email_papers.title: Spectral-Spatial Interpretation
email_papers.abstract: Post-hoc image explanations usually show where a model looks using spatial heatmaps or indicate which channels matter using global channel scores. These separate views are limiting for multispectral data because channel relevance is often spatially localized and physically meaningful. We introduce Spectral-Spatial Interpretation (SSI), a full-grid attribution method over position-channel players (g,c). For each spatial position, SSI fixes the observed surrounding context, defines a conditional game over the channels at that position, and applies the Shapley value to this local game. The result is a full spectral-spatial attribution matrix rather than a single heatmap or a global channel ranking. SSI has a clear local interpretation. It satisfies Shapley fairness within each position, and aggregating its channel attributions exactly recovers the position-level contextual contrast obtained by replacing that position with the baseline. SSI also differs from context-averaged Owen-style hierarchical accounting, which uses the same position-channel grouping but averages over external spatial coalitions. On HLS Burn Scar, SSI outperforms an MC-Owen estimator across retained attribution metrics while using only about 6% of its evaluation budget. Across CUB-200, EuroSAT, and HLS Burn Scar under both per-channel mean and zero baselines, SSI achieves the best joint deletion and insertion AUC over dense, flat, and rank-1 baselines, yields the strongest spectral hit rates and channel deletion, and leads spatial localization on both annotated datasets. Code is available at https://github.com/AtheavenMa/Spectral-Spatial-Interpretation.

Introduction
Modern vision models increasingly operate on inputs with multiple physically
meaningful channels, from RGB fine-grained recognition to Sentinel-2 land-cover
classification and burn-scar mapping. Existing post-hoc explanations usually
answer
where
the model looks, but not
which spectral channels
support the prediction at each location. For these data, high attribution to near-infrared at a vegetation boundary or
to short-wave infrared within a burn scar reflects different physical evidence
from attribution to visible bands. An explanation should therefore identify
where the evidence lies, which channels support it, and how much each channel
contributes at each location.
Existing methods collapse this structure in one of two ways. Spatial
attribution methods such as Grad-CAM
(
Selvaraju et al., 2017
)
,
RISE
(
Petsiuk et al., 2018
)
, and Extremal
Perturbation
(
Fong et al., 2019
)
aggregate over channels and produce
a single heatmap. Spectral or channel attribution methods rank bands globally
using mutual information, attention weights, or SHAP-style
scores
(
Lundberg and Lee, 2017
)
, averaging channel effects across space.

vector assumes a rank-1 structure,

2
Related Work
Post-hoc spatial attribution.
A large family of explanation methods produces spatial heatmaps indicating which image regions drive a prediction. Gradient-based approaches such as Integrated Gradients
(
Sundararajan et al., 2017
)
and Grad-CAM
(
Selvaraju et al., 2017
)
propagate target-class signals to pixels or activation maps. Perturbation-based approaches such as RISE
(
Petsiuk et al., 2018
)
and Extremal Perturbation
(
Fong et al., 2019
)
measure prediction changes under spatial masks.
These methods are effective for identifying where evidence lies, but their explanations either aggregate over channels or treat input elements independently. They therefore do not provide a principled decomposition of which spectral channels matter at each location.
Spectral and channel attribution.
A complementary line of work ranks spectral bands or channels using mutual information
(
Feng et al., 2014
)
, game-theoretic criteria
(
Bruce, 2013
)
, attention weights
(
Hu et al., 2018
;
Woo et al., 2018
)
, or SHAP-style attribution
(
Lundberg and Lee, 2017
)
. Such methods are useful for identifying globally important wavelengths, but they typically average channel relevance over space. This averaging can hide localized spectral evidence because a band may be unimportant on average yet decisive in a small region. SSI instead assigns attribution to each position-channel pair and preserves spatial variation in channel importance.
Joint spectral-spatial modeling.
Architectures such as 3D CNNs
(
Chen et al., 2016
)
, spectral-spatial
transformers
(
Dang et al., 2022
)
, and factorized architecture
search
(
Zhong et al., 2022
)
jointly exploit spectral and spatial
information but focus on prediction performance, and their internal
representations remain opaque.
Propagation-based explanations have been adapted for hyperspectral
classifiers
(
Nagasubramanian et al., 2018
)
, but remain architecture-specific.
SSI instead provides model-agnostic, game-theoretic attribution for
already-trained models.
Game-theoretic and hierarchical attribution.
Shapley values
(
Shapley, 1953
)
and SHAP-style methods
(
Lundberg and Lee, 2017
)
provide additive feature attributions but usually treat all interpretable units as flat players. This flat treatment does not reflect the natural position-channel hierarchy of multispectral images. The Shapley interaction index
(
Grabisch and Roubens, 1999
)
and its higher-order extensions
(
Sundararajan et al., 2020
;
Tsai et al., 2023
)
quantify synergies but do not exploit this two-level structure. Group-level Shapley methods
(
Jullum et al., 2021
)
treat each
predefined group as an atomic player and do not decompose contributions
within groups; methods addressing feature
dependence
(
Aas et al., 2022
)
estimate conditional expectations
rather than fixing observed context. SSI differs from both lines of work in its attribution units
and treatment of context.
Owen value.
The Owen value
(
Owen, 1977
)
, building on games with coalition structures
(
Aumann and Drèze, 1974
)
, respects a priori coalitions by allocating value across and within groups. SSI uses the same position-channel grouping but targets observed-context conditional attribution rather than context-averaged hierarchical accounting.

4.1
Experimental Setup
Datasets and models.
We evaluate SSI on three datasets covering RGB images, multispectral land-cover classification, and burn-scar mapping.
CUB-200-2011
(
Wah et al., 2011
)
contains RGB images of 200 bird species with bounding-box annotations. We fine-tune an ImageNet-pretrained ResNet-18 classifier.
EuroSAT
(
Helber et al., 2019
)
contains 13-band Sentinel-2 patches from 10 land-use/land-cover classes. We train a ResNet-18 classifier from scratch on all bands.
HLS Burn Scar
(
Phillips et al., 2023
)
contains 6-band
Harmonized Landsat–Sentinel-2 patches with burn-scar masks. We train a
lightweight UNet for burn-scar segmentation and use the burn-class logit
averaged over ground-truth mask positions as the scalar response for
attribution. Training details and model performance are reported in Appendix
B
.

Conclusion
We introduced Spectral-Spatial Interpretation (SSI), which explains
predictions of multi-channel image models at the level of joint
position-channel players
(
g
,
c
)
(g,c)
. SSI fixes the observed surrounding context and allocates each
position’s contribution among its channels via the Shapley value, producing a
full attribution matrix whose channel aggregation exactly recovers the
position-level contextual contrast. Across CUB-200, EuroSAT, and HLS Burn
Scar, SSI improves joint faithfulness, spectral hit rates, and channel
deletion over dense, flat, and rank-1 baselines, and outperforms MC-Owen on
HLS Burn Scar with roughly
6
%
6\%
of its evaluation budget.
Although SSI’s estimation error grows only as
ln
⁡
C
\sqrt{\ln C}
and its
per-image cost grows only linearly in
C
C
(Appendix
B.4
), applying SSI to hyperspectral sensors
with hundreds of correlated bands may benefit from channel screening or
adaptive grouping to reduce spectral redundancy before local Shapley
allocation. Validating such extensions on operational hyperspectral
missions remains future work. SSI may also be useful for imaging spectroscopy data from sensors such as EnMAP, where spectral channels carry spatially localized physical information. The observed-context formulation may extend to other multi-channel imaging domains with localized physical meaning, including biomedical microscopy and industrial materials inspection.

CUB-200-2011.

[

contains 11,788 RGB images of 200 bird species. Each image is annotated with a bounding box, part keypoints, and binary attributes, including color attributes. We fine-tune an ImageNet-pretrained ResNet-18 classifier and use the ground-truth class logit as the scalar response for attribution.
EuroSAT.

[
Helber et al., 2019
]
contains 27,000 Sentinel-2 patches from 10 land-use/land-cover classes. We use the 13-band version, including visible RGB, red-edge, near-infrared, short-wave infrared, and atmospheric bands. We train a ResNet-18 classifier from scratch on all 13 bands.

C.3
Spectral Band Priors
The spectral hit-rate evaluation (§
4.3
) requires a set of
prior bands
for each class. These are channels whose reflectance is expected to be positively associated with the target-class decision. We select these priors from established spectral indices and physical reasoning rather than the attribution results themselves.
HLS Burn Scar.
The HLS Burn Scar dataset uses a six-band stack (Blue, Green, Red, Narrow NIR, SWIR
1
, SWIR
2
) derived from the Harmonized Landsat Sentinel-2 product
[
Claverie et al., 2018
]
. For the burn-scar class, we designate Red (band 2), SWIR
1
(band 4), and SWIR
2
(band 5) as prior bands. This selection follows directly from the Normalized Burn Ratio (NBR) and its variants, which are the standard spectral indices for burn severity mapping
[
Key and Benson, 2006
,
García and Caselles, 1991
]
. Burned surfaces exhibit elevated SWIR reflectance due to exposed soil, charcoal, and ash, and elevated red reflectance due to the loss of chlorophyll absorption
[
Trigg and Flasse, 2001
]
. These spectral signatures have been validated across decades of fire-mapping literature using Landsat TM/ETM+/OLI and Sentinel-2 MSI sensors. NIR is excluded from the positive prior because burn scars cause a sharp drop in NIR reflectance (loss of mesophyll scattering), making NIR
negatively
correlated with the burn-scar class.
EuroSAT.
EuroSAT provides 13-band Sentinel-2 imagery spanning the visible, red-edge, NIR, and SWIR spectral regions. We assign class-specific priors based on the physical reflectance properties of each land-cover type:
•
Vegetation classes
(AnnualCrop, Forest, HerbaceousVegetation, Pasture, PermanentCrop). We use the red-edge (B05–B07, 705–783 nm) and NIR (B08/B8A, 842/865 nm) bands as priors. Healthy vegetation produces strong NIR reflectance through mesophyll scattering and exhibits a steep red-edge transition driven by chlorophyll absorption
[
Clevers et al., 2002
,
Delegido et al., 2011
]
. These bands underpin NDVI, NDRE, and related vegetation indices that have been used operationally for crop monitoring and forest mapping for decades
[
Tucker, 1979
,
Rouse et al., 1974
]
.
•
Industrial.
The priors are the SWIR bands (B11, B12; 1610/2190 nm). Impervious surfaces such as concrete, asphalt, and metal roofing reflect strongly in the SWIR due to low moisture content and high mineral reflectance
[
Zha et al., 2003
,
Xu, 2008
]
.
•
Highway, Residential, River, SeaLake.
No positive prior is assigned. These classes are spectrally heterogeneous (Highway, Residential) or uniformly low-reflectance (water bodies), so no single band subset has a reliably positive association with the class decision.
In both datasets, we conservatively include only prior bands with a well-documented, physically grounded positive correlation with the target class. Classes without a clear positive spectral signature receive an empty prior set and are excluded from the hit-rate evaluation. This design ensures that the spectral validity metric tests whether the attribution method recovers known physical relationships, rather than fitting to arbitrary band rankings.

article.headline: 用局部 Shapley 值给出逐位置通道归因矩阵
article.lede: SSI 在每个空间位置固定观测上下文，只对该位置的通道做 Shapley 分配，输出完整的 (g,c) 归因矩阵。
article.problem: 现有的后验图像解释大多只回答「模型看哪里」：Grad-CAM、RISE 一类方法在通道上聚合，得到单张空间热图；而 SHAP、互信息一类通道归因又把通道重要性在空间上平均，给出全局波段排序。对多光谱数据这不够用，因为同一波段在一个区域可能起决定作用、在另一个区域却无关；把热图乘上全局通道向量，等于假设归因矩阵是秩 1 的，在鸟类羽毛或遥感场景中往往不成立。
article.method: SSI 把位置与通道的组合 (g,c) 当作玩家，对每个空间位置 g 固定其余位置的观测值作为上下文，只在 g 处的通道上定义一个条件博弈 w_g，再对这个小型博弈取标准 Shapley 值，得到全网格的 Φ(g,c)。论文证明了两条性质：在每个位置内部满足 Shapley 公平性（效率、对称、零玩家、可加性）；并且对通道求和恰好等于把整个位置替换为基线时的全上下文对比 Δ(g)。它与 Owen 值使用相同的位置—通道分组，但 Owen 要在外部空间联盟上取平均，SSI 只条件于实际观测到的上下文。
article.results: 在 CUB-200、EuroSAT 和 HLS Burn Scar 上，无论用逐通道均值基线还是零基线，SSI 的联合删除 AUC 和插入 AUC 都优于 dense（IG、DeepSHAP）、flat（KernelSHAP）和秩 1（RISE）基线。CUB-200 均值基线下插入 AUC 为 .7132，高于 RISE 的 .6886，而 RISE 用了 8,000 个空间掩码、SSI 为 2048 次前向；HLS Burn Scar 均值基线下联合删除 AUC 为 .1545（IG 为 .2160），对 MC-Owen 为 .155 对 .173，前向评估最多 4,480 次对 76,800 次，约 6% 预算。空间定位上 HLS Burn Scar Top-10% 覆盖的 mIoU 为 .389，DeepSHAP 为 .277、RISE 为 .191；ROAD 评测中 LeRF AUC .657、MoRF AUC .1143，在九种方法中最好。
article.why_it_matters: 对 Sentinel-2、HLS 这类波段带物理含义的影像，解释需要同时说明证据位于哪个区域、由哪些波段支撑，而 SSI 给出的正是这种可分解到位置—波段的归因，并且通道求和有明确的上下文对比含义。它也为「热图 × 全局波段向量」这一常见做法的不足提供了一个可检验的反例：秩 1 投影后删除 AUC 明显变差。
article.limitations: 条件博弈的语义依赖掩码基线的选择（逐通道均值或零），论文自己也承认这是所有扰动式归因的固有问题；Proposition 1 进一步表明，位置级上下文聚合性与全局效率无法同时保证，因此 SSI 不分配整个预测值。采样方面每格最多 K=10 次通道排列，作者指出对数百个相关波段的高光谱传感器可能需要先做通道筛选或自适应分组，这仍是未来工作；而「约 6%」只是前向次数口径下的比较，不是实测耗时，也不能与梯度法的反向传播成本直接对比。
article.figure_caption_zh: SSI 总览：对每个空间位置 g 固定观测到的周边上下文，把局部贡献分配给该位置的各通道，从而得到可用于空间与光谱解释的完整联合归因矩阵 Φ(g,c)。

figure.caption: {Overview of SSI.} For each spatial position \(g\), SSI fixes the observed surrounding context and allocates the local contribution among channels, producing a full joint attribution matrix \( (g,c)\) for spatial and spectral interpretation.

email_papers.title: Agent World Model in the Wild: Computer-Use Agent Environment Synthesis
email_papers.abstract: Agent learning is shifting from learning from human data toward learning through interaction with the world. However, scaling such learning directly in real-world computer systems is challenging and can introduce substantial security risks. We therefore propose Agent World Model in the Wild (WildAWM), a scalable pipeline for synthesizing controllable environments and tasks for training general computer-use agents (CUAs). Whereas existing approaches typically specialize in a single agent interaction interface, we construct executable environments that jointly support graphical user interfaces, model context protocol services, and command-line interfaces, allowing agents to flexibly combine visual interaction, tool use, and code execution. WildAWM is entirely powered by open-source models, demonstrating that high-quality computer-use environments can be generated without proprietary frontier models. Beyond environments, we address three recurring challenges in task synthesis: ensuring solvability, maintaining sufficient difficulty, and producing reliable verifiers, by introducing execution-based quality gates that combine heterogeneous agent rollouts, cross-judge consistency checks, and counterfactual probes of judgment robustness. The resulting pipeline synthesizes 341 long-horizon environment-task pairs that can require over 100 agent steps to solve and remain challenging even for frontier models, with GPT-6-Astra solving only 60% of them. We train two Qwen models of different sizes exclusively in these synthetic worlds. Both models achieve substantial gains across 8 out-of-distribution benchmarks spanning web, claw, and computer-use agents, demonstrating that learning in WildAWM's synthesized worlds generalizes broadly to unseen computer-use tasks. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/MSR-Orchard/WildAWM.
email_papers.content:
Abstract
Agent learning is shifting from learning from human data toward learning through interaction with the world.
However, scaling such learning directly in real-world computer systems is challenging and can introduce substantial security risks.

Introduction
Large language model (LLM) powered agents are shifting from learning from humans to learning from the world
(
Silver & Sutton, 2025
)

(

Zeng et al., 2026
;
Xu et al., 2026
)

However, training directly in the real world is costly and risky: states are hard to reset, online services change over time, and exploratory actions may have unintended consequences.

Synthetic environments and tasks offer a path to controllable, large-scale online RL.
Computer-Use Agents (CUAs) represent a broad setting for environment synthesis, as they operate across applications, websites, and local files on a personal computer.
A single task may be completed through graphical user interface (GUI) interaction, command-line interface (CLI) operations, or calls to model context protocol (MCP) servers, making interface selection and coordination an important capability.
Existing synthesis pipelines often target individual interaction modes, including browser use

Wu et al., 2026

(

(

Prior CUA work, however, often focuses primarily on GUI interaction
(
Aggarwal et al., 2026
;
Wang et al., 2026a
)
.
In this paper, we adopt a broader view of computer use spanning common interfaces on a personal computer, since real computer-use tasks are defined by what can be accomplished rather than by a single interaction modality.
Synthesizing environments and tasks for this broader CUA setting introduces challenges beyond prior synthesis work. Existing approaches often synthesize visually simplified applications and build each application as an isolated environment.
In contrast, realistic computer use spans a connected digital workspace in which websites, applications, MCP services, and local files coexist within an executable personal computer environment.

challenging

reliable

article.headline: 用编码智能体合成电脑使用环境与可验证任务
article.lede: 论文提出两阶段合成流水线，自动生成带 GUI、MCP、CLI 接口的电脑环境与跨接口任务，并用五道质量门筛选。
article.problem: 智能体训练的重心正从「学习人类数据」转向「在环境中交互学习」，但环境供给成了瓶颈：在真实电脑系统里做强化学习成本高、状态难重置、线上服务还会变化，探索性操作可能带来安全后果。手工搭建环境虽可控可验证，却昂贵且难以规模化。已有的合成流水线多针对单一交互方式（浏览器、工具调用、终端），且常把每个应用做成相互隔离的简化环境，与真实电脑使用中网站、应用、MCP 服务与本地文件共存的形态不符。
article.method: 方法分两个阶段。第一阶段是世界合成：用编码智能体构造由人物设定驱动、跨越多个「天」的环境状态，这些状态同时暴露 GUI、MCP 与 CLI 三类接口，形成可执行的个人电脑工作区。第二阶段是跨接口任务合成：围绕可解性、难度与验证器可靠性设计五道质量门来生成任务，其中包含回放确定性检查——从第 N-1 天的同一状态重放 delta.sh 两次，两个世界必须产生完全相同的内容哈希。最终产出 {任务, 环境, 验证器} 三元组用于训练通用电脑使用智能体。
article.results: 论文报告合成了 341 个跨接口（XAI）任务。主结果表中平均分为 53.42，并标出 +10.58 的平均提升；表中各方法分数从 21.73 到 80.77 不等。作者强调的发现之一是「广泛的分布外泛化」。至于合成了多少个环境、训练与合成各花费多少算力，论文未给出具体数字。
article.why_it_matters: 如果环境与验证器能自动合成，强化学习所需的环境供给就有望从手工搭建转为规模化生成，从而绕开在真实电脑系统上训练的成本与安全风险。
article.limitations: 目前公开的规模只有 341 个任务，相对真实电脑使用场景仍偏小；五道质量门中的回放确定性仅以内容哈希一致作为判据，能否代表任务语义上的确定性存疑，验证器可靠性也仍依赖自动筛选而非人工审核。此外，材料中未给出从合成环境到真实系统的迁移证据，也没有与真实世界训练的成本对比，具体环境数量与算力开销论文未给出具体数字。
article.figure_caption_zh: 合成流水线分两步：先用编码智能体构建人物驱动、跨多天、同时提供 GUI、MCP 与 CLI 接口的电脑环境状态，再经五道质量门生成跨接口任务，输出可供训练通用电脑使用智能体的 {任务, 环境, 验证器} 三元组。

figure.caption: Overview of . The synthesis pipeline includes two stages: (1) {World Synthesis}, where we use the coding agent to construct persona-driven, multi-day world states for computer environments that expose GUI, MCP, and CLI interfaces. (2) {XAI Task Synthesis}, where we generate cross-interface tasks through 5 designed quality gates for task solvability, difficulty, and verifier reliability. The synthesized $ \{ {task}, {environment}, {verifier}\}$ triplet enables training general CUA.

email_papers.title: Sage-A1.5: From Long-Horizon Execution to Scientific Exploration with Capability Composition
email_papers.abstract: In this report, we introduce Sage-A1.5, a 35B Mixture-of-Experts agentic model that builds on A1 to advance long-horizon problem solving through adaptive capability composition. Compared with A1, Sage-A1.5 learns not only to solve individual tasks, but also to organize work and revise its approach during execution. Sage-A1.5 highlights three improvements: agentic orchestration, verification, and open scientific discovery. First, agentic orchestration extends single-agent execution through task delegation and parallel collaboration among subagents with isolated contexts, enabling complex tasks to be decomposed and addressed concurrently and supporting efficient execution while reducing interference across concurrent subagents. Second, agentic verification strengthens long-horizon reliability through progress checking, evidence validation, and reflective strategy revision, allowing the agent to recognize unproductive search paths and pursue alternative approaches. Third, open scientific discovery extends agentic capabilities beyond answering predefined questions to conducting exploratory research, connecting scientific inquiry with interactive analysis and inspectable research artifacts. We showcase these capabilities through complicated agentic tasks and multidisciplinary scientific applications. Besides, we hope Sage-A1.5 provides the community with an accessible foundation for open scientific discovery, offering a practical path from long-horizon task execution to collaborative, verifiable, and inspectable scientific exploration.

Sage-A1.5: From Long-Horizon Execution to Scientific Exploration with Capability Composition
Sage-A1.5 Team, Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Laboratory
Abstract
In this report, we introduce Sage-A1.5, a 35B Mixture-of-Experts agentic model that builds on A1 to advance long-horizon problem solving through adaptive capability composition. Compared with A1, Sage-A1.5 learns not only to solve individual tasks, but also to organize work and revise its approach during execution. Sage-A1.5 highlights three improvements: agentic orchestration, verification, and open scientific discovery. First, agentic orchestration extends single-agent execution through task delegation and parallel collaboration among subagents with isolated contexts, enabling complex tasks to be decomposed and addressed concurrently and supporting efficient execution while reducing interference across concurrent subagents. Second, agentic verification strengthens long-horizon reliability through progress checking, evidence validation, and reflective strategy revision, allowing the agent to recognize unproductive search paths and pursue alternative approaches. Third, open scientific discovery extends agentic capabilities beyond answering predefined questions to conducting exploratory research, connecting scientific inquiry with interactive analysis and inspectable research artifacts. We showcase these capabilities through complicated agentic tasks and multidisciplinary scientific applications. Besides, we hope Sage-A1.5 provides the community with an accessible foundation for open scientific discovery, offering a practical path from long-horizon task execution to collaborative, verifiable, and inspectable scientific exploration.

Contents
1
Introduction
In our earlier work, we introduced Agents-A1
[
1
]
, a 35B Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) agent model that improves long-horizon task performance by scaling the agent horizon rather than model parameters. We built a knowledge–action infrastructure
[
2
]
that connects external knowledge, tool calls, observations, and verification feedback, producing training trajectories with an average length of 45K tokens. Agents-A1
[
1
]
showed strong performance in multi-step search, scientific reasoning, instruction following, and tool use, matching or exceeding trillion-parameter models on several benchmarks. These results established a practical path toward capable long-horizon agents at a smaller model scale.
Recent progress
[
3
,
4
,
5
,
2
]
demonstrates that strong domain skills alone are not enough for complicated tasks. Software engineering, machine learning optimization, and scientific research often require agentic model to manage related subtasks, compare different approaches, and revise decisions as new evidence becomes available. A single agentic model working step by step may struggle with a growing context, slow exploration, and errors that affect later decisions. Longer execution also does not always lead to better results: an agent may repeat unproductive searches, build on unsupported assumptions, or accept a conclusion before checking all the evidence. Further progress therefore requires not only stronger intrinsic agentic capabilities and broader skills, but also better ways to organize agent work and check progress.
Task delegation, parallel collaboration, evidence review, and strategy revision should become learned model capabilities rather than depend only on fixed rules in an external framework.
To address these challenges, we introduce Sage-A1.5, a 35B MoE agent model built on Agents-A1, with two key capabilities:
Agentic Orchestration
and
Agentic Verification
.
1)
Agentic Orchestration allows the model to decide how to divide work, delegate subtasks to parallel subagents with separate contexts, and combine their findings toward a shared goal.
2)
Agentic Verification allows the model to recognize when progress has stalled or an important conclusion needs checking, review the available evidence and assumptions, and adjust its next actions. At inference time, this verification takes place within the model’s own reasoning and tool-use process, without an online supervisor or a separate verification tool. These capabilities offer the community a scalable technical pathway for translating model capabilities into agentic capabilities. As shown in Fig.
1
, despite having only 35B parameters, Sage-A1.5 outperforms the substantially larger Kimi-K3
[
4
]
, GLM-5.3
[
6
]
, and GPT-5.6-sol
[
5
]
on FrontierScience-Olympiad
[
7
]
, CMT
[
8
]
, PinchBench
[
9
]
, and IFBench
[
10
]
, while remaining competitive with them on SWE-Bench Pro
[
11
]
and BrowseComp
[
12
]
.
Moreover, Sage-A1.5 matches or surpasses the equally sized Agents-A1
[
1
]
and Ornith-1.5
[
13
]
on all twelve benchmarks.
Our contributions include the following three aspects:
•
We develop Adaptive Agentic Execution, integrating
Agentic Orchestration
and
Agentic Verification
into Sage-A1.5’s execution policy for autonomous coordination of parallel subtasks and evidence-driven self-correction throughout long-horizon problem solving.
•
We build a unified training pipeline that combines multi-domain supervised fine-tuning with mixed-reward reinforcement learning, fusing capabilities across domains, reasoning modes, and agent harnesses into a single agentic model.
•
We demonstrate Sage-A1.5’s potential for agentic scientific discovery through broad benchmark evaluations and scientific case studies, highlighting a shift from isolated task solving toward long-horizon scientific research.
2
Method
Figure 2
:
Overview of the three-stage training pipeline of Sage-A1.5. First, the model is trained on diverse domain data, including coding, long-context reasoning, deep research, scientific reasoning, and co-working, utilizing environment construction, trajectory selection, staged supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning to build multi-domain teachers. Then, these teachers undergo unified outcome-process post-training to produce the final unified model, which features an agent orchestration for collaborative task solving, iterative agentic verification for reasoning reliability, and local deployment for ensuring data privacy, access control, and offline support.
2.1
Adaptive Agentic Execution: From Capability Coverage to Capability Composition
Domain-specific training expands capability coverage—the range of domains and tasks an agent can address. In Sage-A1.5, we extend agent capability development along a second dimension,
capability composition
: how problem-solving capabilities are organized, coordinated, and adapted during execution. This dimension concerns execution structure across task domains. We develop it through Agentic Orchestration and Agentic Verification (Fig.
3
). Agentic Orchestration determines how work is decomposed, delegated, and integrated across agent executions. Agentic Verification determines when to reassess intermediate judgments and exploration strategies, using the findings to revise subsequent actions. As a result, these capabilities make execution organization and feedback-driven adjustment explicit targets of model training alongside domain-specific problem solving.
Figure 3
:
Two complementary dimensions of agent capability. Capability coverage spans task domains, while capability composition concerns how problem-solving capabilities are organized and adapted during execution. Agentic Orchestration coordinates parallel work and integrates results; Agentic Verification reassesses intermediate responses using available evidence and adjusts subsequent actions.
2.1.1
Agentic Orchestration
We propose
Agentic Orchestration
, a foundational capability of Sage-A1.5 for structuring, allocating, and coordinating computation during task execution. The key insight is to make how execution is organized an explicit target of model training:
learning what work to pursue and how to combine the results complements learning to solve individual tasks.
Capability Definition and Composition Patterns.
Agentic Orchestration is the model’s ability to organize multiple agent executions around a shared objective. Its policy determines whether and how to decompose work, which subtasks to delegate, what context to provide, and how to coordinate dependencies and integrate results. The model adapts subsequent work to returned evidence, connecting local execution to the overall task. We distinguish two complementary patterns of parallel agent execution:
•
Exploratory Composition.
The model assigns multiple agents different hypotheses or solution approaches to the same question. Their outputs provide alternative candidates and supporting evidence, which the main agent compares to narrow the investigation and decide which directions to pursue. For example, agents may explore different system architectures against the same requirements, returning candidate designs for comparison.
•
Constructive Composition.
The model decomposes an overall task into complementary subproblems and assigns them to agents for parallel work. Each output contributes a distinct part of the solution; the main agent integrates these parts, coordinating dependencies and checking coverage and consistency. For example, agents may develop the data, interface, and deployment components of one system design, which must fit together to meet the overall requirements.

We develop the Agentic Orchestration capability through two training task families:
Constraint-Guided Long-Horizon Search
and
Multi-Source Research Synthesis
.
1)
Long-horizon search tests whether the model can choose productive angles for parallel investigation, delegate independent investigations of a shared target’s relation constraints, and use returned evidence to narrow candidate answers and guide subsequent searches.
2)
Research synthesis tests whether it can divide a broad research objective into complementary parallel assignments, assess the coverage and consistency of their findings, and integrate them into a report that answers the original research question.
Figure 4
:
Agentic Orchestration in execution and task construction. (a) Independently executing subagents return structured feedback for the main agent’s next decisions. (b) Multiple relation chains are built around a selected answer and combined into one question, with identifying details masked. Their clues provide complementary constraints for parallel investigation.
Orchestration Protocol and Structured Feedback.
The main agent investigates directly or delegates subtasks, specifying their scope and context. Subagents search and read webpages in separate contexts, advancing their model calls and tool interactions independently within a concurrent batch. Once the batch completes, the main agent uses the findings to synthesize an answer or organize further investigation (Fig.
4
a).
Building on the model’s ability to critique its own execution, we ask each subagent to return its result together with a self-assessment, supporting evidence, and remaining issues. This feedback helps the main agent identify gaps and conflicts and provides signals for trajectory selection. Fig.
5
summarizes the interface and structured feedback format.
Task Construction: From Relation Chains to Constraint-Centric Graphs.
For Constraint-Guided Long-Horizon Search, we extend the relation-chain construction method in Agents-A1
[
1
]
. We select an answer entity, identify directly related entities that provide different relation constraints, and extend a chain from each of them. This forms a
starlike tree graph
around the shared answer (Fig.
4
b). Branch descriptions and evidence are combined into one question, with proper names and identifying details masked. The main agent can delegate different constraints for parallel investigation, explore candidates from multiple angles, and combine the findings to recover the shared answer.
Multi-Source Research Synthesis combines evidence from multiple sources into a coherent research report. Agentic Orchestration supports complementary research assignments, comparison of findings across sources, and follow-up investigations to fill gaps or resolve inconsistencies before synthesis. Task construction is described in Section
2.5.1
.
Figure 5
:
Delegation interface and structured subagent feedback.
Trajectory Collection and Role-Specific Supervision.
Teacher model runs within the orchestration harness with role-specific prompts, tools, and execution budgets. It chooses when to investigate directly, delegate, and follow up on returned evidence. We record the complete executions and treat the main-agent trajectory and each subagent trajectory as independent agent samples.
Main-agent samples teach task decomposition, delegation, use of feedback, and synthesis; subagent samples teach independent investigation, evidence organization, and structured reporting. This supervision complements domain expertise with the ability to structure, allocate, and coordinate computation during agentic execution.
2.1.2
Agentic Verification
In long-horizon research tasks, agents must gradually build chains of evidence through multiple rounds of retrieval and reasoning. When an exploration path repeatedly fails to yield useful information, a model may continue searching around the same hypothesis or use unverified assumptions as premises for subsequent reasoning, leading to ineffective exploration and accumulating errors. To address this problem, we propose
Agentic Verification
, which enables the model to adaptively recognize when verification is needed, examine existing evidence and exploration strategies within its own reasoning, and adjust subsequent actions accordingly. When progress stalls or an important intermediate conclusion is reached, the model reviews facts confirmed by evidence, examines earlier judgments for unsupported inferences, identifies unresolved information gaps, and determines which exploration paths have proved ineffective and how to proceed. The central idea is to make verification a learned capability of the model itself:
the model adaptively determines when to verify, what to verify, and how to continue based on the findings, rather than having verification triggered and executed by an external harness according to predefined rules.
This mechanism enables the model to proactively revise its judgments, gather additional evidence, or change its search direction, improving its ability to self-correct during long-horizon tasks.
To train this capability, we construct complete research trajectories containing intermediate reflections and the actions that follow them. During data construction, an execution model conducts research through live search and webpage reading, while a supervisor model examines the exploration process and introduces verification at points involving repetitive searches, sustained lack of progress, or key conclusions requiring confirmation. Each verification relies only on the evidence available at that point, distinguishes confirmed facts from unverified hypotheses, and proposes a concrete direction for further investigation. The execution model then continues exploring based on the verification findings, producing coherent training examples that connect problem recognition, evidence assessment, and action adjustment. After data cleaning and format normalization, external supervision prompts and control messages are removed, and the reflections are incorporated directly into the model’s reasoning text. This allows the model to learn when to verify, what to examine, and how verification should inform subsequent actions. External supervision is used only to construct training data; at inference time, the model performs this process independently.
Note that
we also introduce a conditioning marker during training to enable the capability on demand: for models trained in this way, adding
Verification protocol:enabled
to the system prompt activates Agentic Verification. Once enabled, the model autonomously performs verification within its regular reasoning and tool-use process, without requiring an additional verification tool, an online supervisor model, or a verification procedure implemented by the harness.
Building on this approach, we plan to integrate verification with context management, using intermediate verification points as natural boundaries for organizing the exploration history. After completing an intermediate reflection, the model will autonomously determine whether the preceding exploration segment can be consolidated into a concise stage record. If so, the corresponding history segment will be replaced with the stage record and the current verification, while preserving key evidence, rejected hypotheses, unresolved questions, and the current task state. Compression will apply only to the segment between the two most recent verification points, avoiding repeated compression of earlier history. Through this design, we aim to control context overhead while preserving reasoning continuity and evidence integrity, supporting research tasks over longer horizons.
2.2
Post-training on Engineering Tasks
2.2.1
MLE Tasks
Task Construction.
We design Kaggle-MLE Factory, an automated multi-agent pipeline that converts historical Kaggle competitions into executable tasks with public workspaces, hidden test sets, and a unified evaluation interface. The pipeline assigns distinct roles to competition selection and data acquisition, task analysis, code generation, and execution and validation. The analysis module combines official descriptions with the actual data to form task specifications. The generation module then prepares the data, constructs held-out test splits with hidden labels, and implements task-specific evaluators. The execution and validation modules test the generated tasks on real data and provide feedback for iterative repair. Tasks undergo human review before trajectory collection. We also use MLE-Dojo
[
14
]
as a supplementary task source and exclude competitions that overlap with the full MLE-Bench task set
[
15
]
.
Interaction Harness.
We build an MLE interaction harness for long-horizon experimentation, allowing the model to autonomously refine solutions based on execution feedback. The harness organizes candidate code and execution results into an experiment tree that records solution revisions, supporting branch comparison, backtracking, submission management, and invalidation of candidates with unreliable results. Persistent plans and context compression support sustained interaction, while an analysis sub-agent with an independent context provides data exploration and result diagnosis.
Trajectory Collection and Selection.
We select demonstration trajectories and useful supervision segments based on the actual execution and evaluation results of candidate solutions. If performance degradation after the first best-performing submission exceeds a threshold, we truncate the trajectory at a complete tool-interaction boundary near that submission; otherwise, we retain it through the final submission. This preserves useful exploration and failure recovery while removing persistently degrading tails. Supervision data include initial-solution prefixes that execute successfully and meet quality criteria, long-horizon optimization trajectories, and analysis sub-agent trajectories, covering solution construction, iterative refinement, and experimental diagnosis. Training retains prior interaction context and supervises only newly generated reasoning, text, and tool calls.
Staged Supervised Fine-Tuning.
We adopt two-stage supervised fine-tuning to adapt general interaction capabilities to MLE. The first stage uses general coding and tool-interaction trajectories to establish code revision and tool-use capabilities. The second stage combines MLE trajectories with experimental trajectories from literature-derived scientific tasks to train solution design, result analysis, and sustained optimization, initializing the policy for online reinforcement learning.
Windowed Interaction Reinforcement Learning.
Starting from SFT, we apply Windowed Interaction Reinforcement Learning (WIRL). Since each experimental outcome reflects multiple rounds of analysis, code revision, and tool interaction, WIRL groups interactions between successive experiment results into execution windows with shared outcome-based rewards. Decisions remain conditioned on accumulated history, while completed windows support policy updates before the task ends.
Window rewards combine solution quality measured by task-specific medal thresholds with performance changes relative to the most recent valid submission. Model-induced execution errors and unscorable submissions receive negative rewards. Each window reward directly weights its main-model output tokens during policy optimization, without group-relative normalization.

2.2.2
SWE Tasks
We construct training data for repository-level software-engineering issue resolution. Each task provides a repository snapshot and a natural-language issue description, and the agent interacts with the repository to produce a patch. The patch is evaluated against held-out tests: designated failing tests must pass, while previously passing tests must remain passing.
Task Sources and Environment Construction.
The task pool consists of instances from the public SWE-rebench-V2 dataset
[
17
]
and a separate set of tasks constructed in house. We convert tasks from both sources into a common repair-task format following SWE-bench
[
11
]
. Each task starts from the base commit of its associated pull request and uses the corresponding issue description as the task prompt. The reference diff is split into a solution patch containing changes to non-test files and a test patch reserved for grading.
For each task, we recover or construct the container configuration, installation recipe, and test command. Compatible tasks within a repository release group share environment configurations, with dependency mirrors and runtime settings adapted to our cluster. When a recipe is missing or unusable, we follow the build-and-repair loop of SWE-Factory
[
18
]
. Starting from a validated configuration for a neighboring version when available, we build the container, run the tests, and revise the configuration based on the resulting error logs for a bounded number of rounds. Reference-patch size and modified-file count are used to prioritize task collection rather than as hard exclusion criteria.
Task Validation.
We run both reference-patch and no-op checks on candidate tasks. The reference-patch run checks whether the known fix satisfies the grading criteria in the prepared environment. The no-op run submits an empty patch and checks that it receives zero reward, flagging tasks that can receive reward without a repair. We record both outcomes as task metadata for curation.
Trajectory Collection.
We collect trajectories using two agent harnesses:
mini-swe-agent
[
19
]
, which exposes a single shell-command action per turn, and Claude Code, which provides dedicated editing and shell tools. When both harnesses solve the same task, we retain both trajectories. Rollouts run in per-task isolated containers with turn and wall-clock limits.
Each zero-reward trajectory is re-graded once by replaying its unchanged patch, without further agent interaction, to recover successful patches affected by transient execution or grading failures. If the replay passes, we update the trajectory’s reward label.
The training corpus includes successful trajectories and a filtered subset of unresolved attempts. For unresolved attempts, we require a non-empty patch, substantive task-directed interaction, well-formed structure, a passing leakage check, and additional task or harness coverage. Runs consisting solely of infrastructure failures or bare timeouts are excluded.
Leakage Control.
We restrict access to reference fixes and held-out tests during agent execution. Before each rollout, we remove Git objects that expose these artifacts; resetting the working tree to the base commit alone does not remove them from the object store. Because the grader retrieves the held-out tests from the reference commit, the required objects are restored after the agent exits. The held-out tests are introduced only at grading time.
All outbound traffic from rollout containers is forced through the cluster proxy. During agent execution, we redirect the proxy endpoint to a closed local port to block external access. The separate grading stage retains the connectivity needed to install dependencies. These controls apply to data collection, evaluation, and training-time environment interaction.
We audit trajectories for evidence that reference-solution content reached the agent. Network commands alone are not classified as leakage, since they may be used for dependency installation or connectivity checks. Audit verdicts are stored with the trajectories and used during selection. Instances overlapping the test splits of our evaluation suites are removed before collection.

Scientific Problem Selection.
We first collect a diverse pool of scientific problems spanning mathematics, physics, chemistry, biology, and related disciplines, followed by preliminary quality checks to remove invalid or inconsistent instances. Inspired by ExoMind

20

, we leverage the world-model predictive capabilities of a strong model to evaluate each candidate problem along three dimensions:
(i) Difficulty

(iii) Tool benefit

Based on these assessments, we prioritize medium-to-high difficulty problems that require substantial reasoning or research-oriented exploration and are likely to benefit from tool interactions. This capability-guided selection yields a high-quality scientific training corpus characterized by problem validity, strong relevance to scientific reasoning and research, and close alignment with the target model’s reasoning and tool-use capabilities.
Scientific Research Harness Optimization.
Building on a strong open-source model, we optimize a scientific research harness equipped with four complementary tools:
search
for web retrieval,
visit

code
for computational analysis and executable verification, and
scholar
for academic literature retrieval. We enhance the system prompt to guide scientific reasoning, adaptive tool selection, evidence integration, and multi-step interactions. To improve execution reliability and security, we introduce an isolated code execution sandbox that restricts access to host-local resources and provides a consistent execution environment, mitigating information leakage risks and environment-related failures. Furthermore, we implement a tool-result replay mechanism for
search
,
visit
and
scholar
, which reuses recorded observations for repeated or semantically equivalent requests under consistent retrieval contexts. This mechanism reduces redundant tool calls, improves the stability and reproducibility of tool interactions, and enhances the efficiency of long-horizon scientific research.
Trajectory Distillation and Training.
To develop the science-enhanced teacher model, we adopt a training pipeline comprising two key components: multi-dimensional trajectory filtering and extended multi-epoch training. First, we leverage a strong model with the optimized scientific research harness to distill long-horizon trajectories on the selected high-quality, challenging scientific problems, capturing intermediate reasoning, tool calls, observations, and final answers. We then filter these trajectories along three dimensions:
solution correctness
,
reasoning depth
, and
tool-call success rate
, prioritizing demonstrations that combine accurate solutions, substantive reasoning, and effective tool use. Notably, we also retain selected trajectories involving recoverable tool failures, where the model identifies errors, adjusts its strategy, and successfully retries, providing valuable supervision for robust tool use and self-correction. Finally, we perform token-level supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on Qwen3.5-35B-A3B using the filtered trajectories. Given the high complexity, deep reasoning requirements, and extensive tool interactions of scientific research tasks, we adopt an extended multi-epoch training schedule to repeatedly expose the model to high-quality demonstrations. This sustained training aims to consolidate complex reasoning and tool-use behaviors, improving the stability of long-horizon scientific interactions while preserving the model’s intrinsic reasoning capabilities.
2.4
Recursive Task Evolution for Long-Context Reasoning
Long-context reasoning requires models to locate distributed evidence and integrate it through cross-passage relations and complex dependencies. However, generating questions directly from long documents can produce tasks that rely on local retrieval or shallow evidence aggregation. Repeatedly rewriting such questions may leave their underlying evidence dependencies and solution structure unchanged, yielding little increase in difficulty. We therefore adopt recursive task evolution driven by compositions of atomic capabilities. Diverse scenarios define the task objectives, while atomic capabilities characterize the operations required to solve them. Reference-model feedback then exposes shortcuts that guide subsequent revisions, directing difficulty growth toward changes in evidence organization and reasoning structure.
Task Construction Across Diverse Scenarios.
We construct questions from LongBlocks
[
21
]
documents spanning 16K–128K tokens, using 24 fine-grained task categories. These cover cross-document factual integration, timeline reconstruction, evidence attribution, multi-source consistency checking, rule induction, long-range state tracking, and version-impact analysis, among other scenarios. Each category specifies a solution objective, evidence scope, and answer format. For example, timeline reconstruction requires recovering event order, whereas version-impact analysis requires identifying affected components and their dependencies. We match documents to applicable tasks and generate questions, reference answers, and supporting evidence. This scenario-based organization provides explicit targets for task diversity while preserving a stable objective throughout subsequent evolution.
Atomic Capabilities and Compositional Enhancement.
Solving these tasks requires combining atomic capabilities such as evidence localization, alignment across surface forms, condition evaluation, candidate discrimination, set aggregation, state updating, and dependency propagation. Version-impact analysis, for example, involves locating relevant information, resolving aliases and version correspondences, propagating changes through dependencies, and applying exception conditions. We operationalize difficulty enhancement through ten axes: search-space size, quantifier and answer scope, predicate composition, positional non-locality of evidence, near-miss distractor strength, distractor dispersion, lexical gap between questions and evidence, state-transition depth, computational depth, and the depth of the shortest valid derivation. Each task uses applicable axes and construction operators to increase the demands on individual operations and their composition, while keeping the source document and task objective fixed.
Feedback-Guided Recursive Evolution.
The recursive process uses answerability as a constraint and reference-model performance as a selection signal. We estimate relative difficulty from repeated responses generated by Qwen3.5-35B-A3B. For reviewed questions that remain relatively easy, the generator receives the parent question, reference answer, and response feedback, and is instructed to modify at least two task-relevant enhancement axes to produce a new question, answer, and supporting evidence. Each child question undergoes evidence alignment and two-stage LLM review using the full context, followed by difficulty assessment. The review checks task conformity, answerability, evidential support, and answer correctness and completeness. Candidates that pass review and have an empirical success rate of at most
0.75
0.75
enter the hard-question pool, while valid but easier candidates may seed further evolution. This process yields 3,512 hard QA pairs for subsequent trajectory sampling. Qwen3.5-35B-A3B achieves a mean per-question success rate of 31.57% on this pool.
Trajectory Generation and Joint Selection.
Among correct solutions, we favor trajectories with complete evidential support and minimal redundant reasoning, aiming to teach the model to avoid unproductive context retrieval and repeated derivations. For each selected QA task, we sample three reasoning trajectories from DeepSeek-V4-Pro. We first judge final answers against the reference answer and discard incorrect candidates. The remaining trajectories for the same question are presented jointly to an LLM judge together with the original question and context. The judge decomposes the task into atomic requirements and evaluates evidence coverage, retrieval quality, necessary verification, reasoning consistency, and redundancy. To mitigate presentation-order bias, we conduct a second assessment with the candidate order reversed. Only candidates satisfying the strict quality criteria in both assessments are eligible for selection. We aggregate their scores and select one trajectory per question, preferring a more concise trajectory when quality is comparable. After applying sequence-length constraints, we retain 1949 LongBlocks trajectories for supervised fine-tuning.
2.5
General Agents on Search and Real-World Workflows
2.5.1
Search Agents
Deep search tasks require agents to decompose an open-ended information need, iteratively retrieve and read web content, and synthesize scattered evidence into a well-supported conclusion. Existing open-source search datasets mostly consist of short-answer questions with a single verifiable answer, which can be solved by locating one or a few key facts and provide limited supervision for broad exploration and evidence-grounded synthesis. We therefore complement open-source questions with open-ended research questions constructed by a search-grounded generation pipeline, and pair each question with explicit evaluation criteria that guide both trajectory collection and filtering.
Research Question Collection.
Research questions come from two sources. First, we collect questions from open-source search and deep-research datasets, followed by deduplication and preliminary quality checks to remove ambiguous, outdated, or ill-posed instances. Second, we construct new questions with a research question generation pipeline. Each generation task is seeded with a topic and a keyword, which jointly control topical diversity and anchor the question to a concrete information need. A question proposal agent equipped with web search and page reading tools then explores the seed by issuing queries, reading retrieved pages, and following leads across sources. Rather than relying on the parametric knowledge of the generator, we construct candidate research questions and their criteria from the proposal agent’s trajectories, so that each question is grounded in information that is actually discoverable on the web and the criteria reflect the evidence gathered during exploration. The resulting questions are open-ended, requiring the integration of multiple pieces of evidence rather than the retrieval of a single fact, and each criterion specifies a concrete aspect that a satisfactory answer should cover, such as key facts, supporting evidence, comparisons, or conclusions.
Trajectory Generation.
Using the candidate research questions and their criteria, we collect agentic search trajectories in the same tool environment. For each question, the agent is instructed to conduct multi-turn search and reading, and to produce a detailed report that answers the research question and presents the supporting evidence, including the sources from which key claims are derived. This report-style output encourages the agent to explore the question broadly, cross-check information across sources, and ground its conclusions in retrieved evidence rather than unsupported claims.
Criteria-Based Trajectory Filtering.
An LLM evaluator assesses each trajectory against the criteria associated with its question, checking whether the final report satisfies each criterion and whether its claims are supported by the evidence obtained during the search process. A trajectory is adopted only if its criteria-based score passes a predefined threshold; trajectories that miss key aspects of the question, rely on unsupported claims, or fail to complete the report are discarded. Because the criteria are derived from evidence discovered during question construction, this filtering provides question-specific supervision for open-ended tasks that lack a single reference answer. The retained trajectories are used for supervised fine-tuning on search tasks, teaching the model to plan searches, gather and verify evidence, and synthesize it into comprehensive, evidence-grounded reports.
2.5.2
Economically Valuable and Real-World Tasks
Training agents for real-world tasks is constrained less by the model than by the supply of high-quality tasks.
A useful task must execute in a real environment, admit an objective check on its outcome, and mirror professional work as it is actually practiced.
We therefore synthesize training environments at scale, then collect and select trajectories in them with strong teacher models.
Benchmark and Motivation.
Agents’ Last Exam (ALE)
[
22
]
evaluates agents on long-horizon, economically valuable real-world tasks with verifiable outcomes.
Its tasks span 55 subdomains across 13 industry clusters, covering nonphysical industries defined with reference to O*NET/SOC 2018, the U.S. federal occupational taxonomy.
Each task supplies real input data and a hidden reference.
After the agent finishes, a deterministic grader compares its deliverables against the reference and returns a normalized
[
0

1

score, without any LLM judge.
Compared with the data pipelines above, ALE complements the training distribution with generalist agent behavior on broad professional workflows, where tasks are built around the specialized software used in actual professional practice, require file and data deliverables produced over multiple steps, and are judged by acceptance criteria from real production settings.
We evaluate general agentic capability on ALE-CLI, the CLI task subset of ALE.
Task Environment Synthesis and Scaling.
Training tasks originate from a manual cold start of a few dozen high-quality tasks.
Through
controlled evolution
, these seeds have grown into an environment pool of more than one thousand professional workflow environments.
We pair each seed with retrieved public artifacts such as code, datasets, and scientific workflows.
The seed is then varied along at least two substantive axes drawn from the task object, its data, the required operations, workflow dependencies, and the deliverables and grading.
Every seed anchors a broad population of descendants.
A descendant may surpass its ancestor in scientific validity, fidelity to real professional work, and internal consistency.
Difficulty and coverage rise with the population.
Descendants extend well beyond the scope of the seed set, and diversity grows with every round.
Construction and verification are assigned to distinct agents in every evolution round.
A builder agent assembles each candidate package together with its hidden reference and grader.
An independent reviewer agent audits the finished package without seeing the builder’s reasoning.
A judger agent compares the candidate against its ancestor and rejects descendants that carry material defects, so only sound descendants are admitted.
Qualified descendants serve as the seeds of the next round, and the environment pool compounds.
The separation is deliberate. Bootstrapping, in which a single model both poses a task and certifies its answer, would corrupt the reward signal.
The hidden reference is produced by executing the reference workflow on the final inputs, which doubles as a solvability check in the target environment.
The grader accepts outputs that match the reference and rejects perturbed ones.
Each task is delivered with an isolated sandbox that reproduces its production context and the professional software the task assumes, with pinned tool versions and a time budget set per task.
Solver and evaluator environments are kept separate, so the agent’s execution environment cannot influence grading.
Trajectory Collection and Selection.
We run each task in its own sandbox and collect trajectories from strong teacher models, with Claude Code as the harness.
Many tasks run long enough to exceed the context window, and the harness then compresses the earlier interaction history and continues the task from the compressed context.
We keep every segment of these trajectories, and the model learns to work under both a full context and a compressed one.
Scoring runs in a separate sandbox that receives the hidden reference only after the attempt has finished, keeping grading independent of the collection process and free of answer leakage.
For each task we select the attempt with the highest score, and we also retain a small share of failed attempts that worked actively on the problem and produced substantive deliverables.
We balance the mixture across tasks and domains, with caps on the share of any single family, of any single domain, and of failed attempts.
The final training set amounts to several hundred million supervised tokens.

2.7
Agent Training Infrastructure
Agentic Orchestration expands exploration across concurrent investigations, while Agentic Verification revisits evidence and redirects subsequent actions. In engineering and scientific tasks, these behaviors require files, processes, and intermediate results to remain available as agents test alternatives and revise their approaches. Their logical progress is continuous, but their demand for compute is intermittent. The infrastructure challenge is therefore to preserve many evolving execution contexts without keeping every environment fully resident throughout its lifetime. We build on PolicyVisor (pVisor), an agent-native sandbox framework developed by our infrastructure team, to address this challenge. It provides the default sandbox environments for the agentic rollouts in the experiments section, with MLE-Bench-Lite running on dedicated GPU hosts. Its central principle is to make file and network interactions visible to the host for access control and resource management.
pVisor.
To support agent training and future deployment at larger scales, pVisor combines on-demand environment loading with memory management across execution phases. Shared software dependencies are loaded as needed, while fixed environment versions provide consistent starting points for repeated attempts. Each workspace retains the code and experimental outputs produced along its execution path, allowing subsequent tool calls to inspect results, run additional checks, and refine a solution. Access policies control file and network operations, and workspace changes are retained for review. These mechanisms preserve the execution context and artifacts needed for continued exploration and task-specific evaluation.
While an agent waits for a model response, its environment may continue to occupy substantial memory. pVisor can pause execution, offload memory, and resume from the same point. An experimental integration allows the host to advance model requests during these waits and resume the environment to deliver the response, preserving the agent’s existing tools and control flow. This separates the lifetime of a rollout from continuous residency of its full execution environment. Preliminary static tests, with one run per condition, showed approximately 80% lower resident memory across the VM and supporting processes after offload than in a running baseline with the same application working set. Agent workloads vary widely in memory demand, waiting duration, and concurrent tool activity; actual savings also depend on the cost of managing requests and restoring execution. The model determines which investigations to pursue and when to revise them; the runtime manages the resources needed to maintain those investigations across active and waiting phases.

Together, these mechanisms highlight the potential of Sage-A1.5  to move beyond isolated task execution toward sustained scientific discovery. 4.1
Foundational Capabilities
4.1.1
Agentic Orchestration
To demonstrate how Sage-A1.5 coordinates complex research tasks, we consider a large-scale investigation of the world’s 50 most-viewed YouTube channels, covering channel identities, ownership structures, and commercial relationships. The task requires extensive evidence gathering and cross-entity analysis, where findings from individual investigations may affect subsequent research decisions. Sage-A1.5 decomposes the task into 50 channel-specific investigations, dispatched in six batches of parallel subagents (Fig.
7
). Each subagent independently gathers evidence, while the main agent coordinates their findings and identifies questions requiring further investigation.
Rather than simply aggregating results, the main agent dynamically adjusts the research process based on intermediate findings. For example, it initiates follow-up investigations into relationships among channels sharing commercial partners, distinguishing partnership agreements from common ownership. Subagents also challenge initial assumptions when conflicting evidence emerges. In the
StarPlus
investigation, a subagent corrects the initially assigned operator from
Sony Pictures Networks India
to
Disney Star / JioStar
, and this correction is incorporated into subsequent analysis. The main agent ultimately integrates the findings into a structured report covering channel profiles, ownership relationships, and content-supply models. This case illustrates how agentic orchestration extends beyond parallel task execution, enabling research findings to guide subsequent investigations and refine the overall research process.

4.1.2
Agentic Verification
To examine Agentic Verification in long-horizon exploration, we compare the trajectories of the trained model and a baseline on a multi-hop BrowseComp question. The task asks for the first name of an actor’s first wife, based on clues about his portrayal of a police commissioner in a film, his two marriages, and his second wife’s family history. Solving this question requires cross-checking multiple constraints, where partial matches can lead to incorrect conclusions. As shown in Fig.
8
, Agentic Verification allows the model to assess its progress and revise its strategy when necessary.
The model initially explored broad candidate matches but autonomously initiated verification at turn 20. It recognized that the available evidence supported only parts of the required constraints and that repeated searches had yielded limited progress. Based on this assessment, the model shifted to targeted searches for film credits and marital relationships, ultimately producing
Madhumati
at turn 30, which the case annotation accepts as a spelling variant of the reference answer
Madhumalti
.
In contrast, the baseline continued broad searches and eventually selected Tom Selleck despite unresolved evidence, using a television role to satisfy the film-role constraint. It returned the incorrect answer
Jacqueline
after 48 turns. This comparison illustrates how Agentic Verification can redirect a stalled exploration by identifying evidence gaps and using intermediate assessments to guide subsequent actions.

4.1.3
Local Automated Deployment
Sage-A1.5 is designed to support flexible deployment across diverse local computing environments, ranging from data-center accelerators to consumer-grade workstations. The 35B-A3B model can be served on heterogeneous hardware including domestic NPUs such as Huawei Ascend 910B/910C, mainstream NVIDIA GPUs such as A100, H100, H200, B200, and RTX-series cards, AMD GPUs and Instinct accelerators such as MI300X, and Apple Silicon machines including M-series chips with unified memory. To further reduce memory requirements and broaden hardware compatibility, the model provides multiple quantization variants, including FP8 and 4-bit formats. These options make it feasible to run Sage-A1.5 on local devices with limited accelerator memory while preserving practical inference quality and throughput.
In addition to local model serving, Sage-A1.5 can be integrated with local toolchains to enable fully on-premise agentic workflows, as illustrated in Fig.
9
. Through deployment tools and runtimes such as LM Studio, llama.cpp, and Apple MLX, users can launch the model with minimal configuration and expose it through local inference APIs. Code execution, file access, document retrieval, and other agent tools can likewise be executed in the user’s local environment. This allows the agentic model to complete multi-step scientific and engineering tasks without relying on external cloud inference services, reducing data-leakage risks and supporting privacy-sensitive research, enterprise deployment, and offline scenarios. Together, hardware adaptability, quantization support, and local agent tooling enable end-to-end agentic workflows within the user’s computing environment.

Real-World and Professional Workflows.
We evaluate Sage-A1.5 on ten real-world professional workflows that require domain-specific tools, practical constraints, and verifiable deliverables.
Starting from fixed inputs, the model executes multi-step tasks and produces artifacts that can be independently inspected. These workflows span engineering, scientific computing, planning, financial analysis, cybersecurity, and document processing (Fig.
12

For digital hardware implementation, Sage-A1.5 took a PicoRV32-based SoC through logic synthesis, placement and routing, timing closure, and bitstream generation under fixed iCEBreaker board constraints. The design met timing and pin requirements, with configuration checks confirming correct memory initialization. The deliverables included a loadable bitstream, design files, timing reports, and native tool logs.
In the UAV duct study, Sage-A1.5 evaluated candidate geometries using SU2, assessing thrust, crossload, power, and pressure recovery across operating conditions. After checking feasibility constraints, it selected K17 and corrected a configuration-serialization precision error by regenerating solver inputs and rerunning the simulations. Other engineering cases included clock-gating ECO implementation, transformer thermal-model calibration, and materials defect registry review.
For emergency-response planning, Sage-A1.5 formulated capacity, response-time, coverage, and budget constraints, producing resource-allocation plans with solver certificates and geospatial files. In quantum-compilation auditing, it compared reported results with reproduced workloads, identifying discrepancies that prevented full reproduction of the original claim.
In financial reporting, Sage-A1.5 used SEC Companyfacts data to map filing requests to accounting concepts and periods, producing an auditable data warehouse. For network forensics, it reconciled observations from probes with different clock behavior and recovered a DNS transfer payload with supporting packet evidence. In document security, it generated a redacted PDF and verified that the targeted content had been removed.

5
Limitation and Future Work
In this report, we have developed Sage-A1.5, a 35B MoE model that shifts the focus of agent training from expanding single-task skills to composing capabilities over long horizons. Rather than relying on fixed rules in an external scaffold, we train the model to organize parallel subagents and verify intermediate evidence within its own execution policy, and then merge specialized domain teachers across search, coding, science, and real-world workflows through unified outcome–process post-training. This provides a practical route for a compact open model to tackle complex, multi-stage engineering and scientific problems.
During this effort, we also observed that organizing long-horizon work requires more than task delegation and mid-course verification. On the execution side, our current orchestration and verification training still centers on search and research synthesis, while ultra-long trajectories can still accumulate heavy context overhead; meanwhile, the unified model does not yet fully retain the peak performance of every domain teacher after joint post-training. On the application side, our scientific showcases still operate within computational simulations and historical data replays rather than active physical experiments. In future work, we will use intermediate verification points as natural boundaries to compress completed exploration history into concise stage records, extend learned orchestration to broader engineering workflows while reducing cross-domain distillation loss, and work with scientists to connect Sage-A1.5 with real-world experimental validation.

article.headline: 35B智能体Sage-A1.5：学会分工与验证
article.lede: 上海AI Lab发布35B MoE智能体Sage-A1.5，把子任务并行委派与过程验证纳入训练，多项基准超过前代A1。
article.problem: 此前Agents-A1通过扩展智能体执行长度而非参数规模，在35B MoE上提升长程任务表现；但复杂软件工程、机器学习优化和科研任务还要求管理子任务、比较方案并随证据修改决策。单智能体逐步执行会遭遇上下文增长、探索缓慢和错误累积，长执行也不必然更好：可能重复无效搜索、基于未验证假设推理或过早接受结论。
article.method: Sage-A1.5把执行组织作为训练目标：主智能体学习拆分任务、向隔离上下文的并行子智能体委派，并整合探索性或构造性组合的结果；同时学习在进度停滞或关键结论处自主核查证据、修正策略，推理时不依赖外部监督器或专用验证工具。训练上先做多领域SFT，再用统一的结果奖励RL与多教师on-policy蒸馏进行结果-过程后训练，合并搜索、编码、科学和真实工作流能力。
article.results: 表1中，Sage-A1.5的GAIA为95.1、BrowseComp为81.7、XBench-DS-2510为92.0、MLE-Bench-Lite为65.2、SWE-Bench Pro为61.2、FS-O为81.0、FS-R为48.3、CMT为80.0、CritPt为20.0；前代A1对应为96.0、75.5、86.0、43.9、43.6、79.0、40.0、72.0、4.3。消融显示，启用Agentic Orchestration使BrowseComp从81.7升至82.8、DeepResearch Bench II从43.7升至47.5；Agentic Verification教师使BrowseComp从81.0升至85.5，配对比较中每任务输出token从23,245降至21,962、交互轮次从84.81降至82.14。ALE-CLI严格通过率为19.1%，低于Kimi-K3的27.6%、GLM-5.3的28.5%和GPT-5.6-sol的28.6%；MatTools为42.6，低于A1的47.1。
article.why_it_matters: 意义在于把分工与验证从外部脚手架规则变成可训练能力，让35B级开源模型在长程工程与科研任务上有可复现的路线；本地量化和可检查产物也利于隐私敏感与离线部署。
article.limitations: 论文承认，当前编排与验证训练仍集中在搜索与研究综合，超长轨迹会累积上下文开销，统一模型也未完全保留各领域教师的峰值表现；科学展示仍限于计算模拟和历史数据回放，而非真实物理实验。外部基准上，ALE-CLI 19.1%仍落后于三家更大模型，MatTools 42.6也低于A1的47.1，说明通用专业工作流和材料工具使用仍有短板。
article.figure_caption_zh: 图：Sage-A1.5的三阶段训练流程——先以多领域数据、环境构建、轨迹筛选、分阶段SFT和RL训练出多领域教师，再经统一的结果-过程后训练得到统一模型，支持智能体编排、迭代验证与本地部署。

figure.caption: Overview of the three-stage training pipeline of . First, the model is trained on diverse domain data, including coding, long-context reasoning, deep research, scientific reasoning, and co-working, utilizing environment construction, trajectory selection, staged supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning to build multi-domain teachers. Then, these teachers undergo unified outcome-process post-training to produce the final unified model, which features an agent orchestration for collaborative task solving, iterative agentic verification for reasoning reliability, and local deployment for ensuring data privacy, access control, and offline support.

email_papers.title: Socratic Skill Learning: Interleaving Teaching and Practice for Transferable Agent Skills
email_papers.abstract: Agent Skills improve LLM agents by making task knowledge reusable across sessions. Learning transferable Skills requires evidence about a procedure and its conditions of use, which a successful task attempt can leave untested. We introduce Socratic Skill Learning (SSL), which interleaves expert teaching with Student practice. An Educator guides investigation while the Student remains the sole environment operator and Skill author, able to question, test, and adapt advice. To test reuse beyond the learning task, we construct SkillTransferBench, with 35 task families and 408 executable cases, pairing public variation specifications with held-out evaluation in fresh solver sessions. On the main 22-family, 155-case cohort, Fixed-Window SSL reaches 0.801 utility, versus 0.723 without a Skill, 0.761 for adapted Trace2Skill (trajectory distillation), and 0.751 for adapted SKILL-KD (contrastive distillation). Across three model pairs on shared families, interleaved guidance outperforms expert authoring and post-hoc teaching. Process analysis links guidance to Student writing and package revision; a case study shows the Student testing and refining a proposed procedure for later reuse. As demand for new lessons falls, the cost of fixed-window review grows. Issue-Guided SSL tracks unresolved questions across Skill revisions to select and focus review, reaching 0.805 utility with 61.7% fewer Educator tokens and 16.9% fewer total acquisition tokens than Fixed-Window SSL on the main cohort.
