1
Introduction
Agent Skills extend LLM agents through reusable
instructions and executable resources, without updating model weights
(
Anthropic, 2025
)
. Curated Skills improve
success on tasks requiring specialized expertise
(
Li et al., 2026b
)
. Acquiring transferable Skills requires
identifying which steps to reuse,
under what conditions, and when to adapt them.
Recent methods distill execution trajectories into Skills and refine
packages through testing and feedback
(
Ni et al., 2026
;
Ma et al., 2026
;
Shi et al., 2026
)
. SkillLearnBench’s Teacher
Feedback uses expert advice after failed attempts to guide
revision
(
Zhong et al., 2026
)
. Such refinement depends on
which hypotheses the learner tests and
which failures it investigates. Guidance during an ongoing attempt can
redirect these choices before an untested assumption becomes a reusable
rule. We therefore ask:
how should external expertise guide the
learner while it is still gathering evidence?
We introduce
Socratic Skill Learning (
SSL
)
, interleaving
expert teaching with Student practice (Figure
3
).
1
1
1
Code,
benchmark, and trajectories:
project repository
.
An Educator observes recent Student work and the live Skill, then explains,
challenges, diagnoses, or remains silent. The Student operates the environment
and authors the package. Inspired by Socratic inquiry, the interaction
examines assumptions through dialogue and practical checks; the Student
can question advice, adapt it, and decide what to retain.
We instantiate SSL with
Fixed-Window SSL
, which reviews at regular tool-call
intervals, and
Issue-Guided SSL

Benchmark construction
We construct the benchmark in three stages: adapt source tasks, build task
families through two complementary routes, and validate the resulting cases.
Source adaptation.
We select tasks with clear requirements and meaningful variation from six
benchmarks: Terminal-Bench and AgentIF-OneDay

Task-family construction.
Experts in coding and agent benchmarking collaborate with agents through two
routes (Figure
1

extraction and adaptation

We introduce Socratic Skill Learning (SSL), in which an Educator guides
ongoing investigation while a Student tests the guidance and authors a
transferable Skill. We develop two instantiations:
Fixed-Window SSL
periodically reviews Student progress, while
Issue-Guided SSL
maintains
learning issues to select and focus subsequent reviews. We first describe
their shared learning process (Figure
3
A), then present
each protocol (Figure
3
B).

4.1
Socratic dialogue and Student practice
Both protocols use the target solver’s model as the Student, the sole
environment operator and author of
𝒦
\mathcal{K}
. Guided by the family
specification, it explores the anchor, tests candidate procedures, and
decides what evidence to gather and what knowledge to retain
(Section
3.1
).
Educator review and Student response.
The Educator has read-only access to recent Student work and the live Skill.
It can explain, challenge, diagnose, propose checks, or remain silent.
The Student can question, test, adapt, or reject advice, responding through
dialogue, environment experiments, and package revisions. This interaction
examines the assumptions behind a procedure and the evidence needed to
retain it, with the Student deciding how the evidence changes the Skill.
Rounds and transfer.
A fresh solver tests each round’s package on the reset anchor, checking
whether it carries the procedure beyond the author’s session. The resulting
trajectory and verifier feedback guide the next round. Student and Educator
sessions persist; evaluation sessions are fresh. Only the final package
transfers to held-out family members.
4.2
Fixed-Window SSL
Fixed-Window SSL organizes acquisition as repeated periods of Student
practice and Educator review. After every
g
g
completed Student tool calls,
the Educator examines recent reasoning and tool results alongside the live
Skill, informed by the family specification, prior lessons, and anchor
feedback. This recurring review can challenge an assumption or suggest a
missing check while an investigation is still open, shaping the evidence
gathered before a procedure is retained.
The Student can clarify or contest a lesson, then resumes exploration and
Skill revision. The resulting
work informs the next review. Silence lets practice continue directly.
The schedule thus fixes when review occurs, while guidance responds to
the Student’s progress. The Student determines when to finish the round;
a final review covers any work since the previous review, allowing Student
action before the snapshot (Appendix
C.2
).
4.3
Issue-Guided SSL
Teaching demand changes as a Skill develops: practice can settle a
question, while new evidence can call for further guidance. Issue-Guided
SSL tracks unresolved questions across revisions to select when review
is needed and focus it on relevant evidence.
Persistent learning issues.
An Educator lesson supplies a learning focus and an acceptance criterion:
what to investigate and what observable evidence would resolve it. A learning
issue retains these together with evidence and package revisions for
subsequent review. Issues form a persistent
Learning-Issue Tree
: a concern arising within an investigation becomes a child;
closing it returns attention to the nearest unresolved ancestor. Resolved
branches preserve what has already been addressed.
Revisions and resolution.
The Student groups file edits into a coherent revision, declaring its
summary, evidence, and any issue addressed. An addressed issue can close
with a changed package when the Student verifies the revision, documents
the procedure’s applicability with evidence, or rejects the guidance on
evidential grounds. Verified closure requires a successful post-lesson
check. Investigation can therefore settle a question without another
Educator call.
Selective review and reopening.
An initial review occurs at the first revision or after a warm-up window
of tool calls. Thereafter, an unresolved issue must open, change, or reopen
before further review. The Educator receives the active issue and its
ancestors, the latest revision, and recent local work, with read access to
the complete package. A lesson returns the Student to investigation;
silence closes the current review episode. Contradictory
fresh-solver anchor feedback can reopen the associated issue in the next
round while preserving resolved siblings.
Appendix
C.2
gives event rules and boundary handling.

How should external expertise guide Skill acquisition?

Guidance during practice consistently produces stronger transfer than

Discussion and Conclusion
On shared
SkillTransferBench
families across three model pairs, Socratic
Skill Learning (
SSL
) improves transfer over direct expert authoring
and post-hoc teaching. Process and case analyses show how guidance enters
Skill development: advice identifies a direction to investigate, while
execution evidence informs how the Student tests, adapts, and retains a
procedure.
As teaching demand changes, unresolved questions provide a basis for
allocating expert attention. Issue-Guided SSL tracks these questions across
revisions, retaining transfer utility with 2.75
times the gain per Educator token of Fixed-Window SSL on the main cohort.
The study connects the development of reusable knowledge with decisions
about where further guidance is needed.

Appendix B
Benchmark Assets and Evaluation Cohorts
B.1
Construction routes
Experts in coding and agent benchmarking collaborate with agents to construct
the task families. We first convert source tasks to a common format,
reconciling paths, formats, ordering, precision, and boundary conditions
across the task descriptions, fixtures, and scorers. For example, adapting
the WAL anchor preserves the source database fixtures while revising task
metadata and strengthening checks of the recovered output.
In extraction and adaptation, compatible source cases are grouped into
families, and statements and tests are revised to align their requirements.
In seed expansion, a case from the adapted pool seeds a specification of the
shared invariant and permitted variation; experts and agents then develop
additional cases within this scope. Each task includes a description,
public fixtures, a resettable environment, a reference solution, and a
private verifier.
For example, WAL-recovery cases vary encoding, integrity, and recovery depth
while preserving the reconstruction goal. Acquisition uses a fixed
v01
anchor in each family.

private tests remain outside agent workspaces.

Within an original authoring-protocol run, the package author (the external

Fixed-Window SSL
provides the Educator with the family definition, recent
reasoning and tool calls, prior lessons, feedback from anchor tests by fresh
solvers, and the complete live package. An opening lesson may explain, propose
a test, diagnose, or
challenge an assumption; the Student may clarify, adapt, or contest it,
followed by at most one Educator reply. Subsequent task actions and package
edits remain Student decisions.
Round completion.
The author ends its trajectory when it has finished the current exploration
and package revision. The harness completes the scheduled terminal review,
if any, and the Student’s resulting work, then validates and snapshots the
package for a fresh anchor test. Each round permits at most one terminal
review; resulting Student work is retained without another terminal review.
The tool-call window controls review frequency, while the author determines
trajectory length. All 3 rounds run, with anchor feedback entering
the next round.
The loop below preserves Student package ownership under both schedules.
create Student; create Educator; initialize package K
for round in 1..3:
  give Student public spec, clean anchor, previous feedback
  while the current authoring trajectory is active:
    let Student reason, invoke tools, and edit K
    Fixed-Window SSL: review after g completed tool calls
      or at an unreviewed end-of-round tail
    Issue-Guided SSL: on bootstrap, revision commit, or contradiction:
      resolve addressed active issue if closure conditions hold
      otherwise update, open, or reopen its persistent issue
      request review only for an unresolved transition
    if review requested:
      Educator observes local evidence and complete package
      if lesson: Student responds
        fixed-window permits one Educator follow-up
      else: retain Issue-Guided SSL issue with no-lesson closure reason
      Student resumes its own work
  freeze K; evaluate with fresh target model on clean anchor
  retain trajectory and verifier feedback for the next round
evaluate final K with a fresh target model for each held-out case
Revision declarations and issue state.
During practice, the Student calls
commit_skill_revision
after a
coherent knowledge change to the complete package. The declaration includes
a summary and evidence, plus an issue ID and disposition when it addresses
an existing lesson. Ordinary file edits accumulate until the Student commits
such a revision. The Educator supplies a learning focus and an observable
acceptance criterion when delivering a lesson.
Each persistent issue stores a focus, acceptance criterion, linked revisions,
evidence, and disposition. A child records a concern within ongoing work;
closure returns attention to the nearest unresolved ancestor. In Issue-Guided
SSL, the first-round bootstrap occurs at the first revision or after ten tool
calls, whichever comes first. At the round boundary, an uncommitted package change is processed as
an implicit revision; the runtime also handles any pending bootstrap or anchor
contradiction before the final snapshot. The default Educator view includes up to three active-path nodes, two
recently closed issues, the latest revision, and recent local tool calls;
read access to the complete package remains available. After bootstrap, another
unresolved transition precedes further teaching, so triggers, context, and
follow-up policy change together.
Student-declared closure requires an addressed active issue and a changed
package. A verified disposition additionally requires a successful post-lesson
verification event; bounded and rejected dispositions record stated evidence.
A no-lesson closure records Educator silence rather than verified correctness.
Contradictory feedback from an anchor test by a fresh solver targets the issue
associated with that package and may reopen it while preserving resolved siblings.

E.2
Review decisions and subsequent Student behavior
We relate teaching and silence to the Student’s next action and subsequent
Skill revision. The analysis covers 66
Fixed-Window SSL
runs from
the evaluation manifest, using the latest complete attempt for each family
and repeat. They contain 630 reviews, 254
opening lessons, and 91 follow-ups. Regular ten-tool-call
reviews include 226 teaching and 206
silent decisions; trajectory-end reviews include
28 and 170, respectively.
Observation windows.
Each window begins when the Student receives a lesson or a silent review
completes, and ends at the next review or round boundary. We use event order
and tool-call IDs to identify actions begun within the window. Initial
prompts delimit rounds; recovery messages remain within the current round.
Across 432 regular windows, we classify the first
subsequent tool call as environment, write/edit, read/search, or absent.
Trajectory-end reviews are analyzed separately:
24/28 lessons precede
a tool call, while all 170 silent reviews end the round.
Skill revision over ten tool calls.
The revision analysis uses 193 windows containing
exactly ten calls begun after review, with no continuation of an earlier call.
We compare the Skill versions at the start and end of each window.
Both versions are observable in 112 windows; the other
81 lack a comparable pair. Among these
112 windows, the package changes in
67/69 teaching windows and
27/43 silent windows.
A sensitivity analysis relaxes the ten-call restriction and includes
316 windows with comparable versions.
Estimation.
These observational comparisons measure associations with teaching:
review decisions respond to the Student’s ongoing work. We standardize
contrasts by acquisition round, using rounds with both comparison groups
and weighting them by the eligible sample’s round distribution.

article.headline: 教与练交替：让智能体技能真正可迁移
article.lede: 让教育者在学生实操中途插话指导：主队列效用由0.723升至0.801，教育者token减少61.7%。
article.problem: Agent Skill 能让 LLM 智能体的任务知识跨会话复用，但要习得可迁移的技能，学习者必须弄清「哪些步骤可复用、在什么条件下适用、何时需要调整」，而一次成功的任务尝试往往并不会检验这些前提。现有方法多做轨迹蒸馏或失败后的追补反馈，学习者该验证哪些假设、该追查哪些失败，仍是盲点。
article.method: 作者提出 Socratic Skill Learning（SSL）：学生模型独占环境操作权与 Skill 撰写权，教育者只读观察近期工作与当前 Skill 包，可以解释、质疑、诊断、提议检查或保持沉默，学生则可质疑、实测、改写或拒绝建议。Fixed-Window SSL 每隔 g 个工具调用触发一次审阅；Issue-Guided SSL 则维护一棵持久化的「学习问题树」，记录待解问题与验收标准，只在问题新开、变化或重开时聚焦审阅。作者同时构建 SkillTransferBench：35 个任务族、408 个可执行用例，跨六个领域，每族给出公开的族规格与留出用例，用全新会话的求解器测试冻结后的 Skill 包。
article.results: 在 Qwen 主队列（22 族、155 个留出用例）上，Fixed-Window SSL 取得 0.801 效用，无 Skill 为 0.723，适配版 Trace2Skill 为 0.761，适配版 SKILL-KD 为 0.751；相对 Trace2Skill 高 3.99 个百分点（95% 配对族自助法置信区间 [1.45, 6.49]），相对 SKILL-KD 高 4.99 个百分点。全通过率从 32.50% 升至 49.49%（Fixed-Window）与 50.82%（Issue-Guided）。Issue-Guided SSL 达到 0.805 效用，同时减少 61.7% 的教育者 token 和 16.9% 的总采集 token（每轮 6.89M 降至 5.72M），每教育者 token 的迁移增益为 Fixed-Window 的 2.75 倍；审阅次数减少 47.8%，单次审阅 token 减少 26.7%。在 DeepSeek 与 Kimi 的 10 族共享子集上，两种交替协议同样排名前二，教育者 token 分别减少 63.8% 与 77.4%。
article.why_it_matters: 它把「技能采集」从离线的轨迹蒸馏改成在线的教与练交替，并给出一个可测量留出迁移的基准，说明监督信号何时插入比插入多少更关键。对需要控制专家模型调用成本的智能体技能流水线，问题驱动的选择性审阅提供了一条可操作的降本路径。
article.limitations: 作者自述实验在统一的单锚点设定下比较完整协议，尚未拆解教育者、审阅时机与问题结构各自贡献多少；跨模型结果也不一致，DeepSeek 上 Issue-Guided 虽省教育者 token，但学生 token 增加 39.2%，总采集 token 反而上升，成本优势并非普遍成立。过程分析（教学与写作/修订的关联）本质上是观察性的，不能作为因果结论。
article.figure_caption_zh: 研究总览：(A) 由六个源基准构建任务族，(B) 采集协议比较、外部方法与模型配对，(C) 从教学需求到问题引导式审阅的路径及其效用与成本。

email_papers.title: Harness Scaling for Generalizable Agentic Reinforcement Learning
email_papers.abstract: Agent harnesses have become a central component of modern agentic systems, shaping how models use tools, manage context, and coordinate long-horizon interaction. Realizing the benefits of these harnesses depends on how effectively the underlying model can make use of them, motivating reinforcement learning directly through the harness. However, existing approaches typically train through a single fixed harness, which can lead to specialization and limited transfer across harness configurations. To address this, we introduce \textbf{Harness Scaling}, a new scaling dimension for agentic RL that extends training from a single harness to diverse execution configurations. Concretely, we construct a factorized harness space, select a compact training subset with balanced factorial coverage, and organize cross-harness training to combine global coverage with controlled variation for the same task. Across multiple benchmarks, model scales, and RL algorithms, Harness Scaling consistently improves generalization to unseen white-box configurations. Moreover, models trained through structured white-box variation transfer effectively to unseen external black-box harnesses, outperforming models trained through a single complex black-box harness. These results establish harness diversity as a meaningful scaling dimension for agentic RL and highlight the importance of how this diversity is organized for cross-harness generalization.

Abstract
Agent harnesses have become a central component of modern agentic systems,
shaping how models use tools, manage context, and coordinate long-horizon
interaction. Realizing the benefits of these harnesses depends on how
effectively the underlying model can make use of them, motivating
reinforcement learning directly through the harness. However, existing
approaches typically train through a single fixed harness, which can lead
to specialization and limited transfer across harness configurations.
To address this, we introduce
Harness Scaling
, a new scaling
dimension for agentic RL that extends training from a single harness to
diverse execution configurations.
Concretely, we construct a factorized
harness space, select a compact training subset with balanced factorial
coverage, and organize cross-harness training to combine global coverage
with controlled variation for the same task.
Across multiple benchmarks, model scales, and RL algorithms, Harness Scaling
consistently improves generalization to unseen white-box configurations.
Moreover, models trained through structured white-box variation transfer
effectively to unseen external black-box harnesses, outperforming models
trained through a single complex black-box harness. These results establish
harness diversity as a meaningful scaling dimension for agentic RL and
highlight the importance of how this diversity is organized for
cross-harness generalization.
1
Introduction
Agent harnesses are playing an increasingly central role in modern
agentic systems
[
31
]
. By supporting sustained interaction, tool use, state
maintenance, and recovery from failures
[
4
]
, harnesses have substantially
improved agent performance on complex, long-horizon tasks
[
38
,
32
,
16
]
. Yet the
benefits of a capable harness depend not only on its design, but also on
whether the underlying policy can use it effectively
[
14
]
. This naturally motivates optimizing the policy directly through the harness
with reinforcement learning
[
36
,
39
]
, which strengthens its ability to exploit the
available interaction mechanisms during task solving.
However, existing approaches typically optimize the policy through a
single fixed harness
[
7
,
34
]
. While effective within the training harness, such
optimization may encourage specialization to a particular execution
configuration and weaken transfer across harnesses. We therefore introduce
Harness Scaling
, extending policy optimization from a single
harness to diverse execution configurations.
Unlike task or environment
scaling
[
29
,
6
,
3
,
35
]
, which expands what agents solve or where they operate, Harness
Scaling introduces diversity in how policies execute and interact with the
same underlying task and environment, promoting generalization across
execution configurations.
A key consideration in Harness Scaling is how to model harness variation
and select a compact set of configurations for training.
Given the modular
nature of agent harnesses
[
7
,
23
]
, we factorize harness variation along five
components: system prompt, tool interface, observation, context management, and workflow.
Each component contains multiple realizations, whose combinations define a
factorial space of complete harness configurations. As variation along these
components increases, the space expands rapidly, while exhaustive training
can introduce substantial redundancy under a fixed budget. We therefore
preserve low-order factorial structure in a compact training set, balancing
individual component realizations and their pairwise combinations through
an orthogonal design
[
21
,
8
]
. During reinforcement learning, the same task is paired
with structurally nearby harness configurations, providing controlled local
variation within each task while maintaining broad coverage across the
training space.
To demonstrate the effectiveness of Harness Scaling, we evaluate
cross-harness generalization across multiple benchmarks, model scales, and
RL algorithms. By training across diverse harness configurations, Harness
Scaling reduces specialization to any single harness and encourages more
generalizable agent behavior. Empirically, it consistently outperforms
single-harness RL on unseen white-box configurations.
More importantly, policies trained through structured white-box harness
variation transfer effectively to complex external black-box harnesses
[
18
,
1
]
,
outperforming single-harness black-box training.
These results establish harness diversity as a
meaningful scaling dimension for agentic RL, while showing that effective
scaling depends critically on how this diversity is organized during
training. In summary, our contributions are threefold:
•
We introduce Harness Scaling as a new scaling dimension
for agentic reinforcement learning, distinct from conventional scaling
over tasks and environments, and study how training across diverse
harness configurations affects generalization beyond a single execution
setting.
•
We develop a structured framework for Harness Scaling that
factorizes harness variation, selects a compact training set with balanced
factorial coverage, and organizes cross-harness training by assigning
structurally nearby configurations to the same task across the training space.
•
We demonstrate across benchmarks, model scales, and RL algorithms
that Harness Scaling substantially improves generalization to unseen
white-box and external black-box harnesses, establishing both the value
of scaling across harnesses and the importance of organizing this scaling
structurally.
2
Related Work
2.1
Agentic Reinforcement Learning
Reinforcement learning has emerged as an important paradigm for improving
the capabilities of LLMs
[
40
,
24
]
. Recent work has extended RL from single-turn
reasoning to increasingly complex agentic settings, including tool use
[
2
,
28
]
, web
navigation
[
20
]
, software engineering
[
27
]
, and professional workflows
[
33
]
. As agentic RL moves toward broader
capability, recent efforts have increasingly scaled training along the
task
and
environment
dimensions. Task scaling
[
30
,
3
,
5
]
broadens the
distribution of problems used for policy optimization, while environment
scaling
[
6
,
29
,
35
]
expands the range of external settings in which agents interact and
receive feedback. These directions expand what agents learn to
solve and where they learn to operate, while often retaining a fixed
execution harness. In contrast, we study harness diversity as an additional
scaling dimension for agentic RL, focusing on policy learning and
generalization across execution configurations.
2.2
Harness Design and Optimization
The design of an agent harness can substantially shape how a language model
uses tools, maintains context, and performs long-horizon tasks
[
38
,
14
,
16
]
.
Early agent systems largely relied on manually designed harnesses, while
subsequent work has explored automated harness improvement through search,
editing, and evolution based on task outcomes or execution
trajectories
[
13
,
11
,
23
]
. A complementary line of work directly optimizes
model policies within complex agent harnesses, including reinforcement
learning through black-box harnesses
[
36
,
7
,
26
,
15
,
17
,
9
]
. These directions either
improve the harness itself or adapt a policy to a particular harness.
Harness Scaling instead studies policy optimization over a structured combinatorial space of harness configurations, with the goal of improving generalization to unseen configurations.

Harness Scaling strengthens capabilities that are directly relevant to
operating under different harness configurations.

6
Conclusion
In this work, we study Harness Scaling as a new scaling dimension for agentic
reinforcement learning, motivated by the limitations of optimizing policies
through a single fixed harness. We formalize harness diversity as a structured configuration space and
develop a framework that integrates structured harness selection with
cross-harness policy training. Across benchmarks,
model scales, and RL algorithms, Harness Scaling substantially improves
generalization to unseen white-box configurations and transfers effectively
to complex external black-box harnesses. Our results further show that the
benefits of scaling depend on how harness diversity is selected and incorporated into training, rather than on diversity alone.
More broadly, these findings expand the scope of agentic RL scaling beyond
what agents solve and where they operate to how they interact and execute,
positioning harness variation as a complementary dimension for improving
generalization across diverse execution systems.

Training with Context Compaction.
Context compaction can split a single rollout into multiple training
segments. All segments originating from the same rollout share the same
rollout-level reward and participate in policy optimization, causing the
number of training segments in a batch to vary dynamically. Segment
expansion does not alter the rollout-level grouping used by GRPO: for a
group of eight original rollouts, reward normalization is always computed
over the eight rollout rewards, regardless of how many segments each
rollout produces. Segments inherit the group identity and normalized
advantage of their parent rollout and do not introduce additional entries
when computing the group mean or standard deviation.
Policy loss is aggregated with token-level mean reduction over all valid
policy-generated tokens in the batch. Each valid token therefore
contributes once to the loss regardless of how its parent rollout is
segmented, so splitting a rollout into multiple segments does not introduce
additional sample-level weight. This preserves both the rollout-level
reward semantics and consistent token-level weighting while allowing all
valid post-compaction segments to participate in training.
Black-Box Baselines.
For the black-box baselines, we use OpenClaw v2026.4.5 as the training
harness and reserve Claude Code v2.1.205 as an unseen external harness
for evaluation. Black-Box SFT and Black-Box RL represent two complementary
adaptation strategies to the same single black-box harness: the former
fine-tunes the policy on 12,800 trajectories collected on ClawGym-Task
through OpenClaw for three epochs, while the latter performs online policy
optimization through OpenClaw on the same training set for 300 updates
with 128 rollouts per update. This gives both settings approximately
38,400 trajectory-level training exposures, although SFT reuses a fixed
trajectory set across epochs whereas RL collects trajectories online.
For the comparison in Table
2
, Black-Box RL
uses GRPO, and Harness Scaling uses the corresponding GRPO-trained
checkpoint. Both RL settings use the same backbone models, matched
optimization budgets, the same main GRPO hyperparameters, and the same
evaluation protocol.

Scoring.
We report Pass@1 averaged over three independent evaluation runs. For each
run, every task is executed once under the corresponding harness setting,
and the resulting task-level scores are aggregated following the benchmark
evaluation protocol. The reported score is then obtained by averaging the
Pass@1 results across the three runs. For rubric-based evaluation requiring
a model judge, we use GPT-5.4 with the same judging protocol across all
methods and harness settings.

Appendix D
Additional Analysis Details
D.1
Behavioral Metrics
We use six trajectory-level behavioral metrics to characterize
harness-related capabilities beyond task-level performance.
Instruction Following
measures whether the policy correctly follows
the system instructions and execution constraints specified by the harness.
Interface Handling
measures whether the policy correctly interprets
and uses the available tool interface, particularly when tool names or
schemas differ from the base harness.
Observation Reading
measures whether the policy extracts
task-relevant information from tool feedback despite additional formatting
or distracting metadata.
State Tracking
measures whether the policy maintains an accurate
understanding of task progress, intermediate results, and the evolving
workspace state throughout long-horizon execution.
Workflow Compliance
measures whether the policy follows procedural
requirements imposed by the harness, such as explicit planning or periodic
verification.
Error Recovery
measures whether the policy recognizes execution
failures, adapts its strategy, and continues toward task completion rather
than repeating or propagating the same error.
D.2
Metric Evaluation
We evaluate the six capabilities from complete agent trajectories using
GPT-5.4 as the trajectory judge. For each model scale and each of the
18 held-out in-space harnesses, we collect 200 complete trajectories for
both Single-Harness RL and Harness Scaling on the same 200 ClawGym-Bench
tasks. For each trajectory, the judge is provided with the task instruction,
harness specification, and complete interaction history, including policy
actions, tool calls, and tool observations.
Each capability is scored independently on a five-point scale. A score of
1 indicates that the corresponding capability is largely absent or repeatedly
violated; 2 indicates substantial deficiencies; 3 indicates partial or
inconsistent satisfaction; 4 indicates generally correct behavior with
minor deviations; and 5 indicates consistent and effective satisfaction of
the criterion throughout the trajectory. The judge assigns each dimension
separately rather than producing a single overall trajectory score.
We use the same judging prompt, rubric, and judge model across both
approaches and all harness settings. For each behavioral dimension, we first
average scores over the 200 trajectories within each held-out harness, and
then average equally across all 18 harnesses. For visualization, the
five-point scores are normalized by dividing by five, resulting in values
between 0.2 and 1.0 as reported in

4(b)

article.headline: 跨执行框架训练：智能体RL的新扩展维度
article.lede: 把智能体执行框架拆成五个可变换组件，用正交设计选18种配置做强化学习训练，显著提升对未见框架的泛化。
article.problem: 现有智能体强化学习大多只在单一固定执行框架（harness）下优化策略，容易专门化到特定的工具接口、上下文管理和工作流，一旦更换框架，性能就容易下降。此前关于扩展的研究主要集中在任务扩展和环境扩展，关注「解什么问题」和「在哪里执行」，很少把「怎么执行」当作独立的扩展维度。
article.method: 作者把 harness 分解为系统提示、工具接口、观测、上下文管理、工作流五个组件，每个组件实例化三种实现，构成 3^5=243 个完整配置的组合空间，并以汉明距离定义配置间的结构邻近性。随后用 strength-2 正交设计从中选出 18 个配置组成训练集：每个组件的每种实现各出现 6 次，任意两个组件的实现组合恰好出现 2 次。训练时每个任务随机抽取一个锚点配置，再取与之汉明距离最近的 K=2 个配置，在同一任务上做跨框架 rollout，优化目标仍是标准的 PPO/GRPO 裁剪损失。
article.results: 在 Qwen3-4B-Instruct 上，18 个留出白盒配置的平均 Pass@1 相对单框架 RL 分别提升 +9.80（GRPO）和 +3.57（PPO）分，整体平均从 29.81 升到 39.04、从 33.91 升到 36.93；Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct 上分别提升 +5.21 和 +4.90 分，整体平均从 37.29 升到 42.78、从 36.31 升到 41.89。迁移到未见过的外部黑盒框架 Claude Code 时，两个模型分别取得 37.22 和 41.20 的平均分，高于经由 OpenClaw 训练的 black-box SFT（35.08 / 38.08）和 black-box RL（33.38 / 36.28）。消融显示，在 ClawGym-Bench 上，随机抽取 18 个配置为 47.90/42.78，按本文方法选出的 18 个配置为 52.78/45.37（In-Space/Claude Code）；把邻近分配换成随机分配会掉 2.32/2.20 分；而在基础框架上仅下降 0.19 分。
article.why_it_matters: 它把「执行方式的多样性」提出为一个可与任务扩展、环境扩展并列的智能体 RL 扩展轴，并证明收益取决于多样性如何组织——在固定预算下，穷举全部 243 个配置反而不及结构化的 18 个配置。
article.limitations: 实验只覆盖 Qwen3-4B 与 Qwen3-30B-A3B 两个模型、ClawGym-Task 一个训练集，框架变体由 Opus-4.7 自动生成且仅 5 维 3 档，结论能否外推到更复杂的真实 harness 尚未验证；黑盒对比中的 SFT/RL 基线只基于 OpenClaw 单个黑盒框架，行为分析用 GPT-5.4 作评判也带有主观性。

email_papers.title: Evolving with Open Worlds: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement for Future Forecasting
email_papers.abstract: Most contemporary artificial intelligence (AI) systems are released with frozen parameters and improve through external updates, whereas an ideal system would keep improving from its own experience, a capacity we call recursive self-improvement (RSI). Yet studying RSI requires an environment that is continuously changing, objectively verifiable, and naturally grounded, posing a fundamental challenge for agent evolution. Here we introduce DeepEvolve, a sustainable evolution agent system grounded in future event prediction, in which agents continuously interact with a dynamically evolving environment and improve by internalizing and externalizing the experience gained through these interactions. A living environment synthesizes verifiable tasks, and a recursive-evolution engine turns the reasoning trajectory behind each prediction back into capability: decoupling search from prediction adapts parameter-level evolution to the contamination-prone live environment, while distilling reusable skills lets the agent evolve from the limited live trajectories such an environment affords. On the external FutureX leaderboard, which evaluates predictions against real-world outcomes and is updated weekly, our self-improved forecaster ranked first across all systems over three consecutive weeks, achieving up to a 195% improvement in rating. On our synthesized evaluation, it ranked among the top three across four base LLMs, outperforming the strongest baseline by up to 10.7 Bradley--Terry points. More broadly, these results suggest that a system built for self-improvement is best understood as an agent that co-evolves with a genuinely living, open-ended environment, pointing to a shift in AI from training static models on fixed data toward cultivating agents that grow stronger from their own experience, with such an open world as the indispensable basis of that growth.
email_papers.content:
Abstract
Most contemporary artificial intelligence (AI) systems are released with frozen parameters and improve through external updates, whereas an ideal system would keep improving from its own experience, a capacity we call
recursive self-improvement
(RSI).
Yet studying RSI requires an environment that is continuously changing, objectively verifiable, and naturally grounded, posing a fundamental challenge for agent evolution.

Introduction
Intelligence is often measured by what a system can do at a single moment in time
[
19
,
2
]
.
Yet the more consequential question may not be how capable a model is today, but whether it can become more capable through its own experience
[
23
,
9
,
14
]
.
Across the natural and social sciences, the systems we regard as most powerful (
e.g.,
biological evolution, the scientific method, human expertise) are precisely those that improve themselves cumulatively, correcting past errors and compounding past gains
[
21
,
8
,
25
]
.
This suggests that an ideal artificial system should be measured less by what it can do at any single moment than by how its capabilities form and grow over time.
A system that improves itself from experience is a prerequisite for AI that acts as an autonomous agent and as a genuine instrument of discovery.
In this work, we study this form of
recursive self-improvement
(RSI) in the concrete and demanding setting of real-world event forecasting.
Studying recursive self-improvement, however, is not merely a matter of method.
It places unusually high demands on the research setting itself.
An agent can only improve recursively if its environment keeps posing fresh challenges and can tell, without human intervention, whether the agent is doing better than before.
What this calls for is an interactive environment, yet the fixed datasets that dominate today’s evaluation offer no such thing: inert and unchanging, they neither renew the challenge nor judge progress on their own.
Real-world event forecasting, we argue, is a natural testbed for such study: it is
grounded
in the unfolding world rather than a hand-constructed dataset,
verifiable
through future events whose objective ground truth arrives with time, and
non-stationary
because the world keeps changing.
Together these properties close the loop that recursion requires: the agent observes the world, makes predictions, receives future outcomes, learns from the resulting experience, and improves the predictions it makes next (Figure
1
a).
Whereas prior work on event and time-series forecasting
[
30
,
11

has largely pursued single-shot predictive accuracy, we instead treat forecasting as an environment in which to study how agents improve recursively through continuous interaction with a changing world.
Succeeding in this environment first requires a few foundational capabilities for solving any single forecasting task.

article.headline: 用真实事件预测环境训练自我改进智能体
article.lede: 研究者提出 DeepEvolve，把真实事件预测当作可验证、非平稳的环境，让智能体在预测—结果—更新的闭环中递归自我改进
article.problem: 现有 AI 系统通常在发布时就冻结参数，只能依靠外部更新来变强；而理想系统应当能从自身经验中持续改进，作者称之为递归自我改进（RSI）。但研究 RSI 对研究环境的要求很高：环境必须不断提出新挑战，能无需人工介入就判断智能体是否进步，并且与现实世界自然对应。当前主流评测依赖的固定数据集并不具备这些性质，它们静止不变，既不更新挑战，也不自行判定进步。
article.method: DeepEvolve 由三个模块构成。Prometheus 通过模板和智能体驱动的发现来生成问题，再经时间校验、去重、冲突检测和多样性感知选择。Branchus 把证据搜集与概率预测分开：由调度者、搜索者和批评者组成的 search team 负责对时间敏感的证据检索，predict team 则是时间不变的，只在缓存的证据与推理轨迹上推理；两个团队都会调用相关预测技能。Athena 使用缓存证据和可验证奖励更新 predict team 的参数，把搜索轨迹蒸馏成可复用的预测技能，并把观察到的弱点转化为任务合成技能，再回灌给 Prometheus。
article.results: 作者称 Branchus 在 Qwen3.8-Max 上取得 62.2 的 BT 分数，比表 1 中最强基线高 10.7；评测中，它与 Qwen3.8-Max、GPT-5.6-Sol、DeepSeek-V4-Pro、Claude-Opus-4.6 四个不同规模与厂商的模型配对，并与多类基线比较。作者还报告增益会累积而非饱和：智能体自身在线轨迹不断累积成技能池，蒸馏出的技能逐轮提升预测质量，而不是一次跳升后停滞；但材料中该图（图 6）论文未给出具体数字。技能被组织为从具体到抽象的四级层级（s4 逐字保留的流程、s3 对题型的一般化、s2 领域内一般化、s1 跨领域预测原则）。
article.why_it_matters: RSI 研究长期缺乏一个可以被反复刷新的试验场，而真实世界事件预测把“世界本身”当作评测集，其真值随时间揭晓、无法被人工构造，因此有可能成为智能体自我改进的可扩展环境。
article.limitations: 材料中没有独立的局限性章节；从设计看，这套递归改进高度依赖结果可客观验证，迁移到没有明确真值的领域是否成立尚不清楚。另外，主要增益目前只在 Qwen3.8-Max 上以 BT 单一指标给出，“逐轮累积提升”的具体幅度论文未给出具体数字。

figure.caption: {Overview of {DeepEvolve} for recursive self-improvement in real-world event forecasting.} {a,} The closed loop connects question generation, forecasting, and evolution, with resolved outcomes supplying verifiable rewards and updates feeding into subsequent rounds. {b,} {Prometheus} generates questions through templates and agent-driven discovery, followed by temporal validation, deduplication, conflict detection, and diversity-aware selection. {c,} {Branchus} separates evidence gathering, by a {search team} of a scheduler, searcher, and critic, from probabilistic prediction, by a {predict team}. The search team is time-sensitive, as its result depends on when it runs, while the predict team is time-invariant, reasoning only over the search team's cached evidence and reasoning trajectories. Both teams retrieve relevant forecasting skills. {d,} {Athena} updates the predict team's parameters using cached evidence and verifiable rewards, distills search trajectories into reusable forecasting skills, and converts observed weaknesses into task-synthesis skills for {Prometheus}. Resolved outcomes inform parameter and environment updates but are withheld from the behavior-level judge.

email_papers.title: Which Agent's Skill Should Change? Group-Relative Credit Assignment for Evolving Multi-Agent Teams
email_papers.abstract: Cooperative language-model agents can improve without weight updates by revising reusable skills, but only if a shared team reward is traced to the responsible agent and skill. Existing methods credit the skills present in each trajectory, yet presence is not responsibility: a harmful skill active in successful runs still earns positive credit. We present GRSE, Group-Relative Skill Evolution, which assigns behavioral credit by comparison: inspired by GRPO, it executes each question several times under the same skill libraries and contrasts the executions to credit agent--skill pairs, with structured diagnosis of failures. On HotpotQA and LoCoMo with two open-weight actors, GRSE outperforms MASkills, the closest prior method, on HotpotQA and every LoCoMo category except open-domain, with the largest gains on multi-hop questions (+6.7 and +3.2 F1). Its gains rest on better-grounded retrieval rather than answers given without evidence, and its learned skills transfer between the multi-hop tasks. GRSE is robust to corrupted libraries: starting from planted harmful skills, it credits every planted skill with the correct sign and recovers the score of a clean library (+6.3 points), whereas MASkills misattributes two and falls below its starting point.

Dang et al., 2026
;
Zhang et al., 2026a
;
Xia et al., 2026b
;
Hong et al., 2024
;
Wu et al., 2023
;
Li et al., 2023
)
. Improving such a team requires answering a credit assignment question: which agent’s behavior, and which step of it, produced a success or a failure? The question is classical in multi-agent reinforcement learning, where a shared reward is decomposed with difference rewards or counterfactual baselines
(
Wolpert and Tumer, 2001
;
Foerster et al., 2018
;
Rashid et al., 2020
)
, and it has recently been posed for language-model teams as automated failure attribution
(
Zhang et al., 2025
)
. A wrong answer may stem from evidence collection, an incomplete handoff, or downstream reasoning
(
Wang et al., 2026
;
Zhang et al., 2025
)
, and the agent whose output is wrong is often not the agent whose behavior needs to change. For example, reasoner answers wrongly when the retriever misses the evidence.
We study this problem in a setting where model parameters stay fixed and each agent’s behavior is specified by natural-language skills, reusable procedures that the agent reads and follows
(
Zhao et al., 2024
;
Wang et al., 2023
;
Alzubi et al., 2026
;
Yao et al., 2026
)
. Skills make behavior editable, so credit becomes actionable: once responsibility is located, the responsible procedure can be revised. Existing experience- and skill-learning methods, however, assign credit coarsely, which often distill lessons from whole trajectories, and mainly focus on single-agent setting
(
Shinn et al., 2023
;
Xu et al., 2026
;
Ouyang et al., 2026
)
. Meanwhile MASkill, the recent two-agent SOTA, credits each skill from single trajectory in isolation
(
Yao et al., 2026
)
. However, without a contrast, a skill that is present in every execution also receives credit for the successes it did not cause: in our robustness study, MASkills raises the utility of a planted harmful skill over three iterations, whereas our method labels it harmful and prunes it (Appendix
C
). Comparison between executions already guide experience distillation, skill refinement, and prompt optimization
(
Cai et al., 2025
;
Chen et al., 2026
;
Li et al., 2026
;
Zehle, 2026
)
, but they have not been used to localize a team’s outcome to individual agents’ behaviors.
Behavioral credit assignment in agent teams poses two challenges. First, attribution must look past where an error surfaces. In Figure
1
, Agent 2 answers “not mentioned” in three of four executions of the same question, yet Agent 2 behaves correctly given its input. The decisive difference lies in Agent 1’s search query, which retrieves the answer only in the successful execution. Second, an attribution must be specific and checkable before it can drive a revision. A defective procedure, a missing capability, and a tool failure call for different responses, and an explanation that cites no execution step cannot be verified. Across questions, attributions must also be aggregated without counting repeated executions of one question as independent evidence.

A structured diagnosis grounds each attribution in a failure type, cited failed and successful steps, and an edit action, and reference checks reject attributions that the executions do not support (§

across agents

within an agent
, a previously learned skill is later credited as harmful and diagnosed as a skill defect. Our contributions are threefold:
•
We formulate skill evolution for cooperative agents as
behavioral credit assignment
: with model parameters fixed and skills as editable units, a shared team outcome must be attributed to the agent and skills responsible for it. We address this by jointly comparing same-question team executions, which produces agent–skill feedback while preserving the handoffs needed to interpret each agent’s behavior and the proposed revision.
•
We make these attributions verifiable and actionable: a structured failure analysis links each attribution to a failure type, checked step references, and an edit action, and cross-question aggregation weighs attributions by the number of distinct questions that support them.
•
We evaluate GRSE on HotpotQA and LoCoMo with two open-weight actors. GRSE outperforms MASkills on HotpotQA and every LoCoMo category except open-domain. Its credit identifies and removes harmful skills that MASkills retains. Answer-transition and learned-skill analyses show that GRSE’s gains come from fewer broken answers and better-grounded retrieval.
2
Related Work
2.1
Reflection and Experience Memory
Experience-based adaptation stores information from past interactions to guide future decisions. Reflexion
(
Shinn et al., 2023
)
records verbal reflections for subsequent attempts. ExpeL
(
Zhao et al., 2024
)
extracts reusable insights from successes and failures, including comparisons on the same task. A-MEM
(
Xu et al., 2026
)
constructs linked notes and updates their contextual attributes as new memories arrive. ReasoningBank
(
Ouyang et al., 2026
)
distills reasoning strategies, and its memory-aware test-time scaling uses multiple executions to enrich memory curation. These methods actively transform experience rather than simply retaining raw traces. Memory and skills also interact: MemSkill
(
Zhang et al., 2026b
)
learns to select memory-management skills and revises its skill bank, while MSCE
(
Tang et al., 2026
)
promotes evidence-supported procedural policies into skills and maintains them using feedback. These methods decide
what
experience to keep and how to organize it, whereas GRSE instead decides
where
execution evidence should act, assigning it to editable skills owned by individual agents.
2.2
Reusable Skill Discovery and Evolution
Skill libraries turn experience into procedures that can be invoked and revised. Voyager
(
Wang et al., 2023
)
maintains executable code skills, and EvoSkill
(
Alzubi et al., 2026
)
uses an executor, proposer, and skill builder to discover and refine skills from task feedback. SkillRL
(
Xia et al., 2026a
)
distills failed trajectories into lessons, organizes skills into general and task-specific categories, and evolves the library alongside reinforcement learning of the agent policy. These methods learn skills for a single executing agent, so they never have to decide which agent’s skill to revise. MASkills
(
Yao et al., 2026
)
extends skill learning to cooperative teams through skill-conditioned credit, hierarchical aggregation, and skill editing, but it credits each trajectory on its own. We retain its skill representation and editing operators and change how credit is formed: GRSE jointly compares same-question team executions, and structured diagnosis links each failure to an agent–skill target, cited execution steps, and a checked edit action.
2.3
Group-Relative and Contrastive Feedback
GRPO
(
Shao et al., 2024
)
uses within-question rewards to optimize model parameters. Training-Free GRPO
(
Cai et al., 2025
)
instead distills semantic feedback from rollout groups into experiential context. Several methods already apply comparisons to skills: SkillCAT
(
Chen et al., 2026
)
contrasts same-task success/failure pairs, evaluates patches through replay, and organizes skills for routing. SkillCome
(
Li et al., 2026
)
combines within-group contrast with memories of failure and contrast patterns. CANTANTE
(
Zehle, 2026
)
contrasts joint prompt configurations on the same query to provide per-agent optimization signals. In these methods, the contrast either compares outcomes or varies the configuration being optimized. GRSE holds the skills fixed and contrasts the team’s behavior across executions, so that an outcome difference can be traced to an agent, a skill, and a cited step.

4
Experiment
4.1
Experimental Setup
We follow the setting of MASkills
(
Yao et al., 2026
)
, the closest prior SOTA for multi-agent skill evolution. Each method consists of two agents with task-specific roles that communicate sequentially, and the second agent produces the final answer. The agents are executed by one of two open-weight actors, Qwen3.8-27B
(
Qwen Team, 2026
)
and Gemma-4-31B-it
(
Gemma Team, 2026
)
, each conditioned on its own skill library. We use these two recent released open-weight model of similar size from different families to test whether credit assignment depends on the actor. A fixed Qwen3.8-27B model serves as critic and skill optimizer for all methods. Model parameters and agent roles stay fixed. The agents change only through their skills, which are revised according to the assigned credit.
All skill-evolution methods start from empty libraries and run for five iterations. GRSE samples four team trajectories per question, whereas MASkills samples one. Final libraries are evaluated with temperature-zero decoding. Detailed model, data and optimization settings appear in Appendix
A
.
4.2
Benchmarks
Datasets and metrics.
We evaluate on HotpotQA
(
Yang et al., 2018
)
for multi-hop question answering and LoCoMo
(
Maharana et al., 2024
)
for long-memory conversational reasoning. We use the distractor–hard subset and report the answer-token F1 for HotpotQA. LoCoMo covers multi-hop, temporal, open-domain, and single-hop questions. We report the category-specific F1 and smoothed BLEU.
Baselines.
We group baselines by whether they use the agent team.
Single-model baselines
answer with one model and no agents or skills. On HotpotQA, we run four prompting methods with the same actor, questions, passages, answer-format instruction, and metric as the
agent teams
, including IO (direct answer), Chain-of-Thought(CoT;
(
Wei et al., 2022
)
), CoT with self-consistency (CoT-SC;
(
Wang et al., 2022
)
; majority vote over five samples), and Self-Refine
(
Madaan et al., 2023
)
(at most three feedback-and-revision rounds). On LoCoMo, the full-context baseline follows the benchmark protocol
(
Maharana et al., 2024
)
with the actor model reads the entire conversation and answers directly.
Two-agent baselines
share the team, roles, and actor with GRSE. The empty-library team is this team before any skill is learned (iteration 0). For HotpotQA, all teams follow the agent prompts and short-answer instructions from the MASkills implementation, with questions and distractor passages supplied by the dataset. For LoCoMo, agent teams use category-specific task prompts. All the prompts are detailed in Appendix
F
. We report each
two-agent
method as the mean over three training runs, because the learned libraries vary with the sampled rollouts and the critic’s outputs, whereas
single-model
baselines have no training stage and are evaluated once.

GRSE w/o structure analysis

Conclusion
We studied behavioral credit assignment in cooperative language-model teams whose agents keep fixed parameters and act through natural-language skills. GRSE executes each question several times under the same skill libraries, compares the executions agent by agent, and attributes the team’s outcome to individual agent–skill pairs. Structured diagnosis grounds each attribution in checked execution steps, and the resulting credit drives targeted, validated skill updates. On HotpotQA and LoCoMo with two open-weight actors, GRSE outperforms MASkills on HotpotQA and every LoCoMo category except multi-hop, with the largest gains on multi-hop questions, where the answer depends on evidence passed between the two agents. Its gains also rest on better retrieval rather than on fewer declined answers alone. Accurate credit also makes GRSE robust: starting from a library with planted harmful skills, it credits every planted skill with the correct sign and restores the score of a clean library, whereas MASkills, which credits each trajectory on its own, rewards a harmful skill for successes in which it is merely present and ends below its starting point. Learned libraries also transfer between HotpotQA and LoCoMo multi-hop questions without harm, and only GRSE gains further from training on the target task itself. These results suggest that comparing executions of the same task is a practical way to determine which agent, and which of its behaviors, should change.
Limitations
GRSE trades training compute for more accurate credit: executing each question
G
=
4
G{=}4
times raises actor-token cost by 1.6–2.9
×
\times
over MASkills and wall-clock time by 1.3–1.8
×

Furthermore, GRSE is defined for any number of agents, but we evaluate two-agent sequential teams on two question-answering benchmarks with two open-weight actors and one critic model. Larger teams, non-sequential communication, longer tool-heavy tasks, and other critic models remain to be tested in the future.
Ethical Considerations
In our experiments, we use only publicly available benchmarks, HotpotQA and LoCoMo, under their respective licenses. All models are open-weight and run locally. Because GRSE writes skills in natural language, humans can inspect and edit the learned libraries for safety before deployment.

Answer states.
A final answer is
declined
if it is empty or contains “not mentioned”, “not specified”, “not available”, “not found”, “not stated”, “no information”, “unknown” or “cannot be determined”. Otherwise it is
correct

evidence
if the retriever’s output cites at least one dialogue turn (
[D
session
:
turn

NO_EVIDENCE
, print a grep call instead of running it, or return nothing usable count as no evidence.

verification
(checking that an answer is grounded in the evidence),
reasoning

5.2
. Both use the first run of each configuration and greedy decoding.
Case A: fetching the answer turn (Gemma4, LoCoMo single-hop, GRSE).
On
What type of pizza is James’ favorite?
(gold:
Pepperoni
), the answer turn does not contain the keyword of the question: John asks “Which one do you love the most?” and James replies “Pepperoni of course!” (Figure
2
). With the empty library, the retriever greps
pizza
, which matches the turns around the answer but not the answer itself, tries two narrower patterns that match nothing, and returns
NO_EVIDENCE
, so the reasoner declines. With the final library, the retriever recognizes the matched turn as a question and fetches the turns that follow it, as its learned skill
adjacent-context-expansion
prescribes, and the reasoner answers correctly. This question is one of the 56 declined questions that GRSE turns correct with cited evidence (§
5.2
), and the responsible skill is a retrieval procedure, the most common skill type on LoCoMo (Table
9
). The skill performs the same question–answer expansion that repairs the perturbed library in Robustness Case 1 (Appendix
C
, Figure
5
).
Case B: a more specific answer (Qwen3.8, HotpotQA, GRSE).
On
What occupation was shared by David Yates and Pietro Germi?
(gold:
director
), the passages call Yates a “filmmaker who has directed” films and Germi an “actor, screenwriter, and director”. With the empty library, Agent 1 offers “Filmmaker (or director)” and Agent 2 keeps the broader term (Figure
3
). With the final library, Agent 1 follows the steps of two learned skills,
answer-disambiguation-and-minimalism
and
constraint-based-entity-validation
: it classifies the question as asking for an attribute, checks each person’s stated roles against the passages, and keeps the role both passages support. Agent 2 answers “director”. This is the typical HotpotQA gain in Table
3
: a wrong answer becomes correct without new evidence, through a more precise reading of the passages that the empty library already had.

Agent 1 (harmful)
Name:
focused-latest-session-retrieval
Description:
Use when retrieving evidence: keeps the grep budget small and avoids stale, superseded facts.
Focused Retrieval Protocol
Long conversations contain outdated statements; the most recent session reflects the speaker’s current state.
1.
Pick the single most distinctive keyword from the question (one word, no alternation). Example: for “What instrument does Sam play?” use
<grep>instrument</grep>
.
2.
Issue exactly ONE grep. Additional searches waste budget and pull in contradictory older turns.
3.
From the hits, keep only lines from the highest-numbered session; discard all earlier sessions as outdated.
4.
Hand off at most two evidence lines.

For each training question, the critic receives the instructions in Figure

and a JSON payload. article.headline: 多智能体技能演化：用组内对比定位该改谁的技能
article.lede: 同一问题跑 4 次团队执行，用组内相对优势把成败归到具体智能体—技能对；HotpotQA F1 83.7，比 MASki
article.problem: 多智能体团队只拿到一个共享的团队奖励，想靠修改自然语言技能来改进，就必须回答 credit assignment：哪个智能体的哪段行为决定了成败。现有技能学习方法按「技能是否出现在轨迹里」给 credit，于是一个在成功轨迹中同样出现的有害技能也会拿到正分。而且这类方法大多面向单智能体。
article.method: GRSE 对每个问题在固定技能库下采样 G=4 次完整团队执行，按 GRPO 的归一化方式计算组内相对优势，把高、低优势执行之间的行为差异当作反事实基线。一个 critic 跨执行逐个智能体比较行为与交接，把 credit 落到智能体—技能对，并给出结构化诊断：8 类失败类型、经步骤存在性与奖励符号校验的失败/成功步骤引用，以及 refine、induce、no edit 的编辑动作。credit 按支持的问题数跨问题聚合（重复 rollout 不重复计数），再由 MASkills 的编辑算子生成候选技能库，经验证门只保留不降低验证分的更新。
article.results: HotpotQA 上 GRSE 的 F1 为 83.7±0.5（Qwen3.8 作 actor），MASkills 为 80.6±0.6；换 Gemma4 作 actor 则是 82.8±0.4 对 82.3±0.2。LoCoMo 多跳类别提升 +6.7 F1（53.4 对 46.7）与 +5.3 BLEU，Gemma4 下为 +3.2 F1；时序类别在两个 actor 上均为最高（73.4 与 67.4 F1），但 open-domain（52 题）上 MASkills 更好。在植入有害技能的鲁棒性实验中，GRSE 对 5 个植入技能全部给出正确符号、两类技能效用分离 0.31（MASkills 错 2 个、仅分离 0.03），F1 从 60.6 恢复到 66.9，高于 MASkills 的 58.4。
article.why_it_matters: 权重不动、只改自然语言技能，就能让协作智能体团队变强；把 credit 落到具体的智能体—技能对，使「改谁的技能」成为一个可引用步骤、可校验、可回滚的编辑动作，而不是笼统的整条轨迹反思。
article.limitations: 代价在训练算力：每问题 4 次 rollout 使 actor token 消耗达 MASkills 的 1.6–2.9 倍、wall-clock 1.3–1.8 倍（仅训练阶段，推理不变）。实验只覆盖两智能体顺序团队、两个问答基准与单一 critic，更大团队与非顺序通信未验证；且摘要称 LoCoMo 唯一未超过 MASkills 的类别是 open-domain、结论段却写成 multi-hop，这处不一致需要作者澄清。
article.figure_caption_zh: 每轮迭代：（1）对每个问题采样一组团队执行；（2）对比这些执行给智能体—技能对记 credit，并以结构化形式诊断失败；（3）跨问题聚合 credit 成技能编辑，仅保留不降低验证分的改动。

figure.caption: Each iteration (1) samples a group of team executions per question ( {sec:method-groups}), (2) credits agent--skill pairs by contrasting these executions and diagnoses failures in a structured form ( {sec:method-credit}), and (3) aggregates the credit across questions into skill edits, each kept only if it does not lower the validation score ( {sec:method-organization}-- {sec:method-evolution}). The example is from one training run on LoCoMo single-hop questions, in which Agent~1 retrieves evidence and Agent~2 answers. In iteration~1, a failure that surfaces in Agent~2's answer is traced to Agent~1's retrieval, and a new retrieval skill is induced. In iteration~3, this skill is credited as harmful in the shown group but helpful across the iteration's 16 groups, so it is refined rather than pruned. In Agent~1's search queries, {|} denotes OR.

email_papers.title: DeLoop: Repeated Actions as Self-Supervision for Long-Horizon Agents
email_papers.abstract: Language-model agents that run long tasks often redo work they have already done: they re-issue a tool call they made earlier and get back exactly the same observation, a step that adds no new information. We identify this failure as a loop. Loops appear natively in Qwen, Llama, and Gemini agents and become far more common once the agent's history is compressed to fit its context window. To reduce these loops, we propose DeLoop, a self-supervised training method. DeLoop builds on a simple observation: the agent's own rollout can provide the supervision needed to learn from its loops. We use a looping action as a negative example and the first later non-looping action in the same rollout as a positive example. DeLoop learns from these pairs through direct preference optimization and does not require task rewards, gold answers, or LLM judges. On CodeGym under compression, DeLoop reduces the share of Qwen3-8B tasks containing loops from 57.3% to 6.1%. It also uses about one third as many steps per task, with similar task success. On Qwen3-32B, DeLoop reduces loops and steps while raising task success from 37.7% to 44.8%.
email_papers.content:
DeLoop: Repeated Actions as Self-Supervision for Long-Horizon Agents
Tianle Chen
Pushkar Singh
Ketan Todi
Biswajit Paria
Qijia He
Wenqi Wang
Yuwen Tan
Jike Zhong
Sugato Basu
Deepti Ghadiyaram
Arjun Akula
Abstract
Language-model agents that run long tasks often redo work they have already done: they re-issue a tool call they made earlier and get back exactly the same observation, a step that adds no new information.
We identify this failure as a
loop
.
Loops appear natively in Qwen, Llama, and Gemini agents and become far more common once the agent’s history is compressed to fit its context window.
To reduce these loops, we propose
DeLoop
, a self-supervised training method.
DeLoop builds on a simple observation: the agent’s own rollout can provide the supervision needed to learn from its loops.
We use a looping action as a negative example and the first later non-looping action in the same rollout as a positive example.
DeLoop learns from these pairs through direct preference optimization and does not require task rewards, gold answers, or LLM judges.
On CodeGym under compression, DeLoop reduces the share of Qwen3-8B tasks containing loops from 57.3% to
6.1%
.
It also uses about one third as many steps per task, with similar task success.
On Qwen3-32B,
DeLoop
reduces loops and steps while raising task success from 37.7% to 44.8%. Code and data will be publicly available.
1
Google,
2
Boston University,
3
University of Washington,
4
University of Southern California,
5
Google DeepMind,
†
Project lead
Keywords:
LLM agents, long-horizon agents, agent memory, context compression, agent loops, repeated actions, preference optimization
Figure 1:
Training an agent on its own loops breaks the loop.
(Left)
A repeated search and the later action that marks the server as visited form a preference pair. DPO trains the agent to prefer the recovery.
(Right)
Qwen3-8B on CodeGym: DeLoop and the baseline summarize at 4,096 tokens; full history is the uncompressed reference.
1
Introduction
Language-model agents increasingly solve tasks over long interaction
horizons: they inspect repositories, execute commands, call tools, and act on
environment feedback across many steps
(
Yao et al., 2023
;
Yang et al., 2024a
;
Jimenez et al., 2024
;
Du et al., 2025
)
.
Yet they often redo work they have already done. The agent calls the same tool with the same arguments, receives the same observation, and then issues the same call again (
Figure
1
). Each repeated call is a
looping action
: it gets back an observation the agent already has and adds no new information. We formulate this failure as a
loop
.
The failure is already present even when the full, uncompressed history is available, but compression makes it worse. On CodeGym
(
Du et al., 2025
)
, the loop rate of Qwen3-8B
(
Yang et al., 2025
)
, the share of tasks with at least one loop, rises from
29.0
%
29.0\%
with the full history (no summarization) to
57.3%
under summarization, while looping actions per task increase
more than 3.5
×
\times
!
More importantly, in addition to wasted tool calls, we empirically observed that trajectories that enter a loop fail in all six Qwen3 and Gemini models we evaluate: on average,
59.5%
of looping runs fail, compared with 33.4% of loop-free runs (
Figure
2
).
Thus, context compression
makes looping more likely and increases the chances of task failure.
Recent work manages growing interaction histories through external memory
(
Packer et al., 2023
;
Fox et al., 2026
)
, hierarchical or summarized working context
(
Hu et al., 2025
;
Wu et al., 2025
;
Sun et al., 2026
)
, compact learned state
(
Zhou et al., 2025
)
, and learned context compression or management
(
Kang et al., 2026
;
Lu et al., 2026
;
Liu et al., 2025
)
.
These works study
what
history should an agent retain to continue acting well under a bounded context window. In contrast, we study a complementary question about how the agent’s policy uses its history after compression. That is,
when the history records an action, does the agent use that record to avoid repeating it?
We find that most agents do so only partly.
Another way to reduce looping is to improve the agent’s policy. Some methods address agent failures at inference time through reflection
(
Shinn et al., 2023
)
or early stopping
(
Lu et al., 2025
)
. Others train agents using demonstrations
(
Zeng et al., 2024
;
Chen et al., 2023
)
, search-based training data
(
Yuan et al., 2025
)
, or step-level supervision
(
Xiong et al., 2024
;
Chen and Yuille, 2026
;
Tang, 2026
)
. We instead ask:
can the failure itself provide a useful signal to improve agent’s policy?
Based on these observations, we propose
DeLoop
, a self-supervised training method. Our key observation is that loops can provide their own training signal. We note that a loop is a simple trajectory-level event that can be identified directly from the action-observation trace, without requiring post-hoc failure attribution
(
Barke et al., 2026
;
Hou et al., 2026
)
. Within a single rollout, we pair a looping action with the
first later non-looping
action that differs from it. The looping action provides a natural negative, while the later action provides a positive signal. Figure
1
illustrates this. These pairs are mined directly from the interaction, without gold answers, LLM judges, external rewards, or task-success labels. We train the policy on these pairs through direct preference optimization (DPO
Rafailov et al., 2023
).
On Qwen3-8B, DeLoop cuts the loop rate
9.4
×
\times
while lowering interaction cost, with similar task success. On Qwen3-32B, the self-mined pairs alone reduce loop rate from
38.5
%
38.5\%
to
12.9%
and raise task success from
37.7
%
37.7\%
to
44.8%
, while also lowering interaction cost.
Adding cross-domain pairs (DeLoop-Mix) raises Qwen3-8B task success from
25.1
%
25.1\%
to
30.3%
.
Our contributions are:
1.
Identifying loops in long-horizon agents:
we identify and characterize loops, a simple failure in which an agent repeats an earlier action and receives the same observation. We show that loops occur even with the full history, grow sharply under compression, and are associated with task failure.
2.
Mining loop actions as self-supervision:
we introduce a simple mining
method that turns discovered loops into preference pairs from the agent’s own
rollouts, with no external supervision.
3.
Reducing loops in long-horizon agents:
DeLoop reduces loops (57.3% to
6.1%
on Qwen3-8B) while lowering interaction cost. The gains also extend to larger models, where there is pronounced improvement in task success (45.1% to
52.3%
on Qwen3-14B and 37.7% to
44.8%
on Qwen3-32B).
2
Related work
Repeated actions in agents.
Repetition is a known failure of LLM agents. AgentBench found that agents
mainly exceed their task limit because they repeat earlier
content
(
Liu et al., 2024
)
. MAST also lists step repetition as a failure
mode of multi-agent systems
(
Cemri et al., 2025
)
, and RAGEN shows that multi-turn
RL can trap agents in repetitive reasoning
(
Wang et al., 2025b
)
. Closest to our
setting,
Min et al. (2026)
find that repeated context compression increases
repeated exploration and improve the compression prompt to reduce it; we keep
the compressor fixed and change the policy. IAL-Scan finds code paths that can
run without bound
(
Hou et al., 2026
)
, and other work locates agent
failures in execution traces
(
Deshpande et al., 2025
;
Barke et al., 2026
;
Yeh et al., 2026
;
Liu et al., 2026
;
Zhang et al., 2025
)
.
At inference time, agents can reflect, stop early, or escalate to a stronger
model
(
Shinn et al., 2023
;
Lu et al., 2025
;
He et al., 2026
)
. OpenHands flags an agent as “stuck”
when the same action returns the same observation four times in a
row
(
Wang et al., 2025a
)
. These methods do not change the agent policy. Even with a
blocker that refuses repeated calls and returns their earlier result, Qwen3-8B
on CodeGym still proposes an already executed call in 71.3% of tasks, as often
as without the blocker (69.8%); DeLoop lowers this to 13.6%
(Appendix
J.2
). We define a loop as a repeated tool call
that returns the same observation. Loops persist even with summaries designed
to keep past actions (Section
3.3
), so we train the agent
policy itself to break the loop.
Context management.
Long-horizon agents need to fit their history into a limited context. Common context management methods
store the history in external memory or searchable logs
(
Packer et al., 2023
;
Fox et al., 2026
;
Wang et al., 2026b
)
,
summarize older interactions
(
Hu et al., 2025
;
Wu et al., 2025
;
Sun et al., 2026
;
Su et al., 2026
)
,
keep a compact learned state
(
Zhou et al., 2025
)
, learn what to
keep
(
Kang et al., 2026
;
Lu et al., 2026
;
Liu et al., 2025
)
, or validate their
summaries
(
Chen et al., 2026
)
. However, removing plans from the context sharply hurts
performance
(
Mehta and Datta, 2026
)
. These methods decide
what
history to keep. We instead ask whether the agent uses the kept history to avoid repeating actions.
Learning from agent trajectories.
Most methods that train agents on trajectories need an external signal to
pick the better action. Agent tuning uses filtered or teacher-generated
trajectories
(
Zeng et al., 2024
;
Chen et al., 2023
;
Fu et al., 2025
)
, or successful attempts and
outcome feedback
(
Zelikman et al., 2022
;
Yang et al., 2024b
;
Guo et al., 2025
;
Le et al., 2026
;
Wang et al., 2024
;
Jung et al., 2025
)
. ETO and
Agentic-DPO take the better action from experts
(
Song et al., 2024
;
Chen and Yuille, 2026
)
.
Step-DPO, IPR, and ToolGraph use step-level labels or
rewards
(
Lai et al., 2024
;
Xiong et al., 2024
;
Tang, 2026
)
. Agent-R and Agent Q use tree
search guided by rewards or critiques
(
Yuan et al., 2025
;
Putta et al., 2024
)
, and SCoRe
trains self-correction with online RL
(
Kumar et al., 2025
)
. DeLoop instead
takes the better action from the agent’s own later recovery in the same
rollout and trains with DPO
(
Rafailov et al., 2023
)
. Its only label is the exact-repeat
rule of Section
3.1
, so it needs no rewards, expert actions,
or step labels. Like hindsight experience replay
(
Andrychowicz et al., 2017
)
, it also
learns from failed rollouts.
Penalizing repetition.
Repetition can also be penalized directly. RLTR adds a penalty on redundant
tool calls to its reward
(
Li et al., 2025
)
. In text generation, penalized
sampling
(
Keskar et al., 2019
)
, unlikelihood training
(
Welleck et al., 2020
)
,
and DITTO
(
Xu et al., 2022
)
reduce repeated tokens and sentences. These
penalties mark what to avoid; DeLoop also supplies the agent’s own alternative
action. Using our loop flag as a per-step penalty in online RL (GRPO) lowers the
Qwen3-8B loop rate on CodeGym from 57.3% to 15.0%, against 6.1% for DeLoop
(Section
5.3
).
3
Loops in Long-Horizon Agents
3.1
Defining a Loop
A loop occurs when the agent repeats a previous tool call with identical
arguments and receives the same observation. Thus, that step adds no new
information.
For example, consider an agent counting clusters of online servers on a grid.
The agent has tools to find unvisited servers and mark them as visited.
In one rollout, it issues the same search three times without marking the
returned server. Because that server remains unmarked, each call returns
the same coordinates. The latter two calls therefore add no new information.
This rollout comes from a Qwen3-8B agent on CodeGym
(
Du et al., 2025
)
,
where agents solve tasks through sequences of tool calls.
Appendix
B
shows the rollout excerpt.
We detect such repetitions by comparing each tool call and its observation
with earlier steps.

We then label any run containing at least one looping action as a

3.2
Loops Are Costly
Each looping action consumes tokens and a tool execution without yielding
a new observation. Under a fixed interaction budget, these repeated calls leave fewer
opportunities to take actions that could advance the task.
We compare looping and loop-free Qwen3-8B runs on CodeGym under
summarization at 4,096 tokens. Both groups include successful and failed runs.
Looping runs contain

They execute

Their interaction transcripts also contain

The same pattern holds for all six models in the cost comparison

Within each model’s compressed setting, looping runs are also more likely

The gap appears in all six Qwen3 and Gemini models: Qwen3-8B fails

Gemini 3.1 Pro shows a wider gap:
48%
against 12%.
A loop thus marks a run that is more likely to fail and has a higher
execution cost.
3.3
Compression Makes Loops More Common
An agent’s interaction history records what it has already done.
To keep long rollouts within a context budget, the agent summarizes earlier
interactions (Appendix
D
). We examine whether this compression
makes the agent more likely to repeat completed actions.
On CodeGym, Qwen3-8B loops in 29.0% of runs with the full history.
Summarization at 4,096 tokens raises the loop rate to
57.3%
.
Lowering the threshold to 2,048 tokens raises it further to
64.7%
(Figure
3
a).
The same pattern appears in all three Gemini models that we run with and without compression
(Figure
3
b). We compare CodeGym runs with the full
history against the subset of summarization runs in which compression fires.
Gemini 3.1 Pro loops least with the full history yet shows the largest
increase,
2.9
×
\times
.
To investigate this increase, we ask whether removing a completed action’s
record makes the agent more likely to repeat it.
We reconstruct 300 histories from 253 CodeGym tasks after compression.
Each ends just before Qwen3-8B chooses its next action.
One version of each history keeps the most recent completed tool call and
its observation. The other removes this record.
We sample the next action eight times from each version.
The agent repeats that call in 3.3% of samples with the record present
and
48.8%
with it removed
(Appendix
F
).
The record therefore helps the agent avoid an immediate repeat. This explains
why compression causes more loops. However, over a whole episode, keeping the
record is not enough: Qwen3-8B still loops in 29.0% of runs with the full
history. Under compression, a quarter of runs (25.2%) repeat a call
that is still in the context word for word (Appendix
J.1
).
Better context management does not close this gap. Summaries that keep an
explicit record of past actions, such as a trace of every executed call or a
ledger of tried actions, still loop in 52.0% to 62.7% of runs, close to
standard summarization at 57.3% (Appendix Table
4
). The
compressors ACON
(
Kang et al., 2026
)
and LLMLingua-2
(
Pan et al., 2024
)
lower the
loop rate to 46.3% and 46.7%, still well above the 29.0% with the full
history. The agent often fails to use a record it has, so we train the policy
itself (Section
4
). This complements better compression:
DeLoop-Mix lowers the loop rate under every memory policy we test
(Section
6.1
).

5.1
Experimental Setup
Benchmarks and models.
CodeGym
(
Du et al., 2025
)
is our primary benchmark for both mining
and evaluation: its tasks require many act–observe rounds, so the history
grows until compression fires. We also evaluate on four further agent
environments: ALFWorld
(
Shridhar et al., 2021
)
, Open-AgentRL
(
Wang et al., 2026a
)
,
AppWorld
(
Trivedi et al., 2024
)
, and ScienceWorld
(
Wang et al., 2022
)
.
Terminal-Bench
(
Merrill et al., 2026
)
and BrowseComp-Plus
(
Chen et al., 2025
)
provide further evaluations in their native agent harnesses
(Section
6.3
). Our main agent is Qwen3-8B, and we
repeat the CodeGym study with Qwen3-14B and Qwen3-32B
(
Yang et al., 2025
)
.
Training variants.
DeLoop trains on self-mined CodeGym pairs (Section
4.2
).
We also evaluate
DeLoop-Mix
, a variant trained with additional
cross-domain pairs (Section
5.4
). Its training data include
pairs mined from Terminal-Bench rollouts.
Evaluation protocol and metrics.
In our standard
compressed setting, the agent summarizes its history whenever it exceeds
4,096 tokens; the same model writes the summary and continues from it. Unless
noted otherwise, each policy in the main CodeGym comparison acts in this
setting on 300 held-out tasks, and the full-history agent serves as the
uncompressed reference. We
report four metrics: the loop rate (Section
3
), task
success, steps per task, and estimated tokens per task
(Appendix
A
).
Baselines.
Training-free context methods change what the agent
keeps from its history, including retrieval memory, ACON
(
Kang et al., 2026
)
, and
LLMLingua-2
(
Pan et al., 2024
)
. Training-free inference-time controls act during
inference, including an exact duplicate blocker and
Reflexion
(
Shinn et al., 2023
)
. Trained baselines learn from task outcomes, solved
trajectories, or gold actions, and distillation SFT on full-history traces
is, like DeLoop, label-free. We do not run GRPO on task success: its reward
arrives only once per episode, and even a per-step gold-action reward leaves
only 2.7% of GRPO groups informative (Appendix
G.10
).
The full battery is in Appendix
Tables
4
and
18
.
