6.1
Generalization Across Compression Settings and Memory Policies
We first evaluate
our Qwen3-8B DeLoop policy on CodeGym under five context settings, from
the full history to summarization at 2,048 tokens and truncation at 4,096
tokens. The loop rate falls in every setting, remaining between 4.7% and
12.8% while the untrained baseline reaches 65.3% (Figure
6
b).
Beyond the amount of retained history, we vary how it is represented.
We run DeLoop-Mix (
Section
5.4
) under seven
alternative memory policies, from retrieval memory and Claude-style
compaction to summaries augmented with an action ledger. The loop rate,
steps per task, and tokens per task fall under all seven
(Figure
6
c); with the action ledger,
the loop rate falls from 62.7% to
11.3%
and task success rises by
5.7
points.
6.2
The Improvement Extends to Other Agent Environments
The context comparisons above all use CodeGym. We next run DeLoop-Mix in
four further environments,
ALFWorld, Open-AgentRL,
AppWorld, and ScienceWorld, scored with
each environment’s native loop and success metrics (Table
3
). ALFWorld and Open-AgentRL
are evaluated on unseen games, disjoint from the training games behind their pairs
(Appendix
G.1
). Loops fall in all four, by up
to 32.8 points on AppWorld. Tokens per task fall wherever recorded, and task
success on Open-AgentRL rises from 43.9% to
45.5%
.
6.3
The Repair Transfers to New Benchmarks
Finally, we test DeLoop and DeLoop-Mix in native agent harnesses with different
tools and interactions. Terminal-Bench tests
terminal tasks, and BrowseComp-Plus tests web research.
On Terminal-Bench,
DeLoop cuts unproductive duplicate calls from 16.6 to
6.9
per task. On all 830 BrowseComp-Plus queries,
DeLoop-Mix lowers the loop rate from 22.4% to
1.2%
while matching the untrained model’s accuracy;
DeLoop, trained on CodeGym pairs alone, already lowers it to
6.4%. We also test zero-shot transfer from CodeGym to ALFWorld.
DeLoop on Qwen3-32B, trained only on CodeGym pairs, lowers the ALFWorld loop rate from
64.9% to
54.5%
and raises task success from
33.6% to
42.5%
.
7
Conclusion
Long-horizon agents that compress their history fall into loops: they
re-issue an action they already ran and receive the same result. On
CodeGym, summarizing the history raises the loop rate of Qwen3-8B from
29.0% to 57.3%, and better context management alone does
not remove it. Our key observation is that the loop labels itself: the
looping action is the rejected action, and the agent’s later loop-breaking
action is the chosen one. Trained on these self-mined pairs, DeLoop cuts the loop rate
9.4
×
\times
, from 57.3% to 6.1%, at about one third of the steps per task while
maintaining task success, and raises task success by 7.2 points at 14B and
7.1 points at 32B. An agent’s own loops become its supervision: break the
loop, keep the progress. We believe our work could help the community better
understand and reduce loops in long-horizon agents.

Evaluation Details
Evaluation runs.
Unless noted otherwise, every number comes from the 300 held-out CodeGym
tasks under summarization at 4,096 tokens. When a number averages several
evaluation runs, each run evaluates the same trained policy on the same tasks.
In
Table
1
, the full-history agent, the compressed baseline,
DeLoop, and DeLoop-Mix each average three runs, history truncation
averages two, and every other row is one run. In Table
2
and Figure
8
, DPO (DeLoop) and KTO average three runs, while IPO and
the looping-action penalty GRPO are one run each; the KTO tokens per task
come from one of its three runs. In Figure
5
, the Qwen3-14B
compressed baseline averages three runs and its DeLoop policy is one run; the
Qwen3-32B compressed baseline averages two runs and its DeLoop policy three. In
Figure
6
, the summarization cells at 8,192 and 2,048 tokens and
the seven memory policies are one run each. In Table
3
, each
cell is one run except ScienceWorld, the AppWorld DeLoop-Mix cells, and the
Open-AgentRL base, which average three.
Steps and tokens per task.
Steps per task count the actions the agent executes in a task. We estimate
tokens per task by counting the logged trajectory with the Qwen tokenizer; the
trajectory holds the task prompt, the observations, and the model’s outputs,
each counted once.
Open-AgentRL does not record
tokens, so Table
3
leaves its token cells empty.

Table
3
uses its own native repeat detector.

Appendix B
A Real Loop from CodeGym
The episode below is excerpted from a training rollout of the
compressed Qwen3-8B agent. The task is to count clusters of online servers on
a grid:
⋯
\cdots
13 earlier act–observe turns compressed
⋯
\cdots
FindUnvisitedOnlineServer(start_row=3, start_col=0)
→
\rightarrow
3,0
⋯
\cdots
further act–observe turns of real work
⋯
\cdots
FindUnvisitedOnlineServer(start_row=3, start_col=0)
→
\rightarrow
3,0
FindUnvisitedOnlineServer(start_row=3, start_col=0)
→
\rightarrow
3,0
later in the episode:
MarkVisited(row=3, col=0)
The agent runs the same search three times and gets
3,0
back every
time: nothing has marked that server as visited, so the search can only
return the same cell. The loop sits inside an otherwise productive episode,
and the action the search was waiting for,
MarkVisited
, appears later
in the same rollout. This is the structure DeLoop mines
(Section
4
): the repeated search is the looping action, and
MarkVisited
is the loop-breaking action.
Loop-breaking actions range from tool calls that make progress to final
answers. Another self-mined pair rejects a looping
FindUnvisitedLand()
call and chooses the agent’s later
Done(answer=1)
.

Environment and agent.
CodeGym
(
Du et al., 2025
)
turns static coding problems into
interactive tool-use environments. Each task exposes a function API with
Observe()
, task-specific actions, and
Done()
, and the
environment server scores the agent’s answer against the task’s gold answer.
Unless noted otherwise, the agent is Qwen3-8B with greedy decoding and a budget
of 30 rounds, where a round is one model turn and a step is one executed
action. Training and evaluation tasks share no task instance or code ID.
Appendix
A
lists the evaluation runs behind each result.
Loop detector.
The canonicalization
κ
\kappa
of Section
3.1
normalizes each
tool call for whitespace and argument order. A step is a looping action when
its canonical call appeared earlier in the episode and the environment returns
a byte-identical observation.
Practical agent frameworks use a similar rule: the OpenHands stuck detector
flags an agent when the same action returns the same observation four or
more times
(
Wang et al., 2025a
)
.
Compression.
When the estimated history exceeds the threshold, the harness keeps the system
prompt, the task, and the six most recent messages, and replaces everything in
between with a summary. The same served model writes the summary at
temperature zero, following an instruction that asks it to keep exact values,
environment returns, and executed actions. The standard threshold is 4,096
tokens; Figures
3
a and
6
b also use 8,192
and 2,048 tokens and hard truncation at 4,096 tokens. Every comparison holds
the model and the threshold fixed. Table

lists, for each
context method, the share of episodes in which compression fired.

These probes, which complement
Section
I.1
, ask how Qwen3-8B uses the
record of an action it has already run.
The record matters, its wording does not.
We take 150 looping points from training-side tasks that never appear in
evaluation and rebuild the context in five length-matched variants: (A) the
original action–observation block; (B) a one-line assertion of the action and
its result; (C) no record; (D) the assertion inside the summary; and (E) the
returned value without saying that the agent ran the action. We sample 16
completions per point at temperature 0.7 and measure re-issue, the share of
completions that repeat the looping action. For the compressed baseline,
deleting the record raises re-issue from 15.3% (A) to 43.3% (C), while
rewording it keeps re-issue close to the verbatim rate (17.6% for B, 16.5%
for D, 18.9% for E).
Training lowers re-issue in every condition.
On the same points (
Table
8
), DeLoop
re-issues 3.4% of the time with the verbatim record, 4.5% with the
assertion, and 15.0% with the record deleted, against 15.3%, 17.6%, and
43.3% for the compressed baseline.
The deletion effect holds on an unselected sample.
To avoid selecting on loops, we fix 300 decision points after compression from
253 tasks before any model call, stratified by whether the episode eventually
loops. At each point, the untrained policy chooses its next action with the
most recent completed action–observation record present or deleted (eight
samples each). It re-issues that action 3.3% of the time with the record
present and 48.8% with it deleted in this stratified sample; weighting the two
strata by their population shares gives a difference of 44.3 points.
F.1
Training Suppresses the Looping Action
Two probes at 250 loop points from tasks outside all preference-training data
ask what training changes (
Table
9
). First, we score the recorded loop-breaking action
against the looping action. The untrained policy ranks the loop-breaking
action higher at 49.6% of points, a coin flip; the two-source DeLoop-Mix variant (CodeGym,
ALFWorld, and Open-AgentRL pairs) raises this to 69.2%. Second, we freeze each loop prefix
and take one greedy action. Every trained policy re-issues the looping action
less often than the untrained one (15.6%): 6.0% for DeLoop, 5.2%
for DeLoop-Mix, and 5.6% for looping-action penalty GRPO. The share
that copies the recorded loop-breaking action stays between 18.8% and 20.8%
for every policy, while calls to
Done()
rise from 3.6% to between
12.4% and 26.0%. Training thus suppresses the looping action rather than
teaching one memorized recovery.

Mining.

flag looping actions with the detector of Section

G.7
Per-Step Selectivity
Not every repeated call is wasted: re-checking a state the agent has changed
returns a new observation. We split repeated calls into looping actions, which
get back the same observation, and informative repeats, which get back a new
one. Selectivity is the share of repeats that are informative, pooled over all
scored steps.
Training removes looping actions far more than informative repeats
(
Table
17
). DeLoop lowers looping actions from

I.1
The Policy Reacts to the Record of Its Own Executed Action
We probe the moments at which the agent loops. Unlike the training-side points
of

F

300 evaluation tasks: 150 looping points, one per task at its first loop. We add 80 retry points, at which an earlier call to the same

At each point we rebuild the context from the raw history in six conditions:
not yet executed
(the history before the action was first run);
proposed only
(the same history plus a note that the action was
proposed but not run, padded to the same length);
proposed +
observation
(the note also states what the action would return);
just
executed

lowers re-issue only from 68.4% to 51.7%, while a stated observation alone
lowers it to 20.6% and blocks retries that are worth making. The executed
record, together with what it returned, is what tells the policy whether an
action is finished or worth checking again.

article.headline: 把循环变监督：DeLoop 减少智能体重复动作
article.lede: DeLoop 把循环动作与其后的恢复动作组成偏好对，用 DPO 训练，在 CodeGym 上将 Qwen3-8B 循环率
article.problem: 长程智能体常重复已执行过的工具调用，拿回相同观察，浪费步骤与 token；历史压缩会显著放大这一问题。论文在 CodeGym 上报告，Qwen3-8B 的含循环任务比例从完整历史的 29.0% 升到 4096 token 摘要下的 57.3%，且含循环的运行更易失败。
article.method: DeLoop 把一次循环动作作为负例，把同一 rollout 中之后第一个非循环且不同的动作作为正例，直接用 DPO 训练策略。配对只依赖动作与观察的结构匹配，不需要任务奖励、标准答案或 LLM 评审；作者在 Qwen3-8B 上用 8,000 个自挖掘 CodeGym 对做 LoRA DPO。
article.results: 在 CodeGym 的 4096 token 摘要设置下，Qwen3-8B 的循环率从 57.3% 降至 6.1%（9.4×），每任务步数从 15.00 降至 4.67，token 约降 47%，任务成功率从 25.1% 变为 25.9%。Qwen3-14B 成功率从 45.1% 升至 52.3%，Qwen3-32B 从 37.7% 升至 44.8%，循环率分别从 42.9% 降至 12.3%、从 38.5% 降至 12.9%。加入跨域配对的 DeLoop-Mix 将 8B 成功率从 25.1% 提到 30.3%，在 BrowseComp-Plus 上把循环率从 22.4% 降至 1.2%，准确率与未训练模型相当。
article.why_it_matters: 它把失败轨迹本身变成无需外部标签的训练信号，为长程智能体的上下文压缩与策略修复提供互补思路，并直接减少重复工具调用与 token 消耗。
article.limitations: 循环被定义为同一工具调用返回字节级相同观察，近重复调用与更广泛的低效探索不计入；主要评测集中在 CodeGym，8B 上成功率仅从 25.1% 到 25.9%，且部分消融和跨环境结果仅单次运行。

email_papers.title: Know What You Don't Know: Agentic Data Synthesis by Evolving Generation Space for Closed-Loop Learning
email_papers.abstract: The continued improvement of large language models increasingly depends on synthetic experience, yet effective data synthesis for interactive agents requires not only executable and verifiable trajectories, but also interactions that provide learning value for the current task agent. Existing methods increasingly incorporate environment feedback, data validation, or learner failures, but still face a feedback-to-decision gap: observed weaknesses do not directly specify how future synthesis should change, or whether they can be represented by the current synthesis space. To address this gap, we propose EvoSyn, a learning-feedback-driven multi-agent framework that organizes synthesis around a revisable state specifying what interaction factors can be deliberately generated and where synthesis effort should be allocated. A role-specialized multi-agent system translates learner feedback into synthesis revisions, while a Designer allocates synthesis directions and a Planner grounds them into executable experience. This process enables within-space adaptation toward weak or under-covered regions and synthesis-space expansion that promotes newly discovered factors into explicit generation controls. Experiments on $τ^2$-Bench and CAR-Bench show that EvoSyn improves average task success by 13.3 points over the strongest synthesis baseline, while producing higher-quality and structurally broader synthetic experience and discovering controllable factors missed without learner feedback.

article.headline: EvoSyn：用学习者反馈重塑合成空间
article.lede: 把数据合成与智能体训练连成闭环，让学习者表现反过来改写合成空间，两个智能体基准上平均任务成功率提升13.3个百分点。
article.problem: 面向交互式智能体的合成数据不只要可执行、可验证、符合领域策略，还必须对当前任务智能体具有学习价值。已有方法会引入环境反馈、数据校验或学习者失败案例，但仍存在「反馈到决策的缺口」：观测到的弱点并不能直接说明未来的合成应当如何改变，也无法判断现有合成空间能否表示这种改变。
article.method: EvoSyn 把合成与学习组织成闭环 S_r→D_r→π_θr+1→F_r→S_r+1：每一轮用一个可修订的合成状态来连接学习者诊断与生成控制，并由角色分工的多个智能体分别承担其中的异质决策（作者称为决策抽象）。学习者反馈随后驱动两种动作——在现有合成空间内做自适应调整，或扩展合成空间本身，从而让合成过程与任务智能体在多轮中共同进化。
article.results: 在 τ²-Bench 与 CAR-Bench 上，EvoSyn 相比最强合成基线平均任务成功率提升 13.3 个百分点；为保证比较一致，所有合成方法的下游任务智能体均为 Qwen3-8B。附录的规模实验中，基座从 Qwen3-8B 扩到 14B、30B，平均成功率由 39.4% 升至 48.6% 和 57.1%，作者称仍有相当的后训练空间。论文材料未给出各基准分项的绝对数值，也未给出每一轮的具体增益。
article.why_it_matters: 它把「合成什么数据」从一次性设计变成随学习者状态演化的决策问题，为智能体后训练提供了一种可复用的闭环范式，而不只是堆更多可执行轨迹。
article.limitations: 评测只覆盖 τ²-Bench 与 CAR-Bench 两个智能体基准，合成侧使用的是 Opus 4.5 这类强闭源模型，闭环轮数与总采样成本在材料中未给出，方法在更弱合成模型下是否仍成立尚不清楚。13.3 个百分点是跨基准平均值，分项提升与方差未见报告，30B 基座上也仍留有较大提升空间。
article.figure_caption_zh: EvoSyn 总览：每一轮实例化一次「合成—学习」闭环，可修订的合成状态居中协调学习者诊断与生成控制，角色分工的智能体产出可验证经验，反馈则驱动空间内自适应或合成空间扩展，使合成与任务智能体共同进化。

figure.caption: Overview of {EvoSyn}. Each round instantiates a closed-loop synthesis--learning process in which a revisable synthesis state mediates learner diagnosis and generation control, role-specialized agents realize verified experience, and feedback drives within-space adaptation or synthesis-space expansion to co-evolve synthesis with task-agent learning.

email_papers.title: Agent Sociodrama: Social-Dynamics-Guided Persona Recasting for LLM Agent Teams
email_papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly deployed as teams, yet they fail in characteristically social ways: information holders stay silent, dominant speakers anchor groups on wrong answers, and norm violations go unsanctioned. We present Agent Sociodrama, a framework for modeling and validating evolving social dynamics in LLM agent teams. Under fixed personas, agents' emotional states and directed, asymmetric relationships are updated every round by a unified external LLM judge and shape their subsequent interactions. Across six LLM backbones and five social scenarios, we assess social fidelity through classical social-theory patterns and agreement with human judgments. The resulting trajectories exhibit structured social patterns and model-specific differences. We then introduce Trajectory-Guided Persona Recasting (TPR), which diagnoses group-dynamic failures from interaction transcripts and social trajectories and recasts agent personas before rerunning the task. Across four collaborative benchmarks, TPR improves performance from both heterogeneous and randomly initialized agent persona compositions, yielding up to 83.3%p of accuracy improvement over the initial casting. On representative distributed-information cooperation and mixed-motive bargaining tasks, we outperform SOTOPIA and AgentVerse in three of four comparisons, by up to 37.5%p in Pareto rate. These results show that validated social trajectories provide actionable signals for repairing LLM agent teams.

Abstract
Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly deployed as teams, yet they fail in characteristically social ways: information holders stay silent, dominant speakers anchor groups on wrong answers, and norm violations go unsanctioned.
We present Agent Sociodrama, a framework for modeling and validating evolving social dynamics in LLM agent teams.
Under fixed personas, agents’ emotional states and directed, asymmetric relationships are updated every round by a unified external LLM judge and shape their subsequent interactions.
Across six LLM backbones and five social scenarios, we assess social fidelity through classical social-theory patterns and agreement with human judgments.
The resulting trajectories exhibit structured social patterns and model-specific differences.
We then introduce Trajectory-Guided Persona Recasting (TPR), which diagnoses group-dynamic failures from interaction transcripts and social trajectories and recasts agent personas before rerunning the task.
Across four collaborative benchmarks, TPR improves performance from both heterogeneous and randomly initialized agent persona compositions, yielding up to 83.3%p of accuracy improvement over the initial casting.
On representative distributed-information cooperation and mixed-motive bargaining tasks, we outperform SOTOPIA and AgentVerse in three of four comparisons, by up to 37.5%p in Pareto rate.
These results show that validated social trajectories provide actionable signals for repairing LLM agent teams.

Corresponding authors.
1
Introduction
Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly deployed in teams
(
Wu et al., 2024
;
Hong et al., 2024
)
: they debate answers
(
Du et al., 2024
)
, pool distributed evidence, teach one another,
negotiate, and manage shared resources. Yet sustained multi-agent
interaction requires more than assigning each agent an initial role.
For a team to function as a social system over time, its members must
form, maintain, and revise relationships in ways that remain coherent
with the interaction. Existing agent systems often encode social
context through static role instructions or unstructured memory,
without an explicit and validated account of how directed relationships
evolve over time.
We take a different route. We argue that longitudinal role play requires treating a team not as a collection of fixed personas, but as a dynamic social system. A persona specifies who an agent is, but not how its relationships with others develop over time, including whom it comes to trust, avoid, align with, or oppose. These relationships must therefore be represented as evolving interaction states. The key challenge is not merely to model changing relations, but to ensure that those changes remain socially faithful over time.
Figure 1:
Motivation and overview of Agent Sociodrama.
Agent Sociodrama models multi-agent interaction through stable personas,
evolving emotions, and directed relationships.
We assess the social fidelity of these dynamics against
social-theory patterns and human judgments, and use social
trajectories to guide team composition optimization for better
collaboration.
To instantiate this idea, we propose Agent Sociodrama, a longitudinal
role-playing framework for LLM agent teams. Agent Sociodrama operationalizes
stable personas together with evolving emotional and relational states,
providing a structured account of how a team’s social configuration
develops over repeated interaction.
These dynamics also matter for task-oriented teams. A growing body of
evidence suggests that LLM teams often fail in ways that resemble
classic small-group pathologies rather than limits of individual model
capability: groups that collectively possess the information required
for a correct decision can still converge on an incorrect one
(
Pappu et al., 2026
;
Li et al., 2026
)
, while individually capable
agents can collectively deplete a shared resource until cooperation
collapses
(
Piatti et al., 2024
)
. These failures have a distinctly
social character. Over repeated interaction, overlooked members can
withdraw, early deference to dominant voices can harden into consensus,
and unchallenged violations can progressively erode cooperation. Yet
dominant approaches to improving multi-agent systems optimize prompts,
topologies, or workflows
(
Zhou et al., 2026
;
Zhang et al., 2025
)
, treating
the team as a black box and leaving the social mechanisms behind these
failures largely unexamined. Building on Agent Sociodrama’s explicit social
trajectories, we further introduce Trajectory-Guided Persona Recasting
(TPR), a casting controller that diagnoses team composition and
recasts personas to seek more effective task-oriented collaboration.
Our empirical study has two parts. First, we assess the social fidelity of Agent Sociodrama across six LLM drivers and five social scenarios, using a shared external LLM judge with human cross-validation. We test whether the resulting trajectories recover four established regularities of social interaction: structural balance
(
Heider, 1946
;
Cartwright & Harary, 1956
)
, reciprocity
(
Gouldner, 1960
)
, conflict-driven polarization
(
Krackhardt & Stern, 1988
)
, and divergent repair-versus-escalation dynamics
(
Gottman, 1994
;
Pruitt & Kim, 2004
)
. These analyses establish Agent Sociodrama as a socially faithful framework for longitudinal multi-agent role play. Second, across four collaborative task families, our controller converts evolving social states into persona recasting decisions that substantially improve team performance. These results demonstrate that socially faithful trajectory modeling can directly inform persona recasting and improve multi-agent collaboration.
Our contributions are:
•
A dynamic multi-agent role-playing framework for LLM teams.
Agent Sociodrama jointly models stable personas, evolving emotional states, and directed, asymmetric relational states, allowing multi-agent interaction to unfold as a sustained social process.
•
Cross-model validation of social fidelity.
Across six LLMs and five social scenarios, we validate
Agent Sociodrama against social theory and human evaluation, showing that its long-horizon relational dynamics are structured, interpretable, and socially coherent.
•
Trajectory-guided team composition optimization.
We use social trajectories to guide persona casting, making team chemistry directly controllable. Across four collaborative task families, our controller substantially improves team performance.

Social dynamics fidelity evaluation.
We evaluate how faithfully LLMs model emotional and relational dynamics across five scenarios spanning shared-goal coordination to open factional conflict. The scenarios draw on established paradigms in social psychology
(
Heider, 1946
;

;

(

(

, covering consensus under divergent risk preferences, contested resources, value conflict, mixed-motive bargaining, and factional opposition.
They include a hospital ethics review, inheritance dispute, adventurer-party quest, solar-farm negotiation, and demolition standoff. We evaluate six LLM backbones: GPT-4o, GPT-5-mini, Claude Sonnet 4.6, Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite, Grok 4.20, and DeepSeek V4-Flash, with all five agents in each run instantiated by the same backbone. A GPT-4o judge evaluates the emotional and relational trajectories from every run.
Each scenario–model condition comprises five independent nine-round episodes, yielding 150 team trajectories and 1,350 team-level interaction rounds.

Conclusion
We present Agent Sociodrama, a new framework for modeling and validating evolving social dynamics in LLM agents. We track directed, asymmetric relationships and emotional states, validating cross-model comparability under a unified judge, agreement with classical social theory, and statistical reliability. The casting controller then turns these trajectories into targeted interventions: using relational and emotional trajectories and transcripts, it identifies problematic agents and relationships and recasts their personas, matching or surpassing the strongest manual casting or published reference in collaborative tasks. These results show that social dynamics can serve not only as measurable properties of LLM teams, but also as actionable signals for improving their composition.

Appendix A
Limitations
Several limitations point to future work.
The fidelity evaluation relies on a single unified LLM judge and five designed scenarios; replicating the observed regularities with additional judges and structurally different scenarios would strengthen the external validity of the measurements.
The optimization experiments use 12 episodes per casting, which remains small relative to the variance of LLM interaction; we therefore report consistent directions across tasks, backbones, and initializations rather than per-cell significance claims.
Finally, casting is a coarse, episode-level intervention; the same measured trajectories could drive finer-grained repairs such as runtime mediation, targeted information routing, or norm enforcement, which we view as the natural next step for measurement-driven multi-agent optimization.

Appendix C
Fidelity Evaluation Protocol
The fidelity evaluation crosses five social scenarios with six
LLM drivers, yielding 30 scenario–model conditions.
Each condition includes five independent episodes, with five agents
interacting over nine rounds per episode.
The full design therefore comprises 150 team trajectories,
1,350 team-level interaction rounds, and 6,750 agent-round observations.

Appendix E

Tasks.
Tab.
5
summarizes the four collaborative tasks. Student Council, NASA Moon Survival, and Lost at Sea are information-integration tasks in which decisive knowledge is privately distributed across members; Solar-farm Negotiation is a mixed-motive task in which parties with private preferences must reach a feasible and Pareto-efficient agreement. Each task is played by four agents, Avery, Blake, Casey, and Drew. Private knowledge remains fixed under recasting.In the three information-integration tasks, each episode consists of an individual ranking before discussion, four discussion rounds, and a final individual ranking; the team answer aggregates the four final rankings with a Borda count. article.headline: 用社会动力学轨迹重铸LLM智能体团队角色
article.lede: Agent Sociodrama让情绪与有向关系逐轮演化，并据轨迹重选人格，团队准确率最高提升83.3个百分点。
article.problem: LLM智能体组队时常出现典型的社会性失败：掌握信息者保持沉默，强势发言者把团队锚定在错误答案上，规范违反也无人制裁。现有系统多以静态角色指令或无结构记忆来承载社会语境，缺少对指导性关系如何随时间演化的显式且可验证的刻画。
article.method: 框架为每个智能体保留固定人格，同时由统一的外部LLM评委每轮更新其情绪状态与有向、非对称关系，这些状态再影响后续交互。在此之上，轨迹引导的人格重铸（TPR）从对话记录与社会轨迹中诊断团队失败，重铸智能体人格后重跑任务，最多迭代三次。
article.results: 保真度评估覆盖6个LLM骨干与5个社会场景，共150条团队轨迹、1350个团队级交互轮次。从医院伦理审查到拆迁对峙，平均终局好感度由0.75降至0.23，E-I指数由-0.10变为-2.25，结构平衡由100.0%降至71.7%，修复率由58.5%降至18.9%。在四个协作基准上，TPR从异构与随机两种初始人格出发均带来提升，最高准确率提升83.3个百分点（GPT-5-mini在学生议会任务上由16.7%升至100.0%）；与SOTOPIA、AgentVerse的四项比较中三项占优，Pareto率最高提升37.5个百分点。
article.why_it_matters: 这表明团队“化学”不只是事后描述，而是可测量、可搜索的设计变量，社会轨迹能直接用于定位并修复智能体团队的协作失败。
article.limitations: 保真度评估只依赖单一统一LLM评委和五个设计场景，外部效度有待更多评委与结构不同的场景检验；优化实验每种人格配置仅跑12个episode，作者因此只报告跨任务、骨干与初始化的一致方向，而非逐格显著性，且人格重铸是episode级的粗粒度干预。

page_papers.title: Spectral-Spatial Interpretation
page_papers.abstract: Post-hoc image explanations usually show where a model looks using spatial heatmaps or indicate which channels matter using global channel scores. These separate views are limiting for multispectral data because channel relevance is often spatially localized and physically meaningful. We introduce Spectral-Spatial Interpretation (SSI), a full-grid attribution method over position-channel players (g,c). For each spatial position, SSI fixes the observed surrounding context, defines a conditional game over the channels at that position, and applies the Shapley value to this local game. The result is a full spectral-spatial attribution matrix rather than a single heatmap or a global channel ranking. SSI has a clear local interpretation. It satisfies Shapley fairness within each position, and aggregating its channel attributions exactly recovers the position-level contextual contrast obtained by replacing that position with the baseline. SSI also differs from context-averaged Owen-style hierarchical accounting, which uses the same position-channel grouping but averages over external spatial coalitions. On HLS Burn Scar, SSI outperforms an MC-Owen estimator across retained attribution metrics while using only about 6% of its evaluation budget. Across CUB-200, EuroSAT, and HLS Burn Scar under both per-channel mean and zero baselines, SSI achieves the best joint deletion and insertion AUC over dense, flat, and rank-1 baselines, yields the strongest spectral hit rates and channel deletion, and leads spatial localization on both annotated datasets. Code is available at https://github.com/AtheavenMa/Spectral-Spatial-Interpretation.

Introduction
Modern vision models increasingly operate on inputs with multiple physically
meaningful channels, from RGB fine-grained recognition to Sentinel-2 land-cover
classification and burn-scar mapping. Existing post-hoc explanations usually
answer
where
the model looks, but not
which spectral channels
support the prediction at each location. For these data, high attribution to near-infrared at a vegetation boundary or
to short-wave infrared within a burn scar reflects different physical evidence
from attribution to visible bands. An explanation should therefore identify
where the evidence lies, which channels support it, and how much each channel
contributes at each location.
Existing methods collapse this structure in one of two ways. Spatial
attribution methods such as Grad-CAM
(
Selvaraju et al., 2017
)
,
RISE
(
Petsiuk et al., 2018
)
, and Extremal
Perturbation
(
Fong et al., 2019

using mutual information, attention weights, or SHAP-style
scores
(
Lundberg and Lee, 2017
)
, averaging channel effects across space.

vector assumes a rank-1 structure,

2
Related Work
Post-hoc spatial attribution.
A large family of explanation methods produces spatial heatmaps indicating which image regions drive a prediction. Gradient-based approaches such as Integrated Gradients
(
Sundararajan et al., 2017
)
and Grad-CAM
(
Selvaraju et al., 2017
)
propagate target-class signals to pixels or activation maps. Perturbation-based approaches such as RISE
(
Petsiuk et al., 2018
)
and Extremal Perturbation
(
Fong et al., 2019
)
measure prediction changes under spatial masks.
These methods are effective for identifying where evidence lies, but their explanations either aggregate over channels or treat input elements independently. They therefore do not provide a principled decomposition of which spectral channels matter at each location.
Spectral and channel attribution.
A complementary line of work ranks spectral bands or channels using mutual information
(
Feng et al., 2014
)
, game-theoretic criteria
(
Bruce, 2013
)
, attention weights
(
Hu et al., 2018
;
Woo et al., 2018
)
, or SHAP-style attribution
(
Lundberg and Lee, 2017
)
. Such methods are useful for identifying globally important wavelengths, but they typically average channel relevance over space. This averaging can hide localized spectral evidence because a band may be unimportant on average yet decisive in a small region. SSI instead assigns attribution to each position-channel pair and preserves spatial variation in channel importance.
Joint spectral-spatial modeling.
Architectures such as 3D CNNs
(
Chen et al., 2016
)
, spectral-spatial
transformers
(
Dang et al., 2022
)
, and factorized architecture
search
(
Zhong et al., 2022
)
jointly exploit spectral and spatial
information but focus on prediction performance, and their internal
representations remain opaque.
Propagation-based explanations have been adapted for hyperspectral
classifiers
(
Nagasubramanian et al., 2018
)
, but remain architecture-specific.
SSI instead provides model-agnostic, game-theoretic attribution for
already-trained models.
Game-theoretic and hierarchical attribution.
Shapley values
(
Shapley, 1953
)
and SHAP-style methods
(
Lundberg and Lee, 2017
)
provide additive feature attributions but usually treat all interpretable units as flat players. This flat treatment does not reflect the natural position-channel hierarchy of multispectral images. The Shapley interaction index
(
Grabisch and Roubens, 1999
)
and its higher-order extensions
(
Sundararajan et al., 2020
;
Tsai et al., 2023
)
quantify synergies but do not exploit this two-level structure. Group-level Shapley methods
(
Jullum et al., 2021
)
treat each
predefined group as an atomic player and do not decompose contributions
within groups; methods addressing feature
dependence
(
Aas et al., 2022
)
estimate conditional expectations
rather than fixing observed context. SSI differs from both lines of work in its attribution units
and treatment of context.
Owen value.
The Owen value
(
Owen, 1977
)
, building on games with coalition structures
(
Aumann and Drèze, 1974
)
, respects a priori coalitions by allocating value across and within groups. SSI uses the same position-channel grouping but targets observed-context conditional attribution rather than context-averaged hierarchical accounting.

Conclusion
We introduced Spectral-Spatial Interpretation (SSI), which explains
predictions of multi-channel image models at the level of joint
position-channel players
(
g
,
c
)
(g,c)
. SSI fixes the observed surrounding context and allocates each
position’s contribution among its channels via the Shapley value, producing a
full attribution matrix whose channel aggregation exactly recovers the
position-level contextual contrast. Across CUB-200, EuroSAT, and HLS Burn
Scar, SSI improves joint faithfulness, spectral hit rates, and channel
deletion over dense, flat, and rank-1 baselines, and outperforms MC-Owen on
HLS Burn Scar with roughly
6
%
6\%
of its evaluation budget.
Although SSI’s estimation error grows only as
ln
⁡
C
\sqrt{\ln C}
and its
per-image cost grows only linearly in
C
C
(Appendix
B.4
), applying SSI to hyperspectral sensors
with hundreds of correlated bands may benefit from channel screening or
adaptive grouping to reduce spectral redundancy before local Shapley
allocation. Validating such extensions on operational hyperspectral
missions remains future work. SSI may also be useful for imaging spectroscopy data from sensors such as EnMAP, where spectral channels carry spatially localized physical information. The observed-context formulation may extend to other multi-channel imaging domains with localized physical meaning, including biomedical microscopy and industrial materials inspection.

[
Helber et al., 2019
]
contains 27,000 Sentinel-2 patches from 10 land-use/land-cover classes. We use the 13-band version, including visible RGB, red-edge, near-infrared, short-wave infrared, and atmospheric bands. We train a ResNet-18 classifier from scratch on all 13 bands.

C.3
Spectral Band Priors
The spectral hit-rate evaluation (§
4.3
) requires a set of
prior bands
for each class. These are channels whose reflectance is expected to be positively associated with the target-class decision. We select these priors from established spectral indices and physical reasoning rather than the attribution results themselves.
HLS Burn Scar.
The HLS Burn Scar dataset uses a six-band stack (Blue, Green, Red, Narrow NIR, SWIR
1
, SWIR
2
) derived from the Harmonized Landsat Sentinel-2 product
[
Claverie et al., 2018
]
. For the burn-scar class, we designate Red (band 2), SWIR
1
(band 4), and SWIR
2
(band 5) as prior bands. This selection follows directly from the Normalized Burn Ratio (NBR) and its variants, which are the standard spectral indices for burn severity mapping
[
Key and Benson, 2006
,
García and Caselles, 1991
]
. Burned surfaces exhibit elevated SWIR reflectance due to exposed soil, charcoal, and ash, and elevated red reflectance due to the loss of chlorophyll absorption
[
Trigg and Flasse, 2001
]
. These spectral signatures have been validated across decades of fire-mapping literature using Landsat TM/ETM+/OLI and Sentinel-2 MSI sensors. NIR is excluded from the positive prior because burn scars cause a sharp drop in NIR reflectance (loss of mesophyll scattering), making NIR
negatively
correlated with the burn-scar class.
EuroSAT.
EuroSAT provides 13-band Sentinel-2 imagery spanning the visible, red-edge, NIR, and SWIR spectral regions. We assign class-specific priors based on the physical reflectance properties of each land-cover type:
•
Vegetation classes
(AnnualCrop, Forest, HerbaceousVegetation, Pasture, PermanentCrop). We use the red-edge (B05–B07, 705–783 nm) and NIR (B08/B8A, 842/865 nm) bands as priors. Healthy vegetation produces strong NIR reflectance through mesophyll scattering and exhibits a steep red-edge transition driven by chlorophyll absorption
[
Clevers et al., 2002
,
Delegido et al., 2011
]
. These bands underpin NDVI, NDRE, and related vegetation indices that have been used operationally for crop monitoring and forest mapping for decades
[
Tucker, 1979
,
Rouse et al., 1974
]
.
•
Industrial.
The priors are the SWIR bands (B11, B12; 1610/2190 nm). Impervious surfaces such as concrete, asphalt, and metal roofing reflect strongly in the SWIR due to low moisture content and high mineral reflectance
[
Zha et al., 2003
,
Xu, 2008
]
.
•
Highway, Residential, River, SeaLake.
No positive prior is assigned. These classes are spectrally heterogeneous (Highway, Residential) or uniformly low-reflectance (water bodies), so no single band subset has a reliably positive association with the class decision.
In both datasets, we conservatively include only prior bands with a well-documented, physically grounded positive correlation with the target class. Classes without a clear positive spectral signature receive an empty prior set and are excluded from the hit-rate evaluation. This design ensures that the spectral validity metric tests whether the attribution method recovers known physical relationships, rather than fitting to arbitrary band rankings.

article.headline: 用局部 Shapley 值给出逐位置通道归因矩阵
article.lede: SSI 在每个空间位置固定观测上下文，只对该位置的通道做 Shapley 分配，输出完整的 (g,c) 归因矩阵。
article.problem: 现有的后验图像解释大多只回答「模型看哪里」：Grad-CAM、RISE 一类方法在通道上聚合，得到单张空间热图；而 SHAP、互信息一类通道归因又把通道重要性在空间上平均，给出全局波段排序。对多光谱数据这不够用，因为同一波段在一个区域可能起决定作用、在另一个区域却无关；把热图乘上全局通道向量，等于假设归因矩阵是秩 1 的，在鸟类羽毛或遥感场景中往往不成立。
article.method: SSI 把位置与通道的组合 (g,c) 当作玩家，对每个空间位置 g 固定其余位置的观测值作为上下文，只在 g 处的通道上定义一个条件博弈 w_g，再对这个小型博弈取标准 Shapley 值，得到全网格的 Φ(g,c)。论文证明了两条性质：在每个位置内部满足 Shapley 公平性（效率、对称、零玩家、可加性）；并且对通道求和恰好等于把整个位置替换为基线时的全上下文对比 Δ(g)。它与 Owen 值使用相同的位置—通道分组，但 Owen 要在外部空间联盟上取平均，SSI 只条件于实际观测到的上下文。
article.results: 在 CUB-200、EuroSAT 和 HLS Burn Scar 上，无论用逐通道均值基线还是零基线，SSI 的联合删除 AUC 和插入 AUC 都优于 dense（IG、DeepSHAP）、flat（KernelSHAP）和秩 1（RISE）基线。CUB-200 均值基线下插入 AUC 为 .7132，高于 RISE 的 .6886，而 RISE 用了 8,000 个空间掩码、SSI 为 2048 次前向；HLS Burn Scar 均值基线下联合删除 AUC 为 .1545（IG 为 .2160），对 MC-Owen 为 .155 对 .173，前向评估最多 4,480 次对 76,800 次，约 6% 预算。空间定位上 HLS Burn Scar Top-10% 覆盖的 mIoU 为 .389，DeepSHAP 为 .277、RISE 为 .191；ROAD 评测中 LeRF AUC .657、MoRF AUC .1143，在九种方法中最好。
article.why_it_matters: 对 Sentinel-2、HLS 这类波段带物理含义的影像，解释需要同时说明证据位于哪个区域、由哪些波段支撑，而 SSI 给出的正是这种可分解到位置—波段的归因，并且通道求和有明确的上下文对比含义。它也为「热图 × 全局波段向量」这一常见做法的不足提供了一个可检验的反例：秩 1 投影后删除 AUC 明显变差。
article.limitations: 条件博弈的语义依赖掩码基线的选择（逐通道均值或零），论文自己也承认这是所有扰动式归因的固有问题；Proposition 1 进一步表明，位置级上下文聚合性与全局效率无法同时保证，因此 SSI 不分配整个预测值。采样方面每格最多 K=10 次通道排列，作者指出对数百个相关波段的高光谱传感器可能需要先做通道筛选或自适应分组，这仍是未来工作；而「约 6%」只是前向次数口径下的比较，不是实测耗时，也不能与梯度法的反向传播成本直接对比。
article.figure_caption_zh: SSI 总览：对每个空间位置 g 固定观测到的周边上下文，把局部贡献分配给该位置的各通道，从而得到可用于空间与光谱解释的完整联合归因矩阵 Φ(g,c)。

figure.caption: {Overview of SSI.} For each spatial position \(g\), SSI fixes the observed surrounding context and allocates the local contribution among channels, producing a full joint attribution matrix \( (g,c)\) for spatial and spectral interpretation.

page_papers.title: Agent World Model in the Wild: Computer-Use Agent Environment Synthesis
page_papers.abstract: Agent learning is shifting from learning from human data toward learning through interaction with the world. However, scaling such learning directly in real-world computer systems is challenging and can introduce substantial security risks. We therefore propose Agent World Model in the Wild (WildAWM), a scalable pipeline for synthesizing controllable environments and tasks for training general computer-use agents (CUAs). Whereas existing approaches typically specialize in a single agent interaction interface, we construct executable environments that jointly support graphical user interfaces, model context protocol services, and command-line interfaces, allowing agents to flexibly combine visual interaction, tool use, and code execution. WildAWM is entirely powered by open-source models, demonstrating that high-quality computer-use environments can be generated without proprietary frontier models. Beyond environments, we address three recurring challenges in task synthesis: ensuring solvability, maintaining sufficient difficulty, and producing reliable verifiers, by introducing execution-based quality gates that combine heterogeneous agent rollouts, cross-judge consistency checks, and counterfactual probes of judgment robustness. The resulting pipeline synthesizes 341 long-horizon environment-task pairs that can require over 100 agent steps to solve and remain challenging even for frontier models, with GPT-6-Astra solving only 60% of them. We train two Qwen models of different sizes exclusively in these synthetic worlds. Both models achieve substantial gains across 8 out-of-distribution benchmarks spanning web, claw, and computer-use agents, demonstrating that learning in WildAWM's synthesized worlds generalizes broadly to unseen computer-use tasks. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/MSR-Orchard/WildAWM.
page_papers.content:
Abstract
Agent learning is shifting from learning from human data toward learning through interaction with the world.
However, scaling such learning directly in real-world computer systems is challenging and can introduce substantial security risks.

Introduction
Large language model (LLM) powered agents are shifting from learning from humans to learning from the world
(
Silver & Sutton, 2025
)
. Early agents learned from human data, which are expensive to collect and limited by demonstrator’s ability. Recent agents instead gain much of their capability through reinforcement learning (RL) in executable environments
(
Team et al., 2026
;
Zeng et al., 2026
;
Xu et al., 2026
)
, making environment supply a key bottleneck.
However, training directly in the real world is costly and risky: states are hard to reset, online services change over time, and exploratory actions may have unintended consequences.

Manually built environments restore control and verifiability
(
Yao et al., 2024
;
Zhou et al., 2024
;
Xie et al., 2024
)
, but remain expensive and hard to scale.
Synthetic environments and tasks offer a path to controllable, large-scale online RL.
Computer-Use Agents (CUAs) represent a broad setting for environment synthesis, as they operate across applications, websites, and local files on a personal computer.
A single task may be completed through graphical user interface (GUI) interaction, command-line interface (CLI) operations, or calls to model context protocol (MCP) servers, making interface selection and coordination an important capability.
Existing synthesis pipelines often target individual interaction modes, including browser use
(
Zhou, 2026
;
Wu et al., 2026
)
, tool calling
(
Du et al., 2026
;
Wang et al., 2026d
)
, and terminal workflows
(
Li et al., 2026
;
Zhu et al., 2026
)
.
Prior CUA work, however, often focuses primarily on GUI interaction
(
Aggarwal et al., 2026
;
Wang et al., 2026a
)
.
In this paper, we adopt a broader view of computer use spanning common interfaces on a personal computer, since real computer-use tasks are defined by what can be accomplished rather than by a single interaction modality.
Synthesizing environments and tasks for this broader CUA setting introduces challenges beyond prior synthesis work. Existing approaches often synthesize visually simplified applications and build each application as an isolated environment.
In contrast, realistic computer use spans a connected digital workspace in which websites, applications, MCP services, and local files coexist within an executable personal computer environment.
Meanwhile, synthesized tasks should be
solvable
under the synthesized environment state, sufficiently
challenging
to provide useful learning signals, and paired with
reliable
verifiers to distinguish successful completion from incorrect outcomes, all without relying on simplistic assumptions such as “a frontier model is necessarily correct.”

article.headline: 用编码智能体合成电脑使用环境与可验证任务
article.lede: 论文提出两阶段合成流水线，自动生成带 GUI、MCP、CLI 接口的电脑环境与跨接口任务，并用五道质量门筛选。
article.problem: 智能体训练的重心正从「学习人类数据」转向「在环境中交互学习」，但环境供给成了瓶颈：在真实电脑系统里做强化学习成本高、状态难重置、线上服务还会变化，探索性操作可能带来安全后果。手工搭建环境虽可控可验证，却昂贵且难以规模化。已有的合成流水线多针对单一交互方式（浏览器、工具调用、终端），且常把每个应用做成相互隔离的简化环境，与真实电脑使用中网站、应用、MCP 服务与本地文件共存的形态不符。
article.method: 方法分两个阶段。第一阶段是世界合成：用编码智能体构造由人物设定驱动、跨越多个「天」的环境状态，这些状态同时暴露 GUI、MCP 与 CLI 三类接口，形成可执行的个人电脑工作区。第二阶段是跨接口任务合成：围绕可解性、难度与验证器可靠性设计五道质量门来生成任务，其中包含回放确定性检查——从第 N-1 天的同一状态重放 delta.sh 两次，两个世界必须产生完全相同的内容哈希。最终产出 {任务, 环境, 验证器} 三元组用于训练通用电脑使用智能体。
article.results: 论文报告合成了 341 个跨接口（XAI）任务。主结果表中平均分为 53.42，并标出 +10.58 的平均提升；表中各方法分数从 21.73 到 80.77 不等。作者强调的发现之一是「广泛的分布外泛化」。至于合成了多少个环境、训练与合成各花费多少算力，论文未给出具体数字。
article.why_it_matters: 如果环境与验证器能自动合成，强化学习所需的环境供给就有望从手工搭建转为规模化生成，从而绕开在真实电脑系统上训练的成本与安全风险。
article.limitations: 目前公开的规模只有 341 个任务，相对真实电脑使用场景仍偏小；五道质量门中的回放确定性仅以内容哈希一致作为判据，能否代表任务语义上的确定性存疑，验证器可靠性也仍依赖自动筛选而非人工审核。此外，材料中未给出从合成环境到真实系统的迁移证据，也没有与真实世界训练的成本对比，具体环境数量与算力开销论文未给出具体数字。
article.figure_caption_zh: 合成流水线分两步：先用编码智能体构建人物驱动、跨多天、同时提供 GUI、MCP 与 CLI 接口的电脑环境状态，再经五道质量门生成跨接口任务，输出可供训练通用电脑使用智能体的 {任务, 环境, 验证器} 三元组。

figure.caption: Overview of . The synthesis pipeline includes two stages: (1) {World Synthesis}, where we use the coding agent to construct persona-driven, multi-day world states for computer environments that expose GUI, MCP, and CLI interfaces. (2) {XAI Task Synthesis}, where we generate cross-interface tasks through 5 designed quality gates for task solvability, difficulty, and verifier reliability. The synthesized $ \{ {task}, {environment}, {verifier}\}$ triplet enables training general CUA.

page_papers.title: Sage-A1.5: From Long-Horizon Execution to Scientific Exploration with Capability Composition
page_papers.abstract: In this report, we introduce Sage-A1.5, a 35B Mixture-of-Experts agentic model that builds on A1 to advance long-horizon problem solving through adaptive capability composition. Compared with A1, Sage-A1.5 learns not only to solve individual tasks, but also to organize work and revise its approach during execution. Sage-A1.5 highlights three improvements: agentic orchestration, verification, and open scientific discovery. First, agentic orchestration extends single-agent execution through task delegation and parallel collaboration among subagents with isolated contexts, enabling complex tasks to be decomposed and addressed concurrently and supporting efficient execution while reducing interference across concurrent subagents. Second, agentic verification strengthens long-horizon reliability through progress checking, evidence validation, and reflective strategy revision, allowing the agent to recognize unproductive search paths and pursue alternative approaches. Third, open scientific discovery extends agentic capabilities beyond answering predefined questions to conducting exploratory research, connecting scientific inquiry with interactive analysis and inspectable research artifacts. We showcase these capabilities through complicated agentic tasks and multidisciplinary scientific applications. Besides, we hope Sage-A1.5 provides the community with an accessible foundation for open scientific discovery, offering a practical path from long-horizon task execution to collaborative, verifiable, and inspectable scientific exploration.

Sage-A1.5: From Long-Horizon Execution to Scientific Exploration with Capability Composition
Sage-A1.5 Team, Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Laboratory
Abstract
In this report, we introduce Sage-A1.5, a 35B Mixture-of-Experts agentic model that builds on A1 to advance long-horizon problem solving through adaptive capability composition. Compared with A1, Sage-A1.5 learns not only to solve individual tasks, but also to organize work and revise its approach during execution. Sage-A1.5 highlights three improvements: agentic orchestration, verification, and open scientific discovery. First, agentic orchestration extends single-agent execution through task delegation and parallel collaboration among subagents with isolated contexts, enabling complex tasks to be decomposed and addressed concurrently and supporting efficient execution while reducing interference across concurrent subagents. Second, agentic verification strengthens long-horizon reliability through progress checking, evidence validation, and reflective strategy revision, allowing the agent to recognize unproductive search paths and pursue alternative approaches. Third, open scientific discovery extends agentic capabilities beyond answering predefined questions to conducting exploratory research, connecting scientific inquiry with interactive analysis and inspectable research artifacts. We showcase these capabilities through complicated agentic tasks and multidisciplinary scientific applications. Besides, we hope Sage-A1.5 provides the community with an accessible foundation for open scientific discovery, offering a practical path from long-horizon task execution to collaborative, verifiable, and inspectable scientific exploration.
Homepage
Token-plan
Model
Figure 1
:
Benchmark performance of Sage-A1.5.
Contents
1
Introduction
In our earlier work, we introduced Agents-A1
[
1
]
, a 35B Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) agent model that improves long-horizon task performance by scaling the agent horizon rather than model parameters. We built a knowledge–action infrastructure
[
2
]
that connects external knowledge, tool calls, observations, and verification feedback, producing training trajectories with an average length of 45K tokens. Agents-A1
[
1
]
showed strong performance in multi-step search, scientific reasoning, instruction following, and tool use, matching or exceeding trillion-parameter models on several benchmarks. These results established a practical path toward capable long-horizon agents at a smaller model scale.
Recent progress
[
3
,
4
,
5
,
2
]
demonstrates that strong domain skills alone are not enough for complicated tasks. Software engineering, machine learning optimization, and scientific research often require agentic model to manage related subtasks, compare different approaches, and revise decisions as new evidence becomes available. A single agentic model working step by step may struggle with a growing context, slow exploration, and errors that affect later decisions. Longer execution also does not always lead to better results: an agent may repeat unproductive searches, build on unsupported assumptions, or accept a conclusion before checking all the evidence. Further progress therefore requires not only stronger intrinsic agentic capabilities and broader skills, but also better ways to organize agent work and check progress.
Task delegation, parallel collaboration, evidence review, and strategy revision should become learned model capabilities rather than depend only on fixed rules in an external framework.
To address these challenges, we introduce Sage-A1.5, a 35B MoE agent model built on Agents-A1, with two key capabilities:
Agentic Orchestration
and
Agentic Verification
.
1)
Agentic Orchestration allows the model to decide how to divide work, delegate subtasks to parallel subagents with separate contexts, and combine their findings toward a shared goal.
2)
Agentic Verification allows the model to recognize when progress has stalled or an important conclusion needs checking, review the available evidence and assumptions, and adjust its next actions. At inference time, this verification takes place within the model’s own reasoning and tool-use process, without an online supervisor or a separate verification tool. These capabilities offer the community a scalable technical pathway for translating model capabilities into agentic capabilities. As shown in Fig.
1
, despite having only 35B parameters, Sage-A1.5 outperforms the substantially larger Kimi-K3
[
4
]
, GLM-5.3
[
6
]
, and GPT-5.6-sol
[
5
]
on FrontierScience-Olympiad
[
7
]
, CMT
[
8
]
, PinchBench
[
9
]
, and IFBench
[
10
]
, while remaining competitive with them on SWE-Bench Pro
[
11
]
and BrowseComp
[
12
]
.
Moreover, Sage-A1.5 matches or surpasses the equally sized Agents-A1
[
1
]
and Ornith-1.5
[
13
]
on all twelve benchmarks.
Our contributions include the following three aspects:
•
We develop Adaptive Agentic Execution, integrating
Agentic Orchestration
and
Agentic Verification
into Sage-A1.5’s execution policy for autonomous coordination of parallel subtasks and evidence-driven self-correction throughout long-horizon problem solving.
•
We build a unified training pipeline that combines multi-domain supervised fine-tuning with mixed-reward reinforcement learning, fusing capabilities across domains, reasoning modes, and agent harnesses into a single agentic model.
•
We demonstrate Sage-A1.5’s potential for agentic scientific discovery through broad benchmark evaluations and scientific case studies, highlighting a shift from isolated task solving toward long-horizon scientific research.
2
Method
Figure 2
:
Overview of the three-stage training pipeline of Sage-A1.5. First, the model is trained on diverse domain data, including coding, long-context reasoning, deep research, scientific reasoning, and co-working, utilizing environment construction, trajectory selection, staged supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning to build multi-domain teachers. Then, these teachers undergo unified outcome-process post-training to produce the final unified model, which features an agent orchestration for collaborative task solving, iterative agentic verification for reasoning reliability, and local deployment for ensuring data privacy, access control, and offline support.
2.1
Adaptive Agentic Execution: From Capability Coverage to Capability Composition
Domain-specific training expands capability coverage—the range of domains and tasks an agent can address. In Sage-A1.5, we extend agent capability development along a second dimension,
capability composition
: how problem-solving capabilities are organized, coordinated, and adapted during execution. This dimension concerns execution structure across task domains. We develop it through Agentic Orchestration and Agentic Verification (Fig.
3
). Agentic Orchestration determines how work is decomposed, delegated, and integrated across agent executions. Agentic Verification determines when to reassess intermediate judgments and exploration strategies, using the findings to revise subsequent actions. As a result, these capabilities make execution organization and feedback-driven adjustment explicit targets of model training alongside domain-specific problem solving.
Figure 3
:
Two complementary dimensions of agent capability. Capability coverage spans task domains, while capability composition concerns how problem-solving capabilities are organized and adapted during execution. Agentic Orchestration coordinates parallel work and integrates results; Agentic Verification reassesses intermediate responses using available evidence and adjusts subsequent actions.
2.1.1
Agentic Orchestration
We propose
Agentic Orchestration
, a foundational capability of Sage-A1.5 for structuring, allocating, and coordinating computation during task execution. The key insight is to make how execution is organized an explicit target of model training:
learning what work to pursue and how to combine the results complements learning to solve individual tasks.
Capability Definition and Composition Patterns.
Agentic Orchestration is the model’s ability to organize multiple agent executions around a shared objective. Its policy determines whether and how to decompose work, which subtasks to delegate, what context to provide, and how to coordinate dependencies and integrate results. The model adapts subsequent work to returned evidence, connecting local execution to the overall task. We distinguish two complementary patterns of parallel agent execution:
•
Exploratory Composition.
The model assigns multiple agents different hypotheses or solution approaches to the same question. Their outputs provide alternative candidates and supporting evidence, which the main agent compares to narrow the investigation and decide which directions to pursue. For example, agents may explore different system architectures against the same requirements, returning candidate designs for comparison.
•
Constructive Composition.
The model decomposes an overall task into complementary subproblems and assigns them to agents for parallel work. Each output contributes a distinct part of the solution; the main agent integrates these parts, coordinating dependencies and checking coverage and consistency. For example, agents may develop the data, interface, and deployment components of one system design, which must fit together to meet the overall requirements.

Trajectory Collection and Role-Specific Supervision.
Teacher model runs within the orchestration harness with role-specific prompts, tools, and execution budgets. It chooses when to investigate directly, delegate, and follow up on returned evidence. We record the complete executions and treat the main-agent trajectory and each subagent trajectory as independent agent samples.
Main-agent samples teach task decomposition, delegation, use of feedback, and synthesis; subagent samples teach independent investigation, evidence organization, and structured reporting. This supervision complements domain expertise with the ability to structure, allocate, and coordinate computation during agentic execution.
2.1.2
Agentic Verification
In long-horizon research tasks, agents must gradually build chains of evidence through multiple rounds of retrieval and reasoning. When an exploration path repeatedly fails to yield useful information, a model may continue searching around the same hypothesis or use unverified assumptions as premises for subsequent reasoning, leading to ineffective exploration and accumulating errors. To address this problem, we propose
Agentic Verification
, which enables the model to adaptively recognize when verification is needed, examine existing evidence and exploration strategies within its own reasoning, and adjust subsequent actions accordingly. When progress stalls or an important intermediate conclusion is reached, the model reviews facts confirmed by evidence, examines earlier judgments for unsupported inferences, identifies unresolved information gaps, and determines which exploration paths have proved ineffective and how to proceed. The central idea is to make verification a learned capability of the model itself:
the model adaptively determines when to verify, what to verify, and how to continue based on the findings, rather than having verification triggered and executed by an external harness according to predefined rules.
This mechanism enables the model to proactively revise its judgments, gather additional evidence, or change its search direction, improving its ability to self-correct during long-horizon tasks.
To train this capability, we construct complete research trajectories containing intermediate reflections and the actions that follow them. During data construction, an execution model conducts research through live search and webpage reading, while a supervisor model examines the exploration process and introduces verification at points involving repetitive searches, sustained lack of progress, or key conclusions requiring confirmation. Each verification relies only on the evidence available at that point, distinguishes confirmed facts from unverified hypotheses, and proposes a concrete direction for further investigation. The execution model then continues exploring based on the verification findings, producing coherent training examples that connect problem recognition, evidence assessment, and action adjustment. After data cleaning and format normalization, external supervision prompts and control messages are removed, and the reflections are incorporated directly into the model’s reasoning text. This allows the model to learn when to verify, what to examine, and how verification should inform subsequent actions. External supervision is used only to construct training data; at inference time, the model performs this process independently.
Note that
we also introduce a conditioning marker during training to enable the capability on demand: for models trained in this way, adding
Verification protocol:enabled
to the system prompt activates Agentic Verification. Once enabled, the model autonomously performs verification within its regular reasoning and tool-use process, without requiring an additional verification tool, an online supervisor model, or a verification procedure implemented by the harness.
Building on this approach, we plan to integrate verification with context management, using intermediate verification points as natural boundaries for organizing the exploration history. After completing an intermediate reflection, the model will autonomously determine whether the preceding exploration segment can be consolidated into a concise stage record. If so, the corresponding history segment will be replaced with the stage record and the current verification, while preserving key evidence, rejected hypotheses, unresolved questions, and the current task state. Compression will apply only to the segment between the two most recent verification points, avoiding repeated compression of earlier history. Through this design, we aim to control context overhead while preserving reasoning continuity and evidence integrity, supporting research tasks over longer horizons.
2.2
Post-training on Engineering Tasks
2.2.1
MLE Tasks
Task Construction.
We design Kaggle-MLE Factory, an automated multi-agent pipeline that converts historical Kaggle competitions into executable tasks with public workspaces, hidden test sets, and a unified evaluation interface. The pipeline assigns distinct roles to competition selection and data acquisition, task analysis, code generation, and execution and validation. The analysis module combines official descriptions with the actual data to form task specifications. The generation module then prepares the data, constructs held-out test splits with hidden labels, and implements task-specific evaluators. The execution and validation modules test the generated tasks on real data and provide feedback for iterative repair. Tasks undergo human review before trajectory collection. We also use MLE-Dojo
[
14
]
as a supplementary task source and exclude competitions that overlap with the full MLE-Bench task set
[
15
]
.
Interaction Harness.
We build an MLE interaction harness for long-horizon experimentation, allowing the model to autonomously refine solutions based on execution feedback. The harness organizes candidate code and execution results into an experiment tree that records solution revisions, supporting branch comparison, backtracking, submission management, and invalidation of candidates with unreliable results. Persistent plans and context compression support sustained interaction, while an analysis sub-agent with an independent context provides data exploration and result diagnosis.
Trajectory Collection and Selection.
We select demonstration trajectories and useful supervision segments based on the actual execution and evaluation results of candidate solutions. If performance degradation after the first best-performing submission exceeds a threshold, we truncate the trajectory at a complete tool-interaction boundary near that submission; otherwise, we retain it through the final submission. This preserves useful exploration and failure recovery while removing persistently degrading tails. Supervision data include initial-solution prefixes that execute successfully and meet quality criteria, long-horizon optimization trajectories, and analysis sub-agent trajectories, covering solution construction, iterative refinement, and experimental diagnosis. Training retains prior interaction context and supervises only newly generated reasoning, text, and tool calls.
Staged Supervised Fine-Tuning.
We adopt two-stage supervised fine-tuning to adapt general interaction capabilities to MLE. The first stage uses general coding and tool-interaction trajectories to establish code revision and tool-use capabilities. The second stage combines MLE trajectories with experimental trajectories from literature-derived scientific tasks to train solution design, result analysis, and sustained optimization, initializing the policy for online reinforcement learning.
Windowed Interaction Reinforcement Learning.
Starting from SFT, we apply Windowed Interaction Reinforcement Learning (WIRL). Since each experimental outcome reflects multiple rounds of analysis, code revision, and tool interaction, WIRL groups interactions between successive experiment results into execution windows with shared outcome-based rewards. Decisions remain conditioned on accumulated history, while completed windows support policy updates before the task ends.
Window rewards combine solution quality measured by task-specific medal thresholds with performance changes relative to the most recent valid submission. Model-induced execution errors and unscorable submissions receive negative rewards. Each window reward directly weights its main-model output tokens during policy optimization, without group-relative normalization.

We asynchronously collect completed windows with trusted feedback and correct policy differences using token probability ratios between the pre-update and rollout policies. 2.2.2
SWE Tasks
We construct training data for repository-level software-engineering issue resolution. Each task provides a repository snapshot and a natural-language issue description, and the agent interacts with the repository to produce a patch. The patch is evaluated against held-out tests: designated failing tests must pass, while previously passing tests must remain passing.
Task Sources and Environment Construction.
The task pool consists of instances from the public SWE-rebench-V2 dataset
[
17
]
and a separate set of tasks constructed in house. We convert tasks from both sources into a common repair-task format following SWE-bench
[
11
]
. Each task starts from the base commit of its associated pull request and uses the corresponding issue description as the task prompt. The reference diff is split into a solution patch containing changes to non-test files and a test patch reserved for grading.
For each task, we recover or construct the container configuration, installation recipe, and test command. Compatible tasks within a repository release group share environment configurations, with dependency mirrors and runtime settings adapted to our cluster. When a recipe is missing or unusable, we follow the build-and-repair loop of SWE-Factory
[
18
]
. Starting from a validated configuration for a neighboring version when available, we build the container, run the tests, and revise the configuration based on the resulting error logs for a bounded number of rounds. Reference-patch size and modified-file count are used to prioritize task collection rather than as hard exclusion criteria.
Task Validation.
We run both reference-patch and no-op checks on candidate tasks. The reference-patch run checks whether the known fix satisfies the grading criteria in the prepared environment. The no-op run submits an empty patch and checks that it receives zero reward, flagging tasks that can receive reward without a repair. We record both outcomes as task metadata for curation.
Trajectory Collection.
We collect trajectories using two agent harnesses:
mini-swe-agent
[
19
]
, which exposes a single shell-command action per turn, and Claude Code, which provides dedicated editing and shell tools. When both harnesses solve the same task, we retain both trajectories. Rollouts run in per-task isolated containers with turn and wall-clock limits.
Each zero-reward trajectory is re-graded once by replaying its unchanged patch, without further agent interaction, to recover successful patches affected by transient execution or grading failures. If the replay passes, we update the trajectory’s reward label.
The training corpus includes successful trajectories and a filtered subset of unresolved attempts. For unresolved attempts, we require a non-empty patch, substantive task-directed interaction, well-formed structure, a passing leakage check, and additional task or harness coverage. Runs consisting solely of infrastructure failures or bare timeouts are excluded.
Leakage Control.
We restrict access to reference fixes and held-out tests during agent execution. Before each rollout, we remove Git objects that expose these artifacts; resetting the working tree to the base commit alone does not remove them from the object store. Because the grader retrieves the held-out tests from the reference commit, the required objects are restored after the agent exits. The held-out tests are introduced only at grading time.
All outbound traffic from rollout containers is forced through the cluster proxy. During agent execution, we redirect the proxy endpoint to a closed local port to block external access. The separate grading stage retains the connectivity needed to install dependencies. These controls apply to data collection, evaluation, and training-time environment interaction.
We audit trajectories for evidence that reference-solution content reached the agent. Network commands alone are not classified as leakage, since they may be used for dependency installation or connectivity checks. Audit verdicts are stored with the trajectories and used during selection. Instances overlapping the test splits of our evaluation suites are removed before collection.

Scientific Research

Scientific research requires models to combine deep scientific reasoning, effective tool use, and long-horizon problem-solving capabilities. To enhance these capabilities, we develop a science-enhanced teacher model through a three-stage pipeline
