page_papers.title: Evolving with Open Worlds: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement for Future Forecasting
page_papers.abstract: Most contemporary artificial intelligence (AI) systems are released with frozen parameters and improve through external updates, whereas an ideal system would keep improving from its own experience, a capacity we call recursive self-improvement (RSI). Yet studying RSI requires an environment that is continuously changing, objectively verifiable, and naturally grounded, posing a fundamental challenge for agent evolution. Here we introduce DeepEvolve, a sustainable evolution agent system grounded in future event prediction, in which agents continuously interact with a dynamically evolving environment and improve by internalizing and externalizing the experience gained through these interactions. A living environment synthesizes verifiable tasks, and a recursive-evolution engine turns the reasoning trajectory behind each prediction back into capability: decoupling search from prediction adapts parameter-level evolution to the contamination-prone live environment, while distilling reusable skills lets the agent evolve from the limited live trajectories such an environment affords. On the external FutureX leaderboard, which evaluates predictions against real-world outcomes and is updated weekly, our self-improved forecaster ranked first across all systems over three consecutive weeks, achieving up to a 195% improvement in rating. On our synthesized evaluation, it ranked among the top three across four base LLMs, outperforming the strongest baseline by up to 10.7 Bradley--Terry points. More broadly, these results suggest that a system built for self-improvement is best understood as an agent that co-evolves with a genuinely living, open-ended environment, pointing to a shift in AI from training static models on fixed data toward cultivating agents that grow stronger from their own experience, with such an open world as the indispensable basis of that growth.
page_papers.content:
Abstract
Most contemporary artificial intelligence (AI) systems are released with frozen parameters and improve through external updates, whereas an ideal system would keep improving from its own experience, a capacity we call
recursive self-improvement
(RSI).
Yet studying RSI requires an environment that is continuously changing, objectively verifiable, and naturally grounded, posing a fundamental challenge for agent evolution.

Introduction
Intelligence is often measured by what a system can do at a single moment in time
[
19
,
2
]
.
Yet the more consequential question may not be how capable a model is today, but whether it can become more capable through its own experience
[
23
,
9
,
14
]
.
Across the natural and social sciences, the systems we regard as most powerful (
e.g.,
biological evolution, the scientific method, human expertise) are precisely those that improve themselves cumulatively, correcting past errors and compounding past gains
[
21
,
8
,
25
]
.
This suggests that an ideal artificial system should be measured less by what it can do at any single moment than by how its capabilities form and grow over time.
A system that improves itself from experience is a prerequisite for AI that acts as an autonomous agent and as a genuine instrument of discovery.
In this work, we study this form of
recursive self-improvement
(RSI) in the concrete and demanding setting of real-world event forecasting.
Studying recursive self-improvement, however, is not merely a matter of method.
It places unusually high demands on the research setting itself.
An agent can only improve recursively if its environment keeps posing fresh challenges and can tell, without human intervention, whether the agent is doing better than before.
What this calls for is an interactive environment, yet the fixed datasets that dominate today’s evaluation offer no such thing: inert and unchanging, they neither renew the challenge nor judge progress on their own.
Real-world event forecasting, we argue, is a natural testbed for such study: it is
grounded
in the unfolding world rather than a hand-constructed dataset,
verifiable
through future events whose objective ground truth arrives with time, and
non-stationary
because the world keeps changing.
Together these properties close the loop that recursion requires: the agent observes the world, makes predictions, receives future outcomes, learns from the resulting experience, and improves the predictions it makes next (Figure
1
a).
Whereas prior work on event and time-series forecasting
[
30
,
11
]
has largely pursued single-shot predictive accuracy, we instead treat forecasting as an environment in which to study how agents improve recursively through continuous interaction with a changing world.
Succeeding in this environment first requires a few foundational capabilities for solving any single forecasting task.

Our experiments trace this improvement to how environment, parameters, and skills evolve together, each by its own means.

article.headline: 用真实事件预测环境训练自我改进智能体
article.lede: 研究者提出 DeepEvolve，把真实事件预测当作可验证、非平稳的环境，让智能体在预测—结果—更新的闭环中递归自我改进
article.problem: 现有 AI 系统通常在发布时就冻结参数，只能依靠外部更新来变强；而理想系统应当能从自身经验中持续改进，作者称之为递归自我改进（RSI）。但研究 RSI 对研究环境的要求很高：环境必须不断提出新挑战，能无需人工介入就判断智能体是否进步，并且与现实世界自然对应。当前主流评测依赖的固定数据集并不具备这些性质，它们静止不变，既不更新挑战，也不自行判定进步。
article.method: DeepEvolve 由三个模块构成。Prometheus 通过模板和智能体驱动的发现来生成问题，再经时间校验、去重、冲突检测和多样性感知选择。Branchus 把证据搜集与概率预测分开：由调度者、搜索者和批评者组成的 search team 负责对时间敏感的证据检索，predict team 则是时间不变的，只在缓存的证据与推理轨迹上推理；两个团队都会调用相关预测技能。Athena 使用缓存证据和可验证奖励更新 predict team 的参数，把搜索轨迹蒸馏成可复用的预测技能，并把观察到的弱点转化为任务合成技能，再回灌给 Prometheus。
article.results: 作者称 Branchus 在 Qwen3.8-Max 上取得 62.2 的 BT 分数，比表 1 中最强基线高 10.7；评测中，它与 Qwen3.8-Max、GPT-5.6-Sol、DeepSeek-V4-Pro、Claude-Opus-4.6 四个不同规模与厂商的模型配对，并与多类基线比较。作者还报告增益会累积而非饱和：智能体自身在线轨迹不断累积成技能池，蒸馏出的技能逐轮提升预测质量，而不是一次跳升后停滞；但材料中该图（图 6）论文未给出具体数字。技能被组织为从具体到抽象的四级层级（s4 逐字保留的流程、s3 对题型的一般化、s2 领域内一般化、s1 跨领域预测原则）。
article.why_it_matters: RSI 研究长期缺乏一个可以被反复刷新的试验场，而真实世界事件预测把“世界本身”当作评测集，其真值随时间揭晓、无法被人工构造，因此有可能成为智能体自我改进的可扩展环境。
article.limitations: 材料中没有独立的局限性章节；从设计看，这套递归改进高度依赖结果可客观验证，迁移到没有明确真值的领域是否成立尚不清楚。另外，主要增益目前只在 Qwen3.8-Max 上以 BT 单一指标给出，“逐轮累积提升”的具体幅度论文未给出具体数字。
article.figure_caption_zh: DeepEvolve 总览：问题生成（Prometheus）、预测（Branchus）与进化（Athena）构成闭环，已揭晓的结果提供可验证奖励并回流到后续轮次。

figure.caption: {Overview of {DeepEvolve} for recursive self-improvement in real-world event forecasting.} {a,} The closed loop connects question generation, forecasting, and evolution, with resolved outcomes supplying verifiable rewards and updates feeding into subsequent rounds. {b,} {Prometheus} generates questions through templates and agent-driven discovery, followed by temporal validation, deduplication, conflict detection, and diversity-aware selection. {c,} {Branchus} separates evidence gathering, by a {search team} of a scheduler, searcher, and critic, from probabilistic prediction, by a {predict team}. The search team is time-sensitive, as its result depends on when it runs, while the predict team is time-invariant, reasoning only over the search team's cached evidence and reasoning trajectories. Both teams retrieve relevant forecasting skills. {d,} {Athena} updates the predict team's parameters using cached evidence and verifiable rewards, distills search trajectories into reusable forecasting skills, and converts observed weaknesses into task-synthesis skills for {Prometheus}. Resolved outcomes inform parameter and environment updates but are withheld from the behavior-level judge.

page_papers.title: Which Agent's Skill Should Change? Group-Relative Credit Assignment for Evolving Multi-Agent Teams
page_papers.abstract: Cooperative language-model agents can improve without weight updates by revising reusable skills, but only if a shared team reward is traced to the responsible agent and skill. Existing methods credit the skills present in each trajectory, yet presence is not responsibility: a harmful skill active in successful runs still earns positive credit. We present GRSE, Group-Relative Skill Evolution, which assigns behavioral credit by comparison: inspired by GRPO, it executes each question several times under the same skill libraries and contrasts the executions to credit agent--skill pairs, with structured diagnosis of failures. On HotpotQA and LoCoMo with two open-weight actors, GRSE outperforms MASkills, the closest prior method, on HotpotQA and every LoCoMo category except open-domain, with the largest gains on multi-hop questions (+6.7 and +3.2 F1). Its gains rest on better-grounded retrieval rather than answers given without evidence, and its learned skills transfer between the multi-hop tasks. GRSE is robust to corrupted libraries: starting from planted harmful skills, it credits every planted skill with the correct sign and recovers the score of a clean library (+6.3 points), whereas MASkills misattributes two and falls below its starting point.

1
Introduction

In iteration 1, a failure that surfaces in Agent 2’s answer is traced to Agent 1’s retrieval, and a new retrieval skill is induced. In iteration 3, this skill is credited as harmful in the shown group but helpful across the iteration’s 16 groups, so it is refined rather than pruned. In Agent 1’s search queries,

Language-model agents increasingly work in teams: one agent collects evidence, another reasons over it, and the team is judged by a single outcome
(
Cemri et al., 2026
;
Ghareeb et al., 2026
;
Tran et al., 2025
;
Dang et al., 2026
;
Zhang et al., 2026a
;
Xia et al., 2026b
;
Hong et al., 2024
;
Wu et al., 2023
;
Li et al., 2023
)
. Improving such a team requires answering a credit assignment question: which agent’s behavior, and which step of it, produced a success or a failure? The question is classical in multi-agent reinforcement learning, where a shared reward is decomposed with difference rewards or counterfactual baselines
(
Wolpert and Tumer, 2001
;
Foerster et al., 2018
;
Rashid et al., 2020
)
, and it has recently been posed for language-model teams as automated failure attribution
(
Zhang et al., 2025
)
. A wrong answer may stem from evidence collection, an incomplete handoff, or downstream reasoning
(
Wang et al., 2026
;
Zhang et al., 2025
)
, and the agent whose output is wrong is often not the agent whose behavior needs to change. For example, reasoner answers wrongly when the retriever misses the evidence.
We study this problem in a setting where model parameters stay fixed and each agent’s behavior is specified by natural-language skills, reusable procedures that the agent reads and follows
(
Zhao et al., 2024
;
Wang et al., 2023
;
Alzubi et al., 2026
;
Yao et al., 2026
)
. Skills make behavior editable, so credit becomes actionable: once responsibility is located, the responsible procedure can be revised. Existing experience- and skill-learning methods, however, assign credit coarsely, which often distill lessons from whole trajectories, and mainly focus on single-agent setting
(
Shinn et al., 2023
;
Xu et al., 2026
;
Ouyang et al., 2026
)
. Meanwhile MASkill, the recent two-agent SOTA, credits each skill from single trajectory in isolation
(
Yao et al., 2026
)
. However, without a contrast, a skill that is present in every execution also receives credit for the successes it did not cause: in our robustness study, MASkills raises the utility of a planted harmful skill over three iterations, whereas our method labels it harmful and prunes it (Appendix
C
). Comparison between executions already guide experience distillation, skill refinement, and prompt optimization
(
Cai et al., 2025
;
Chen et al., 2026
;
Li et al., 2026
;
Zehle, 2026
)
, but they have not been used to localize a team’s outcome to individual agents’ behaviors.
Behavioral credit assignment in agent teams poses two challenges. First, attribution must look past where an error surfaces. In Figure
1
, Agent 2 answers “not mentioned” in three of four executions of the same question, yet Agent 2 behaves correctly given its input. The decisive difference lies in Agent 1’s search query, which retrieves the answer only in the successful execution. Second, an attribution must be specific and checkable before it can drive a revision. A defective procedure, a missing capability, and a tool failure call for different responses, and an explanation that cites no execution step cannot be verified. Across questions, attributions must also be aggregated without counting repeated executions of one question as independent evidence.
We introduce
GRSE
,
G
roup-
R
elative
S
kill
E
volution, a training-free framework that evolves cooperative agents’ skills through group relative behavioral credit assignment. Following GRPO
(
Shao et al., 2024
)
, GRSE samples multiple complete team rollouts of the same question under fixed skill libraries and compute relative within-group advantages (§
3.1
). A group-relative critic compares agent behavior and handoffs across these rollouts to assign feedback to individual agent–skill pairs. A structured diagnosis grounds each attribution in a failure type, cited failed and successful steps, and an edit action, and reference checks reject attributions that the executions do not support (§
3.2
). The accepted attributions are aggregated across questions (§
3.3
) and applied as skill updates through the editing operators and validation gate of MASkills (§
3.4
). Figure
1
shows both levels of attribution within a single run:
across agents
, responsibility shifts from the answering agent to the retrieving agent;
within an agent
, a previously learned skill is later credited as harmful and diagnosed as a skill defect. Our contributions are threefold:
•
We formulate skill evolution for cooperative agents as
behavioral credit assignment
: with model parameters fixed and skills as editable units, a shared team outcome must be attributed to the agent and skills responsible for it. We address this by jointly comparing same-question team executions, which produces agent–skill feedback while preserving the handoffs needed to interpret each agent’s behavior and the proposed revision.
•
We make these attributions verifiable and actionable: a structured failure analysis links each attribution to a failure type, checked step references, and an edit action, and cross-question aggregation weighs attributions by the number of distinct questions that support them.
•
We evaluate GRSE on HotpotQA and LoCoMo with two open-weight actors. GRSE outperforms MASkills on HotpotQA and every LoCoMo category except open-domain. Its credit identifies and removes harmful skills that MASkills retains. Answer-transition and learned-skill analyses show that GRSE’s gains come from fewer broken answers and better-grounded retrieval.
2
Related Work
2.1
Reflection and Experience Memory
Experience-based adaptation stores information from past interactions to guide future decisions. Reflexion
(
Shinn et al., 2023
)
records verbal reflections for subsequent attempts. ExpeL
(
Zhao et al., 2024
)
extracts reusable insights from successes and failures, including comparisons on the same task. A-MEM
(
Xu et al., 2026
)
constructs linked notes and updates their contextual attributes as new memories arrive. ReasoningBank
(
Ouyang et al., 2026
)
distills reasoning strategies, and its memory-aware test-time scaling uses multiple executions to enrich memory curation. These methods actively transform experience rather than simply retaining raw traces. Memory and skills also interact: MemSkill
(
Zhang et al., 2026b
)
learns to select memory-management skills and revises its skill bank, while MSCE
(
Tang et al., 2026
)
promotes evidence-supported procedural policies into skills and maintains them using feedback. These methods decide
what
experience to keep and how to organize it, whereas GRSE instead decides
where
execution evidence should act, assigning it to editable skills owned by individual agents.
2.2
Reusable Skill Discovery and Evolution
Skill libraries turn experience into procedures that can be invoked and revised. Voyager
(
Wang et al., 2023
)
maintains executable code skills, and EvoSkill
(
Alzubi et al., 2026
)
uses an executor, proposer, and skill builder to discover and refine skills from task feedback. SkillRL
(
Xia et al., 2026a
)
distills failed trajectories into lessons, organizes skills into general and task-specific categories, and evolves the library alongside reinforcement learning of the agent policy. These methods learn skills for a single executing agent, so they never have to decide which agent’s skill to revise. MASkills
(
Yao et al., 2026
)
extends skill learning to cooperative teams through skill-conditioned credit, hierarchical aggregation, and skill editing, but it credits each trajectory on its own. We retain its skill representation and editing operators and change how credit is formed: GRSE jointly compares same-question team executions, and structured diagnosis links each failure to an agent–skill target, cited execution steps, and a checked edit action.
2.3
Group-Relative and Contrastive Feedback
GRPO
(
Shao et al., 2024
)
uses within-question rewards to optimize model parameters. Training-Free GRPO
(
Cai et al., 2025
)
instead distills semantic feedback from rollout groups into experiential context. Several methods already apply comparisons to skills: SkillCAT
(
Chen et al., 2026
)
contrasts same-task success/failure pairs, evaluates patches through replay, and organizes skills for routing. SkillCome
(
Li et al., 2026
)
combines within-group contrast with memories of failure and contrast patterns. CANTANTE
(
Zehle, 2026
)
contrasts joint prompt configurations on the same query to provide per-agent optimization signals. In these methods, the contrast either compares outcomes or varies the configuration being optimized. GRSE holds the skills fixed and contrasts the team’s behavior across executions, so that an outcome difference can be traced to an agent, a skill, and a cited step.
3

1

3.1
); a group-relative critic assigns behavioral credit to agent–skill pairs and grounds it in structured failure analysis (§
3.2
); and the attributions are aggregated across questions (§
3.3
) and applied as validated skill updates (§
3.4
). Algorithm

4
Experiment
4.1
Experimental Setup
We follow the setting of MASkills
(
Yao et al., 2026
)
, the closest prior SOTA for multi-agent skill evolution. Each method consists of two agents with task-specific roles that communicate sequentially, and the second agent produces the final answer. The agents are executed by one of two open-weight actors, Qwen3.8-27B
(
Qwen Team, 2026
)
and Gemma-4-31B-it
(
Gemma Team, 2026
)
, each conditioned on its own skill library. We use these two recent released open-weight model of similar size from different families to test whether credit assignment depends on the actor. A fixed Qwen3.8-27B model serves as critic and skill optimizer for all methods. Model parameters and agent roles stay fixed. The agents change only through their skills, which are revised according to the assigned credit.
All skill-evolution methods start from empty libraries and run for five iterations. GRSE samples four team trajectories per question, whereas MASkills samples one. Final libraries are evaluated with temperature-zero decoding. Detailed model, data and optimization settings appear in Appendix
A
.
4.2
Benchmarks
Datasets and metrics.
We evaluate on HotpotQA
(
Yang et al., 2018
)
for multi-hop question answering and LoCoMo
(
Maharana et al., 2024
)
for long-memory conversational reasoning. We use the distractor–hard subset and report the answer-token F1 for HotpotQA. LoCoMo covers multi-hop, temporal, open-domain, and single-hop questions. We report the category-specific F1 and smoothed BLEU.
Baselines.
We group baselines by whether they use the agent team.
Single-model baselines
answer with one model and no agents or skills. On HotpotQA, we run four prompting methods with the same actor, questions, passages, answer-format instruction, and metric as the
agent teams
, including IO (direct answer), Chain-of-Thought(CoT;
(
Wei et al., 2022
)
), CoT with self-consistency (CoT-SC;
(
Wang et al., 2022
)
; majority vote over five samples), and Self-Refine
(
Madaan et al., 2023
)
(at most three feedback-and-revision rounds). On LoCoMo, the full-context baseline follows the benchmark protocol
(
Maharana et al., 2024
)
with the actor model reads the entire conversation and answers directly.
Two-agent baselines
share the team, roles, and actor with GRSE. The empty-library team is this team before any skill is learned (iteration 0). For HotpotQA, all teams follow the agent prompts and short-answer instructions from the MASkills implementation, with questions and distractor passages supplied by the dataset. For LoCoMo, agent teams use category-specific task prompts. All the prompts are detailed in Appendix
F
. We report each
two-agent
method as the mean over three training runs, because the learned libraries vary with the sampled rollouts and the critic’s outputs, whereas
single-model
baselines have no training stage and are evaluated once.
GRSE variants.
We report GRSE and
GRSE w/o structure analysis
, which retains group-relative feedback but omits the prescribed failure-diagnosis schema and its checks, in main analysis. We report
GRSE w/o structure
and the other three variants in ablation studies:
GRSE w/ label
retains structured diagnosis and additionally uses dataset labels to condition the critic and organize update evidence;
GRSE with
G
=

G{=}1
samples one trajectory per question; and
DAPO filter
keeps four rollouts but, following the dynamic sampling of DAPO
(
Yu et al., 2025
)
, sends only groups whose rewards differ to the critic.

Robustness Analysis
A skill library may contain flawed or irrelevant skills, for example when skills are written by hand or reused from another task. We test whether skill evolution can repair such a library on LoCoMo single-hop questions, the category with the largest test set (453 questions), with the Qwen3.8 actor. Instead of an empty library, both methods start from the same corrupt library: each agent keeps one helpful skill and receives two harmful or irrelevant skills phrased as plausible advice, and neither the critic nor the optimizer is told which skills are perturbed. 6
Conclusion
We studied behavioral credit assignment in cooperative language-model teams whose agents keep fixed parameters and act through natural-language skills. GRSE executes each question several times under the same skill libraries, compares the executions agent by agent, and attributes the team’s outcome to individual agent–skill pairs. Structured diagnosis grounds each attribution in checked execution steps, and the resulting credit drives targeted, validated skill updates. On HotpotQA and LoCoMo with two open-weight actors, GRSE outperforms MASkills on HotpotQA and every LoCoMo category except multi-hop, with the largest gains on multi-hop questions, where the answer depends on evidence passed between the two agents. Its gains also rest on better retrieval rather than on fewer declined answers alone. Accurate credit also makes GRSE robust: starting from a library with planted harmful skills, it credits every planted skill with the correct sign and restores the score of a clean library, whereas MASkills, which credits each trajectory on its own, rewards a harmful skill for successes in which it is merely present and ends below its starting point. Learned libraries also transfer between HotpotQA and LoCoMo multi-hop questions without harm, and only GRSE gains further from training on the target task itself. These results suggest that comparing executions of the same task is a practical way to determine which agent, and which of its behaviors, should change.

Larger teams, non-sequential communication, longer tool-heavy tasks, and other critic models remain to be tested in the future.

In our experiments, we use only publicly available benchmarks, HotpotQA and LoCoMo, under their respective licenses. All models are open-weight and run locally. Because GRSE writes skills in natural language, humans can inspect and edit the learned libraries for safety before deployment.

C

(gold:
director

This appendix lists the prompts used in our experiments (Figures

). Placeholders such as

.
Agent roles.
Each agent’s system prompt is its fixed role followed by its current skill library: the role, a heading
## Skills
, and the bodies of all skills in the library. Roles do not change during training. On HotpotQA (Figure
7
), the two agents act in sequence: Agent 1 sees the question and passages, and Agent 2 additionally sees Agent 1’s response and gives the final answer. On LoCoMo (Figures
8
and
9
), Agent 1 searches the conversation with
<grep>
calls (at most three, each returning up to 20 matching turns), and Agent 2 answers from the retrieved evidence only. The environment appends the question, its category, and the tool-call instructions to these roles.
Single-model baselines.
These baselines send one user message per call, with no system prompt, agents, or skills (Figure
10
). On HotpotQA,
{context}
holds the same ten distractor-setting passages that the agents see. CoT-SC samples the CoT prompt five times and returns the majority answer. Self-Refine starts from the CoT answer, then alternates feedback and refinement until the feedback is
CORRECT
or three rounds have passed. The LoCoMo full-context baseline follows the benchmark’s own QA protocol
(
Maharana et al., 2024
)
:
{conversation}
is the whole conversation, with each session rendered as
DATE: {date}
, then
CONVERSATION:
, then one line per turn,
{speaker} said, "{text}"
. Answers are limited to 32 tokens.
Group-relative credit assignment.
For each training question, the critic receives the instructions in Figure
11
, followed by
INPUT:
and a JSON payload. The payload holds the task (question and passages, or the LoCoMo question without the conversation), each agent’s current skill library, and all rollouts of the group with their reward, group-relative advantage, agent steps, and recorded skill use. Repeated text (the passages inside each step, identical system prompts) is replaced by references to keep the payload within the context window. The critic decodes in JSON mode. On HotpotQA, an answer-length note is appended.
Structured failure diagnosis.
GRSE with structured analysis appends the instructions in Figure
12
to the critic prompt and adds two fields to the payload:
citation_constraints
, which lists the legal full- and non-full-reward rollout indices and the agent of each step, and
task_category
. Without the category label,
task_category
is
not_grouped
; with it,
task_category
is the question category for LoCoMo. Diagnoses that violate the constraints are returned to the critic once for repair.
Skill update operators.
Induction creates a new skill from the induction evidence collected for an agent, refinement applies anchored edits to an existing skill, and consolidation merges overlapping skills (Figure
13
). Induction and consolidation end with an output skeleton so that every new skill is a well-formed skill file. On LoCoMo, the operators use category-specific prompts followed by the output-format note.

article.headline: 多智能体技能演化：用组内对比定位该改谁的技能
article.lede: 同一问题跑 4 次团队执行，用组内相对优势把成败归到具体智能体—技能对；HotpotQA F1 83.7，比 MASki
article.problem: 多智能体团队只拿到一个共享的团队奖励，想靠修改自然语言技能来改进，就必须回答 credit assignment：哪个智能体的哪段行为决定了成败。现有技能学习方法按「技能是否出现在轨迹里」给 credit，于是一个在成功轨迹中同样出现的有害技能也会拿到正分。而且这类方法大多面向单智能体。
article.method: GRSE 对每个问题在固定技能库下采样 G=4 次完整团队执行，按 GRPO 的归一化方式计算组内相对优势，把高、低优势执行之间的行为差异当作反事实基线。一个 critic 跨执行逐个智能体比较行为与交接，把 credit 落到智能体—技能对，并给出结构化诊断：8 类失败类型、经步骤存在性与奖励符号校验的失败/成功步骤引用，以及 refine、induce、no edit 的编辑动作。credit 按支持的问题数跨问题聚合（重复 rollout 不重复计数），再由 MASkills 的编辑算子生成候选技能库，经验证门只保留不降低验证分的更新。
article.results: HotpotQA 上 GRSE 的 F1 为 83.7±0.5（Qwen3.8 作 actor），MASkills 为 80.6±0.6；换 Gemma4 作 actor 则是 82.8±0.4 对 82.3±0.2。LoCoMo 多跳类别提升 +6.7 F1（53.4 对 46.7）与 +5.3 BLEU，Gemma4 下为 +3.2 F1；时序类别在两个 actor 上均为最高（73.4 与 67.4 F1），但 open-domain（52 题）上 MASkills 更好。在植入有害技能的鲁棒性实验中，GRSE 对 5 个植入技能全部给出正确符号、两类技能效用分离 0.31（MASkills 错 2 个、仅分离 0.03），F1 从 60.6 恢复到 66.9，高于 MASkills 的 58.4。
article.why_it_matters: 权重不动、只改自然语言技能，就能让协作智能体团队变强；把 credit 落到具体的智能体—技能对，使「改谁的技能」成为一个可引用步骤、可校验、可回滚的编辑动作，而不是笼统的整条轨迹反思。
article.limitations: 代价在训练算力：每问题 4 次 rollout 使 actor token 消耗达 MASkills 的 1.6–2.9 倍、wall-clock 1.3–1.8 倍（仅训练阶段，推理不变）。实验只覆盖两智能体顺序团队、两个问答基准与单一 critic，更大团队与非顺序通信未验证；且摘要称 LoCoMo 唯一未超过 MASkills 的类别是 open-domain、结论段却写成 multi-hop，这处不一致需要作者澄清。
article.figure_caption_zh: 每轮迭代：（1）对每个问题采样一组团队执行；（2）对比这些执行给智能体—技能对记 credit，并以结构化形式诊断失败；（3）跨问题聚合 credit 成技能编辑，仅保留不降低验证分的改动。

figure.caption: Each iteration (1) samples a group of team executions per question ( {sec:method-groups}), (2) credits agent--skill pairs by contrasting these executions and diagnoses failures in a structured form ( {sec:method-credit}), and (3) aggregates the credit across questions into skill edits, each kept only if it does not lower the validation score ( {sec:method-organization}-- {sec:method-evolution}). The example is from one training run on LoCoMo single-hop questions, in which Agent~1 retrieves evidence and Agent~2 answers. In iteration~1, a failure that surfaces in Agent~2's answer is traced to Agent~1's retrieval, and a new retrieval skill is induced. In iteration~3, this skill is credited as harmful in the shown group but helpful across the iteration's 16 groups, so it is refined rather than pruned. In Agent~1's search queries, {|} denotes OR.

page_papers.title: DeLoop: Repeated Actions as Self-Supervision for Long-Horizon Agents
page_papers.abstract: Language-model agents that run long tasks often redo work they have already done: they re-issue a tool call they made earlier and get back exactly the same observation, a step that adds no new information. We identify this failure as a loop. Loops appear natively in Qwen, Llama, and Gemini agents and become far more common once the agent's history is compressed to fit its context window. To reduce these loops, we propose DeLoop, a self-supervised training method. DeLoop builds on a simple observation: the agent's own rollout can provide the supervision needed to learn from its loops. We use a looping action as a negative example and the first later non-looping action in the same rollout as a positive example. DeLoop learns from these pairs through direct preference optimization and does not require task rewards, gold answers, or LLM judges. On CodeGym under compression, DeLoop reduces the share of Qwen3-8B tasks containing loops from 57.3% to 6.1%. It also uses about one third as many steps per task, with similar task success. On Qwen3-32B, DeLoop reduces loops and steps while raising task success from 37.7% to 44.8%.
page_papers.content:
DeLoop: Repeated Actions as Self-Supervision for Long-Horizon Agents
Tianle Chen
Pushkar Singh
Ketan Todi
Biswajit Paria
Qijia He
Wenqi Wang
Yuwen Tan
Jike Zhong
Sugato Basu
Deepti Ghadiyaram
Arjun Akula
Abstract
Language-model agents that run long tasks often redo work they have already done: they re-issue a tool call they made earlier and get back exactly the same observation, a step that adds no new information.
We identify this failure as a
loop
.
Loops appear natively in Qwen, Llama, and Gemini agents and become far more common once the agent’s history is compressed to fit its context window.
To reduce these loops, we propose
DeLoop
, a self-supervised training method.
DeLoop builds on a simple observation: the agent’s own rollout can provide the supervision needed to learn from its loops.
We use a looping action as a negative example and the first later non-looping action in the same rollout as a positive example.
DeLoop learns from these pairs through direct preference optimization and does not require task rewards, gold answers, or LLM judges.
On CodeGym under compression, DeLoop reduces the share of Qwen3-8B tasks containing loops from 57.3% to
6.1%
.
It also uses about one third as many steps per task, with similar task success.
On Qwen3-32B,
DeLoop
reduces loops and steps while raising task success from 37.7% to 44.8%. Code and data will be publicly available.
1
Google,
2
Boston University,
3
University of Washington,
4
University of Southern California,
5
Google DeepMind,
†
Project lead
Keywords:
LLM agents, long-horizon agents, agent memory, context compression, agent loops, repeated actions, preference optimization
Figure 1:
Training an agent on its own loops breaks the loop.
(Left)
A repeated search and the later action that marks the server as visited form a preference pair. DPO trains the agent to prefer the recovery.
(Right)
Qwen3-8B on CodeGym: DeLoop and the baseline summarize at 4,096 tokens; full history is the uncompressed reference.
1
Introduction
Language-model agents increasingly solve tasks over long interaction
horizons: they inspect repositories, execute commands, call tools, and act on
environment feedback across many steps
(
Yao et al., 2023
;
Yang et al., 2024a
;
Jimenez et al., 2024
;
Du et al., 2025
)
.
Yet they often redo work they have already done. The agent calls the same tool with the same arguments, receives the same observation, and then issues the same call again (
Figure
1
). Each repeated call is a
looping action
: it gets back an observation the agent already has and adds no new information. We formulate this failure as a
loop
.
The failure is already present even when the full, uncompressed history is available, but compression makes it worse. On CodeGym
(
Du et al., 2025
)
, the loop rate of Qwen3-8B
(
Yang et al., 2025
)
, the share of tasks with at least one loop, rises from
29.0
%
29.0\%
with the full history (no summarization) to
57.3%
under summarization, while looping actions per task increase
more than 3.5
×
\times
!
More importantly, in addition to wasted tool calls, we empirically observed that trajectories that enter a loop fail in all six Qwen3 and Gemini models we evaluate: on average,
59.5%
of looping runs fail, compared with 33.4% of loop-free runs (
Figure
2
).
Thus, context compression
makes looping more likely and increases the chances of task failure.
Recent work manages growing interaction histories through external memory
(
Packer et al., 2023
;
Fox et al., 2026
)
, hierarchical or summarized working context
(
Hu et al., 2025
;
Wu et al., 2025
;
Sun et al., 2026
)
, compact learned state
(
Zhou et al., 2025
)
, and learned context compression or management
(
Kang et al., 2026
;
Lu et al., 2026
;
Liu et al., 2025
)
.
These works study
what
history should an agent retain to continue acting well under a bounded context window. In contrast, we study a complementary question about how the agent’s policy uses its history after compression. That is,
when the history records an action, does the agent use that record to avoid repeating it?
We find that most agents do so only partly.
Another way to reduce looping is to improve the agent’s policy. Some methods address agent failures at inference time through reflection
(
Shinn et al., 2023
)
or early stopping
(
Lu et al., 2025
)
. Others train agents using demonstrations
(
Zeng et al., 2024
;
Chen et al., 2023
)
, search-based training data
(
Yuan et al., 2025
)
, or step-level supervision
(
Xiong et al., 2024
;
Chen and Yuille, 2026
;
Tang, 2026
)
. We instead ask:
can the failure itself provide a useful signal to improve agent’s policy?
Based on these observations, we propose
DeLoop
, a self-supervised training method. Our key observation is that loops can provide their own training signal. We note that a loop is a simple trajectory-level event that can be identified directly from the action-observation trace, without requiring post-hoc failure attribution
(
Barke et al., 2026
;
Hou et al., 2026
)
. Within a single rollout, we pair a looping action with the
first later non-looping
action that differs from it. The looping action provides a natural negative, while the later action provides a positive signal. Figure
1
illustrates this. These pairs are mined directly from the interaction, without gold answers, LLM judges, external rewards, or task-success labels. We train the policy on these pairs through direct preference optimization (DPO
Rafailov et al., 2023
).
On Qwen3-8B, DeLoop cuts the loop rate
9.4
×
\times
while lowering interaction cost, with similar task success. On Qwen3-32B, the self-mined pairs alone reduce loop rate from
38.5
%
38.5\%
to
12.9%
and raise task success from
37.7
%
37.7\%
to
44.8%
, while also lowering interaction cost.
Adding cross-domain pairs (DeLoop-Mix) raises Qwen3-8B task success from
25.1
%
25.1\%
to
30.3%
.
Our contributions are:
1.
Identifying loops in long-horizon agents:
we identify and characterize loops, a simple failure in which an agent repeats an earlier action and receives the same observation. We show that loops occur even with the full history, grow sharply under compression, and are associated with task failure.
2.
Mining loop actions as self-supervision:
we introduce a simple mining
method that turns discovered loops into preference pairs from the agent’s own
rollouts, with no external supervision.
3.
Reducing loops in long-horizon agents:
DeLoop reduces loops (57.3% to
6.1%
on Qwen3-8B) while lowering interaction cost. The gains also extend to larger models, where there is pronounced improvement in task success (45.1% to
52.3%
on Qwen3-14B and 37.7% to
44.8%
on Qwen3-32B).
2
Related work
Repeated actions in agents.
Repetition is a known failure of LLM agents. AgentBench found that agents
mainly exceed their task limit because they repeat earlier
content
(
Liu et al., 2024
)
. MAST also lists step repetition as a failure
mode of multi-agent systems
(
Cemri et al., 2025
)
, and RAGEN shows that multi-turn
RL can trap agents in repetitive reasoning
(
Wang et al., 2025b
)
. Closest to our
setting,
Min et al. (2026)
find that repeated context compression increases
repeated exploration and improve the compression prompt to reduce it; we keep
the compressor fixed and change the policy. IAL-Scan finds code paths that can
run without bound
(
Hou et al., 2026
)
, and other work locates agent
failures in execution traces
(
Deshpande et al., 2025
;
Barke et al., 2026
;
Yeh et al., 2026
;
Liu et al., 2026
;
Zhang et al., 2025
)
.
At inference time, agents can reflect, stop early, or escalate to a stronger
model
(
Shinn et al., 2023
;
Lu et al., 2025
;
He et al., 2026
)
. OpenHands flags an agent as “stuck”
when the same action returns the same observation four times in a
row
(
Wang et al., 2025a
)
. These methods do not change the agent policy. Even with a
blocker that refuses repeated calls and returns their earlier result, Qwen3-8B
on CodeGym still proposes an already executed call in 71.3% of tasks, as often
as without the blocker (69.8%); DeLoop lowers this to 13.6%
(Appendix
J.2
). We define a loop as a repeated tool call
that returns the same observation. Loops persist even with summaries designed
to keep past actions (Section
3.3
), so we train the agent
policy itself to break the loop.
Context management.
Long-horizon agents need to fit their history into a limited context. Common context management methods
store the history in external memory or searchable logs
(
Packer et al., 2023
;
Fox et al., 2026
;
Wang et al., 2026b
)
,
summarize older interactions
(
Hu et al., 2025
;
Wu et al., 2025
;
Sun et al., 2026
;
Su et al., 2026
)
,
keep a compact learned state
(
Zhou et al., 2025
)
, learn what to
keep
(
Kang et al., 2026
;
Lu et al., 2026
;
Liu et al., 2025
)
, or validate their
summaries
(
Chen et al., 2026
)
. However, removing plans from the context sharply hurts
performance
(
Mehta and Datta, 2026
)
. These methods decide
what
history to keep. We instead ask whether the agent uses the kept history to avoid repeating actions.
Learning from agent trajectories.
Most methods that train agents on trajectories need an external signal to
pick the better action. Agent tuning uses filtered or teacher-generated
trajectories
(
Zeng et al., 2024
;
Chen et al., 2023
;
Fu et al., 2025
)
, or successful attempts and
outcome feedback
(
Zelikman et al., 2022
;
Yang et al., 2024b
;
Guo et al., 2025
;
Le et al., 2026
;
Wang et al., 2024
;
Jung et al., 2025
)
. ETO and
Agentic-DPO take the better action from experts
(
Song et al., 2024
;
Chen and Yuille, 2026
)
.
Step-DPO, IPR, and ToolGraph use step-level labels or
rewards
(
Lai et al., 2024
;
Xiong et al., 2024
;
Tang, 2026
)
. Agent-R and Agent Q use tree
search guided by rewards or critiques
(
Yuan et al., 2025
;
Putta et al., 2024
)
, and SCoRe
trains self-correction with online RL
(
Kumar et al., 2025
)
. DeLoop instead
takes the better action from the agent’s own later recovery in the same
rollout and trains with DPO
(
Rafailov et al., 2023
)
. Its only label is the exact-repeat
rule of Section
3.1
, so it needs no rewards, expert actions,
or step labels. Like hindsight experience replay
(
Andrychowicz et al., 2017
)
, it also
learns from failed rollouts.
Penalizing repetition.
Repetition can also be penalized directly. RLTR adds a penalty on redundant
tool calls to its reward
(
Li et al., 2025
)
. In text generation, penalized
sampling
(
Keskar et al., 2019
)
, unlikelihood training
(
Welleck et al., 2020
)
,
and DITTO
(
Xu et al., 2022
)
reduce repeated tokens and sentences. These
penalties mark what to avoid; DeLoop also supplies the agent’s own alternative
action. Using our loop flag as a per-step penalty in online RL (GRPO) lowers the
Qwen3-8B loop rate on CodeGym from 57.3% to 15.0%, against 6.1% for DeLoop
(Section
5.3
).

3.1
Defining a Loop
A loop occurs when the agent repeats a previous tool call with identical
arguments and receives the same observation. Thus, that step adds no new
information.
For example, consider an agent counting clusters of online servers on a grid.
The agent has tools to find unvisited servers and mark them as visited.
In one rollout, it issues the same search three times without marking the
returned server. Because that server remains unmarked, each call returns
the same coordinates. The latter two calls therefore add no new information.

3.2
Loops Are Costly
Each looping action consumes tokens and a tool execution without yielding
a new observation. Under a fixed interaction budget, these repeated calls leave fewer
opportunities to take actions that could advance the task.
We compare looping and loop-free Qwen3-8B runs on CodeGym under
summarization at 4,096 tokens. Both groups include successful and failed runs.
Looping runs contain
6.5
looping actions on average.
They execute
10.5
more actions per task on average than loop-free runs.
Their interaction transcripts also contain
11k
more tokens.
The same pattern holds for all six models in the cost comparison
(Appendix Figure
7
).
Within each model’s compressed setting, looping runs are also more likely
to fail than loop-free runs (Figure
2
).
The gap appears in all six Qwen3 and Gemini models: Qwen3-8B fails
85%
of looping runs against 68% of loop-free runs.
Gemini 3.1 Pro shows a wider gap:
48%
against 12%.
A loop thus marks a run that is more likely to fail and has a higher
execution cost.
3.3
Compression Makes Loops More Common
An agent’s interaction history records what it has already done.
To keep long rollouts within a context budget, the agent summarizes earlier
interactions (Appendix
D
). We examine whether this compression
makes the agent more likely to repeat completed actions.
On CodeGym, Qwen3-8B loops in 29.0% of runs with the full history.
Summarization at 4,096 tokens raises the loop rate to
57.3%
.
Lowering the threshold to 2,048 tokens raises it further to
64.7%
(Figure
3
a).
The same pattern appears in all three Gemini models that we run with and without compression
(Figure
3
b). We compare CodeGym runs with the full
history against the subset of summarization runs in which compression fires.
Gemini 3.1 Pro loops least with the full history yet shows the largest
increase,
2.9
×
\times
.
To investigate this increase, we ask whether removing a completed action’s
record makes the agent more likely to repeat it.
We reconstruct 300 histories from 253 CodeGym tasks after compression.
Each ends just before Qwen3-8B chooses its next action.
One version of each history keeps the most recent completed tool call and
its observation. The other removes this record.
We sample the next action eight times from each version.
The agent repeats that call in 3.3% of samples with the record present
and
48.8%
with it removed
(Appendix
F
).
The record therefore helps the agent avoid an immediate repeat. This explains
why compression causes more loops. However, over a whole episode, keeping the
record is not enough: Qwen3-8B still loops in 29.0% of runs with the full
history. Under compression, a quarter of runs (25.2%) repeat a call
that is still in the context word for word (Appendix
J.1
).
Better context management does not close this gap. Summaries that keep an
explicit record of past actions, such as a trace of every executed call or a
ledger of tried actions, still loop in 52.0% to 62.7% of runs, close to
standard summarization at 57.3% (Appendix Table

(

history. The agent often fails to use a record it has, so we train the policy
itself (Section
4
). This complements better compression:
DeLoop-Mix lowers the loop rate under every memory policy we test
(Section
6.1
).

5.1
Experimental Setup
Benchmarks and models.
CodeGym
(
Du et al., 2025
)
is our primary benchmark for both mining
and evaluation: its tasks require many act–observe rounds, so the history
grows until compression fires. We also evaluate on four further agent
environments: ALFWorld
(
Shridhar et al., 2021
)
, Open-AgentRL
(
Wang et al., 2026a
)
,
AppWorld
(
Trivedi et al., 2024
)
, and ScienceWorld
(
Wang et al., 2022
)
.
Terminal-Bench
(
Merrill et al., 2026
)
and BrowseComp-Plus
(
Chen et al., 2025
)
provide further evaluations in their native agent harnesses
(Section
6.3
). Our main agent is Qwen3-8B, and we
repeat the CodeGym study with Qwen3-14B and Qwen3-32B
(
Yang et al., 2025
)
.
Training variants.
DeLoop trains on self-mined CodeGym pairs (Section
4.2
).
We also evaluate
DeLoop-Mix
, a variant trained with additional
cross-domain pairs (Section
5.4
). Its training data include
pairs mined from Terminal-Bench rollouts.
Evaluation protocol and metrics.
In our standard
compressed setting, the agent summarizes its history whenever it exceeds
4,096 tokens; the same model writes the summary and continues from it. Unless
noted otherwise, each policy in the main CodeGym comparison acts in this
setting on 300 held-out tasks, and the full-history agent serves as the
uncompressed reference. We
report four metrics: the loop rate (Section
3
), task
success, steps per task, and estimated tokens per task
(Appendix
A
).
Baselines.
Training-free context methods change what the agent
keeps from its history, including retrieval memory, ACON
(
Kang et al., 2026
)
, and
LLMLingua-2
(
Pan et al., 2024
)
. Training-free inference-time controls act during
inference, including an exact duplicate blocker and
Reflexion
(
Shinn et al., 2023
)
. Trained baselines learn from task outcomes, solved
trajectories, or gold actions, and distillation SFT on full-history traces
is, like DeLoop, label-free. We do not run GRPO on task success: its reward
arrives only once per episode, and even a per-step gold-action reward leaves
only 2.7% of GRPO groups informative (Appendix
G.10
).
The full battery is in Appendix
Tables
4
and
18
.

6.3
The Repair Transfers to New Benchmarks
Finally, we test DeLoop and DeLoop-Mix in native agent harnesses with different
tools and interactions. Terminal-Bench tests
terminal tasks, and BrowseComp-Plus tests web research.
On Terminal-Bench,
DeLoop cuts unproductive duplicate calls from 16.6 to
6.9
per task. On all 830 BrowseComp-Plus queries,
DeLoop-Mix lowers the loop rate from 22.4% to
1.2%
while matching the untrained model’s accuracy;
DeLoop, trained on CodeGym pairs alone, already lowers it to
6.4%. We also test zero-shot transfer from CodeGym to ALFWorld.
DeLoop on Qwen3-32B, trained only on CodeGym pairs, lowers the ALFWorld loop rate from
64.9% to
54.5%
and raises task success from
33.6% to
42.5%
.
7
Conclusion
Long-horizon agents that compress their history fall into loops: they
re-issue an action they already ran and receive the same result. On
CodeGym, summarizing the history raises the loop rate of Qwen3-8B from
29.0% to 57.3%, and better context management alone does
not remove it. Our key observation is that the loop labels itself: the
looping action is the rejected action, and the agent’s later loop-breaking
action is the chosen one. Trained on these self-mined pairs, DeLoop cuts the loop rate
9.4
×
\times
, from 57.3% to 6.1%, at about one third of the steps per task while
maintaining task success, and raises task success by 7.2 points at 14B and
7.1 points at 32B. An agent’s own loops become its supervision: break the
loop, keep the progress. We believe our work could help the community better
understand and reduce loops in long-horizon agents.

Environment and agent.
CodeGym
(
Du et al., 2025
)
turns static coding problems into
interactive tool-use environments. Each task exposes a function API with
Observe()
, task-specific actions, and
Done()
, and the
environment server scores the agent’s answer against the task’s gold answer.
Unless noted otherwise, the agent is Qwen3-8B with greedy decoding and a budget
of 30 rounds, where a round is one model turn and a step is one executed
action. Training and evaluation tasks share no task instance or code ID.
Appendix
A
lists the evaluation runs behind each result.
Loop detector.
The canonicalization
κ
\kappa
of Section
3.1
normalizes each
tool call for whitespace and argument order. A step is a looping action when
its canonical call appeared earlier in the episode and the environment returns
a byte-identical observation.
Practical agent frameworks use a similar rule: the OpenHands stuck detector
flags an agent when the same action returns the same observation four or
more times
(
Wang et al., 2025a
)
.
Compression.
When the estimated history exceeds the threshold, the harness keeps the system
prompt, the task, and the six most recent messages, and replaces everything in
between with a summary. The same served model writes the summary at
temperature zero, following an instruction that asks it to keep exact values,
environment returns, and executed actions. The standard threshold is 4,096
tokens; Figures
3
a and
6
b also use 8,192
and 2,048 tokens and hard truncation at 4,096 tokens. Every comparison holds
the model and the threshold fixed. Table
4
lists, for each
context method, the share of episodes in which compression fired.

These probes, which complement
Section
I.1
, ask how Qwen3-8B uses the
record of an action it has already run.
The record matters, its wording does not.
We take 150 looping points from training-side tasks that never appear in
evaluation and rebuild the context in five length-matched variants: (A) the
original action–observation block; (B) a one-line assertion of the action and
its result; (C) no record; (D) the assertion inside the summary; and (E) the
returned value without saying that the agent ran the action. We sample 16
completions per point at temperature 0.7 and measure re-issue, the share of
completions that repeat the looping action. For the compressed baseline,
deleting the record raises re-issue from 15.3% (A) to 43.3% (C), while
rewording it keeps re-issue close to the verbatim rate (17.6% for B, 16.5%
for D, 18.9% for E).
Training lowers re-issue in every condition.
On the same points (
Table
8
), DeLoop
re-issues 3.4% of the time with the verbatim record, 4.5% with the
assertion, and 15.0% with the record deleted, against 15.3%, 17.6%, and
43.3% for the compressed baseline.
The deletion effect holds on an unselected sample.
To avoid selecting on loops, we fix 300 decision points after compression from
253 tasks before any model call, stratified by whether the episode eventually
loops. At each point, the untrained policy chooses its next action with the
most recent completed action–observation record present or deleted (eight
samples each). It re-issues that action 3.3% of the time with the record
present and 48.8% with it deleted in this stratified sample; weighting the two
strata by their population shares gives a difference of 44.3 points.
F.1
Training Suppresses the Looping Action
Two probes at 250 loop points from tasks outside all preference-training data
ask what training changes (
Table
9
). First, we score the recorded loop-breaking action
against the looping action. The untrained policy ranks the loop-breaking
action higher at 49.6% of points, a coin flip; the two-source DeLoop-Mix variant (CodeGym,
ALFWorld, and Open-AgentRL pairs) raises this to 69.2%. Second, we freeze each loop prefix
and take one greedy action. Every trained policy re-issues the looping action
less often than the untrained one (15.6%): 6.0% for DeLoop, 5.2%
for DeLoop-Mix, and 5.6% for looping-action penalty GRPO. The share
that copies the recorded loop-breaking action stays between 18.8% and 20.8%
for every policy, while calls to
Done()
rise from 3.6% to between
12.4% and 26.0%. Training thus suppresses the looping action rather than
teaching one memorized recovery.

G.1
Training Details
Mining.
We run the compressed agent on CodeGym training tasks and
flag looping actions with the detector of Section
3.1
,
comparing canonicalized calls (whitespace and argument order normalized) and
exact observations. Each looping action that the agent later breaks yields one pair: the prompt is the
history just before it, the rejected action is the looping action, and the
chosen action is the first later action in the same rollout that is neither a
looping action nor the same call. Without the second condition, a later repeat
that returns a new observation could be chosen, and both sides of the pair
would be the same text.
No labels.
The miner reads only actions and observations. It never
reads the reward, the task status, or a gold answer, and no LLM judge takes
part. Of the 8,000 CodeGym pairs, 82.6% come from runs that fail.

G.7
Per-Step Selectivity
Not every repeated call is wasted: re-checking a state the agent has changed
returns a new observation. We split repeated calls into looping actions, which
get back the same observation, and informative repeats, which get back a new
one. Selectivity is the share of repeats that are informative, pooled over all
scored steps.
Training removes looping actions far more than informative repeats
(
Table
17
). DeLoop lowers looping actions from
24.9% to 2.5% of steps and informative repeats from 10.6% to 5.8%, so
selectivity rises from 29.9% to 69.8%; DeLoop-Mix reaches
74.2%. The trained policies still re-check the environment, but they rarely
re-issue a call whose answer they already have.

G.10
GRPO Variants
We train Qwen3-8B with online GRPO
(
Shao et al., 2024
)
under summarization at 4,096 tokens and
vary the reward, sampling, or prompts (
Table
19
).
Looping-action penalty GRPO penalizes every looping action; one version also
mixes in prompts from other environments. Episode-level loop reward GRPO gives
one sparse reward per episode, and loop-weighted SFT replaces RL with weighted
imitation. Gold-action GRPO, the labeled baseline of Table
1
,
rewards an exact match with a gold action; its variants add partial credit and
more diverse sampling. A group is informative when its rewards differ, so that
it yields a gradient.
The per-step penalty is the strongest signal.
It cuts the loop
rate to 15.0%, and to 18.3% with 28.3% task success when prompts are mixed.
A sparse episode-level reward leaves 47.3% of runs looping, and loop-weighted
SFT 42.3%.
Gold-action rewards give GRPO little to learn from.
With exact
matching, only 2.7% of groups are informative and the loop rate stays at
52.7%. Partial credit raises informative groups to 5.3% and diverse sampling
to 20.5%, and the loop rate falls with them, to 49.3% and 32.7%.
The penalty holds across context settings.
Trained once under
summarization at 4,096 tokens, the policy loops in 13.7% of tasks with the
full history and in 11.3%, 15.0%, and 16.0% under summarization at 8,192,
4,096, and 2,048 tokens, against 29.0%, 51.0%, 57.3%, and 64.7% for the
untrained agent in the same settings. Under truncation, which it never saw in
training, it loops in 24.7% of tasks against 65.3%. Task success rises from
20.0% to 24.3% at 2,048 tokens and from 18.0% to 25.7% under
truncation.

G.13
A Likelihood Anchor Brings Loops Back
Plain DPO suits self-mined pairs better than DPO with a likelihood anchor.
RPO adds a negative log-likelihood term on the chosen action to the DPO loss,
with weight
α
=
1.0
\alpha=1.0
. On the same 8,000 self-mined CodeGym pairs, the
anchor raises the loop rate of Qwen3-8B from 6.1% to 27.0%, steps per task
from 4.67 to 7.90, and tokens per task from 12.7k to 24.8k, and task
success goes from 25.9% to 21.3%. The anchor raises loops on other training
data as well: from 19.0% to 42.1% on a two-source mixed corpus, and from
34.7% to 37.3% on the outcome-ranked pairs of Table
1
.
The training logs show what the anchor changes. Plain DPO pushes the looping
action far down and lowers the loop-breaking action only slightly; with the
anchor, the loop-breaking action rises toward imitation.

Planning an action does not stop the agent from
issuing it: with the action only proposed, the untrained Qwen3-8B re-issues it
in 73.9% of completions, the same as before the action was ever run
(73.7%). Stating the observation lowers re-issue to 29.0%, and the record of
the agent’s own execution lowers it further, to 16.5%. Deleting that record
brings re-issue back to 53.3%. The effect is strongest right after the run
(4.9%) and fades as history accumulates.
The record also separates loops from reasonable retries. At retry points it
lowers re-issue only from 68.4% to 51.7%, while a stated observation alone
lowers it to 20.6% and blocks retries that are worth making. The executed
record, together with what it returned, is what tells the policy whether an
action is finished or worth checking again.
Trained policies.
Both trained policies still tell loops from
retries. With the record present, DeLoop re-issues a looping action in
8.3% of completions and DeLoop-Mix in 6.8%, against 36.1% and
38.0% at retry points. Deleting the record raises re-issue at looping points
only to 20.7% and 23.9%, against 53.3% for the untrained model, while
retries return to 54.2% and 56.1%. The trained policies thus avoid most
loops even when the record of the earlier run is missing.

article.headline: 把循环变监督：DeLoop 减少智能体重复动作
article.lede: DeLoop 把循环动作与其后的恢复动作组成偏好对，用 DPO 训练，在 CodeGym 上将 Qwen3-8B 循环率
article.problem: 长程智能体常重复已执行过的工具调用，拿回相同观察，浪费步骤与 token；历史压缩会显著放大这一问题。论文在 CodeGym 上报告，Qwen3-8B 的含循环任务比例从完整历史的 29.0% 升到 4096 token 摘要下的 57.3%，且含循环的运行更易失败。
article.method: DeLoop 把一次循环动作作为负例，把同一 rollout 中之后第一个非循环且不同的动作作为正例，直接用 DPO 训练策略。配对只依赖动作与观察的结构匹配，不需要任务奖励、标准答案或 LLM 评审；作者在 Qwen3-8B 上用 8,000 个自挖掘 CodeGym 对做 LoRA DPO。
article.results: 在 CodeGym 的 4096 token 摘要设置下，Qwen3-8B 的循环率从 57.3% 降至 6.1%（9.4×），每任务步数从 15.00 降至 4.67，token 约降 47%，任务成功率从 25.1% 变为 25.9%。Qwen3-14B 成功率从 45.1% 升至 52.3%，Qwen3-32B 从 37.7% 升至 44.8%，循环率分别从 42.9% 降至 12.3%、从 38.5% 降至 12.9%。加入跨域配对的 DeLoop-Mix 将 8B 成功率从 25.1% 提到 30.3%，在 BrowseComp-Plus 上把循环率从 22.4% 降至 1.2%，准确率与未训练模型相当。
article.why_it_matters: 它把失败轨迹本身变成无需外部标签的训练信号，为长程智能体的上下文压缩与策略修复提供互补思路，并直接减少重复工具调用与 token 消耗。
article.limitations: 循环被定义为同一工具调用返回字节级相同观察，近重复调用与更广泛的低效探索不计入；主要评测集中在 CodeGym，8B 上成功率仅从 25.1% 到 25.9%，且部分消融和跨环境结果仅单次运行。

page_papers.title: Know What You Don't Know: Agentic Data Synthesis by Evolving Generation Space for Closed-Loop Learning
page_papers.abstract: The continued improvement of large language models increasingly depends on synthetic experience, yet effective data synthesis for interactive agents requires not only executable and verifiable trajectories, but also interactions that provide learning value for the current task agent. Existing methods increasingly incorporate environment feedback, data validation, or learner failures, but still face a feedback-to-decision gap: observed weaknesses do not directly specify how future synthesis should change, or whether they can be represented by the current synthesis space. To address this gap, we propose EvoSyn, a learning-feedback-driven multi-agent framework that organizes synthesis around a revisable state specifying what interaction factors can be deliberately generated and where synthesis effort should be allocated. A role-specialized multi-agent system translates learner feedback into synthesis revisions, while a Designer allocates synthesis directions and a Planner grounds them into executable experience. This process enables within-space adaptation toward weak or under-covered regions and synthesis-space expansion that promotes newly discovered factors into explicit generation controls. Experiments on $τ^2$-Bench and CAR-Bench show that EvoSyn improves average task success by 13.3 points over the strongest synthesis baseline, while producing higher-quality and structurally broader synthetic experience and discovering controllable factors missed without learner feedback.

article.headline: EvoSyn：用学习者反馈重塑合成空间
article.lede: 把数据合成与智能体训练连成闭环，让学习者表现反过来改写合成空间，两个智能体基准上平均任务成功率提升13.3个百分点。
article.problem: 面向交互式智能体的合成数据不只要可执行、可验证、符合领域策略，还必须对当前任务智能体具有学习价值。已有方法会引入环境反馈、数据校验或学习者失败案例，但仍存在「反馈到决策的缺口」：观测到的弱点并不能直接说明未来的合成应当如何改变，也无法判断现有合成空间能否表示这种改变。
article.method: EvoSyn 把合成与学习组织成闭环 S_r→D_r→π_θr+1→F_r→S_r+1：每一轮用一个可修订的合成状态来连接学习者诊断与生成控制，并由角色分工的多个智能体分别承担其中的异质决策（作者称为决策抽象）。学习者反馈随后驱动两种动作——在现有合成空间内做自适应调整，或扩展合成空间本身，从而让合成过程与任务智能体在多轮中共同进化。
article.results: 在 τ²-Bench 与 CAR-Bench 上，EvoSyn 相比最强合成基线平均任务成功率提升 13.3 个百分点；为保证比较一致，所有合成方法的下游任务智能体均为 Qwen3-8B。附录的规模实验中，基座从 Qwen3-8B 扩到 14B、30B，平均成功率由 39.4% 升至 48.6% 和 57.1%，作者称仍有相当的后训练空间。论文材料未给出各基准分项的绝对数值，也未给出每一轮的具体增益。
article.why_it_matters: 它把「合成什么数据」从一次性设计变成随学习者状态演化的决策问题，为智能体后训练提供了一种可复用的闭环范式，而不只是堆更多可执行轨迹。
article.limitations: 评测只覆盖 τ²-Bench 与 CAR-Bench 两个智能体基准，合成侧使用的是 Opus 4.5 这类强闭源模型，闭环轮数与总采样成本在材料中未给出，方法在更弱合成模型下是否仍成立尚不清楚。13.3 个百分点是跨基准平均值，分项提升与方差未见报告，30B 基座上也仍留有较大提升空间。
article.figure_caption_zh: EvoSyn 总览：每一轮实例化一次「合成—学习」闭环，可修订的合成状态居中协调学习者诊断与生成控制，角色分工的智能体产出可验证经验，反馈则驱动空间内自适应或合成空间扩展，使合成与任务智能体共同进化。

Each round instantiates a closed-loop synthesis--learning process in which a revisable synthesis state mediates learner diagnosis and generation control, role-specialized agents realize verified experience, and feedback drives within-space adaptation or synthesis-space expansion to co-evolve synthesis with task-agent learning.

page_papers.title: Agent Sociodrama: Social-Dynamics-Guided Persona Recasting for LLM Agent Teams
page_papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly deployed as teams, yet they fail in characteristically social ways: information holders stay silent, dominant speakers anchor groups on wrong answers, and norm violations go unsanctioned. We present Agent Sociodrama, a framework for modeling and validating evolving social dynamics in LLM agent teams. Under fixed personas, agents' emotional states and directed, asymmetric relationships are updated every round by a unified external LLM judge and shape their subsequent interactions. Across six LLM backbones and five social scenarios, we assess social fidelity through classical social-theory patterns and agreement with human judgments. The resulting trajectories exhibit structured social patterns and model-specific differences. We then introduce Trajectory-Guided Persona Recasting (TPR), which diagnoses group-dynamic failures from interaction transcripts and social trajectories and recasts agent personas before rerunning the task. Across four collaborative benchmarks, TPR improves performance from both heterogeneous and randomly initialized agent persona compositions, yielding up to 83.3%p of accuracy improvement over the initial casting. On representative distributed-information cooperation and mixed-motive bargaining tasks, we outperform SOTOPIA and AgentVerse in three of four comparisons, by up to 37.5%p in Pareto rate. These results show that validated social trajectories provide actionable signals for repairing LLM agent teams.

Corresponding authors.
1
Introduction
Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly deployed in teams
(
Wu et al., 2024
;
Hong et al., 2024
)
: they debate answers
(
Du et al., 2024
)
, pool distributed evidence, teach one another,
negotiate, and manage shared resources. Yet sustained multi-agent
interaction requires more than assigning each agent an initial role.
For a team to function as a social system over time, its members must
form, maintain, and revise relationships in ways that remain coherent
with the interaction. Existing agent systems often encode social
context through static role instructions or unstructured memory,
without an explicit and validated account of how directed relationships
evolve over time.
We take a different route. We argue that longitudinal role play requires treating a team not as a collection of fixed personas, but as a dynamic social system. A persona specifies who an agent is, but not how its relationships with others develop over time, including whom it comes to trust, avoid, align with, or oppose. These relationships must therefore be represented as evolving interaction states. The key challenge is not merely to model changing relations, but to ensure that those changes remain socially faithful over time.
Figure 1:
Motivation and overview of Agent Sociodrama.
Agent Sociodrama models multi-agent interaction through stable personas,
evolving emotions, and directed relationships.
We assess the social fidelity of these dynamics against
social-theory patterns and human judgments, and use social
trajectories to guide team composition optimization for better
collaboration.
To instantiate this idea, we propose Agent Sociodrama, a longitudinal
role-playing framework for LLM agent teams. Agent Sociodrama operationalizes
stable personas together with evolving emotional and relational states,
providing a structured account of how a team’s social configuration
develops over repeated interaction.
These dynamics also matter for task-oriented teams. A growing body of
evidence suggests that LLM teams often fail in ways that resemble
classic small-group pathologies rather than limits of individual model
capability: groups that collectively possess the information required
for a correct decision can still converge on an incorrect one
(
Pappu et al., 2026
;
Li et al., 2026
)
, while individually capable
agents can collectively deplete a shared resource until cooperation
collapses
(
Piatti et al., 2024
)
. These failures have a distinctly
social character. Over repeated interaction, overlooked members can
withdraw, early deference to dominant voices can harden into consensus,
and unchallenged violations can progressively erode cooperation. Yet
dominant approaches to improving multi-agent systems optimize prompts,
topologies, or workflows
(
Zhou et al., 2026
;
Zhang et al., 2025
)
, treating
the team as a black box and leaving the social mechanisms behind these
failures largely unexamined. Building on Agent Sociodrama’s explicit social
trajectories, we further introduce Trajectory-Guided Persona Recasting
(TPR), a casting controller that diagnoses team composition and
recasts personas to seek more effective task-oriented collaboration.
Our empirical study has two parts. First, we assess the social fidelity of Agent Sociodrama across six LLM drivers and five social scenarios, using a shared external LLM judge with human cross-validation. We test whether the resulting trajectories recover four established regularities of social interaction: structural balance
(
Heider, 1946
;
Cartwright & Harary, 1956
)
, reciprocity
(
Gouldner, 1960
)
, conflict-driven polarization
(
Krackhardt & Stern, 1988
)
, and divergent repair-versus-escalation dynamics
(
Gottman, 1994
;
Pruitt & Kim, 2004
)
. These analyses establish Agent Sociodrama as a socially faithful framework for longitudinal multi-agent role play. Second, across four collaborative task families, our controller converts evolving social states into persona recasting decisions that substantially improve team performance. These results demonstrate that socially faithful trajectory modeling can directly inform persona recasting and improve multi-agent collaboration.
Our contributions are:
•
A dynamic multi-agent role-playing framework for LLM teams.
Agent Sociodrama jointly models stable personas, evolving emotional states, and directed, asymmetric relational states, allowing multi-agent interaction to unfold as a sustained social process.
•
Cross-model validation of social fidelity.
Across six LLMs and five social scenarios, we validate
Agent Sociodrama against social theory and human evaluation, showing that its long-horizon relational dynamics are structured, interpretable, and socially coherent.
•
Trajectory-guided team composition optimization.
We use social trajectories to guide persona casting, making team chemistry directly controllable. Across four collaborative task families, our controller substantially improves team performance.
2

We evaluate how faithfully LLMs model emotional and relational dynamics across five scenarios spanning shared-goal coordination to open factional conflict. The scenarios draw on established paradigms in social psychology

They include a hospital ethics review, inheritance dispute, adventurer-party quest, solar-farm negotiation, and demolition standoff. We evaluate six LLM backbones: GPT-4o, GPT-5-mini, Claude Sonnet 4.6, Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite, Grok 4.20, and DeepSeek V4-Flash, with all five agents in each run instantiated by the same backbone. Conclusion
We present Agent Sociodrama, a new framework for modeling and validating evolving social dynamics in LLM agents. We track directed, asymmetric relationships and emotional states, validating cross-model comparability under a unified judge, agreement with classical social theory, and statistical reliability. The casting controller then turns these trajectories into targeted interventions: using relational and emotional trajectories and transcripts, it identifies problematic agents and relationships and recasts their personas, matching or surpassing the strongest manual casting or published reference in collaborative tasks. These results show that social dynamics can serve not only as measurable properties of LLM teams, but also as actionable signals for improving their composition.

Appendix A
Limitations
Several limitations point to future work.
The fidelity evaluation relies on a single unified LLM judge and five designed scenarios; replicating the observed regularities with additional judges and structurally different scenarios would strengthen the external validity of the measurements.
The optimization experiments use 12 episodes per casting, which remains small relative to the variance of LLM interaction; we therefore report consistent directions across tasks, backbones, and initializations rather than per-cell significance claims.
Finally, casting is a coarse, episode-level intervention; the same measured trajectories could drive finer-grained repairs such as runtime mediation, targeted information routing, or norm enforcement, which we view as the natural next step for measurement-driven multi-agent optimization.

Tasks.

Student Council, NASA Moon Survival, and Lost at Sea are information-integration tasks in which decisive knowledge is privately distributed across members; Solar-farm Negotiation is a mixed-motive task in which parties with private preferences must reach a feasible and Pareto-efficient agreement. Each task is played by four agents, Avery, Blake, Casey, and Drew. Private knowledge remains fixed under recasting.In the three information-integration tasks, each episode consists of an individual ranking before discussion, four discussion rounds, and a final individual ranking; the team answer aggregates the four final rankings with a Borda count. article.headline: 用社会动力学轨迹重铸LLM智能体团队角色
article.lede: Agent Sociodrama让情绪与有向关系逐轮演化，并据轨迹重选人格，团队准确率最高提升83.3个百分点。
article.problem: LLM智能体组队时常出现典型的社会性失败：掌握信息者保持沉默，强势发言者把团队锚定在错误答案上，规范违反也无人制裁。现有系统多以静态角色指令或无结构记忆来承载社会语境，缺少对指导性关系如何随时间演化的显式且可验证的刻画。
article.method: 框架为每个智能体保留固定人格，同时由统一的外部LLM评委每轮更新其情绪状态与有向、非对称关系，这些状态再影响后续交互。在此之上，轨迹引导的人格重铸（TPR）从对话记录与社会轨迹中诊断团队失败，重铸智能体人格后重跑任务，最多迭代三次。
article.results: 保真度评估覆盖6个LLM骨干与5个社会场景，共150条团队轨迹、1350个团队级交互轮次。从医院伦理审查到拆迁对峙，平均终局好感度由0.75降至0.23，E-I指数由-0.10变为-2.25，结构平衡由100.0%降至71.7%，修复率由58.5%降至18.9%。在四个协作基准上，TPR从异构与随机两种初始人格出发均带来提升，最高准确率提升83.3个百分点（GPT-5-mini在学生议会任务上由16.7%升至100.0%）；与SOTOPIA、AgentVerse的四项比较中三项占优，Pareto率最高提升37.5个百分点。
article.why_it_matters: 这表明团队“化学”不只是事后描述，而是可测量、可搜索的设计变量，社会轨迹能直接用于定位并修复智能体团队的协作失败。
article.limitations: 保真度评估只依赖单一统一LLM评委和五个设计场景，外部效度有待更多评委与结构不同的场景检验；优化实验每种人格配置仅跑12个episode，作者因此只报告跨任务、骨干与初始化的一致方向，而非逐格显著性，且人格重铸是episode级的粗粒度干预。

page_papers.title: Answering in the User's Variety: Calibrated Accommodation Pairs for Post-Training
page_papers.abstract: People adapt how they talk to the person in front of them. However, chat models tend to respond in Standard English regardless of the dialect used by the user. A uniform answer can hide whether training treats these users alike, and output audits cannot tell as well. We trace how each post-training stage, from supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to preference optimization (DPO) and reinforcement learning, changes a model's tendency to match the user, and read what each update prefers from two content-matched replies, one matching the user and one not. Across 10 open model lineages, post-training standardizes replies to every informal cue, yet after adjusting for how likely each reply already was, the DPO update still favours matching British and Australian spelling over AAE and Singlish on 10 lineages, and models still produce AAE features when asked. We then introduce calibrated accommodation pairs (CAP), preference data that reward matching users' dialect density while preserving Standard English for Standard-English users. On a fully open model, CAP raises convergence on features it was not trained on without a detectable increase in dialect for Standard-English users or a cost in instruction following. In contrast, one-sided pairs reach a similar gain only by overshooting the user and imposing dialect. Our findings show that uniform replies can hide selective updates and audits should read the update as well as the output. Code: https://github.com/kouzhizhuo/cap-accommodation.
page_papers.content:
Abstract
People adapt how they talk to the person in front of them. However, chat models tend to respond in Standard English regardless of the dialect used by the user. A uniform answer can hide whether training treats these users alike, and output audits cannot tell as well. We trace how each post-training stage, from supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to preference optimization (DPO) and reinforcement learning, changes a model’s tendency to match the user, and read what each update prefers from two content-matched replies, one matching the user and one not. Across 10 open model lineages, post-training standardizes replies to every informal cue, yet after adjusting for how likely each reply already was, the DPO update still favours matching British and Australian spelling over AAE and Singlish on all 10 lineages, and models still produce AAE features when asked. We then introduce calibrated accommodation pairs (CAP), preference data that reward matching users’ dialect density while preserving Standard English for Standard-English users. On a fully open model, CAP raises convergence on features it was not trained on without a detectable increase in dialect for Standard-English users or a cost in instruction following. In contrast, one-sided pairs reach a similar gain only by overshooting the user and imposing dialect. Our findings show that uniform replies can hide selective updates and audits should read the update as well as the output. Code:
cap-accommodation
.

Discussion
Output audits find one Standard-English answer for every user; the update diagnostic, read from public checkpoints without retraining, shows training moving the policy toward matching some users and away from others. Model releases should report it next to output audits. The standard default arises with little dialect-specific data (under 1% of preference prompts) and is not inevitable, since deployed chatbots answer Nigerian Pidgin in kind. The prestige ordering in the update is consistent with prestige-directed convergence but does not identify prestige as its cause, and raw and adjusted contrasts answer different questions, so update diagnostics should report both (

Conclusion
Along every released stage of open model lineages, post-training standardizes replies to every informal cue, prestige spelling included, while the training update favours matching prestige spelling over stigmatized varieties, and models still produce AAE features on request; adding accommodation-consistent pairs to a third of the DPO data raises held-out convergence over matched controls in every run, though without calibrating it.
Calibrated accommodation pairs address that failure: on OLMo-2-1B they raise held-out convergence with no detectable increase in dialect for Standard-English users, though explicit requests for Standard English still receive some, whereas one-sided pairs built the same way reach a similar gain only by overshooting the user’s density and imposing it.
Uniform replies can hide a selective update; audits should read the update as well as the output.

article.headline: 后训练抹平方言，更新仍偏爱英式拼写
article.lede: 10 个开源模型谱系显示，后训练把回复统一成标准英语，但 DPO 更新仍偏向英式拼写；作者提出 CAP 偏好数据来校准迁
article.problem: 人会根据对话对象调整说话方式，聊天模型却不论用户用什么方言都回标准英语。统一的回复既掩盖了训练是否在差别对待不同用户，也让只审计输出的做法看不出问题。
article.method: 作者沿 SFT、DPO 到强化学习逐阶段追踪开源模型谱系匹配用户方言的倾向，并从内容配对的「匹配」与「不匹配」两条回复中读出每次更新偏好什么。随后构造校准式迁就配对（CAP）偏好数据，按用户的方言密度给奖励，同时对标准英语用户保留标准英语。实验用 287 条第一人称请求，覆盖六类任务与 150 条正式、137 条随意语境，方言特征由 Multi-VALUE 施加，eWAVE 权重缩放 0.8。
article.results: 在 10 个开源模型谱系上，后训练把所有非正式线索统一为标准英语；校正每条回复原本的似然后，DPO 更新在全部 10 个谱系上仍更偏向匹配英式与澳式拼写，而非 AAE 与 Singlish，方言相关数据在偏好提示中占比不到 1%。在 OLMo-2-1B 上把 CAP 加入三分之一的 DPO 数据后，每个 run 在未训练特征上的 held-out 收敛都相对匹配对照提升，且未检出标准英语用户方言增加或指令遵循变差——论文未给出具体提升幅度数字。单边配对同样能取得相近增益，但代价是超出用户密度、强加方言。
article.why_it_matters: 只审计输出会漏掉训练更新里的选择性偏好：同一个标准英语答案背后，更新可能正在靠近一部分用户、远离另一部分用户。作者主张把从公开 checkpoint 读出的「更新诊断」与输出审计并列发布。
article.limitations: 方言变换未按真实特征密度校准，渲染文本也未做自然度评分；人类审计中 40 对里 25 对被判为同等正式，其余 15 对的 κ=0.196（bootstrap 95% CI [−0.316, 0.700]），低于预设门槛，语域结论只能放附录。作者也指出声望排序与 prestige-directed convergence 一致但无法确定因果，CAP 提升了收敛却未校准密度，显式要求标准英语时仍会收到部分方言。
