page_papers.title: Looking Ahead: Modeling Future Evolution in Autoregressive Video Generation
page_papers.abstract: Autoregressive video diffusion models generate videos chunk by chunk, yet producing plausible continuations does not guarantee that they capture how scenes evolve. Under teacher forcing, strong temporal redundancy may allow local visual continuity to serve as a shortcut for current-chunk denoising, reducing the pressure to model visual evolution. We introduce Future Chunk Prediction (FCP), an auxiliary objective jointly optimized with teacher-forced denoising that predicts temporally separated chunks without access to the intervening visual context. Drawing supervision directly from training videos, FCP requires no additional pretrained visual encoder and leaves autoregressive inference unchanged. Our method achieves superior physical plausibility over standard teacher-forced autoregressive training with a lower overall training compute budget, highlighting the effectiveness and efficiency of future-chunk supervision for modeling visual evolution. Intriguingly, our visualizations suggest that FCP fosters a more structured representation space, which may be valuable for building autoregressive world models.
page_papers.content:
Looking Ahead: Modeling Future Evolution
in Autoregressive Video Generation
Ruopeng Gao
1,∗
, Yukun Huang
2,‡
, Jiarui Hu
3
, Shuai Wang
1
,
Wenbo Hu
2
, Ying Shan
2
, Limin Wang
1,†
1
Nanjing University
2
ARC Lab, Tencent IEG
3
Zhejiang University
Project page:
https://hellorpg.github.io/looking-ahead/
Code:
https://github.com/TencentARC/Looking-Ahead
Abstract
Autoregressive video diffusion models generate videos chunk by chunk, yet producing plausible continuations does not guarantee that they capture how scenes evolve.
Under teacher forcing, strong temporal redundancy may allow local visual continuity to serve as a shortcut for current-chunk denoising, reducing the pressure to model visual evolution.
We introduce Future Chunk Prediction (FCP), an auxiliary objective jointly optimized with teacher-forced denoising that predicts temporally separated chunks without access to the intervening visual context.
Drawing supervision directly from training videos, FCP requires no additional pretrained visual encoder and leaves autoregressive inference unchanged.
Our method achieves superior physical plausibility over standard teacher-forced autoregressive training with a lower overall training compute budget, highlighting the effectiveness and efficiency of future-chunk supervision for modeling visual evolution.
Intriguingly, our visualizations suggest that FCP fosters a more structured representation space, which may be valuable for building autoregressive world models.
1
Introduction
Autoregressive video generation
(
Yang et al., 2025
;
Huang et al., 2025
;
Zhu et al., 2026
;
Yuan et al., 2026
)
has emerged as an important direction in video generation, offering a flexible paradigm in which visual sequences can be extended continuously.
It typically operates through chunk-wise temporal rollout, where each new chunk is generated conditioned on preceding visual context.
As an important pathway toward generative world modeling
(
Bruce et al., 2024
;
Valevski et al., 2025
)
, such a history-conditioned generator is expected not merely to produce plausible successive chunks, but also to model how visual scenes evolve over time.
However, the ability to extend a video does not by itself guarantee that the model has learned how the scene should evolve.
We argue that a key reason is standard teacher forcing, where the current chunk is denoised given ground-truth history.
Due to the strong temporal redundancy in videos, neighboring chunks often share highly similar appearance and motion patterns.
As a result, the model may rely heavily on local visual continuity to recover the current chunk, creating a shortcut that provides limited pressure to capture the underlying dynamics of scene evolution.
This motivates us to seek supervision that goes beyond what can be readily inferred from local visual continuity.
A natural place to look is farther into the future.
As the prediction target moves farther from the observed history, local appearance and motion continuity provide less direct support for recovering the target, thereby placing greater pressure on the model to capture temporal progression.
Importantly, this supervision comes directly from the training video itself, without requiring external pretrained representations or semantic alignment
(
Yu et al., 2025
;
Zhang et al., 2025a
)
.
Motivated by this intuition, we introduce Future Chunk Prediction (FCP), a simple auxiliary objective for autoregressive video diffusion training.
In addition to denoising the target chunk under standard teacher forcing, FCP uses the learned intermediate representation to predict a target beyond the current chunk, without exposing the model to the intervening ground-truth visual context.
This complementary objective places additional training pressure on the learned representations to capture information relevant to visual evolution, a capability fundamental to effective temporal rollout in autoregressive video generation.
Importantly, FCP is introduced only during training and leaves the original autoregressive inference process unchanged.
To assess whether this additional supervision improves the modeling of visual evolution, we focus on physical plausibility as a concrete and challenging evaluation dimension.
Our method demonstrates improved physical plausibility over standard teacher-forced autoregressive training under matched data exposure and training budget, highlighting the effectiveness and efficiency of future-chunk supervision.
These results highlight the potential of exploiting richer predictive supervision from existing video data, rather than relying solely on increased training resources.
Beyond the improvements in generation quality, we further examine how FCP affects the intermediate video representations.
Interestingly, the introduced supervision induces more pronounced spatiotemporal organization in the representation space, suggesting that FCP also meaningfully reshapes the representations learned during training.
This finding highlights the potential of future prediction for learning representations better suited to autoregressive video generation, which may further benefit generative world modeling.
2
Related Work
2.1
Autoregressive Video Diffusion
Conventional video diffusion models typically synthesize fixed-duration clips in a single denoising process
(
Ho et al., 2022
;
Blattmann et al., 2023
;
Team, 2025
;
Wang et al., 2025a
)
.
Autoregressive video diffusion instead extends video chunk by chunk, conditioning on preceding visual context
(
Voleti et al., 2022
;
Chen et al., 2024
;
Teng et al., 2025
)
.
This formulation supports streaming generation and provides a basis for interactive visual simulation and generative world modeling
(
Bruce et al., 2024
;
He et al., 2025
;
Yang et al., 2025
;
Valevski et al., 2025
)
.
Prior work addresses rollout quality by adapting bidirectional models into causal few-step generators through distribution matching or adversarial training
(
Yin et al., 2025
;
Lin et al., 2025
)
, exposing models to self-generated histories or extended student rollouts
(
Huang et al., 2025
;
Cui et al., 2025
;
Liu et al., 2025
)
, and examining the causal compatibility of teacher supervision with student generation
(
Zhu et al., 2026
;
Zheng et al., 2026
)
.
Other approaches manage historical context through active windows, cached states, or global anchors
(
Gao et al., 2025
;
Yang et al., 2025
;
Liu et al., 2025
)
, while selective retrieval and cache compression balance long-range consistency against computational and memory costs
(
Cai et al., 2025
;
Samuel et al., 2026
;
Ji et al., 2026
)
.
Our approach complements these directions by adding future-chunk supervision to teacher-forced training without prescribing rollout distillation or inference-time context management.
2.2
Representation Alignment for Generation
Aligning intermediate diffusion features with vision foundation models can accelerate training and improve generation quality
(
Yu et al., 2025
)
.
Video extensions use cross-frame and multi-feature alignment
(
Hwang et al., 2025
;
Lee et al., 2025
)
, or relational supervision targeting physical plausibility
(
Zhang et al., 2025a
)
.
These methods rely on targets from external pretrained encoders
(
Oquab et al., 2024
;
Wang et al., 2023
)
, which may complicate scaling to large video corpora.
Our approach instead derives supervision from future chunks in the training videos, without an additional pretrained vision model, offering a data-native path toward scaling.
Our work was developed independently of and concurrently with Next Forcing
(
Xu et al., 2026
)
, the closest related approach. We include relevant comparisons in our experiments and provide a more detailed discussion in the appendix.

4.1
Future Chunk Prediction
Building upon the teacher-forced formulation in Section
3.3
, each target chunk is denoised conditioned on its temporally contiguous ground-truth history.
As discussed in Section
1
, the strong temporal redundancy of video allows this immediately preceding correct context to provide substantial support for current-chunk denoising, reducing the pressure to capture temporal progression and potentially hindering the learning of representations that capture visual evolution.
This observation suggests a simple design principle: we seek a learning signal that is less directly supported by such immediately preceding context, yet remains intrinsic to the training video itself, allowing the supervision to scale naturally with video data without relying on external pretrained representations.
To this end, we introduce Future Chunk Prediction (FCP), which supplements next-chunk denoising with an auxiliary task of predicting temporally more distant chunks from the same video.
By excluding the intervening chunks from the visual context, this task discourages reliance on local temporal continuity and encourages stronger predictive representations of visual evolution.

Feature Conditioning.
To capture information at different semantic levels, we extract features from multiple generator layers, concatenate them along the channel dimension at corresponding token positions, and fuse them with an MLP.
Inspired by prior AdaLN-based conditioning designs
(
Wang et al., 2026b
;
Pan et al., 2026
;
Wang et al., 2026a
)
, we inject the fused features into every auxiliary DiT block through token-wise AdaLN modulation, preserving fine-grained conditioning across spatiotemporal positions.
Asymmetric Text Conditioning.
Unlike the text-conditioned main generator, the auxiliary predictors omit text cross-attention from every DiT block.
Consistent with equation
6
, this asymmetry blocks a direct pathway through which text prompts could leak cues about future events, encouraging the predictors to rely on the generator’s source representations instead.
This design also reduces the predictors’ parameter count and computational cost.

At inference, we discard all FCP-specific modules, retaining the same autoregressive generator and rollout procedure as the teacher-forcing baseline without additional overhead.
Qualitative visualizations of the auxiliary predictors suggest that they capture plausible future evolution despite limited visual fidelity.

5
Experiments
5.1
Implementation Details
We initialize our autoregressive generators from official Wan checkpoints
(
Wang et al., 2025a
)
.
For our implementation, we choose the image-to-video setting, treating the initial frame as fixed clean context and generating subsequent chunks of three latent frames.
Each auxiliary predictor contains three DiT blocks initialized from the corresponding generator; the generators and predictors are then jointly optimized.
Further model and training details are provided in Appendix
A
.
5.2
Benchmarks
Modeling visual evolution involves diverse aspects of temporal dynamics, making its comprehensive evaluation an open challenge
(
Li et al., 2025b
;
Ma et al., 2026
;
Wu et al., 2026
)
.
In this work, we focus primarily on physical plausibility
(
Brooks et al., 2024
;
Kang et al., 2025
;
Agarwal et al., 2025
)
, motivated by the availability of dedicated benchmarks and systematic research on its evaluation.
This choice is further motivated by the role of physical plausibility in shaping the perceived realism of generated videos.
We adopt Physics-IQ Verified
(
Rädsch et al., 2026
)
as our primary benchmark because its reference-based numerical metrics assess generated continuations against real-world recordings without relying on VLM-based judgments.
We further evaluate on WorldModelBench
(
Li et al., 2025a
)
, PAI-Bench-G
(
Zhou et al., 2025
)
, and PhyGround
(
Lin et al., 2026
)
as complementary physics-related benchmarks.

Datasets
We train our models on a mixture of internally sourced videos and WISA-80K
(
Wang et al., 2025b
)
, using the original text annotations from each source.
The training data primarily comprises general-purpose real-world videos, without using data from physics simulators.
We select videos longer than five seconds and use approximately the first five seconds, sampled at the default frame rate of the corresponding model.
Incorporating physics-simulator data
(
Aditi et al., 2026
)
may further improve physical plausibility as training scales, but we leave this possibility to future work.

Figure

FCP preserves the direction of domino toppling and captures the water-level rise visible in the ice-melting sequence, whereas the teacher-forcing baseline exhibits an anomalous central collapse in the former and misses the subtle level change in the latter.
Together, these examples suggest that FCP better captures physically plausible visual evolution, which is central to the perceived realism of generated videos.

5.6
Representation Space Analysis
Beyond physical-plausibility evaluation, we visualize the generator’s intermediate representations using query-to-token similarity maps.
As shown in Figure
5
, teacher forcing produces diffuse responses extending into unrelated regions, whereas FCP yields more selective responses aligned with the queried object and visually related instances.
Figure
6
further shows that high-similarity regions remain aligned with corresponding content as it moves across frames.
Together, these visualizations suggest that FCP-trained representations capture clearer spatial structure and meaningful temporal correspondence.
We believe that such semantically structured representations may provide a useful foundation for future world models.
6
Conclusion
We introduced Future Chunk Prediction (FCP), an auxiliary objective that predicts temporally separated chunks from the same training video in autoregressive video diffusion.
Optimized jointly with the standard teacher-forced denoising objective, FCP provides complementary supervision to the generator’s intermediate representations without requiring an additional pretrained encoder.
The auxiliary predictors are removed at inference, leaving the autoregressive generation process unchanged.
Controlled comparisons show improved physical plausibility across model scales and conditioning settings.
More surprisingly, our visualizations suggest that FCP also induces a more structured representation space, which we believe may be important for autoregressive world models.
Together, these findings support future prediction as a promising training principle for autoregressive video generation.

The 1.3B and 5B configurations may appear to follow different design principles.
These differences arise from choices made at different stages of development.
For source-layer selection, the 1.3B configuration evolved from an early single-layer variant using layer 15, subsequently expanded to include both shallower and deeper features.
For the 5B model, we select approximately evenly spaced layers backward from the final block to provide direct auxiliary supervision across the generator’s depth, while excluding the earliest blocks whose features may not yet be sufficiently semantically informative.
Computational constraints have prevented a systematic comparison of these source-layer selection strategies, which we may revisit in future scaling efforts.
For auxiliary initialization, the 1.3B configuration follows the early variant using source features from layer 15, with blocks 17–19 used to initialize the auxiliary predictor.
For the 5B model, we instead initialize from the final backbone blocks, decoupling this choice from the source-layer configuration and simplifying subsequent scale-up.
These blocks are also closer to the output and are chosen to better match the output head, which is likewise initialized from the original generator.
Preliminary experiments suggest that this initialization strategy may offer a modest improvement in early-stage convergence.

Appendix C
Limitations and Discussions
C.1
Comparison with Next Forcing
As discussed in Section
2.2
, Next Forcing
(
Xu et al., 2026
)
explores a closely related future-prediction idea.
Importantly, our work was developed independently of and concurrently with Next Forcing
(
Xu et al., 2026
)
. The initial FCP prototype design was completed before the Next Forcing paper became publicly available. While both works explore future prediction for autoregressive video generation, we target different tasks and adopt distinct methodological and experimental designs. First, Next Forcing is primarily framed around world-action modeling and robotic action learning, whereas we focus on autoregressive video generation as a pathway toward generative world modeling.
Conditioning Context and Efficiency.
Second, Next Forcing conditions its auxiliary predictors on the full visible history
𝐡
≤
k
\mathbf{h}_{\leq k}
, whereas ours use only
𝐡
k
\mathbf{h}_{k}
. As discussed in Section
4.1
, this choice encourages the source-chunk representation itself to compactly encode information predictive of future evolution. Beyond this design rationale, we test the context choice with a full-context FCP variant shown in Figure
4
. At matched training steps, the two FCP variants achieve comparable IQ scores, but ours requires roughly 40–50% less training compute to attain the same performance. Our source-chunk-only design thus offers a more efficient and scalable form of future-prediction supervision, an important consideration when training larger video generators.
Parallel versus Chained Prediction.
Third, Next Forcing adopts a chained prediction architecture inspired by language-model MTP
(
DeepSeek-AI, 2024
)
, whereas our offset-specific predictors operate in parallel from
𝐡
k
\mathbf{h}_{k}
. Unlike discrete-token prediction, diffusion-based video prediction gives each auxiliary predictor a partially noised future latent. Chaining may therefore pass information from an intermediate future chunk to later predictors along the red path in Figure
2(a)
, weakening the intended predictive supervision on
𝐡
k
\mathbf{h}_{k}
.
Consistent with this concern, the chained variant retains a gain at 1.3B with three offsets, but offers only a marginal I2V gain and no V2V gain at 5B models. This decline suggests that information leakage in chained prediction may become more consequential at larger model scales, as higher-capacity models can more readily exploit intermediate future information and thereby weaken the intended supervision.
Parallel prediction, by contrast, remains effective in both settings (Tables
4
and
2
), supporting its use for visual future prediction.
Other Differences.
Our different task emphasis also shapes several design and evaluation choices.
We supervise both clean-context and noisy-target representations, and use token-wise AdaLN to inject source features into the auxiliary predictors, drawing on prior experience in visual generation
(
Wang et al., 2026b
;
Pan et al., 2026
)
.
Our evaluation focuses on the physical plausibility of generated videos, reflecting our interest in visual evolution rather than action-planning performance.
C.2
Potential Inference-Time Applications
Figure
11
suggests that the auxiliary predictors can anticipate future dynamics, although their outputs do not yet reach the visual fidelity expected of final video generation.
Replacing the main generator with these branches throughout denoising may therefore compromise output quality.
One possibility is to use them during early, high-noise denoising before handing the sample to the main generator for refinement, potentially reducing sampling cost.
Alternatively, combining their predictions with those of the main generator may improve the reliability of the resulting future evolution.
These inference-time applications remain untested and are left for future work.
C.3
From-Scratch Pretraining and Further Scaling
Due to computational constraints, our experiments do not cover larger model scales or training on substantially longer videos.
We therefore leave broader scaling and evaluation across longer temporal horizons to future work.
All current models are initialized from pretrained bidirectional video diffusion checkpoints rather than pretrained from scratch.
In our experiments, adapting these checkpoints for autoregressive training led to early-stage performance degradation.
We suspect that bidirectional and autoregressive models may organize their representations differently, so this initialization could limit the extent to which FCP’s benefits emerge.
We aim to investigate large-scale from-scratch pretraining with FCP as a native objective for autoregressive world models, together with more diverse, higher-quality data tailored to this setting.

article.headline: 用未来块预测约束自回归视频生成
article.lede: 南大与腾讯ARC提出FCP：训练时让模型预测被隔开的未来块，推理流程不变，物理合理性提升。
article.problem: 自回归视频扩散模型按块逐步生成，但标准教师强制训练下，当前块去噪可以依赖真实且紧邻的历史块。由于视频存在强时间冗余，局部外观与运动连续性足以构成一条「捷径」，模型因此缺少建模场景如何演化的压力。能生成看似合理的后续片段，并不等于学到了视觉演化规律。
article.method: 作者提出未来块预测（FCP）作为与教师强制去噪联合优化的辅助目标：从同一训练视频中取时间上相隔 Δ 个块的未来块作为预测目标，且不把中间块作为条件输入，从而削弱对局部连续性的依赖。实现上用一个参数独立的轻量DiT辅助预测器，以生成器第 k 块的中间隐状态（clean 与 noisy 两种）为条件，通过逐token AdaLN 注入特征，并去掉文本交叉注意力以防文本泄露未来信息。辅助损失经隐状态回传至生成器，推理时全部FCP模块被丢弃，不增加开销。
article.results: 在 Physics-IQ Verified 上，1.3B 模型的 IQ 从教师强制的 27.6 提升到 30.9；5B 模型的图生视频（I2V）从 30.4 提升到 33.8，视频生视频（V2V）从 40.6 提升到 44.4。消融显示，只正则化 clean 上下文或 noisy 目标分别带来 1.2 和 2.3 分提升，二者合用提升 3.3 分；链式预测版本在 5B 上仅有微弱 I2V 增益且 V2V 无提升。在达到相同 IQ 29 与 30 时，作者的 h_k 条件方案比全历史 h_≤k 变体分别少用 42.6% 与 50.7% 的训练算力。其他基准上，WorldModelBench 总分从 7.22 升至 7.64，PAI-Bench-G 域分数从 81.13 升至 82.38，PhyGround 物理项从 2.75 升至 2.80。
article.why_it_matters: 它提示一条不依赖外部预训练视觉编码器、直接从视频数据本身获取监督的训练路径，并可作为一种面向自回归世界模型的表征正则化手段。
article.limitations: 实验仅覆盖图像生视频设定，模型全部从 Wan 双向预训练 checkpoint 初始化而非从零预训练，作者也承认这种初始化可能限制 FCP 收益；训练数据含不可公开的内部视频，精确复现受限，且评测集中在物理合理性这一维度，VLM 评判类基准对物理变化时序不够敏感，部分指标增益有限。

page_papers.title: Memory-Centric Continual Learning for AI Agents
page_papers.abstract: Autonomous agents powered by foundation models can reason, plan, and use tools, but their fixed weights and context limits hinder sustained learning from experience over long-term deployment. While external memory systems attempt to bridge this gap, they mostly act as passive retrieval caches, evaluated primarily by whether they can recall stored facts or past interactions. Whether memory can drive genuine continual learning remains an open question. In this paper, we introduce Memory-Centric Continual Learning (MCCL), arguing that memory should be judged by whether it improves future actions, not merely what it retrieves. MCCL has three main parts. First, a three-axis taxonomy organizes memory by where state is stored (substrates), what form it takes (assets), and how it is managed (policies). This defines a two-loop lifecycle that updates memory state in an inner loop while refining management policies in an outer loop based on task feedback. Second, an evaluation protocol measures retention under interference, adaptation to change, and task transfer to isolate genuine behavioral gains from simple context expansion. Third, a memory scaling framework models how agent performance scales with experience, storage capacity, and compute budgets across non-parametric and parametric memory. Together, these components reframe agent memory from passive lookup to continuous learning, offering a principled route toward self-improving autonomous agents.

Abstract
Autonomous agents powered by foundation models can reason, plan, and use tools, but their fixed weights and context limits hinder sustained learning from experience over long-term deployment. While external memory systems attempt to bridge this gap, they mostly act as passive retrieval caches, evaluated primarily by whether they can recall stored facts or past interactions. Whether memory can drive genuine continual learning remains an open question. In this paper, we introduce
Memory-Centric Continual Learning

Second, an evaluation protocol measures retention under interference, adaptation to change, and task transfer to isolate genuine behavioral gains from simple context expansion. Third, a memory scaling framework models how agent performance scales with experience, storage capacity, and compute budgets across non-parametric and parametric memory. Together, these components reframe agent memory from passive lookup to continuous learning, offering a principled route toward self-improving autonomous agents.
Non-parametric memory

Conclusion

Empirical Study
Experimental Protocol & Controls

Consolidation
: Replay, abstract, and bake verified memories into model weights via modular adapters.

Conclusion
In this paper, we reframe agent memory as an evolving learning
infrastructure for continual learning, rather than a passive storage or
retrieval component. We argue that experience accumulation cannot be equated
with static recall, but requires a closed-loop dynamic of retention,
adaptation, and transfer, explaining why current memory agents fail under
delay, interference, and environmental drift. To address this, we establish
a unified framework spanning physical substrates, reusable assets, and
lifecycle policies, coupled with a behavior-centric evaluation methodology
to isolate genuine experiential gains and a memory scaling law that relates
those gains to experience and memory resources. By adopting this memory-centric
lens, the field shifts its central question from whether an agent can
remember to whether it can continually learn, paving a more principled path
towards building resilient, self-improving intelligent systems.

article.headline: 把智能体记忆当作持续学习系统来评估
article.lede: 论文提出以记忆为中心的持续学习框架MCCL，主张用记忆是否改善未来行动来评判它，而非只看检索准确率。
article.problem: 基于基础模型的智能体能够推理、规划和调用工具，但权重固定、上下文有限，难以在长期部署中持续从经验里学习。现有的外部记忆系统大多只是被动的检索缓存，评价标准停留在能否回忆起存过的事实或历史交互。记忆能否真正驱动持续学习，仍是一个未解的问题。
article.method: 作者提出以记忆为中心的持续学习（MCCL），用三个维度组织记忆：状态存在哪里（substrate）、以什么形式存在（asset）、如何被管理（policy），并由此定义一个双环生命周期——内环更新记忆状态，外环依据任务反馈改进管理策略。配套一套评测协议，分别测量干扰下的保持、对变化的适应和任务迁移，以把真实的行为收益与单纯的上下文扩张区分开。此外还提出记忆扩展框架，刻画智能体性能如何随经验量、存储容量和算力预算变化，覆盖非参数化与参数化记忆。
article.results: 论文未给出具体数字：材料中没有报告任何实验结果或性能指标。从框架层面看，作者给出的是3维记忆分类法、2层循环生命周期，以及由保持、适应、迁移3项构成的评测协议；记忆扩展框架也只是建模思路，未提供拟合或验证数据。
article.why_it_matters: 它把智能体记忆的核心问题从「能不能记住」换成「能不能持续学习」，为构建可自我改进的智能体提供了一个可操作的评测与设计视角。
article.limitations: 从现有材料看，这是一篇立场与框架型论文，缺少实证结果来支撑「现有记忆智能体在延迟、干扰和环境漂移下失败」这一论断。所提评测协议和记忆扩展框架是否可实际测量、能否在不同任务上复现，仍有待验证。
article.figure_caption_zh: 图示将记忆为中心的持续学习刻画为一个耦合动力系统：任务流产生结果反馈，经验以情景、语义和程序性资产的形式跨上下文、激活、外部与参数化基质持久存在，内环对记忆状态进行形成、巩固、再激活与修正，外环则利用任务反馈更新记忆管理策略。

figure.caption: Memory-centric continual learning as a coupled dynamical system. A task stream is executed by the agent and produces outcome feedback. Experience is organized as episodic, semantic, and procedural assets that persist across contextual, activation, external, and parametric substrates. An inner memory-state loop forms, consolidates, reactivates, and revises these assets, while prescribed, deliberative, or learned policies govern the corresponding operations. An outer policy-adaptation loop uses task feedback to update memory management.

page_papers.title: DONIC: Generalist Dexterous Bimanual Tracking Control from Human Demonstrations
page_papers.abstract: Despite recent progress in dexterous reference tracking, existing models focus primarily on single-hand manipulation and a limited range of interactions, leaving the bimanual dexterous behaviors common in real life unaddressed. The scarcity of contact-rich bimanual manipulation data and the increased complexity of coordinating contacts make developing a generalist bimanual tracker particularly challenging. Therefore, we present 1) DONIC, the first generalist bimanual tracker jointly trained across operation categories and human-motion sources, together with 2) BiHOI, a multi-view dataset of 1,575 sequences spanning 229 objects and emphasizing sustained bimanual interaction, where reconstructed interactions are retargeted into robot references. DONIC combines proximal policy optimization with behavioral cloning in a feedback loop that recycles verified successful executions into training demonstrations. An object-centered per-hand reward maintains object-motion feedback while supervising each hand according to its reference contact role. Clip-Centered Advantages remove reference-dependent advantage offsets while preserving within-trajectory differences. Together, these designs enable one single policy to learn coordinated manipulation across heterogeneous references. Without finetuning, a single checkpoint achieves 86.79% success on unseen trajectories of training objects and 57.32% on held-out objects, surpassing the state-of-the-art bimanual tracking baselines by 77.36 and 45.73 percentage points.

Dexterous manipulation supports household assistance, industrial assembly, and assistive care. Unlike gripper-based manipulation, it requires precise coordination of finger motions and changing hand–object contacts to grasp, reorient, and reposition objects

Unequal clip difficulty also creates advantage offsets that can weaken updates for useful actions in harder sequences. 6
Conclusion, Limitations and Future Work
We presented
DONIC
, a generalist bimanual tracker, and BiHOI, a multi-view bimanual interaction dataset. Object-centered per-hand rewards and CCA support iterative PPO+BC training, yielding one checkpoint that generalizes to unseen trajectories and objects without fine-tuning and substantially outperforms adapted baselines. Ablations support both learning signals and the benefit of additional BiHOI data.
However, our quantitative evaluation focuses on simulated single-object interactions and relies on reconstructed, retargeted motion references.
We aim to extend
DONIC
to longer-horizon and multi-object manipulation, evaluate on an independent benchmark, and investigate transfer to physical bimanual systems.

Appendix A
Additional Related Work
Executable human references and shared control.
Human demonstrations provide motion targets but do not directly specify robot actions: differences in hand kinematics and simulated contact can make a kinematically plausible reference physically difficult to execute. Reference-based trackers address this gap through closed-loop control. DexTrack
[
19
]
combines trajectory-specific demonstration generation with generalist learning; Dexplore
[
38
]
expands exploration around reference motions; and AdaDexTrack
[
1
]
combines specialist distillation with reference modulation. Our reference-conditioned action interface and iterative reinforcement–imitation learning loop build on this line of work. Our contributions within that loop are the object-centered per-hand reward and Clip-Centered Advantages (CCA), designed for shared bimanual tracking across heterogeneous references.
What generalization means here.
Generalization across grasped objects, manipulation skills, and complete reference trajectories imposes different requirements. UniDexGrasp++
[
33
]
studies generalizable dexterous grasping, while BiDexHD
[
43
]
learns trajectory-conditioned bimanual policies within operation categories. Our controller is jointly trained across operation categories and human-motion sources. We evaluate new trajectories of training objects and trajectories involving held-out objects with the same checkpoint. These two splits test reference and object generalization; they do not, by themselves, establish generalization to held-out operation categories or arbitrary manipulation goals.
Interaction capture and usable control data.
GRAB, GigaHands, OakInk2, TACO, and H2O provide complementary sources of hand–object interaction
[
32
,
10
,
41
,
20
,
13
]
. HOI4D and HO-Cap further broaden capture settings and annotation tools
[
21
,
34
]
. Our comparison distinguishes the inventory of a source dataset from the subset retained for robot training. A clip enters our bimanual pool only if the required hand and object tracks are available and both hands contact the object at some point. This allows sequential as well as simultaneous hand participation. BiHOI complements these sources with a higher measured proportion of simultaneous bimanual contact in the analyzed recordings.

Single-object representation.
For multi-object recordings, conversion retains one primary object: TACO keeps the tool rather than the target, and OakInk2 selects the main object from its hand-role program annotations. The controller represents the selected object by a fixed mesh and a rigid pose. Articulation and deformation are not modeled explicitly, even when the captured object belongs to those categories.
B.2
Multi-View Reconstruction and Annotation
The reconstruction pipeline uses learned image predictions to initialize geometry, then calibrated multi-view observations to recover physical scale and temporal consistency. Its five stages are mask/depth extraction, object reconstruction and tracking, participant-specific hand calibration, hand-motion reconstruction, and joint refinement. Figure
S1
summarizes the complete calibrated multi-view reconstruction and annotation pipeline.
Figure S1:
Reconstruction and annotation pipeline.
Synchronized multi-view RGB observations are processed to obtain SAM3 object masks and metric depth maps. The object branch performs metric reconstruction followed by robust multi-view 6D tracking, while the hand branch performs participant-specific hand calibration and multi-view hand-pose reconstruction. The two branches are finally refined jointly using depth-guided hand–object optimization.

article.headline: DONIC：单一策略实现双手灵巧参考跟踪
article.lede: 首个跨操作类别与人类动作来源联合训练的双手灵巧参考跟踪器 DONIC 提出，并配套 1575 条序列的 BiHOI 数据
article.problem: 现有灵巧参考跟踪模型多集中在单手操作，难以覆盖日常生活中普遍存在的双手协作行为。双手接触丰富的数据稀缺，且一个共享策略还需应对两只手角色不同、接触时机异步的协调难题。
article.method: 作者用 32 个校准 RGB 相机采集构建 BiHOI 多视角手物交互数据集，重建双手与物体后重定向为机器人参考，并与公开数据混合成训练池。DONIC 以 PPO 加行为克隆的迭代闭环训练单一双手策略，把验证成功的执行回收进示范库。方法核心是物体中心的逐手奖励与 Clip-Centered Advantages（CCA）：前者按参考接触角色分别监督每只手，后者在 GAE 后减去每个片段的优势均值，去除参考难度带来的偏移。
article.results: 在 unseen-traj 上，DONIC 单检查点达到 86.79% 成功率（SR）和 67.62% 完成度（Comp），比更强的 Dexplore-bi 基线分别高 77.36 和 39.75 个百分点；在 unseen-obj 上达到 57.32% SR 和 54.69% Comp。加入全部 1575 条 BiHOI 序列后，两个 split 的 SR 升至 88.68% 和 59.76%，Comp 为 68.72% 和 55.35%，未见物体平移误差从 15.74 cm 降到 13.96 cm。消融中移除 CCA 使 SR 从 86.79% 降到 81.13%（unseen-traj）、从 57.32% 降到 48.17%（unseen-obj）。
article.why_it_matters: 这是首个跨操作类别与人类动作来源联合训练的双手参考跟踪器，单一检查点无需微调即可泛化到新轨迹与新物体。它把双手协作中的接触角色与片段难度差异显式纳入奖励和优势估计，为通用双手操作策略提供了可复用的训练范式。
article.limitations: 定量评估仅限仿真中的单刚体物体跟踪，参考来自重建并重定向的人类动作，接触监督使用净力加距离的代理，重建阶段没有显式接触或碰撞损失。作者也承认尚未验证留出操作类别、长时程与多物体场景，以及向真实机器人系统的迁移。
article.figure_caption_zh: DONIC 流程：BiHOI 多视角采集重建重定向后与公开数据构成训练池，单一双手策略在 PPO+BC 迭代闭环中学习，物体中心的逐手奖励、CCA 与行为克隆提供互补信号。

figure.caption: {Overview of .} {Top:} BiHOI captures are reconstructed and retargeted, then combined with public-data references to form the training pool. {Middle:} A shared bimanual policy learns through simulated interaction and verified demonstrations in an iterative PPO+BC loop. {Bottom:} An object-centered per-hand reward, Clip-Centered Advantages (CCA), and behavioral cloning provide complementary learning signals.

page_papers.title: Latent Bridge: From Video Latents to 3D Geometry via Feature Alignment
page_papers.abstract: Video generation and feed-forward 3D reconstruction typically use separate representations, requiring RGB decoding and visual re-encoding to recover geometry from generated latents. We propose Latent Bridge, which connects video generative latent spaces with geometric feature spaces to directly predict 3D geometry from video latents. We develop representation-specific bridges for Wan2.1 and V-RAE, enabling feed-forward prediction of cameras, depth, and 3D point clouds without the intermediate RGB pathway. Each bridge is trained on RGB videos through feature distillation, while the video encoder and geometry model remain frozen. Training requires neither ground-truth geometry nor execution of the downstream geometric aggregator or prediction heads. At inference, the same video latents support both RGB decoding and geometry prediction. The same trained bridge can be reused for image-to-video and text-to-video generation within the same video latent space, without bridge retraining. Experiments on Co3Dv2 and WildRGB-D demonstrate competitive geometric reconstruction quality, efficient end-to-end generation and reconstruction, and faster latent-to-geometry decoding, highlighting latent alignment as a practical and reusable interface between video generation and 3D reconstruction. Our code is available at: https://github.com/hustvl/Latent-Bridge.
page_papers.content:
Latent Bridge: From Video Latents to 3D Geometry via Feature Alignment
Shuai Zhang, Zhanpeng Ouyang, Zhengqing Chen,
Ruohong Mei, Shaoyu Chen, Weiqiang Ren, Hui Sun,
Qian Zhang, Wenyu Liu, Xinggang Wang
Huazhong University of Science and Technology
Horizon Robotics
{shuaizhang,xgwang}@hust.edu.cn
Project leader
 Corresponding author
Abstract
Video generation and feed-forward 3D reconstruction typically use separate representations, requiring RGB decoding and visual re-encoding to recover geometry from generated latents. We propose Latent Bridge, which connects video generative latent spaces with geometric feature spaces to directly predict 3D geometry from video latents. We develop representation-specific bridges for Wan2.1 and V-RAE, enabling feed-forward prediction of cameras, depth, and 3D point clouds without the intermediate RGB pathway. Each bridge is trained on RGB videos through feature distillation, while the video encoder and geometry model remain frozen. Training requires neither ground-truth geometry nor execution of the downstream geometric aggregator or prediction heads. At inference, the same video latents support both RGB decoding and geometry prediction. The same trained bridge can be reused for image-to-video and text-to-video generation within the same video latent space, without bridge retraining. Experiments on Co3Dv2 and WildRGB-D demonstrate competitive geometric reconstruction quality, efficient end-to-end generation
and reconstruction, and faster latent-to-geometry decoding,
highlighting latent alignment as a practical and reusable
interface between video generation and 3D reconstruction. Our code is available at: https://github.com/hustvl/Latent-Bridge.
1
Introduction
Recent advances in video generation and feed-forward 3D reconstruction
have enabled compelling visual synthesis and efficient geometric inference.
Video generation models, such as CogVideoX
(
Yang et al., 2025
)
and Wan2.1
(
Wan et al., 2025
)
, combine spatiotemporally compressed
latent representations with diffusion transformers to synthesize
high-quality, temporally coherent videos.
Meanwhile, feed-forward reconstruction models, such as
VGGT
(
Wang et al., 2025
)
, jointly predict camera parameters,
depth maps, and 3D point maps from multi-view images in a single forward pass.
Recent work has begun to explore the joint execution of these two tasks: generating videos while simultaneously reconstructing the generated content.
Despite their complementary goals, video generation and feed-forward
3D reconstruction typically rely on different representations.
Video generators synthesize content in spatiotemporally compressed
latent spaces, whereas reconstruction models often aggregate
features from visual foundation models such as
DINOv2
(
Oquab et al., 2024
)
to infer scene geometry.
This representational gap means that combining the two models
typically involves decoding generated latents into RGB frames
and re-encoding them into geometric features, introducing
additional computation. This raises the question:
Can scene geometry be generated directly without RGB decoding?
Recent work has begun to integrate video generation with explicit geometry prediction. Gen3R
(
Huang et al., 2026
)
compresses intermediate VGGT features into geometric latents, aligns their distribution with video appearance latents, and fine-tunes a video diffusion model to jointly generate both. As shown in Fig.
1
(a), joint generation in a shared latent space requires additional training and can reduce efficiency due to the increased number of tokens.
FantasyWorld
(
Dai et al., 2026
)
introduces a geometric branch into video generation. VGGRPO
(
An et al., 2026
)
uses latent-space geometry predictions to construct rewards for video model post-training, while Beyond Pixels
(
Liu et al., 2026
)
combines latent alignment, LoRA adaptation, and geometry-supervised fine-tuning of prediction heads for direct latent-to-4D prediction. As shown in Fig.
1
(b), these methods all aim to train a 3D/4D decoder module, requiring substantial data and retraining of the decoder, while also raising concerns about generalization.
Unlike the aforementioned methods, we argue that the key lies in aligning the generative and reconstruction latent spaces. We propose Latent Bridge, which directly maps video latents into the representation space of a frozen feed-forward geometry model (Fig.
1
(c)). The frozen downstream VGGT aggregator and depth head can then be used to reconstruct the scene. This provides an elegant solution that eliminates the need for joint feature training or training downstream decoder heads. It also generalizes well, enabling the reuse of existing generative models and downstream tasks built on the same representation. Specifically, we adapt our framework to two representative video encoders, the Wan2.1 VAE and V-RAE
(
Guo et al., 2026
)
, by designing a dedicated Bridge network for each. This enables models built upon either encoder to directly generate scene geometry.
Figure 1:
Bypass the video decoder and directly align latent spaces to generate 3D outputs.
Our contributions can be summarized as follows:
•
We propose Latent Bridge, which aligns the generative latent space with the representation space of a reconstruction model, enabling geometry to be recovered directly from generated latents. The Bridge module is trained through feature distillation and requires only video data for training. This substantially reduces the cost of recovering geometry from the latent spaces of generative models.
•
We adapt our framework to two video encoders, Wan2.1 and V-RAE, by designing a dedicated Latent Bridge network for each. Both variants achieve strong performance, demonstrating that the Latent Bridge framework can effectively accommodate different generative latent spaces.
•
Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed Latent Bridge enables high-quality and efficient reconstruction. It also exhibits strong generalization: within the same latent space, it can support generative models designed for different generation tasks, as well as other downstream tasks, without retraining.
2
Related Work
Generative latent space.
Modern video generation models commonly extend latent diffusion to the
spatiotemporal domain, where a video VAE compresses RGB frames into compact
latent representations and a diffusion transformer models their temporal
dynamics. Stable Video Diffusion
(
Blattmann et al., 2023
)
establishes a
scalable latent video diffusion framework, while
HunyuanVideo
(
Kong et al., 2024
)
demonstrates the effectiveness of
large diffusion transformers and progressive training for high-fidelity video
generation. Wan2.1
(
Wan et al., 2025
)
follows this paradigm and combines a
causal spatiotemporal VAE with a diffusion transformer to support both
text-to-video and image-to-video generation. REPA
(
Yu et al., 2025
)
and VA-VAE
(
Yao et al., 2025
)
align diffusion features and VAE latents, respectively, with pretrained
visual representations to improve generative modeling.
RAE
(
Zheng et al., 2026
)
directly adopts frozen visual encoders,
while V-RAE
(
Guo et al., 2026
)
extends this paradigm to video through
temporal pooling.
Feed-forward reconstruction.
DUSt3R
(
Wang et al., 2024
)
formulates 3D reconstruction as pointmap
regression, jointly predicting dense 3D points for an image pair in a
shared coordinate frame without requiring known camera parameters.
Moving beyond pairwise prediction,
VGGT
(
Wang et al., 2025
)
, built upon a DINOv2-pretrained visual
encoder
(
Oquab et al., 2024
)
, jointly predicts camera parameters,
depth maps, 3D point maps, and point tracks from multiple RGB images
in a single forward pass, without per-scene optimization. VGGT-
Ω
\Omega
(
Wang et al., 2026
)
further initializes its trainable visual backbone from
DINOv3
(
Siméoni et al., 2026
)
and introduces scene registers, register
attention, and a shared dense prediction head. Together with large-scale
self-supervised video training, these designs improve the scalability and
efficiency of feed-forward geometry reconstruction for both static and
dynamic scenes.
Joint generative-reconstructive method
Recent work has explored video and 3D co-generation through complementary approaches. FantasyWorld
(
Dai et al., 2026
)
couples video and geometry latents through a trainable geometry branch on a frozen Wan2.1 backbone, while LYRA
(
Bahmani et al., 2026
)
introduces a self-distilled 3D Gaussian decoder. Gen3R
(
Huang et al., 2026
)
jointly generates video and geometry in a unified latent space, whereas PixWorld
(
Gao et al., 2026a
)
operates in pixel space to avoid VAE-induced detail loss. VGGT-World
(
Sun et al., 2026
)
instead forecasts geometry-centric VGGT tokens and decodes future geometry using frozen heads, without synthesizing RGB frames. VGGRPO
(
An et al., 2026
)
uses latent-space geometry predictions to construct rewards for video DiT post-training, while Beyond Pixels
(
Liu et al., 2026
)
directly decodes geometry from video latents. VIST3A
(
Go et al., 2026
)
connects video latents to a selected intermediate reconstruction layer and jointly trains the stitching layer and downstream LoRA adapters using teacher-predicted geometry. Pano2World
(
Li et al., 2026
)
aligns diffusion hidden features with a pretrained reconstruction model’s token space through feature distillation, followed by joint fine-tuning of the adapter and Gaussian decoder under rendering supervision. In contrast, we map video latents to a predefined geometric feature interface through feature alignment, keeping the downstream geometric aggregator and prediction heads entirely frozen.
3
Preliminaries
3.1
Video Latent Representations
Video generation models typically use an encoder to compress videos into a latent space. We define an RGB video with
T
T
frames, height
H
H
, and width
W
W
as
𝐗
∈
ℝ

\mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times 3\times H\times W}
.
In this paper, we focus on two types of VAEs: the convolutional VAE used in Wan2.1
(
Wan et al., 2025
)
and the representation-based autoencoder V-RAE
(
Guo et al., 2026
)
.
Wan2.1 VAE.
Wan2.1
(
Wan et al., 2025
)
employs a causal spatiotemporal VAE with a spatial compression factor of
8

and
16

We propose an alignment framework between generative latents and the representations of a feed-forward geometry model, which we term the
Latent Bridge
. The key idea is to jointly support video generation and 3D reconstruction by aligning generative and reconstruction representations, without retraining the existing vision autoencoder, generative model, or 3D reconstruction heads. For the Wan2.1 VAE and V-RAE, we design distinct Latent Bridge networks and develop a corresponding training procedure, as illustrated in Fig.
2
. At inference, the bridge enables the frozen geometry model to predict 3D geometry directly from generated video latents.

Ablation study and Generalization Evaluation
Parameter settings.
In this ablation study, we investigate how bridge capacity affects latent-space alignment. As shown in Fig.
4
, we vary only the internal hidden width of the bridge network to control its capacity, keeping all other settings fixed within each model family. For the Wan Bridge, widths of 256, 512, and 768 yield 9.11M, 35.65M, and 79.62M trainable parameters, respectively. For the VRAE Bridge, we vary the hidden width of the spatial mapping MLP and temporal FFN across 1024, 2048, 4096, and 6144, yielding 12.61M, 16.80M, 25.20M, and 33.59M parameters. All alignment variants are trained from scratch on a mixture of four datasets and evaluated for teacher-depth consistency on a fixed set of 64 validation videos. We compute teacher-normalized L1 and AbsRel over all pixels in all 49 frames, without foreground masking or prediction-scale fitting.

We conduct structural ablations of the Bridge on the Wan branch. Starting from the full Bridge, we separately replace spatial packing with average pooling, causal phase expansion with fixed linear interpolation, and spatiotemporal mixing with a token-wise MLP to assess each component’s contribution.
All variants are trained from scratch using the same training data, frozen Wan encoder, VGGT-

We evaluate them at matched training steps on a fixed validation set of 64 videos, each containing 49 frames, using full-image teacher-normalized L1 and depth AbsRel to measure depth distillation consistency. Conclusion
We presented Latent Bridge, a framework that connects video generation and feed-forward 3D reconstruction through latent-space feature alignment. By mapping Wan2.1 and V-RAE video representations to a predefined geometric feature interface, our method enables direct prediction of cameras, depth, and point clouds while keeping the downstream geometric model frozen. This design bypasses RGB decoding and visual re-encoding in the geometry branch, allowing a shared video latent representation to support both video synthesis and geometry prediction. Experiments on Co3Dv2 and WildRGB-D demonstrate competitive reconstruction quality with improved inference efficiency. More broadly, our results suggest that feature alignment offers a practical route to reusing pretrained geometric models with generative video representations.

A.1
Comparison with Existing Methods
As shown in Tab.
5
, we compare our method with existing approaches from two perspectives: compatibility with existing models and training overhead. Cross-DiT checkpoint reuse refers to whether the method can produce 3D outputs using different generative DiT checkpoints without retraining. FantasyWorld trains a geometry branch and cross-branch adapters while keeping the video backbone frozen, whereas Gen3R fine-tunes the video DiT to jointly generate appearance and geometry latents. Beyond Pixels and our method instead learn geometry pathways from video latents without updating the DiT, enabling reuse across compatible generators that share the same VAE checkpoint and latent conventions. We demonstrate this reuse by applying the same Wan Bridge checkpoint to camera-conditioned generation and the official Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B model without additional Bridge training. Pretrained task-head reuse refers to the ability to reuse existing downstream heads because our method outputs features in VGGT’s DINO feature space. Consequently, the resulting features can be used not only for reconstruction with VGGT but also for cross-view segmentation with VGGT-S, as shown in Section
A.2
. Gen3R reconstructs intermediate VGGT geometry tokens, which are decoded by pretrained geometry heads. In contrast, FantasyWorld and Beyond Pixels incorporate their decoder heads into training and therefore do not offer this advantage. Therefore, our method offers substantially greater versatility than existing approaches.
In addition, we compare the additional training costs required to support both generation and reconstruction. FantasyWorld trains a geometry branch and cross-branch adapters, while Gen3R fine-tunes the video DiT for joint video and geometry generation. Beyond Pixels trains an alignment module, LoRA adapters, and geometry prediction heads. In contrast, we train only the Bridge through feature alignment, keeping the video encoder, geometric aggregator, and prediction heads frozen. Keeping the decoder heads frozen further reduces the training cost. Furthermore, FantasyWorld and Gen3R introduce additional geometry tokens. Our bridge is trained using feature supervision alone, without executing the downstream geometric aggregator or prediction heads during optimization.

Limitation.
Our Bridge network has the following limitations:
First, our model depends on a pretrained geometry model.
The bridge learns to match teacher features while keeping the downstream geometry model frozen, and therefore cannot be expected to correct the teacher’s geometric errors. Second, inconsistencies in generated videos are not automatically corrected. Our method extracts geometry from generated latents but does not explicitly constrain the video generation process. Therefore, if the generated content exhibits structural changes or object inconsistencies across frames, the Bridge cannot guarantee the reconstruction of a coherent 3D scene.

article.headline: 潜空间搭桥：视频潜变量直通三维几何
article.lede: 不经过RGB解码，把视频生成潜变量直接映射到冻结几何模型的特征空间，一次生成同时得到深度、相机参数与点云。
article.problem: 视频生成在时空压缩的潜空间里合成内容，而前馈式三维重建依赖DINO类视觉特征，两套表征之间存在鸿沟。因此从生成潜变量取几何通常要先解码成RGB再重新编码，带来额外计算。此前的联合生成方案要么联合训练DiT与几何分支、引入额外几何token，要么训练专门的3D/4D解码头，代价高且泛化性存疑。
article.method: 作者提出Latent Bridge：只训练一个小型桥接网络，把Wan2.1 VAE与V-RAE的潜变量映射到冻结VGGT-Ω patch编码器的token空间（49×1225×1024）。训练采用特征蒸馏，只用RGB视频，不需要真值几何，也不执行下游几何聚合器与预测头，视频编码器和几何模型全程冻结。推理时同一份潜变量既能解码RGB，也能直接输出深度、相机内外参与点云。
article.results: 在300条Co3Dv2与158条WildRGB-D序列上，V-RAE版本取得两个数据集上最低的Chamfer Distance（Co3Dv2 0.2662，WildRGB-D 0.0657），Wan2.1版本在WildRGB-D上取得最低Accuracy（0.0189）。端到端延迟上Wan2.1版本为70.09秒，低于Gen3R的189.57秒、Aether的181.33秒与FantasyWorld的448.63秒。在相同生成潜变量下，桥接把潜变量到几何的耗时从7.92秒降到4.92秒（1.61倍加速），V-RAE从5.76秒降到4.64秒（1.24倍），重建精度与RGB解码路径接近。生成质量方面，Wan2.1版本在Co3Dv2上PSNR为17.0388、SSIM为0.6166、LPIPS为0.4121。桥接网络约35.65M可训练参数，Wan2.1分支训练约1501 GPU小时，V-RAE分支约498 GPU小时。
article.why_it_matters: 这把潜空间对齐做成了一个可复用接口：同一个桥接无需重训就能服务图生视频、文生视频以及共用同一VAE的其他生成模型，并可直接接上冻结的下游任务头（如VGGT-S跨视角分割），省去重复的RGB解码与特征重编码。
article.limitations: 方法依赖预训练的冻结几何模型，桥接学的是拟合教师特征，无法纠正教师本身的几何误差；它也不约束视频生成过程，若生成结果跨帧出现结构或物体不一致，无法保证重建出连贯的三维场景。此外表中端到端延迟还受生成器与输出帧数差异影响（Aether仅用41帧），作者也承认不能把延迟优势全部归因于桥接本身。

page_papers.title: RubatoCodec: Budgeted Adaptive Speech Tokenization with Streaming Decoding
page_papers.abstract: Neural speech codecs provide discrete tokens for speech generation. Lower frame rates shorten token sequences, but each token must then carry more linguistic and acoustic information. Variable-frame-rate codecs address this trade-off by adapting token allocation to speech content, but threshold-based allocation lets content determine the token count, so the sequence length a speech generator must produce varies across utterances and datasets at a fixed setting. We present RubatoCodec, a variable-frame-rate speech codec built on X-Codec-2 with an exact utterance-level event budget and streaming decoding. Its Adaptive Firing mechanism uses changes in codec features and waveform spectra to divide speech into variable-duration events without a learned boundary predictor. Discrete codes and an explicit duration represent each event, allowing a speech generator to predict and decode one event at a time. Controlled experiments show that adaptive allocation outperforms fixed-rate coding in reconstruction fidelity and intelligibility at low event rates. A model trained on large-scale multilingual speech achieves competitive reconstruction quality across English, Japanese, and Mandarin, with the best intelligibility preservation among the compared codecs on the evaluated English and Japanese benchmarks at comparable bitrates. In a matched text-to-speech comparison, the adaptive representation yields lower WER and higher UTMOS and UTMOSv2 with comparable speaker similarity. The speech generator also learns the codec's utterance-level event budget without an explicit generation-time rate constraint. These results demonstrate that budgeted adaptive speech representations support both high-quality reconstruction and streaming text-to-speech generation. Code and weights are available at https://github.com/third-intelligence/RubatoCodec and https://huggingface.co/third-intelligence/RubatoCodec.
page_papers.content:
Abstract
Neural speech codecs provide discrete tokens for speech generation. Lower frame rates shorten token sequences, but each token must then carry more linguistic and acoustic information. Variable-frame-rate codecs address this trade-off by adapting token allocation to speech content, but threshold-based allocation lets content determine the token count, so the sequence length a speech generator must produce varies across utterances and datasets at a fixed setting. We present RubatoCodec, a variable-frame-rate speech codec built on X-Codec-2 with an exact utterance-level event budget and streaming decoding. Its Adaptive Firing mechanism uses changes in codec features and waveform spectra to divide speech into variable-duration events without a learned boundary predictor. Discrete codes and an explicit duration represent each event, allowing a speech generator to predict and decode one event at a time. Controlled experiments show that adaptive allocation outperforms fixed-rate coding in reconstruction fidelity and intelligibility at low event rates. A model trained on large-scale multilingual speech achieves competitive reconstruction quality across English, Japanese, and Mandarin, with the best intelligibility preservation among the compared codecs on the evaluated English and Japanese benchmarks at comparable bitrates. In a matched text-to-speech comparison, the adaptive representation yields lower WER and higher UTMOS and UTMOSv2 with comparable speaker similarity. The speech generator also learns the codec’s utterance-level event budget without an explicit generation-time rate constraint. These results demonstrate that budgeted adaptive speech representations support both high-quality reconstruction and streaming text-to-speech generation. Code and weights are available at
https://github.com/third-intelligence/RubatoCodec
and
https://huggingface.co/third-intelligence/RubatoCodec
.
1

Introduction
Neural speech codecs encode waveforms as discrete tokens for reconstruction
[
1
,
2
,
3
]
and language-model-based generation, including AudioLM
[
4
]
, VALL-E
[
5
]
, and recent synthesis and spoken dialogue systems
[
6
,
7
,
8
,
9
]
. For generation, the codec’s frame rate determines the temporal sequence length: ten seconds of speech requires 500 positions at 50 Hz. Lower rates shorten this sequence but require each position to represent a longer acoustic interval. Recent tokenizers operate at 12.5 Hz
[
6
,
8
,
9
]
, where each token spans 80 ms. At this resolution, where boundaries fall relative to speech content matters: a fixed grid can merge a rapid phonetic transition into a single token while spending as many tokens on a pause as on the transition.
Speech is temporally nonstationary: pauses and steady vowels change slowly, whereas transitions change rapidly. Variable-rate representations and variable-frame-rate codecs exploit this by assigning different durations to frames
[
10
,
11
,
12
,
13
,
14
,
15
]
. Threshold-based allocation, however, lets content determine the frame count, so rates vary across utterances and datasets at a fixed setting
[
14
,
15
]
. For example, one released threshold-based codec ranges from 46.1 to 81.5 events/s under a single threshold across our five evaluation datasets (Section
5.4.1
). Calibrating the threshold on representative data can match an average rate, but it neither fixes the count for an individual utterance nor preserves that average when the data distribution shifts. Sequence length, and with it downstream modeling cost, then cannot be determined from audio duration alone. An explicit event budget removes this dependence: placement adapts to content, while utterance duration determines the sequence length.
Prescribed-count segmentation has been explored in codecs and speech representation methods
[
11
,
12
,
16
]
. We build on this principle with a codec that uses a deterministic firing signal to allocate events, learns duration-aware representations of those events, and decodes them causally.
RubatoCodec separates the number of events from their placement. A retention ratio
R
R
fixes the number of events for
T
T
latent frames at
K
=
round
⁡
(
R
​
T
)
K=\operatorname{round}(RT)
(Section
3.3.2
), and Adaptive Firing places them by cumulative allocation of a signal derived from latent dissimilarity and waveform spectral flux, without a learned boundary predictor. The default
R
=
0.25
R=0.25
yields 12.5 events/s on average from a 50-Hz latent grid, with variable event durations. The name reflects the musical term rubato: local timing flexes while the overall tempo is preserved.
RubatoCodec builds on X-Codec-2
[
7
]
, retaining its acoustic/semantic encoder and spectral synthesis backbone while introducing adaptive aggregation and causal decoding. Each event carries discrete codes and an explicit duration, allowing a downstream model to predict and decode completed events incrementally. We evaluate the design through controlled codec comparisons, multilingual reconstruction, and downstream TTS training.
Our contributions are:

Discussion
7.1
Adaptive allocation under an explicit budget
An exact event budget leaves useful freedom to distribute temporal resolution within an utterance. This freedom matters most at lower event rates: the gains over fixed-rate downsampling appear at 6.25 and 12.5 Hz and narrow at 25 Hz (Section
5.2.1
). Those comparisons change placement, interval aggregation, and decoding grid together, and the adaptive codec has lower speaker similarity there. With aggregation and grid held fixed, however, adaptive placement raises speaker similarity relative to uniform stride (Section
5.2.2
). Although the two comparisons use different training data and lengths, this suggests that the SIM gap in Section
5.2.1
stems from interval aggregation and grid design rather than from placement itself.
The uniform-stride comparison (Section
5.2.2
) supports content-dependent event placement with aggregation and decoding grid held fixed. The firing-rule comparison (Appendix
A.4
) separately favors cumulative allocation over the tested level-thresholding rule. Cumulative allocation produces approximately uniform spacing under a constant firing signal and adjusts that spacing with the cumulative bounded increments. Broad temporal coverage combined with content-dependent placement is one possible explanation for its performance, but these experiments do not isolate that mechanism.
The firing analysis shows how the budget is used: events longer than 300 ms predominantly cover low-energy regions across all five datasets, leaving more events for the remaining speech (Section
5.4.2
). Budgeted and threshold-based allocation also make different trade-offs. A prescribed count gives predictable sequence lengths without dataset-specific calibration, but equally long utterances receive the same budget regardless of acoustic complexity. Threshold-based methods can instead spend more events on difficult utterances.
7.2
Temporal resolution and quantizer depth for speech generation
Temporal resolution and quantizer depth are not interchangeable ways of spending a bitrate budget. In the evaluated configurations, additional residual layers do not fully compensate for coarser segmentation: 12.5 Hz approaches 25 Hz near 1.2 kbit/s, but 6.25 Hz falls clearly behind, and 25 Hz regains a fidelity advantage near 2.4 kbit/s (Section
5.2.3
).
For generation, these choices also distribute computation differently. Hierarchical models such as Moshi, Qwen3-TTS, and MOSS-TTS predict codebook tokens with a smaller within-event module
[
6
,
8
,
56
]
. Increasing depth adds predictions there, whereas increasing event rate adds steps to the larger temporal backbone. The reconstruction results therefore motivate 12.5 Hz as a practical compromise between quality and sequence length, without establishing it as optimal. Because RubatoCodec’s waveform decoder still operates on a 50-Hz grid, the shorter sequence reduces downstream modeling cost but not waveform-decoder computation.
The inference-time ratio experiment (Appendix
A.5
) shows asymmetric tolerance to event rates outside the training setting: raising the rate improves reconstruction at additional bitrate, whereas aggressive reduction degrades it sharply even at greater quantizer depth. The model thus tolerates higher, but not lower, inference rates.
7.3
From encoded durations to generated timing
The matched TTS comparison shows that codes and durations can be generated jointly while improving intelligibility and predicted quality over the fixed-rate codec (Section
6.2
). Each completed event can be passed directly to the causal waveform decoder, so the same representation serves both temporal compression and incremental synthesis.
The generator also learns the codec’s utterance-level event budget. Generated event counts match the codec’s budget rule for 88.3% of utterances and fall within one event for 99.9% (Section
6.3
), so the generator offsets long events with short ones within each utterance. Generated sequence length therefore remains predictable, although no rate constraint is imposed during generation. Long events also predominantly correspond to low-energy regions in both encoded speech and generated audio under the same measurement criterion (Sections
5.4.2
and
6.3
), indicating that the generator reproduces the codec’s use of long events for near-silence. The concentration of long events at utterance boundaries is consistent with learning leading and trailing silence from HiFiTTS-2, although that training-data correspondence has not been measured directly.
Pause placement, however, is not always natural: informal listening revealed an unnatural within-phrase pause associated with a long event (Section
6.3
). Efficiently representing silence and placing pauses naturally are therefore distinct modeling concerns.
7.4
Reconstruction quality and multilingual performance
On the English benchmarks, RubatoCodec combines strong intelligibility preservation with high predicted-quality scores, while the strongest comparators retain higher signal fidelity and speaker similarity (Section
5.3
). On the Japanese benchmarks, its intelligibility advantage extends to both read and emotional speech, whereas predicted-quality rankings depend on the dataset. In Mandarin, intelligibility preservation remains competitive, although the strongest alternatives achieve lower dCER. These patterns distinguish preservation of linguistic content, speaker characteristics, and waveform detail; improvements in one need not imply improvements in the others. RubatoCodec’s UTMOSv2 scores exceed those of the original recordings on LibriSpeech, indicating that higher predicted quality should not be interpreted as greater fidelity to the source. The 44.1-kHz output rate is a synthesis capability, not evidence of full-band source recovery. Encoding uses 16-kHz input, so higher frequencies must be inferred.
The English, Japanese, and Mandarin results establish reconstruction across languages with a shared model and allocation rule. Combined with the cross-dataset rate analysis (Section
5.4.1
), they demonstrate both predictable encoded sequence lengths and content preservation across the evaluated languages.
7.5

Conclusion
We introduced RubatoCodec, a speech codec that combines content-adaptive event placement, an exact utterance-level event budget, and streaming waveform decoding. By representing speech as discrete codes paired with durations, it allows temporal resolution to follow speech content while keeping sequence length predictable.
Controlled experiments support the value of adaptive allocation for reconstruction at low event rates. Multilingual evaluation demonstrates competitive reconstruction quality, with the best intelligibility preservation among the compared codecs on the evaluated English and Japanese benchmarks at comparable bitrates. Signal fidelity remains an area for improvement relative to the strongest alternatives. In matched text-to-speech experiments, the adaptive representation improves intelligibility and predicted speech quality with comparable speaker similarity. The generator also learns the codec’s utterance-level event budget without an explicit rate constraint.
These results support budgeted adaptive speech tokenization as a practical representation for both reconstruction and speech generation. Combining content-dependent timing with predictable sequence length provides a basis for compact speech modeling and streaming synthesis.

article.headline: 可变帧率语音编码器用事件预算锁定序列长度
article.lede: RubatoCodec 在 X-Codec-2 上用固定事件预算做内容自适应分词，平均 12.5 事件/秒，可流式解码。
article.problem: 神经语音编解码器用离散 token 表示语音，降低帧率能缩短序列，但每个 token 要承载更多信息。现有可变帧率方案靠阈值分配事件，事件数由内容决定，因此固定设置下不同话语、不同数据集的序列长度会漂移，生成模型难以预知建模成本。
article.method: 作者在 X-Codec-2 的编码器与解码器骨架上加入 Adaptive Firing：用隐特征的差异与波形频谱通量构造触发信号，按累积分配把语音切成变长事件，不使用可学习的边界预测器。每个事件用离散码加一个显式时长表示，用保留率 R 把 T 个隐帧的事件数固定为 K=round(RT)，默认 R=0.25，从而把「在哪里放事件」与「放多少个事件」解耦。事件级表示再经区间聚合与上采样恢复到 50 Hz 解码网格，因此可以逐个事件因果解码。
article.results: 默认 R=0.25 时，从 50 Hz 隐网格得到平均 12.5 事件/秒。阈值式编解码器在五个评测数据集、同一阈值下事件率在 46.1 至 81.5 事件/秒之间波动。受控实验显示自适应分配在低事件率下重建保真度与可懂度优于固定帧率，优势出现在 6.25 与 12.5 Hz，在 25 Hz 时收窄；12.5 Hz 在约 1.2 kbit/s 附近接近 25 Hz，6.25 Hz 明显落后，25 Hz 在约 2.4 kbit/s 附近重获保真优势。多语言模型在英语、日语、普通话上取得有竞争力的重建质量，在相近码率下于所评测的英语与日语基准中可懂度保持最好。在匹配的 TTS 对比中，自适应表示 WER 更低、UTMOS 与 UTMOSv2 更高，说话人相似度相当；生成器在无显式速率约束下，88.3% 的话语事件数与编解码器预算规则完全一致，99.9% 落在±1 个事件内。
article.why_it_matters: 它让序列长度可以由音频时长直接推算，同时保留内容自适应的时域分辨率，这对流式 TTS 的延迟与计算规划尤其关键。生成器还能在无速率约束下学会这套预算规则，说明该表示可以直接接到语言模型式语音生成上。
article.limitations: 信号保真度仍是短板：最强对比方法在波形细节与说话人相似度上更高，普通话的 dCER 也不及最优方案；论文还指出 LibriSpeech 上 UTMOSv2 超过原始录音，说明预测质量分不等于对源信号的还原度。此外波形解码器仍工作在 50 Hz 网格上，缩短序列只降低下游建模成本而非解码器算力；非正式听测发现过长事件会带来不自然的句内停顿，且等长话语无论声学复杂度如何都拿到同样预算。
article.figure_caption_zh: RubatoCodec 架构：在 X-Codec-2 编解码骨架上以默认 0.25 保留率，用隐特征变化与波形频谱通量引导预算化事件分配，区间聚合器把事件起始特征与基于该特征、帧特征均值及时长的学习式修正结合，量化后的事件表示与时长恢复 50 Hz 解码网格，再由上采样器提高合成特征率。

page_papers.title: Automating ML for Science: Can Frontier Agents Climb Scientific Hills in the Wild?
page_papers.abstract: Frontier coding agents are increasingly framed as end-to-end automated researchers, and ML for science offers a demanding test of that promise: improving a scientific model often requires domain insight beyond routine ML engineering. We introduce Agent4Sci, a long-horizon testbed for measuring how far today's agents can improve the published best models on scientific ML benchmarks, spanning 20 benchmarks across 11 domains. Rather than ranking agents on a leaderboard, Agent4Sci asks what kinds of progress agents can make on these tasks under in-the-wild conditions, and where they fall short. Empirically, today's frontier agents advance the published best on every benchmark, with Claude Opus reaching 10.4% mean relative improvement and no run flagged for academic misconduct. These gains, however, come almost entirely from a bag of ML-engineering tricks rather than research-level insight. Trajectory analysis surfaces three recurring limitations in this setting: novelty miscalibration, resource under-utilization, and rapid collapse into local engineering sweeps. Lightweight plug-in skills for research ideation, experiment management, and scheduled checklists raise Claude Opus from 10.4% to 20.1% and Codex from 4.4% to 8.1%, while yielding more diverse, domain-relevant interventions. Agent4Sci gives the community a way to track and push frontier agents from ML engineering toward domain insight on real-world ML-for-science problems. Code and data are available on GitHub (https://github.com/maszhongming/agent4sci) and Hugging Face (https://huggingface.co/datasets/MingZhong/agent4sci).

Abstract
Frontier coding agents are increasingly framed as end-to-end automated researchers, and ML for science offers a demanding test of that promise: improving a scientific model often requires domain insight beyond routine ML engineering. We introduce
Agent4Sci
, a long-horizon testbed for measuring how far today’s agents can improve the published best models on scientific ML benchmarks, spanning 20 benchmarks across 11 domains. Rather than ranking agents on a leaderboard,
Agent4Sci
asks what kinds of progress agents can make on these tasks under in-the-wild conditions, and where they fall short. Empirically, today’s frontier agents advance the published best on every benchmark, with Claude Opus reaching 10.4% mean relative improvement and no run flagged for academic misconduct. These gains, however, come almost entirely from a bag of ML-engineering tricks rather than research-level insight. Trajectory analysis surfaces three recurring limitations in this setting: novelty miscalibration, resource under-utilization, and rapid collapse into local engineering sweeps. Lightweight plug-in skills for research ideation, experiment management, and scheduled checklists raise Claude Opus from 10.4% to 20.1% and Codex from 4.4% to 8.1%, while yielding more diverse, domain-relevant interventions.
Agent4Sci
gives the community a way to track and push frontier agents from ML engineering toward domain insight on real-world ML-for-science problems. Code and data are available on

Introduction
Recent advances in frontier coding agents are turning automated research into an executable workflow: agents can read papers and repositories, modify implementations, run experiments, interpret quantitative feedback, and iterate. A growing body of recent work suggests a common recipe for this vision: cast research as a feedback loop in which an agent operates in a workspace, pursues a measurable objective, and improves through experimentation
