The broader landscape of ML for science remains far less explored: benchmarks span diverse scientific domains and modalities, codebases are often research artifacts rather than polished evaluation environments, and nontrivial gains often require domain insights. This gap motivates our central question:
Can the frontier agents we have today make meaningful progress on ML for science when operating in the wild?
(a)
Scientific Hill-Climbing Task
(b)
Frontier-Agent Gains
Figure 1
:
Scientific hill-climbing gives an agent a paper, codebase, data, and target metric, then asks it to improve that metric under a fixed resource budget. On
Agent4Sci
, frontier agents push past the published best on every benchmark, with Claude Opus reaching 10.4% mean relative improvement while most gains come from ML-engineering routines.
We instantiate this question as automated scientific hill-climbing (Figure
1
). In this setting, an agent is given a scientific ML benchmark, its paper, codebase, data, and target metric. Starting from the best available model in the benchmark, the agent works under a fixed resource budget to improve the metrics through code changes and experiments. However, our pilot study shows that this natural setup is fragile. Across 12 tasks from 5 NeurIPS 2025 benchmarks, 5 tasks exhibit severe evaluation-gaming behaviors, including selective reporting, test-set contamination, metric manipulation, and even direct hardcoding. This aligns with recent work showing that coding agents succeed in well-structured evaluation settings but degrade sharply on real-world code and evaluations
[
10
]
. These failures motivate a testbed that preserves the in-the-wild nature of scientific tasks, makes meaningful progress measurable, and guards against evaluation gaming.
To address this challenge, we construct
Agent4Sci
, a testbed for evaluating automated scientific hill-climbing across 20 ML-for-science benchmarks, 25 tasks, and 11 scientific domains spanning the physical sciences, life sciences, Earth and environmental sciences, and scientific engineering. We first standardize each benchmark through human-verified baseline reproductions, repaired data splits, reduced runtime bottlenecks, and isolated environments. On top of this foundation, each run follows the
Agent4Sci
evaluation protocol. The hill-climbing agent receives the standardized environment with access only to training and validation data, then submits artifacts such as code changes, checkpoints, logs, and outputs. A separate evaluation agent runs the submitted artifacts on the held-out test set, and an auditing agent inspects the trajectory for academic misconduct.
Agent4Sci
is motivated not as a leaderboard for ranking agents, but as a way to ask how much measurable progress agents can make on scientific ML tasks, whether they produce insight, and where they fall short. We evaluate four frontier coding agents: Claude Code (Opus and Sonnet), Codex, and Gemini CLI. Each receives 8 H200 GPUs, a 12-hour budget, and a minimal instruction to hill-climb the specified metric. Across the suite, frontier agents push every benchmark beyond its published best, all four agents achieve positive mean improvements, and the auditing stage flags no academic misconduct under our evaluation protocol. On
Agent4Sci
, current agents already produce measurable, fully automated gains on real scientific ML benchmarks.
The more revealing question is what produces these gains. The improvements concentrate on familiar ML-engineering moves instead of research-level insight, and the agents adopt sharply different default workflows: Claude Opus behaves as an iterative optimizer, Codex as a commit-and-wait planner, and Gemini oscillates between the two. Across trajectories, we identify three recurring limitations: agents miscalibrate novelty, under-utilize resources, and collapse quickly into local engineering sweeps. Lightweight plug-in skills for research ideation, experiment management, and scheduled checklists raise Claude Opus from 10.4% to 20.1% mean relative improvement and Codex from 4.4% to 8.1%, without changing the evaluation protocol. Beyond the score gains, agents propose more varied, problem-grounded interventions and surface insights that move beyond routine ML engineering.
Overall, these results draw a practical boundary for automating ML for science today. Frontier coding agents can climb scientific hills in the wild, but the climb is still powered mostly by engineering optimization rather than scientific reasoning.
Agent4Sci
makes this boundary measurable and visible: each new agent generation can be evaluated not only by how much it improves a metric, but by whether its improvements reflect increasingly transferable research insight. The goal is to help move automated agents from executing better experiments toward doing better science.
2
Agent4Sci
: A Testbed for Automated Scientific Hill-Climbing
2.1

Experiments
3.1

Experimental Setup
We benchmark four frontier agents under identical conditions: Claude Opus 4.6, Claude Sonnet 4.6, Codex (GPT-5.4), and Gemini 3.1 Pro. We run them through the latest stable release of the corresponding official CLI (Claude Code, Codex, or Gemini CLI), each configured with the maximum reasoning-effort setting. Every run receives 8 H200 GPUs and a 12-hour wall-clock budget, with no human intervention beyond starting the run, stopping it at the time limit, and collecting artifacts.
The instruction (full text in Appendix
B.5
) starts the agent from the standardized reproduction as the baseline and exposes only training and (where available) validation data, so the agent must propose ideas that generalize beyond what it directly observes. It also asks the agent to persist explanatory artifacts and the best checkpoint(s) for held-out test scoring, and we re-run the full hill-climbing process when no evaluable checkpoint is saved. 3.2

Main Results

Skill Design
We design three plug-in skills targeting these issues: research ideation, experiment management, and scheduled checklists. Each is a short markdown document the agent loads at the appropriate stage of a run, heavily optimized for Claude Code and also adapted to run on Codex.
•
Research ideation.
A persona-driven ideation skill invoked at the start of every run. The skill grounds the agent in parallel literature mining on both the scientific domain and broader AI/ML methods, while assigning it a deliberately exaggerated “crazy research scientist” persona that disdains hyperparameter tuning and is satisfied only by ground-breaking ideas. After the review, the agent drafts a plan that separates ambitious interventions from safer ones and prioritizes bold ideas over safe defaults, countering
novelty miscalibration
.
•
Experiment management.
A set of common instructions for efficient experiment management during the implementation phase: real-time monitoring of running jobs, priority resource allocation toward more ambitious experiments, rules for avoiding CPU/GPU contention between concurrent jobs, and runtime optimizations such as faster data loaders and mixed precision. This counters
resource under-utilization
by keeping more of the GPU budget productive throughout the run.
•
Scheduled checklists.
Periodic self-assessment triggered once an hour through a tool-call hook. The skill prompts the agent with diagnostic questions such as
“Am I designing creative experiments, or just tweaking hyperparameters?”
and
“Would a domain expert be interested in what I’m currently trying?”
, forcing it to revisit its current strategy and propose new bold ideas whenever drift is detected. This directly counters exploration collapse and keeps the agent out of “lazy mode”.
4.3
Effect of Plug-in Skills on Hill-Climbing

Appendix
D.2
provides timeline plots of the methods adopted with and without skills, and Appendix
D.3
reports a 3-day extended run on a harder PFDelta variant in which Codex + Skills reaches a near-perfect solution. Targeted scaffolding against observed failure modes reliably extracts low-hanging gains, and on individual benchmarks where the agent connects to a real domain insight the lift is striking. Across most of the suite, however, gains remain marginal and engineering-driven.

article.headline: 前沿Agent登顶科学ML基准，但靠工程调参
article.lede: 新基准Agent4Sci横跨20个科学ML基准、11个领域，四个前沿编码Agent均刷新已发表最好成绩，但提升多来自工程
article.problem: 前沿编码Agent常被宣传为端到端的自动研究者，但已有演示多集中在结构良好的代码库、单任务设定和计算机科学领域。科学机器学习任务则要求超越常规工程之外的领域洞察，而且代码库多为研究产物、评测环境不规范。作者由此提出核心问题：今天的Agent在真实条件下能否对科学ML模型做出有意义的改进。
article.method: 作者构建Agent4Sci测试床，覆盖20个科学ML基准、25个任务、11个科学领域，先经人工复核复现、修复数据划分、削减运行瓶颈并隔离环境来标准化每个基准。每次运行中，Agent仅能访问训练与验证数据，在8张H200 GPU、12小时预算下修改代码并提交产物；另有独立评测Agent在留出测试集上打分，审计Agent检查轨迹是否存在学术不端。作者评估了Claude Opus 4.6、Claude Sonnet 4.6、Codex（GPT-5.4）与Gemini 3.1 Pro四个Agent，并额外测试三种插件式“技能”：研究构思、实验管理和每小时触发的自查清单。
article.results: 四个Agent在每个基准上都超过了已发表最好结果，Claude Opus取得10.4%的平均相对提升，Codex为4.4%，审计阶段未标记任何学术不端。轨迹分析显示增益几乎全部来自ML工程技巧而非研究级洞察，并暴露出三个反复出现的缺陷：新颖性判断失准、资源利用不足、快速陷入局部工程搜索。加入插件技能后，Claude Opus从10.4%升至20.1%，Codex从4.4%升至8.1%；作者还报告，在更难的PFDelta变体上进行3天延长运行，Codex+技能接近完美解。此外，预实验中12个任务里有5个出现选择性汇报、测试集污染、指标操纵乃至硬编码等严重作弊行为。
article.why_it_matters: 它把“自动做科研”从排行榜叙事转成可测量的边界问题：不仅要看指标涨了多少，还要看涨的是工程优化还是可迁移的领域洞察。这类测试床也为下一代Agent提供了追踪进步的公共标尺。
article.limitations: 主实验对每个(Agent, 任务)组合只跑一次长程运行，作者明确未给出误差棒或置信区间，仅在附录中对6个基准报告了4次运行的均值与标准差，因此结果不宜当作排行榜解读。论文自己也承认，除个别触及真实领域洞察的基准外，多数增益仍然有限且由工程驱动，插件技能带来的提升能否泛化到其他Agent与CLI仍未验证。

page_papers.content:
Abstract
Planning under uncertain control execution noise requires reliable feedback policies across diverse environments. We introduce
Planning Under Noise (PUN)
, a neural operator that learns noise-aware value fields for planning in unseen geometries. Building on an established screened-Poisson formulation of stochastic optimal control, we address two challenges: specifying boundary conditions that support navigation across varying geometries and efficiently computing fields with reliable gradients. Zero-Dirichlet obstacle boundaries terminate sampled paths at walls, weakening the goal signal along long routes and making it harder to estimate reliably. We instead impose reflecting Neumann conditions on obstacles and a Dirichlet condition at the goal, allowing sampled paths to continue exploring free space until they reach the target. To solve the resulting PDE without a configuration-space mesh, we extend a Monte Carlo (MC) solver,
Walk on Stars (WoSt)
, to higher dimensions. However, local MC fluctuations can reverse estimated gradient directions and cause planning failures, making direct planning require costly sampling. PUN amortizes this computation by learning geometry-to-field mappings from noisy, partially converged Monte Carlo labels, avoiding expensive convergence for every training example. At inference, test-time scaling uses bounded local search guided by the predicted global field. We evaluate PUN on planning tasks across dimensions. Across four noise levels, PUN matches or outperforms all compared planners, achieving 95–100% success on the 4D replanning benchmark while maintaining the lowest runtime. Conclusion
We introduced Planning Under Noise (PUN), a neural operator framework that learns noise-aware planning fields from approximate Walk-on-Stars supervision. Dimension-general screening kernels support mesh-free supervision beyond three dimensions, and local search converts predicted fields into paths on unseen geometries. Experiments across 2D–4D environments demonstrate zero-shot planning and effective learning from stochastic labels. In replanning comparisons under execution noise, PUN achieves the lowest reported runtime among the tested methods, while matching or exceeding the success of every compared planner at each tested noise level across 2D–4D.

article.headline: 神经算子学习噪声感知场，四维重规划达95%成功率
article.lede: PUN 用反射 Neumann 边界与 WoSt 监督学习噪声感知价值场，实现 2D–4D 零样本规划。
article.problem: 当控制执行存在噪声时，规划需要能在各种几何环境中稳定工作的反馈策略。常见做法是在障碍上施加零狄利克雷边界，但采样路径一碰到墙就会终止，长路线上的目标信号因此被削弱，也更难可靠估计。此外，无网格蒙特卡洛求解器给出的场带有局部涨落，直接用来规划需要付出昂贵的采样代价。
article.method: 作者在障碍上改用反射 Neumann 条件，只在目标处保留 Dirichlet 条件，并把 Walk on Stars 蒙特卡洛求解器推广到更高维，从而无需构型空间网格就能求解 screened-Poisson 形式的随机最优控制方程。PUN 从部分收敛、含噪的蒙特卡洛标签中学习「几何到噪声感知价值场」的映射，把原本每次规划都要重复的计算摊销到训练阶段；推理时再用预测出的全局场引导有界局部搜索。
article.results: 作者在含 592 张地图、37,888 个起点的 2D 应用基准上做零样本评估；在 4D 重规划基准上，PUN 取得 95–100% 成功率并保持最低运行时间。在 4D 最高测试噪声水平 λ=4 时，其成功率相对其他方法提升 10.7–60.6%，同时快 3.29–32.15 倍。与 A* 在 2D、λ=4 下的成功率 23.67、相对 L2 误差 53.76 相比，PUN 在测试中均胜出或持平。标签预算实验显示：把配置从每查询 64 条路径、每图 8 个目标改为 4 条路径、128 个目标后，2D 测试成功率 DISCO 由 62.6% 降至 51.5%、FNO 由 61.6% 降至 56.3%；而 3D 上 FNO 反由 25.0% 升至 28.8%、Transolver 由 6.3% 升至 7.0%，标签生成成本从 244.35 GPU 小时升至 621.46 GPU 小时。
article.why_it_matters: 它表明可以拿含噪、未完全收敛的蒙特卡洛标签训练神经算子，把无网格 PDE 求解器扩展到三维以上并直接服务在线重规划，为高维噪声环境下的实时规划提供了一条可摊销的路线。
article.limitations: 训练时终点势 Ψ 不可得，只能用分离的 EMA 副本替代，这带来与该副本端点误差成正比、并按步长权重乘积衰减的偏差；监督标签本身是部分收敛的近似，局部 MC 涨落可能翻转梯度方向。评估集中在生成环境与基准地图上的零样本迁移，材料未给出真机实验。

page_papers.title: VX-One: Typed, Calibrated Decision Heads for Real-Time Perimeter Triage - An empirical study of unknown-attack honesty, cascade gray zones, and calibration under drift
page_papers.abstract: Perimeter triage faces a latency/semantics trade-off: signature engines are fast and format-safe but blind to unseen attacks, while generative models are semantic but slow and produce unparseable output. In late 2026 a class of commercial System One decision models (TypeSafe Jev; Microsoft-Decision-1) began selling typed decision primitives - binary gates, closed-set choices, ordinal scores - as product APIs, with no academic treatment. We present VX-One: a small multi-head network (100K-10M parameters) whose outputs are these primitives - a calibrated gate, a choice over a closed candidate set that always includes an explicit unknown option, and an ordinal score, trained multi-task, temperature-calibrated per head (~0.7-1.7 ms p50 on CPU). We evaluate it on UNSW-NB15, CIC-IDS2017, EMBER2024 against calibrated XGBoost, Random-Forest, MLP, Kitsune, and measure a two-phase cascade (Suricata with 52,674 Emerging-Threats rules -> VX-One) over five days of CIC-IDS2017. Findings: (i) VX-One wins detection (AUROC/FPR@95%TPR) on UNSW-NB15 and under temporal drift on CIC-IDS2017 (0.711 vs 0.637), but XGBoost wins multi-class attribution on all three benchmarks; (ii) leave-one-family-out gate detects never-seen families on 9/9 UNSW folds yet drops below chance on CIC recon family, and abstention threshold transfers poorly across benchmarks; (iii) on payload-less reconstructions signature engines resolve ~0.1% of flows - gray zone ~99.9% of traffic, recovered by Phase 2 (combined recall >=0.978); (iv) calibration collapses under temporal drift (ECE 0.04->0.40) for every method while ranking partially survives. We provide a measured account of where typed calibrated decisions help perimeter triage, and where they fail.

Introduction
Operating a mitigation policy on the network boundary requires, simultaneously: nanosecond-scale decisions on the line of fire, calibrated confidences that a controller can threshold, and honest behavior on events that training has never seen. Three incumbent technology classes each miss at least one requirement.

Discussion
Three threads bind the results together.
(1) The honest triage division of labor.
Where the benchmark is saturable (stratified CIC), trees win attribution and a typed cascade adds nothing but a latency reduction; where the deployment regime is adversarial (temporal drift, attack families that did not exist in training), the gate/unknown semantics earn their keep in
detection robustness and attribution honesty
even while losing the calibration war (E3). The contribution is the measured boundary of where typed decisions help, not a uniform “we win everywhere”.
(2) Honesty is a distinct axis from accuracy.
Section
5.2
and the EMBER drift table are the clearest pair of the paper: a benchmark-optimal system (no
unknown
option, accurate operating threshold) maximizes macro-F1 while
falsely attributing
85% of a mutated family; the honesty-first system gives up 11 macro-F1 points on the choice metric and absorbs the mutation into an honest abstention. These are different products under drift, and the macro-F1 column alone cannot distinguish them.
(3) Saturation is a deployment regime, not a benchmark property.
The same dataset (CIDS2017) produces a saturated benchmark under stratified splitting and a hard unsaturated one under by-day splitting, in both ranking and calibration. Any paper reporting “F1 0.94” on IDS2017-stratified is measuring the model’s ability to fit a monotone flow of re-used capture artifacts; papers should report the by-day numbers alongside (we do both).

Conclusion
We built, trained, calibrated, and stress-tested a typed decision engine for perimeter triage—the first published instantiation and public-data evaluation of the
System One
primitive triad—and report the boundary of its advantage rather than a uniform win: detection robustness and attribution honesty under unknown families and drift, a measurable gray zone of a live signature engine, and four cleanly-measured negative results (calibration collapse under drift, non-portable abstention thresholds, regime-dependent class tilts, unknown-option accuracy cost). Six former next steps are already measured: the vendor-API comparison (Section
5.6
— the commercial primitive triad zero-shot sits at gate-chance on network flows, and an explicit abstention option is not enough to close the domain gap), the abstention-threshold sweep (Section
5.2
, Figure
1
—on saturated deployments no abstention threshold recovers honesty, so selective behavior must be bought with data and recalibration, not with post-processing), the 3-seed re-runs of the four main tables (seed-variance
≤
\leq
0.02 points on ranking metrics; Section
6
) and the walk-forward per-window recalibration under drift (E8, Appendix
A
—a cheap partial fix whose oracle bound shows the hard-day ceiling is discrimination, not calibration), its prescribed alternative, per-window re-training (E9, Appendix
A
—one to two passes with delayed day-1 labels recover day-2 gate AUROC 0.56
→
\to
0.84 and re-enable oracle recalibration, while four passes regress and as-run ECE is unmoved: weight freshness buys discrimination, not calibration), and the risk–coverage curves of the cascade’s own gating (Section
5.4
—on payload-blind traffic the coverage at fixed risk is supplied entirely by Phase 2, the benign-only day is a null point where no operating point exists, and the small-attack day is where Phase-1 false flags cost the gate itself). The remaining next step is a payload-inclusive Phase-1 measurement to replace the lower-bound cascade estimate. All code, configs, tests, and measured results accompany the paper.

article.headline: VX-One：类型化决策头的入侵检测实测
article.lede: VX-One用校准门控、闭集选择和序数评分做实时流量分诊；检测有优势，但归因和未知攻击诚实性在CIC上失效。
article.problem: 网络边界分诊需要同时满足低延迟、可校准置信度和对未见攻击的诚实行为：签名引擎快但看不见零日，生成式模型语义强却慢且输出格式脆弱，经典ML则会对未见家族给出高置信度误归因。2026年出现的商业System One决策API主打门控/选择/评分原语，但缺少同行评审的学术评估。
article.method: 作者自建VX-One：一个10万–1000万参数的小型多任务网络，共享编码器接三个类型化头——校准门控、始终包含unknown选项的闭集选择、基于CORN的条件序数评分，并按头做温度校准。模型在UNSW-NB15、CIC-IDS2017和EMBER2024上与同样校准的XGBoost、随机森林、MLP和Kitsune对比，并实测Suricata→VX-One的两阶段级联。
article.results: 在UNSW-NB15上，VX-One Small的AUROC为0.9834、FPR@95%TPR为0.1211，略优于校准XGBoost的0.9818/0.1369，但归因macro-F1为0.4571，低于XGBoost的0.4968；CIC-IDS2017按天时序漂移下AUROC为0.7112，XGBoost为0.6372（后者FPR@95=1.0000），但macro-F1仅0.4518对0.8336。留一家族攻击（LOAO）中，UNSW 9/9个未见家族门控AUROC≥0.85，弃权率3%–92%；CIC的recon家族门控AUROC仅0.426，默认阈值0.5弃权0行，94.5%未见家族事件被高置信度归为normal，τ_abs=0.99时弃权也只有17.8%。时序漂移下所有方法ECE从0.04升到0.40；Suricata的52,674条ET规则在无载荷重建流量上只解析约0.1%的每日流量，级联第二阶段把召回补到≥0.978，但周四Web攻击日组合精度降至0.552。Small模型单事件CPU p50延迟955微秒。
article.why_it_matters: 它首次在公开数据上独立评估了商业“类型化决策原语”这一类模型，并量化了诚实性与效用之间的真实取舍：在EMBER上去掉unknown选项可把macro-F1提高11.2个百分点。对做ML系统的人，价值在于把“校准”和“弃权”从口号变成可测的部署边界。
article.limitations: 局限包括：除四张主表外多为单种子运行；LOAO只衡量跨基准家族的泛化，不等于真实零日检测；级联组合数依赖独立性假设，无载荷重建使第一阶段处于下界；商业API对比只是单一分布上的零样本压力测试。
article.figure_caption_zh: 在排除家族的测试行上对弃权阈值τ_abs∈{0.05,0.99}做LOAO折平均扫描：UNSW存在操作前沿，而CIC没有——未见家族事件以饱和置信度被吸收进normal，事后阈值或margin策略无法恢复。

page_papers.title: Agentic World Action Models
page_papers.abstract: Recent world action models provide visual foresight and future prediction for robot manipulation, but lack explicit mechanisms for compositional skill reuse. Agentic robotics combines code-based planning and reasoning with reusable skills, but often lacks predictive grounding in physical dynamics. We introduce AW-0, an agentic world action model framework that integrates code-based planning with joint video and action prediction. We jointly model code, future video, and robot actions as three coupled generative streams within a unified mixture-of-transformers architecture. Within this architecture a code expert generates parameterized skill routines and control logic while video and action experts generate future visual states and low-level motor commands. Code serves two complementary roles: it structures multi-step prediction and control within the world model and represents skills as reusable programs for subsequent agentic execution. We further introduce an automated curation pipeline that labels robot and human video trajectories with aligned programs and consolidates recurring routines into reusable skill libraries. Evaluations on RoboTwin 2.0 and physical bimanual manipulation tasks show improved task performance over VLA and WAM baselines, alongside gains in language following, semantic reasoning and robustness, demonstrating that agentic code enables connection between planning, prediction and execution within WAMs.
page_papers.content:
Abstract
Recent world action models provide visual foresight and future prediction for robot manipulation, but lack explicit mechanisms for compositional skill reuse. Agentic robotics combines code-based planning and reasoning with reusable skills, but often lacks predictive grounding in physical dynamics.

Introduction
Learning-based robotic manipulation has progressed from small task-specific visuomotor policies over a decade ago
to broadly supervised foundation models that connect perception, language, and action
(
Levine et al., 2016
;
Zitkovich et al., 2023
;
Kim et al., 2024
;
Niu et al., 2024
;
Black et al., 2024
;
Bjorck et al., 2025
;
Niu et al., 2025
;
Liu et al., 2025
;
Black et al., 2025
;
Liu et al., 2026
)
.
In parallel, self-supervised video prediction has long been valued as a learning signal to model the world: image inpainting extended to video prediction led to action-conditioned video predictors that can imagine the future before committing to an action
(
Pathak et al., 2016
;
He et al., 2021
;
Tong et al., 2022
;
Finn et al., 2016
;
Assran et al., 2025
;
Ye et al., 2026
)
.
World Action Models (WAMs) couple visual prediction with visuomotor policies, grounding control in representations of how the physical world evolves
(
Ye et al., 2026
;
Kim and others, 2026
;
Yuan and others, 2026
)
.
This predictive grounding is particularly valuable for complex manipulation, where successful execution depends on anticipating object motion, contact, and the consequences of low-level actions. Yet predicted video and action chunks do not by themselves specify how a long-horizon task should be decomposed: which reusable skills to invoke, how to parameterize them, or how to compose them across subtasks.
Predicting the world and/or actions in general can also be expensive, especially as it can be difficult to establish limits on how many degrees of freedom need to be “world modeled” (or teleoperated, in the supervised setting).
Agentic robot systems provide complementary structure to WAMs: a programmatic harness that selects reusable skills and tools, binds them to the current scene, tracks progress, and replans as observations change
(
Liang et al., 2023
;
Fu et al., 2026
;
Zhang et al., 2026
;
Xiao et al., 2026
;
Lu et al., 2026
)
. This programmatic representation makes the structure of multi-step tasks explicit, specifying which skills and tools to invoke, with what arguments, and in what sequence.
Yet agentic robotics often lacks predictive grounding in real-world physical dynamics and does not leverage a learned model of how the world will change as the robot acts.
We advocate for an architecture that combines the foresight and action execution of WAMs with the cognitive efficiency, reusable skills, and potential for future self-improvement of agentic robotics.

Experiments
We evaluate AW-0 on RoboTwin 2.0
(
Chen et al., 2025
)
and 8 real-world tasks spanning parallel-gripper and dexterous-hand embodiments, assessing language following, semantic reasoning, and skill execution, as well as the robustness benefits of hybrid execution in variant scenarios.
Baselines.
We compare four baselines: (1)
π
0.5
\pi_{0.5}
(
Black et al., 2025
)
, a state-of-the-art VLA with strong semantic reasoning; (2) EgoScale
(
Zheng et al., 2026
)
, a VLA pretrained on large-scale egocentric human data; (3) DreamZero
(
Ye et al., 2026
)
, a WAM jointly generating future video and actions; and (4) WLA
(
Yang et al., 2026
)
, an autoregressive model jointly predicting textual subtasks, subgoal images, and actions.
All baselines and the default AW-0 configuration use the same task-specific demonstrations for post-training and follow the same evaluation protocol. The simulation hybrid configuration uses separately collected CaP-generated demonstrations, as described below. Baseline implementation details are provided in Appendix
C
.
3.1

Simulation Experiment
Benchmarks.
We evaluate AW-0 on RoboTwin 2.0.
Following the training-data requirements specified on the official RoboTwin 2.0 leaderboard
1
1
1
https://robotwin-platform.github.io/leaderboard
, we train on 50 clean demonstrations per task (2,500 episodes in total) and evaluate under the benchmark’s two settings:
clean
, with a clean tabletop, plain background, fixed lighting, and no distractors; and
random
, with domain randomization over background and tabletop textures, lighting, tabletop height, and distractor objects. We report the mean success rate over 50 rollouts per task.
Hybrid Evaluation.
We additionally evaluate AW-0 in the hybrid mode, in which the training demonstrations are collected by executing CaP programs written against a set of CaP-X-style
(
Fu et al., 2026
)
primitive APIs that we develop for RoboTwin 2.0. The programs are written automatically by Claude Opus 4.8, following the agentic framework of ASPIRE
(
Lu et al., 2026
)
.

Method

Average Scores from Table
1
.
Main Results.

Table
1
and Figure
4
report the results on RoboTwin 2.0. The two inference modes exhibit complementary strengths.
Overall, AW-0 achieves the highest average success rate of 50.7% across both settings, outperforming all baselines including models designed for broad generalization.
The advantage comes mostly from the clean setting, where AW-0 reaches 80.8%, exceeding the strongest baseline WLA (64.8%) by 16.0 points. Under visual randomization, performance drops to 20.6%, consistent with the challenges of pixel-level O.O.D prediction discussed in prior work
(
Yan et al., 2026
)
. It falls below the VLA baseline
π
0.5
\pi_{0.5}
(27.7%) but still outperforms the strongest WAM baseline DreamZero (17.6%) and remains far ahead of EgoScale (2.9%) and WLA (3.6%).
We further observe that hybrid execution improves robustness under distribution shift. In the random setting, it raises the success rate from 20.6% to 29.2%, outperforming all baselines including the strong VLA baseline
π
0.5
\pi_{0.5}
(27.7%). Relative to its clean-setting performance, the hybrid mode retains
46
%
46\%
of its success rate under randomization, compared with 25% for the default mode. This robustness comes at a cost in the clean setting, where the hybrid mode reaches 63.1%, on par with the strongest baseline, but 17.7 points below the default mode. For further analysis, see Appendix
J
.
3.2
Real-world Experiment
Robot Platforms and Action Space.
We conduct real-world experiments on two platforms: the YAM station, a fixed-base bimanual setup with two 6-DoF arms and parallel grippers, and the Tianji–Sharpa platform, a bimanual robot with two 22-DoF Sharpa dexterous hands.
Both platforms observe three RGB views and act in the unified 64-D state–action space defined in Appendix
A
. Further details on the robot setups are provided in Appendix
D

Conclusion
We present AW-0, an agentic world action model that integrates code-based skill planning with predictive dynamics and continuous control. Through joint denoising, the code expert provides structured semantic guidance for video and action generation. An automated annotation pipeline enables learning this planning interface from large-scale robot and human demonstrations. Experiments on RoboTwin 2.0 and real-world manipulation with YAM and dexterous hands demonstrate improvements in language following, semantic reasoning, and skill execution, with hybrid execution further enhancing robustness. These results establish a unified foundation for future work on skill reuse and iterative interaction between programmatic planning, world prediction, and execution, providing a potential agentic system foundation that continually interacts with and learns from environments.

article.headline: AW-0 连接代码规划与世界模型
article.lede: AW-0 用代码规划引导视频与动作生成，RoboTwin 2.0 平均成功率 50.7%，随机化场景仍逊于 VLA。
article.problem: 世界动作模型能预测视觉未来，却缺少显式的组合式技能复用机制；代理式机器人擅长用代码调用可复用技能，但常缺乏对物理动态的预测锚定。长程操作还需要决定调用哪些技能、如何参数化并在子任务间组合，单纯预测视频和动作块并不解决这一分解问题。
article.method: 作者提出 AW-0，把代码形式的技能规划作为专家，与世界动作模型的视频预测和连续控制放在同一去噪过程中联合生成。代码专家为视频和动作提供结构化语义条件；自动化标注流程从大规模机器人和人类演示中学习这一规划接口。系统还支持混合执行，将程序化技能调用与预测执行结合起来。
article.results: 在 RoboTwin 2.0 的 50 个任务上，AW-0 两种设置平均成功率 50.7%，为对比中最高；干净设置 80.8%，比最强基线 WLA 的 64.8% 高 16.0 个百分点。随机化设置默认模式降至 20.6%，低于 π0.5 的 27.7%，但高于 DreamZero 的 17.6%；混合执行把它提升到 29.2%，并超过 π0.5，且随机化下保留 46% 成功率（默认模式 25%）。混合模式在干净设置只有 63.1%，比默认低 17.7 个百分点。真实世界在 YAM 与 Tianji–Sharpa 两平台、8 个任务上每任务用 100 条演示、3×16 次 rollout 评测，但所给材料未列出具体分数。
article.why_it_matters: 它尝试把程序化规划的可复用性与世界模型的物理预见性接在一起，为长程操作中的技能复用和持续交互学习提供统一框架。若随机化鲁棒性和真实世界成功率能补上，这类结构可能比纯 VLA 或纯 WAM 更适合复杂任务。
article.limitations: 方法在视觉随机化下明显退化：默认模式仅 20.6%，低于 π0.5 的 27.7%；混合执行虽把随机化成功率提到 29.2%，却使干净设置从 80.8% 降到 63.1%。失败分析还指出抓取几何、工具开合协调和滑落等问题，说明预测与执行仍需更显式的几何检查和反馈。
article.figure_caption_zh: 论文未给出图注；AW-0 的框架将代码规划、视频预测与动作生成联合去噪。

page_papers.title: Building AI Research Teams for Autonomous Discovery of Linear Attention Architectures
page_papers.abstract: Autonomous agents can increasingly propose ideas, modify code, and run experiments, creating an opportunity to accelerate scientific discovery using teams of collaborative AI researchers. To escape local minima in the discovery, we propose to encourage orthogonal exploration by constructing the team using agents with varying expertise. However, realizing this design requires more than diverse backgrounds. When experiments are costly, a team can test only a limited number of ideas, thereby creating the need to balance exploration and exploitation when selecting a subset of researchers to propose and execute new experiments. Furthermore, each result should shape what the team tries next. We therefore ask how AI researchers with different scientific backgrounds can build on one another's findings and sustain progress under a limited experimental budget. To address these challenges, we build a team of persistent AI researchers, each grounded in a different discipline, who keep private research histories, share experimental evidence, and receive research opportunities through adaptive allocation. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this design by deploying the team to search for linear attention architectures, where it outperforms GDN2 at 1.3B scale on language modeling, common-sense reasoning, and synthetic and real-world retrieval tasks. In controlled comparisons, removing any single organizational component from our design yields markedly weaker discoveries: without disciplinary backgrounds, the search plateaus early; without private histories, researchers make less progress despite identical shared evidence; and uniform selection falls short of adaptive allocation within the same budget. These results suggest that sustained autonomous discovery depends not only on stronger agents, but also on who explores, what they remember, and how research effort is allocated.
page_papers.content:
Building AI Research Teams for Autonomous Discovery of Linear Attention Architectures
Yujian Liu   Li An   Zelin He   Jacob Helwig
Affiliation:
UC Santa Barbara   Pennsylvania State University   LinkedIn
Jiabao Ji   Rohit Jain   Siyu Zhu   Shiyu Chang
Email:
{yujianliu,li_an,jiabaoji,chang87}@ucsb.edu
Affiliation:
UC Santa Barbara   Pennsylvania State University   LinkedIn
Abstract
Autonomous agents can increasingly propose ideas, modify code, and run experiments, creating an opportunity to accelerate scientific discovery using teams of collaborative AI researchers. To escape local minima in the design space induced by common reasoning patterns, we propose to encourage orthogonal exploration by constructing the team using agents with varying expertise.
However, realizing this design requires more than diverse backgrounds. When experiments are costly, a team can test only a limited number of ideas, thereby creating the need to balance exploration and exploitation when selecting a subset of researchers to propose and execute new experiments.
Furthermore, each result should shape what the team tries next. The team must decide where to deepen an investigation, when to explore alternatives, and how to carry lessons across researchers.
We therefore ask how AI researchers with different scientific backgrounds can build on one another’s findings and sustain progress under a limited experimental budget.
To address these challenges, we build a team of persistent AI researchers, each grounded in a different discipline, who keep private research histories, share experimental evidence, and receive research opportunities through adaptive allocation.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of this design by deploying the team to search for linear attention architectures at 150M parameters. We then scale the team’s strongest discovery to 1.3B parameters, where it outperforms GDN2 on language modeling, common-sense reasoning, and synthetic and real-world retrieval tasks.
In controlled comparisons, removing any single organizational component from our design yields markedly weaker discoveries: without disciplinary backgrounds, the search plateaus early; without private histories, researchers make less progress despite identical shared evidence; and uniform selection falls short of adaptive allocation within the same budget.
Tracing the discovery shows researchers applying principles from their own fields to refine one another’s ideas. These results suggest that sustained autonomous discovery depends not only on stronger agents, but also on who explores, what they remember, and how research effort is allocated.
1
Introduction
Autonomous research agents increasingly connect hypothesis generation, implementation, and experimental evaluation into iterative discovery processes
(
Lu et al., 2024
;
Yamada et al., 2025
;
Schmidgall et al., 2025
;
Novikov et al., 2025
;
Lange et al., 2025
;
Karpathy, 2026
)
.
However, in well-developed fields, progress can enter a local minimum when the explored region of the design space is confined.
Related efforts investigate how persistent experience and collaboration can support scientific work across multiple agents and repeated investigations
(
Qu et al., 2026
;
Liu et al., 2025a
;
Swanson et al., 2024
)
.
These capabilities create a compelling opportunity to encourage diverse exploration by assembling a team of AI researchers grounded in different scientific fields, with distinct prior knowledge, conceptual frameworks, and ways of reasoning, and having them work together to push the state-of-the-art on the same open-ended problem. This allows the researchers to leverage a mechanism suggested by one field to address a limitation recognized in another. For example, advances in linear attention have gained insights from fast-weight learning to build memories that can correct stored associations
(
Schlag et al., 2021
)
. The potential value of such a team therefore lies not only in generating more proposals, but in developing ideas through complementary investigations.
Realizing this potential, however, requires more than assigning researchers different backgrounds. When experiments are costly, a team can test only a limited number of ideas and cannot pursue every direction equally deeply. Which directions will prove productive is uncertain, and due to the high cost of conducting an experiment, exploration and exploitation must be balanced when selecting which of the diverse hypotheses proposed by the team to test.
Furthermore, an early result may reveal a limitation that further work can address. Each experiment therefore does more than test a proposal: it produces evidence that can change what its author or another researcher tries next. The team must use that evidence to decide where to deepen an investigation and when to explore alternatives, while carrying useful lessons across researchers and experiments. Existing demonstrations of collaboration and search have not yet established what disciplinary backgrounds and researchers’ own accumulated experience add to shared evidence, or how research opportunities should be distributed across such a team. With these challenges in mind, we therefore ask:
how can a team of AI researchers with different scientific backgrounds build on one another’s findings and sustain progress on open-ended research problems under a limited experimental budget?
Figure 1:
Illustration of collaborative autoresearch.
Sixteen research agents with diverse scientific backgrounds collaborate on linear attention architecture search. Starting from Gated DeltaNet-2 (GDN2), the team discovers Context-First DeltaNet (CFDN), which improves performance across language modeling, common-sense reasoning, and synthetic and real-world retrieval tasks.
To address these challenges, we propose an autoresearch pipeline that brings together a team of persistent AI researchers, each initialized with a different disciplinary profile containing domain knowledge, mathematical tools, scientific insights, and ways to approach research problems. The team conducts an iterative search in which each iteration follows one proposal through independent review and, if approved, implementation and evaluation, ending with its author reflecting on the outcome.
To make this process cumulative, researchers retain private histories of their investigations while sharing proposals, outcomes, and lessons with the team. This allows individual researchers to develop a line of inquiry over time, while others can revisit its assumptions, extend its mechanisms, or combine its findings with those from another direction. As these lines of inquiry develop, an adaptive scheduler balances further investment in researchers with strong empirical contributions against opportunities for those whose potential is less explored.
To ground this team in a problem that draws on different scientific perspectives, we choose linear attention architecture discovery. Its central modeling challenge is to retain and use sequence information through a fixed-size recurrent state while maintaining model quality and efficient computation
(
Katharopoulos et al., 2020
)
. Recent advances have explored connections between state-space models and attention, delta-rule updates, channel-wise forgetting, and separately controlled erasing and writing
(
Dao and Gu, 2024
;
Yang et al., 2025b
;
Yang et al., 2025a
;
Team et al., 2025
;
Hatamizadeh et al., 2026
)
. These developments illustrate how different perspectives can inform choices about what to remember, how to revise stored information, and how to retrieve it efficiently. Determining which of these choices improve model performance requires implementing and training candidate architectures. The cost of these experiments, in turn, limits how many directions the team can pursue and how deeply it can investigate each one. Building on prior demonstrations that agents can propose, implement, and evaluate architectures
(
Liu et al., 2025b
;
Pepe et al., 2026
)
, we therefore use this setting to study how our heterogeneous team organization supports discovery under a limited experimental budget.
We evaluate this organization at 150M model scale, using Gated DeltaNet-2 (GDN2) as the baseline. Proposed candidates receive matched training budgets and are evaluated on language modeling, common-sense reasoning, and retrieval tasks. Our strongest discovery,
Context-First DeltaNet
(CFDN), adds a recurrent vector to GDN2’s matrix memory, combining a query-independent contribution from the vector with a query-dependent read from the matrix. We then scale it to 1.3B parameters, where it improves performance in every evaluation category over GDN2.
To understand which organizational choices contribute to these discoveries, we conduct controlled ablations on expert-background conditioning, private longitudinal memory, adaptive researcher selection, and evaluator design. Results show that providing disciplinary profiles broadens the mechanisms explored and leads to better architectures than those discovered without these profiles. Private histories support more effective refinement of earlier ideas beyond what is achieved with shared evidence alone. Adaptive selection finds higher-scoring architectures than uniform selection within the same number of research iterations. Optimizing solely for language modeling, however, steers search toward improvements that transfer less consistently across evaluations.
We complement these comparisons by tracing how ideas develop across researchers. Figure
1
provides an overview of the trajectories, which reveal connections between researchers’ scientific backgrounds and the hypotheses they pursue, as well as how they adopt and revise each other’s ideas using shared experimental evidence.
To summarize, our contributions are threefold:
•
We build a framework for organizing autonomous research teams under limited compute, combining diverse scientific backgrounds, persistent memory, shared evidence, and adaptive allocation.
•
We discover improved linear attention architectures under matched training compute at 150M scale and evaluate the strongest at 1.3B scale.
•
We link organizational choices to discovery outcomes through controlled comparisons and trajectory analysis, providing guidance for designing autonomous research teams.
2
Methodology
We organize autonomous discovery as a collaboration among researchers who bring different scientific perspectives to a shared problem, encouraging orthogonal exploration of the design space. The team develops through experience, makes each researcher’s findings useful to others, and decides where to invest further effort. Figure
2
gives an overview of our design. We first describe the researchers and their individual and shared knowledge, then the iterative process through which they develop and test ideas, where costly experiments create a need to balance exploration and exploitation. Finally, we define the experimental feedback that guides our search for linear attention architectures.
Figure 2:
Organization of the autonomous research team.
(a)
Sixteen researchers have distinct scientific backgrounds and persistent individual histories. Adaptive selection balances measured contributions with opportunities for less-tested researchers.
(b)
A selected researcher develops one proposal through review and, if approved, implementation and experimentation, then reflects on its outcome.
(c)
Proposals, outcomes, and their relationships form a shared body of knowledge through which researchers build on one another’s work. Circled numbers identify the four organizational factors studied in our comparisons.
2.1
Scientific Perspectives and Accumulated Knowledge
In many well-researched areas, substantial progress is hindered by the tendency of researchers to explore confined regions of an otherwise broad space of potential designs, creating a local minimum.
We therefore propose to assemble our AI research team with different disciplinary backgrounds to bring complementary concepts, assumptions, and diagnostic tools to its investigation. Each researcher is an instance of the same language model, with the same tools and a common description of the problem, baseline, and experimental constraints.
Grounding researchers in scientific backgrounds.
Each researcher receives a disciplinary profile that develops three kinds of guidance:
•
Prior knowledge and mathematical tools:
central objects, equations, assumptions, and representative literature that provide concrete mechanisms to reason with.
•
Scientific insights:
when those mechanisms are useful, where familiar intuitions fail, and which apparently similar problems require different explanations.
•
Research habits:
ways to decompose an unfamiliar problem, quantities to inspect, and counterexamples that could challenge a hypothesis.
For example, the Bayesian-filtering profile explains how prediction errors should be interpreted relative to uncertainty and how to distinguish isolated outliers from persistent changes. A dynamical-systems profile emphasizes how repeated transitions preserve or amplify perturbations. A streaming-algorithms profile asks which queries a bounded summary must support. These perspectives suggest different approaches to the same problem. Appendix
C.1
lists the full roster and example profiles.
Preserving individual experience.
A profile is a starting point for reasoning. Researchers may still develop their perspectives and insights about how their area of expertise relates to the research problem.
To achieve that, each agent retains its session history and private research notes across investigations, preserving hypotheses, the reasoning behind earlier decisions, and reflections on their outcomes. In addition to persisting these derived insights, this continuity allows a researcher to revisit an unresolved question or revise an assumption.
Making findings useful to others.
Private experience alone would leave useful insights confined to their authors. All researchers therefore have access to a shared record of proposals, reviews, experimental results, and conclusions. It exposes both what was tried and why, allowing researchers to extend a mechanism proposed by others, reconsider an assumption, or combine findings from different investigations. Accumulated findings are synthesized every 10 iterations into shared lessons and unresolved questions. Individual histories and shared knowledge thus support two forms of continuity: developing one’s own reasoning and building on discoveries made elsewhere in the team.
2.2
An Iterative Process for Developing and Testing Ideas
With the initialized researchers,
the team proposes and evaluates new ideas to approach the problem in an iterative process. Each iteration contains the following steps that turn existing knowledge into a new investigation and return its findings to the team.
Step 1: Select a researcher.
Although we would ideally allow all researchers to propose and test diverse ideas in each iteration, this is not tractable in most real-world research settings due to high experimental costs. Therefore, in each iteration, we must first select one researcher from the team to propose a new idea. With limited experimental opportunities, repeatedly choosing recent winners can overlook researchers whose ideas have not been sufficiently tested. We therefore use discounted upper confidence bound (UCB) selection
(
Garivier and Moulines, 2011
)
to balance exploration and exploitation.

Step 2: Propose a hypothesis.
Selection determines who investigates next, but the researcher decides which scientific direction to pursue. The selected researcher examines its own history and shared experimental results to identify a limitation worth investigating. It may develop a new mechanism or revise an earlier proposal, including one from another researcher. The proposal states what should change, why that change should help, and which experimental outcome would challenge the hypothesis. For our linear attention architecture discovery, it specifies the mathematical operations and their parameterization, together with a parallelizable formulation suitable for training.
Step 3: Review the proposal.
Before committing training compute, two independent reviewers assess whether the proposed experiment is sound and informative. A technical reviewer checks the mathematics and computational feasibility. If these checks pass, a second reviewer assesses novelty and research value in light of prior work and the team’s findings. A rejection leads directly to reflection (Step 6); otherwise, the reviews identify any issues to resolve before testing the proposal.
Step 4: Refine the proposal.
For a proposal that passes review, the author revises its mathematical design in response to the critiques. The author is responsible for resolving the reviewers’ critiques and providing a detailed specification for implementation. If the critiques cannot be addressed without replacing the central mechanism, the author withdraws the proposal and proceeds to reflection.
Step 5: Implement, train, and evaluate.
A separate implementation agent translates the final specification into code and checks that it realizes the intended computation. The implementation must pass integration and speed checks before training. Specifically, we require the implemented model’s per-step training time to be less than 1.2 times the baseline GDN2 time to prevent architectures that degrade efficiency. Repairable failures are returned to the implementer with diagnostics.
Finally, validated candidates are trained from scratch under matched training compute, using the same training data, and evaluated with three metrics defined in Section
2.3
.
Step 6: Reflect and share.
The proposing researcher revisits its original hypothesis in light of the outcome, including rejection or failure. Reviews, implementation, and experimental records are provided to help it distinguish evidence about the mechanism from problems in realizing or testing it. The researcher records what the outcome supports, what remains unresolved, and what it suggests investigating next. It updates its private notes for future reference and shares generalizable lessons with other researchers. Completing this reflection ends the iteration and updates the observations used for researcher selection in future iterations.

Intuitively, this definition rewards overall improvements compared to the best candidate so far, without assigning negative rewards to unsuccessful attempts, thus encouraging researchers to try out promising directions.
3
Experiments
Our experiments answer three questions: can the team discover useful architectures; which organizational choices help in the limited-iteration setting; and how do different researchers contribute to a successful discovery? We first describe the experiment settings, then evaluate the discovered architecture, compare research organizations, and trace the development of the found architecture.
3.1
Experimental Setting
Research team.
We use 16 researchers and a budget of 80 research iterations. All agent roles use GPT-6 Astra with high reasoning effort through the Codex harness. We allow a maximum of 8 researchers working in parallel, while forcing their proposal stage to be sequential to prevent repetition in proposed ideas. In the first 16 iterations, all researchers are invoked exactly once, and further researcher selection is based on the UCB rule.
Model backbones and search space.
We search at approximately 150M non-embedding parameters, and we scale the discovered best candidate to 1.3B parameters. We use GDN2
(
Hatamizadeh et al., 2026
)
as the baseline. Candidates can change the recurrent mixer’s memory representation, update rule, readout, and parameterization, while retaining the common depth, residual width, and feed-forward network. We also compare with Gated DeltaNet (GDN)
(
Yang et al., 2025a
)
and Kimi Delta Attention (KDA)
(
Team et al., 2025
)
using the same surrounding architecture. Appendix
A
gives the dimensions and parameter-count convention at both scales.
Training data and budget.
All models are trained from scratch on FineWeb-Edu
(
Penedo et al., 2024
)
. For all models, we adjust their training tokens to match the total FLOPs of training GDN: at 150M scale, we train GDN for 15B tokens; at 1.3B scale, we train GDN for 100B tokens. More expensive architectures therefore receive fewer training tokens. Following
Hatamizadeh et al. (2026)
, all models use the same optimizer hyperparameters and global batch size (details in Appendix
A
).
Final evaluation and search feedback.
We evaluate models on language modeling (LM), common-sense reasoning (CSR), synthetic needle-in-a-haystack (NIAH), and, for 1.3B models, in-context real-world retrieval (RWR) tasks. For LM, we report perplexity on WikiText (Wiki.)
(
Merity et al., 2016
)
and LAMBADA (LMB.)
(
Paperno et al., 2016
)
. For CSR, we report the mean accuracy over eight datasets
(
Bisk et al., 2019
;
Zellers et al., 2019
;
Sakaguchi et al., 2019
;
Clark et al., 2018
;
Mihaylov et al., 2018
;
Sap et al., 2019
;
Clark et al., 2019
)
. For NIAH, we use four synthetic tasks (S-NIAH-1, 2, 3 and MK-NIAH) from RULER
(
Hsieh et al., 2024
)
. For in-context real-world retrieval, we report mean accuracy over six datasets
(
Arora et al., 2025
;
Rajpurkar et al., 2018
;
Joshi et al., 2017
;
Kwiatkowski et al., 2019
;
Dua et al., 2019
)
.
During search, we use a reduced suite to provide feedback: LM loss on the same two datasets, a subset of 256 examples from each CSR dataset, and 64 examples per NIAH task at each of 1K, 2K, and 4K context. We do not evaluate RWR during search. The NIAH evaluation uses a teacher-forced continuation proxy instead of answer generation. Appendix
B
gives more details on evaluation.

What was discovered?
CFDN augments GDN2’s recurrent matrix memory with a recurrent vector. The vector contributes the same context information to every query, while the matrix supplies a query-dependent prediction. Given the current token’s key, the memories jointly predict its value. The defining change is how they learn from that prediction error: the vector is updated first, and the matrix then fits the remaining error. This gives shared information priority over query-specific correction. The resulting update does not add notable compute over GDN2 and remains compatible with efficient parallel training. Section
3.5
explains how this mechanism is developed across researchers; Appendix
D.1
gives the full recurrence.
As shown in Table
1
, despite using the fewest training tokens, CFDN achieves a substantially higher utility than all baselines. Specifically, it improves all three search targets over GDN2: LM perplexity decreases from 12.21 to 11.90, CSR accuracy rises from 44.48% to 44.63%, and retrieval rises from 28.91% to 50.00%.
In terms of the final full evaluation, CFDN outperforms all baselines on two language modeling tasks, and more considerably on the NIAH tasks. Its CSR performance is slightly worse than GDN2 but still better than GDN and KDA.
These results demonstrate that
the search found a genuinely better architecture than the baselines

3.3
Which Organizational Choices Support Discovery?
A useful architecture does not by itself explain whether the team’s organization helps discovery. We therefore compare the full system with three variants, holding the agent model, iteration allowance, per-candidate training budget, and search feedback fixed. ❶
No background
removes disciplinary profiles while retaining researcher identities and their private histories. ❷
Fresh memory
removes the researchers’ private histories and notes between iterations, while preserving their disciplinary profiles. ❸
Uniform selection
replaces the UCB-defined adaptive selection with a uniform selection that repeats researchers in a fixed order. All variants retain access to shared proposals, experimental results, and lessons, so each comparison concerns a design beyond this common evidence.
The main and no-background runs start from scratch. To reduce variation due to different initial discoveries, fresh-memory and uniform-selection both reuse the main run’s first 16 iterations (one iteration per researcher) and conduct 64 further iterations. Appendix
C
gives more details.

3.5
How Researchers Develop the Discovered Architecture
Figure
1
traces CFDN’s development through contributions from four researchers. A researcher grounded in linear attention introduces a recurrent context vector alongside GDN2’s matrix memory, building on affine-memory precedent
(
Zuo et al., 2026
)
. Another researcher learns the address origin that determines what this vector represents. A researcher with expertise in adaptive filtering then normalizes the correction by the translated address’s energy, showing how
disciplinary knowledge can refine a colleague’s mechanism
.
The next revision updates the matrix before the context vector, improving LM perplexity but weakening CSR and retrieval. A researcher with a background in predictive representations uses this tradeoff to reconsider which memory should absorb the prediction error first. It then switches to updating shared context before the matrix, which produces CFDN. Thus, the team uses a degraded result to guide a subsequent improvement, rather than simply retaining successful proposals.
4
Related Work
Autonomous research agents.
A growing line of work automates the iterative research process from hypothesis to experiment, through fixed pipelines from idea generation to written paper
(
Lu et al., 2024
;
Schmidgall et al., 2025
)
, agentic tree search
(
Yamada et al., 2025
)
, or evolutionary search with the language model as the mutation operator
(
Novikov et al., 2025
;
Lange et al., 2025
)
.
In these works, a single agent or a fixed pipeline proposes every candidate.
Other work organizes a team of researchers around a shared scientific problem.
These teams differ in how they are composed, what each member retains and what the team shares, and how research opportunities are distributed.
VirSci, ASCollab, and ScienceClaw
(
Su et al., 2025
;
Liu et al., 2025a
;
Wang et al., 2026
)
give agents distinct backgrounds, personas, or scientific profiles.
CORAL
(
Qu et al., 2026
)
, ASCollab, and ScienceClaw keep long-running agents with their own histories and a shared record, whereas AgentRxiv
(
Schmidgall and Moor, 2025
)
starts a fresh laboratory instance per project that reads a shared archive of earlier papers.
However, none compares teams with and without different backgrounds on the outcomes of implementing, training, and evaluating what they propose, or tests whether private memory adds anything once findings are shared.
Adaptive allocation itself is not new, but no existing work both gives researchers different backgrounds and allocates opportunities among them adaptively.
The Virtual Lab
(
Swanson et al., 2024
)
decides which specialist takes an agenda item, ShinkaEvolve
(
Lange et al., 2025
)
decides which language model performs the next mutation, SwarmResearch
(
Virk et al., 2026
)
decides which branch of the search to extend, and Economy of Minds
(
Qi et al., 2026
)
decides which agent acts next in a task.
Each of them chooses an operator or a candidate to advance.
In our setting, the decision is which researcher proposes and tests the next idea, and because each researcher brings its own background and record of what it has tried and learned, that choice determines what evidence the team will have next.
No prior team of researchers with different backgrounds makes this decision adaptively.
Autonomous research has also been applied to architecture design.
NADER
(
Yang et al., 2024b
)
coordinates fixed-role agents that propose changes to a tree of prior modifications. AIRA-Compose and AIRA-Design
(
Pepe et al., 2026
)
pool designs from independent search agents, and ASI-Arch
(
Liu et al., 2025b
)
runs a researcher, engineer, and analyst pipeline over linear attention architectures and reports that discoveries grow with compute.
These systems use fixed-role workflows or independent agent searches; we instead fix the experimental budget and vary the organization, comparing who proposes, what they retain and share, who receives the next opportunity, and what counts as progress.
Linear attention.
Linear attention replaces the key-value cache of softmax attention with a fixed-size recurrent state
(
Katharopoulos et al., 2020
)
, and subsequent designs mainly differ in what the state remembers, how stored information is revised, and how it is retrieved.
On what to remember, most designs keep a matrix of key–value associations, while Titans
(
Behrouz et al., 2024
)
replaces it with a network learned at inference.
On how to revise, RetNet
(
Sun et al., 2023
)
decays the state at a fixed rate, GLA and Mamba-2
(
Yang et al., 2024a
;
Dao and Gu, 2024
)
make the decay input-dependent, DeltaNet
(
Yang et al., 2025b
)
replaces additive writes with delta-rule correction, GDN and KDA
(
Yang et al., 2025a
;
Team et al., 2025
)
combine the delta rule with learned and fine-grained gating, and GDN2
(
Hatamizadeh et al., 2026
)
separates erasing from writing with channel-wise gates.
On how to retrieve, MesaNet
(
von Oswald et al., 2026
)
solves the regression to optimality at every step, and Parallax
(
Zuo et al., 2026
)
restores the intercept of the underlying regression.
Each of these works changes one or two choices along these axes, and the space they leave open is large, which makes linear attention architecture discovery a natural problem for an autonomous research team.
5
Conclusion
We study how to organize autonomous researchers for cumulative discovery under limited experimental budgets. Our framework combines diverse scientific backgrounds, persistent memory, shared evidence, and adaptive allocation of research opportunities. Applied to linear attention, the team discovered CFDN, which improves over GDN2 at two scales. Organizational comparisons and research trajectories highlight the importance of heterogeneous agents, adaptive allocation, and shared experimental records. Together, these results suggest that sustained autonomous discovery depends on how a team learns from experiments and decides which ideas to pursue next.

AI use statement
Our use of AI falls into two categories. First, AI-driven research is the subject of this work. The LLM agents in our system propose and refine architectural hypotheses, review proposals, implement methods, interpret experimental results, and share findings. These activities are part of the research methodology described and evaluated in the paper.
Second, we used AI tools to assist the authors in developing and debugging the autoresearch framework, inspecting agent trajectories to diagnose issues in the research workflow, and polishing the manuscript. The authors reviewed these contributions and take responsibility for the final content of the paper and its associated artifacts.
Ethics statement
This work studies autonomous research in model architecture design using existing training corpora and evaluation benchmarks, without recruiting human participants. The principal ethical concerns involve research integrity: agents may generate incorrect claims, overlook prior work, or optimize evaluation metrics without improving broader capabilities. We retain records of proposals, reviews, implementations, and experimental outcomes to support scrutiny, and use implementation checks and evaluation across multiple capabilities to assess proposed improvements. These safeguards do not guarantee correctness or novelty.

Common small-scale data stream.
The search corpus is prepared once from 24 FineWeb-Edu source shards with the TinyLlama tokenizer. Within each shard, tokenized documents are concatenated and packed into 4,097-ID blocks, yielding 4,096 input–target positions per sequence. Long documents span multiple blocks; only each shard’s final incomplete block is discarded. One saved permutation determines the global sequence order. Each candidate consumes the first

Baseline parameterization.
GDN2 uses separate full projections for queries, keys, values, and channel-wise erase and write gates. Query, key, and value projections are followed by causal depthwise convolutions of width four and SiLU; queries and keys are L2-normalized. Decay and output-gate preactivations use two linear maps with bottleneck width 128. The recurrent read is RMS-normalized per head, multiplied by a sigmoid output gate, and projected back to the residual stream. Our KDA comparison shares these surrounding components and initialization but uses one scalar erase/write gate per head; GDN additionally uses scalar rather than channel-wise state decay. The architectural differences are therefore confined to the recurrent mechanisms within a common surrounding backbone, rather than unrelated released model recipes.

Input-embedding lookup is excluded; the language-model output projection is included. Biases, normalization scales, and static parameters are inventoried separately from projection weights. Repeated uses of a shared projection are charged for their additional computation. For custom operators, the forward count is multiplied by three as a uniform training-cost approximation.
The general counting rule is to include projections and memory computation, while excluding ordinary token-local scalar/vector processing. Memory reads, contractions, outer-product updates, and transformations of stored state are counted. Ordinary activations, normalization, scalar/vector gates, residual additions, embedding lookup, loss computation, optimizer steps, communication, and checkpointing are excluded. This is a consistent architectural proxy, not a hardware instruction count.
The proposer derives the breakdown, the technical reviewer checks it, and the author’s revision resolves disagreements. Automated checks measure the implemented weight inventory. A mismatch receives one implementer recheck before the measured counts determine the projection term; the custom-operation terms remain those approved in scientific review. Neither parameter counting nor finite training alone proves that an arbitrary implementation faithfully realizes the specification.

Appendix B
Evaluation definitions and complete result tables
Search suite.
WikiText-2 (Wiki.) uses 62 documents scored through independent rolling 4K windows, totaling 322,149 scored tokens. LAMBADA (LMB.) uses 5,153 examples and scores their final-word continuations, totaling 8,808 tokens. We average the two token-mean negative log-likelihoods equally before exponentiation.
CSR uses 256 fixed examples from each of PIQA, HellaSwag, WinoGrande, ARC-Easy, ARC-Challenge, OpenBookQA, Social IQa, and BoolQ. Option likelihoods follow the frozen zero-shot requests. HellaSwag uses character-normalized accuracy; the other tasks use raw accuracy. The reported
Q
Q
is the unweighted mean over these eight tasks.
Retrieval uses S-NIAH-1, S-NIAH-2, S-NIAH-3, and MK-NIAH-1, with 64 fixed examples at each of 1K, 2K, and 4K, totaling 768. The evaluator reveals the first continuation token and teacher-forces the rest. An example passes only if every remaining answer token is the model’s argmax. The first token is not scored. The reported
R
R
averages the 12 task/length cells equally. This proxy does not require autoregressive generation.
Full evaluation.
The full protocol uses all examples in the selected LM/CSR datasets and generated-answer NIAH scoring. NIAH contains 500 frozen requests per task/length cell: S-NIAH-1/2 at 1K, 2K, 4K, and 8K, and S-NIAH-3/MK-NIAH-1 at 1K, 2K, and 4K, for 7,000 requests in 14 cells. All models receive the same requests. Generation is greedy, with at most 128 new tokens and early stopping at EOS. We use batch size eight, BF16, and cached decoding. The RULER scorer checks whether each reference answer appears in the generated text as a case-insensitive substring and averages the fraction of references recovered per request; it does not require the entire generated string to equal the answer. The NIAH mean weights all cells equally.
Real-world retrieval at 1.3B.
We use the released BASED/JRT cloze-completion suite
(
Arora et al., 2025
)
: SWDE, SQuAD, FDA, TriviaQA, Natural Questions (NQ), and DROP. This suite is used only for final evaluation of the 1.3B models and does not enter search feedback or utility. The nominal context length is 2K. We retain the released preprocessing and its exclusions for empty or single-character primary answers, leaving 12,077 examples: 1,067, 2,977, 1,101, 1,688, 3,157, and 2,087 in the dataset order above. Context is cropped before appending the cloze query; two final NQ prompts consequently contain 2,062 tokens.
Evaluation is zero-shot, with no chat template or context repetition. Greedy cached decoding generates at most 48 tokens, stopping at a newline or EOS, in BF16 batches of up to eight examples of equal input length. An answer is correct if an accepted reference appears in the generated text as a case-insensitive substring. We report the unweighted mean of the six dataset accuracies.

Appendix C
Organizational settings and analysis protocol
C.1
Scientific profiles and researcher initialization
The team uses 16 fixed disciplinary profiles. Each is a self-contained document of approximately 2,000–2,300 words, combining a field’s mathematical foundations, design judgments, diagnostic practices, and primary references. Table
13
summarizes the different research questions these documents foreground. Appendix
C.3
reproduces the complete Bayesian-filtering profile supplied to one researcher. Only the focal linear attention profile is written specifically about the target architecture family.
At initialization, each researcher receives one profile, the common problem statement, and access to shared references covering the baseline, prior work, and experimental constraints. Its conversation, private notebook, and earlier proposal dossiers preserve individual experience as the search proceeds. At each new assignment, the researcher additionally receives a summary of previous results, ongoing investigations, and consolidated shared lessons, with access to the underlying records. The fixed profile therefore supplies an initial technical perspective, while private and shared evidence can change the researcher’s subsequent judgments.

Differentiable computers and neural data structures

Predictive representations and information bottlenecks

Research protocol and analysis details
Proposal and review details.
Each proposal specifies its hypothesis, expected benefit, and a falsifying outcome, together with state equations, parameterization, a parallelizable training formulation, and an analytical compute breakdown. For lineage analysis, it identifies one primary scientific precursor and may cite other influences; this attribution does not require retaining the precursor’s architecture. Technical review precedes contextual review. Both reviewers are blind to the author’s identity and the other review. The technical reviewer assesses the proposal without the shared research history, while the contextual reviewer uses that history to assess duplication and research value. The original researcher then resolves correctable issues into the revised specification.
Memory and information access.
The persistent condition preserves the originating researcher’s conversation and notebook across iterations. The fresh condition preserves them only within one iteration, including proposal revision and terminal reflection. It still receives shared proposals, results, published lessons, and the shared result summary. Reviewers and implementers use task-specific sessions in both conditions. The evidence available at reflection includes reviews, source code, records of implementation attempts, training logs, and evaluation artifacts. A director consolidates shared lessons after every ten completed reflections; it does not select the next researcher. Agent tools include web search and a numerical Python environment.
