Bayesian Filtering, Innovations, and Regime Change (researcher profile)
# Bayesian Filtering, Innovations, and Regime Change
Sequential inference is the discipline of maintaining a calibrated belief about an evolving latent process. The state of a filter is not merely its current best estimate. It is a probability distribution—or a controlled approximation to one—whose uncertainty determines how new evidence should be interpreted.
Consider the state-space model
\[
x_t\sim p(x_t\mid x_{t-1}),\qquad
y_t\sim p(y_t\mid x_t).
\]
Bayesian filtering alternates prediction and correction:
\[
p(x_t\mid y_{1:t-1})
=\int p(x_t\mid x_{t-1})p(x_{t-1}\mid y_{1:t-1})\,dx_{t-1},
\]
\[
p(x_t\mid y_{1:t})
\propto p(y_t\mid x_t)p(x_t\mid y_{1:t-1}).
\]
This recursion is exact as an identity. All difficulty lies in representing and updating the posterior.
## Linear–Gaussian filtering and the meaning of innovation
For linear dynamics and Gaussian noise,
\[
x_t=F_tx_{t-1}+w_t,\quad w_t\sim\mathcal N(0,Q_t),
\]
\[
y_t=H_tx_t+v_t,\quad v_t\sim\mathcal N(0,R_t),
\]
the posterior remains Gaussian. After predicting mean \(m_tˆ-\) and covariance \(P_tˆ-\), the innovation and its covariance are
\[
\nu_t=y_t-H_tm_tˆ-,\qquad
C_t=H_tP_tˆ-H_tˆ\top+R_t.
\]
The Kalman gain \(K_t=P_tˆ-H_tˆ\top C_tˆ{-1}\) balances model confidence against measurement confidence, and the corrected mean is \(m_t=m_tˆ-+K_t\nu_t\).
The key quantity is the **normalized innovation**, not the raw residual. A residual of magnitude ten is unremarkable if predicted uncertainty is one hundred and alarming if uncertainty is one tenth. Innovation whiteness is also a diagnostic: persistent temporal structure in normalized innovations signals a misspecified dynamics model, observation model, or noise covariance.
Covariance is computational state, not decorative metadata. Discarding it forces a fixed response to evidence and prevents principled fusion of measurements with different reliability. Square-root filters propagate factors of \(P\) for numerical stability. Information-form filters propagate precision \(J=Pˆ{-1}\) and information vector \(h=Jm\), making independent measurement contributions additive. Choice of form should follow sparsity and conditioning.
Consistency can be tested statistically. Under the assumed model, the normalized innovation squared
\[
\operatorname{NIS}_t=\nu_tˆ\top C_tˆ{-1}\nu_t
\]
has a chi-squared reference distribution with dimension equal to the observation dimension. A sequence of values that is systematically too large indicates overconfidence or mismatch; values that are systematically too small indicate excessive uncertainty. Temporal dependence must be checked separately with innovation-whiteness tests. Coverage and whiteness reveal failures that root-mean-square error cannot.
Even algebraically equivalent covariance updates differ in finite precision. The compact expression \(P_t=(I-K_tH_t)P_tˆ-\) can lose symmetry or positive semidefiniteness. The Joseph form,
\[
P_t=(I-K_tH_t)P_tˆ-(I-K_tH_t)ˆ\top+K_tR_tK_tˆ\top,
\]
is more robust, and square-root implementations are preferable when conditioning is severe. Numerical representation is part of the inferential method because an invalid covariance implies invalid confidence.
## Beyond a single Gaussian
Extended Kalman filtering linearizes nonlinear dynamics locally and can become inconsistent when curvature is strong. Sigma-point methods propagate a designed set of points through the nonlinear map, improving moment approximation without explicit Jacobians but still reducing the posterior to a Gaussian.
Particle filters retain weighted samples:
\[
p(x_t\mid y_{1:t})\approx
\sum_{i=1}ˆ{N}w_tˆ{(i)}\delta(x_t-x_tˆ{(i)}).
\]
They can represent multimodality and non-Gaussian tails, but importance weights degenerate over time. Resampling removes low-weight particles yet causes impoverishment and destroys ancestry diversity. The importance-sampling distribution is therefore central: sampling only from the transition prior wastes particles when the observation is informative. Differentiable or learned filters do not abolish these issues; they can simply hide miscalibration inside an expressive learned sampler.
Rao–Blackwellization is often preferable to brute-force particles. If part of the model is conditionally linear–Gaussian, integrate that part analytically and sample only the discrete or nonlinear component. Expert design exploits conditional structure before increasing particle count.
## Robustness is a modeling decision
An unexpectedly large innovation admits several explanations: the observation
may be corrupted, the latent state may have moved farther than expected, the
dynamics may have changed regime, or the posterior may simply have been
overconfident. A robust filter should not collapse these explanations into one
generic downweighting rule. Each implies a different posterior and a different
prediction for the next observation.
Heavy-tailed likelihoods, such as Student-(t) observation models, reduce the
leverage of isolated outliers. Mixture likelihoods can carry an explicit
contamination indicator. Adaptive process noise can accommodate gradual drift,
while switching dynamics or run-length uncertainty represent persistent
structural change. These mechanisms are not interchangeable. An overly heavy
tail can explain away a genuine change point forever; inflated process noise
can preserve tracking error at the cost of uninformative uncertainty; a reset
rule can mistake one sensor fault for a new regime.
I distinguish these cases through persistence and cross-channel structure. A
single-channel spike with immediate recovery supports contamination. Coherent
innovations across several measurements support latent motion or model error.
A sustained change in the distribution of normalized innovations supports a
regime hypothesis. Posterior predictive checks should reproduce not only
marginal residual magnitudes but also their temporal dependence, direction,
and coincidence across sensors.
Robustness must remain calibrated. A method that never issues a confident
posterior is difficult to falsify but not useful. I report coverage conditioned
on nominal periods, outliers, and transitions, together with detection delay
and false-alarm rate. This makes explicit whether apparent resilience comes
from correct hypothesis management or from indiscriminately broad intervals.
## Switching models and hypothesis management
Abruptly changing systems require uncertainty over both continuous state and discrete regime. If a mode \(z_t\) follows a Markov chain and each mode has its own dynamics, exact filtering yields a mixture whose number of components grows exponentially. The interacting multiple-model method controls this explosion by mixing, filtering within each mode, and merging hypotheses at every step.
This is an important general lesson: bounded inference requires a deliberate **hypothesis management policy**. Pruning, merging, and moment matching are not implementation afterthoughts; they determine which alternative explanations survive. A mode with low current probability may need preservation if it predicts a high-consequence future or is difficult to recover after deletion.
## Change points as uncertainty over run length
Bayesian online change-point detection introduces the run length \(r_t\), the number of observations since the most recent change. A hazard function \(H(r)\) specifies the prior probability of a change after a run of length \(r\). The posterior update combines two possibilities:
\[
p(r_t=0, y_{1:t})
=\sum_{r_{t-1}}
p(r_{t-1},y_{1:t-1})H(r_{t-1})
p(y_t\mid r_{t-1}),
\]
and growth transitions \(r_t=r_{t-1}+1\) weighted by \(1-H(r_{t-1})\).
This is more informative than a reset score. It maintains uncertainty over when the current regime began, and each run-length hypothesis carries its own sufficient statistics. The hazard encodes duration assumptions; a constant hazard implies a geometric regime duration and is often adopted without justification.
Exact run-length support grows by one at every observation. A bounded implementation must prune, merge, or aggregate old hypotheses, and this approximation determines the longest change history the detector can express. Keeping only the most probable run length turns posterior inference into brittle winner-take-all segmentation. A small tail mass spread over many long runs can matter even when no individual run is likely.
Outliers and change points are easily confused. A robust observation model should explain isolated anomalies without resetting the regime, whereas sustained predictive failure should transfer mass toward short run lengths. Heavy-tailed likelihoods, explicit outlier indicators, and hierarchical hazards help separate these phenomena.
## Event-triggered inference
In sensing and networked control, communication or correction can be triggered only when the innovation is informative enough to justify its cost. Crucially, silence can itself be evidence: if a sensor transmits only when a residual leaves a known region, no transmission tells the estimator that the residual remained inside that region. Treating skipped updates as missing at random loses information and biases uncertainty.
Event policies should therefore be designed jointly with the estimator. A threshold on \(\nu_tˆ\top C_tˆ{-1}\nu_t\) has a statistical interpretation, while a threshold on raw magnitude does not. Resource-aware filtering asks for an optimal trade between posterior risk, sensing cost, latency, and energy.
## Filtering, smoothing, and decision delay
Filtering estimates \(x_t\) from \(y_{1:t}\); smoothing permits later observations. Fixed-lag smoothing occupies a useful middle ground: it delays commitment by \(L\) steps and revises recent states using \(y_{t+1:t+L}\). This is often more valuable than making a much larger causal filter, especially near regime boundaries.
The correct comparison therefore fixes decision latency. Zero-lag detection, fixed-lag revision, and retrospective segmentation answer different questions. A change-point method should also state whether it estimates the first affected sample, the time at which evidence became sufficient, or the time at which an alarm was issued.
## Failure modes
- **Overconfidence:** underestimated \(Q\) or \(R\) produces brittle gains and poor coverage.
- **Model mismatch:** a precise posterior under the wrong model is worse than an honest broad posterior.
- **Innovation misuse:** large raw residuals are treated as changes without uncertainty normalization.
- **Particle collapse:** a nominally multimodal filter effectively contains one duplicated hypothesis.
- **Premature merging:** distinct modes with similar current means have incompatible futures.
- **Hazard misspecification:** expected regime duration silently dictates detection latency.
- **Numerical loss of positive definiteness:** naïve covariance updates accumulate roundoff error.
- **Retrospective leakage:** smoothing results are reported as if available to an online filter.
## An expert workflow for sequential inference
When a sequential estimator fails, I first decide which problem it is failing
to solve. State estimation asks where the process is within a trusted model.
Robust inference asks whether an observation is an outlier. Model selection
asks which dynamics explain the data. Change-point detection asks whether the
old regime has ended. These explanations can produce the same large residual,
but they imply different updates.
My operating sequence is:
1. **Write the belief state.** I state which variables are uncertain and which
approximation represents their joint posterior: moments, information
parameters, particles, regime mixtures, run lengths, or a factorization.
A point estimate is acceptable only when uncertainty cannot affect any
subsequent decision.
2. **Predict before observing.** The transition model produces a predictive
distribution, not just a predicted mean. Its spread is the reference against
which the next observation becomes ordinary or surprising.
3. **Correct by relative evidence.** I inspect likelihood ratios or normalized
innovations. Raw residual magnitude has no context. With Gaussian
observations, \(\nu_tˆ\top C_tˆ{-1}\nu_t\) is the natural scalar diagnostic;
for non-Gaussian models, posterior predictive checks play the same role.
4. **Keep explanations alive when their futures differ.** A low-probability
regime, run length, or particle family should not be merged merely because
its present mean resembles the winner. Pruning is a resource decision about
tail mass, recoverability, and future consequence. Conditional analytic
structure should be Rao–Blackwellized before particles are multiplied.
5. **Interpret persistence.** One unlikely observation may call for a
heavy-tailed likelihood or outlier indicator. A sequence of structured
innovations suggests dynamics mismatch or regime change. The hazard model
states how readily persistent failure becomes a reset; it should never be
an invisible constant.
6. **Choose commitment latency.** Filtering, fixed-lag smoothing, and
retrospective segmentation permit different evidence. I compare methods at
equal delay and distinguish the first affected time, the time evidence
became sufficient, and the alarm time.
7. **Audit numerical and statistical consistency.** I preserve symmetry and
positive semidefiniteness with square-root or Joseph-form updates when
needed. I check posterior coverage, normalized-innovation distributions,
innovation whiteness, effective particle diversity, and recovery after
mismatch—not point error alone.
Missingness and silence require an observation model too. If a sensor reports
only outside a threshold region, no report truncates the residual distribution
and is informative. If observations are missing for external reasons, treating
the gap as evidence is wrong. Sensing, communication, and inference policies
must therefore be specified jointly whenever reporting depends on latent
state or innovation.
To falsify an estimator, I vary noise scale, inject isolated heavy-tailed
outliers, switch among regimes with similar current means but different
dynamics, alter regime duration, and withhold informative observations. I
check whether uncertainty broadens before errors grow, whether alternative
hypotheses survive long enough to recover, and whether apparent calibration
comes from inflating \(Q\) or \(R\) to conceal model-form error. Learned
dynamics, observation models, and samplers are useful only if their flexibility
does not make these checks vacuous; epistemic uncertainty and irreducible
observation noise should not be collapsed into one convenient variance.
The unresolved resource problem is hypothesis management. Exact belief support
usually grows, while hard winner-take-all truncation is brittle. Pruning,
merging, moment matching, and learned sampling mechanisms should be judged by
which future distinctions they erase and how their lost tail mass is
accounted for.
The defining principle is that an observation has no fixed importance. Its
importance is the likelihood ratio it induces relative to the current
predictive belief.
## Selected primary references
- Kalman, [“A New Approach to Linear Filtering and Prediction Problems”](https://doi.org/10.1115/1.3662552).
- Gordon, Salmond, and Smith, [“Novel Approach to Nonlinear/Non-Gaussian Bayesian State Estimation”](https://people.bordeaux.inria.fr/pierre.delmoral/gordon-salmond-smith-1993.pdf).
- Blom and Bar-Shalom, [“The Interacting Multiple Model Algorithm for Systems with Markovian Switching Coefficients”](https://doi.org/10.1109/9.1299).
- Adams and MacKay, [“Bayesian Online Changepoint Detection”](https://arxiv.org/abs/0710.3742).
- Jonschkowski et al., [“Differentiable Particle Filters”](https://arxiv.org/abs/1805.11122).

article.headline: 16 人多学科 AI 团队自主搜出线性注意力架构
article.lede: 16 个学科背景各异的 AI 智能体在有限算力下组队，自主发现的新线性注意力架构在 150M 与 1.3B 规模上均优于
article.problem: 现有自主研究智能体多由单一智能体或固定流水线提出全部候选，容易沿同一种推理模式过早收敛到设计空间的局部最优。当实验成本高昂、只能测试有限想法时，如何在探索与利用之间分配研究机会，以及如何让一次实验的结果真正影响团队下一步尝试，仍缺少系统研究。论文因此追问：不同学科背景的 AI 研究者如何在有限实验预算下互相借鉴发现并持续取得进展。
article.method: 团队由 16 个持久化的 AI 研究者组成，每人以不同学科档案初始化，档案包含先验知识、数学工具、研究直觉与研究习惯，各自保留私有研究笔记，同时共享提案、结果与经验，每 10 次迭代把积累综合为共识经验。每次迭代先用折扣 UCB 规则选出下一位研究者，提案经技术评审和情境评审两道独立审查后，由实现智能体编码、在匹配 GDN 参考 FLOPs 的预算下训练评估，最后由作者反思并把结论写回团队。研究者可以修订他人提案，早期失败或被拒的结果也被当作后续改进的证据。
article.results: 主运行在 80 次迭代内完成 63 次候选评估，找到 Context-First DeltaNet（CFDN）：在 GDN2 的矩阵记忆上加一路循环上下文向量，并让上下文先于矩阵吸收预测误差。按搜索反馈协议，CFDN 相对 GDN2 把语言建模困惑度从 12.21 降到 11.90、常识推理从 44.48% 升到 44.63%、检索从 28.91% 升到 50.00%。150M 全量评估中，CFDN 的 NIAH 为 29.76%（GDN2 为 25.79%）、WikiText 困惑度 33.84（GDN2 为 34.93），但常识推理 43.29% 略低于 GDN2 的 43.60%。扩到 1.3B 后，CFDN 在五类指标上均最优：WikiText 15.74、LAMBADA 11.04、常识推理 54.53%、NIAH 67.29%、真实检索 33.41%，对应 GDN2 为 16.05、11.22、52.65%、66.86%、32.52%。消融显示主运行最佳效用为 1.04，去掉学科背景为 0.54、去掉私有记忆为 0.56、改为均匀轮换选择为 0.76；无背景版本在第 22 次迭代达到自身最好结果后便不再进步。
article.why_it_matters: 这项工作把自主科研的瓶颈从「智能体够不够强」换成「谁在探索、记住什么、机会怎么分配」，并用可消融的对照把这些组织选择与最终架构质量挂钩。若结论稳健，未来的架构搜索可以由异质研究者团队在固定算力下承担，而不是靠单个智能体反复试错。
article.limitations: 结论只覆盖线性注意力这一任务族和 GDN2 这一条基线，智能体模型与运行框架也各只有一种；几组关键对比都是单次运行，未给出重复实验的方差，而主运行直到第 68 次迭代才拿出最强候选，说明结果可能对具体调度轨迹敏感。作者自己亦指出，智能体可能生成错误主张、忽略已有工作或只优化指标而不提升更广泛能力，实现检查与多指标评估并不能保证正确性或新颖性。
article.figure_caption_zh: 自主研究团队的组织方式：(a) 16 位研究者各有学科背景与持久私有历史，自适应选择在已测贡献与尚待检验的机会之间平衡；(b) 被选中的研究者让一个提案走完评审，通过后实现并实验，再反思结果；(c) 提案、结果及其关联构成共享知识，供研究者互相借鉴，圈号标出对照实验涉及的四项组织因素。

figure.caption: {Organization of the autonomous research team.} {(a)} Sixteen researchers have distinct scientific backgrounds and persistent individual histories. Adaptive selection balances measured contributions with opportunities for less-tested researchers. {(b)} A selected researcher develops one proposal through review and, if approved, implementation and experimentation, then reflects on its outcome. {(c)} Proposals, outcomes, and their relationships form a shared body of knowledge through which researchers build on one another's work. Circled numbers identify the four organizational factors studied in our comparisons.

page_papers.title: GAD: Geometry Attention Distillation for Consistent Video Generation
page_papers.abstract: Video diffusion models generate visually compelling short-term sequences but often struggle to preserve scene geometry and object structure over time. In this paper, we first demonstrate that current video attention cannot identify reliable correspondences across frames, with responses dispersed across multiple regions even after recognizable scene structure has emerged. We argue that reliable cross-frame associations are essential for information exchange as scene structure forms in video generation. Thus, we introduce Geometry Attention Distillation (GAD), which transfers correspondences from a frozen geometry model's attention to video attention. Extracted from clean videos, these correspondences link the same static surface or moving object across frames. Since structure formation begins in deeper layers at higher noise and shallower layers at lower noise, we apply attention distillation at a student layer selected according to the noise timestep. After training, video attention focuses more consistently on corresponding locations. Experiments across all three video backbones demonstrate improved long-range scene consistency and dynamic temporal consistency, with geometric gains across generation lengths. On Wan2.2 5B, GAD improves cross-frame matching accuracy by at least 30% over the Wan baseline on both long-range benchmarks. Notably, GAD achieves these gains without additional inference modules, offering a promising approach to efficient and consistent video-based world simulation. Project page: https://fantasy-amap.github.io/GAD/.

Abstract
Video diffusion models generate visually compelling short-term sequences but often struggle to preserve scene geometry and object structure over time.
In this paper, we first demonstrate that current video attention cannot identify reliable correspondences across frames, with responses dispersed across multiple regions even after recognizable scene structure has emerged.
We argue that reliable cross-frame associations are essential for information exchange as scene structure forms in video generation.
Thus, we introduce Geometry Attention Distillation (
GAD
), which transfers correspondences from a frozen geometry model’s attention to video attention.
Extracted from clean videos, these correspondences link the same static surface or moving object across frames.
Since structure formation begins in deeper layers at higher noise and shallower layers at lower noise, we apply attention distillation at a student layer selected according to the noise timestep.
After training, video attention focuses more consistently on corresponding locations.
Experiments across all three video backbones demonstrate improved long-range scene consistency and dynamic temporal consistency, with geometric gains across generation lengths.
On Wan2.2 5B,
GAD
improves cross-frame matching accuracy by at least 30% over the Wan baseline on both long-range benchmarks.
Notably,
GAD
achieves these gains without additional inference modules, offering a promising approach to efficient and consistent video-based world simulation.

1  Introduction
Recent video diffusion models
[

33
,
71

57
]
generate visually compelling sequences from text and images, yet struggle to preserve scene geometry over time and maintain coherent object structure during motion. Such consistency is essential for interactive world modeling
[
68
,
49
]
, robotic planning
[
17
,
32
]
, and autonomous driving simulation
[
21
,
64
]
, where generated videos must represent temporally coherent environments.
To improve consistency, existing approaches employ camera-aware positional encoding
[
36
,
72
]
, explicit geometric conditioning
[
53
,
6
,
25
]
, history-conditioned generation
[
37
,
78
]
, and geometry-aware feature alignment
[
65
,
23
]
.
However, such guidance does not ensure that video models reliably associate observations of the same scene element across frames, a capability essential for consistent video generation.
To understand how cross-frame associations develop, we examine attention patterns in video models and the emergence of scene structure across noise levels and network depths.
Our analysis shows that video attention cannot reliably identify the same scene element across frames: its responses are often dispersed across multiple regions, even after recognizable scene structure has emerged.
Such ambiguous associations can mix information from unrelated regions, undermining the preservation of scene geometry and object structure across frames.
Ideally, cross-frame attention should connect observations of the same scene element, enabling information exchange that supports consistent structure formation. We further observe that recognizable scene structure begins to emerge in deeper layers at higher noise and shallower layers at lower noise. This suggests guiding video attention where structure and cross-frame associations are beginning to form, with the guidance depth adapted to the noise level. For a source of this guidance, we turn to geometry foundation models
[
35
,
58
]
with promising multi-view matching capabilities.
Probing VGGT-
Ω
\Omega
[
59
]
reveals attention responses that associate the same static surface or moving object across frames, providing geometric correspondence targets for guiding video attention.
Building on these insights, we introduce Geometry Attention Distillation (
GAD
), an attention distillation framework that guides cross-frame associations during structure formation. During training, we extract correspondence targets from the attention of a frozen geometry model on clean videos. The total attention each source token assigns to a target frame serves as a reliability cue for weighting its supervision. We select the student layer for attention distillation according to the noise timestep, guiding cross-frame associations as scene structure forms. At the selected layer, pairwise supervision encourages spatial discrimination within frame pairs, while trackwise supervision extends temporal coverage by matching a common source to multiple target frames. These complementary distillation objectives are optimized jointly with the original video generation loss, transferring cross-frame relations while preserving the flexibility of video representations. After training, video attention focuses more consistently on corresponding regions across frames, while generated videos better preserve scene geometry and moving-object structure.
We evaluate
GAD
on camera-controlled video generation using RealEstate10K and DL3DV-10K for long-range scene consistency and OmniWorld-Game for dynamic consistency.
Across all three video backbones,
GAD
improves geometric consistency in long-range generation and temporal consistency in dynamic generation.
Geometric improvements across generation lengths further support the applicability of
GAD
across backbone configurations and video durations.
Notably, with Wan2.2 5B,
GAD
delivers at least a 30% relative improvement in cross-frame matching accuracy on both long-range benchmarks, without additional inference modules or computations.
Our main contributions are summarized as follows:
•
We analyze cross-frame associations in video models, revealing persistent geometric ambiguities in attention and a noise-dependent shift in the depth at which scene structure begins to form. These observations motivate geometry attention distillation at layers where structure is emerging.
•
We propose
GAD
, an attention distillation framework that transfers geometric correspondence knowledge to video attention for improved cross-frame consistency.
•
Extensive experiments demonstrate that
GAD
improves long-range scene consistency and dynamic temporal consistency across all three video backbones, with consistent improvements across generation lengths and no additional inference modules.

3  Analysis and Motivation
3.1  Attention Patterns in Video Models
Cross-frame consistency requires associating the same scene element across viewpoint changes or object motion. We examine how video attention establishes these associations across noise levels and network depths.
In
Fig.
2(a)
, we fix a source query and a target frame within a single video generation trajectory, and visualize the target frame’s intermediate token features using PCA alongside query-to-target attention responses. The PCA visualizations reveal recognizable scene structure, while the attention maps show whether responses concentrate near the reference correspondence or favor other regions. Further visualization details are provided in
Section
E.1
.
This joint analysis reveals two key findings. First, video attention cannot reliably identify the same scene element across frames. Its responses can remain dispersed across multiple regions, including those with similar appearance or semantics, even after recognizable scene structure has emerged in the PCA features. Second, the emergence of scene structure and cross-frame associations depends on both noise level and network depth. We distinguish three qualitative regimes.
In the
noise-dominated region
, PCA features show little recognizable scene structure, while attention responses remain scattered rather than concentrated around the corresponding region.
In the
structure-formation region
(red boxes in
Fig.
2(a)
), recognizable scene structure begins to emerge, and attention starts to respond to corresponding regions across frames, although competing responses remain. This region occurs in deeper layers at higher noise and shallower layers at lower noise.
In the
structure-established region
, scene layout is more clearly defined in the PCA features and cross-frame associations are more apparent, but they are not necessarily geometrically accurate.
These observations motivate explicitly guiding video attention toward geometrically corresponding regions to help preserve scene and object structure across frames.
Furthermore, the three observed regimes suggest that the placement of this guidance matters. In the noise-dominated region, weak structural evidence may make correspondence supervision difficult to exploit; in the structure-established region, additional guidance may have less opportunity to shape associations that have already formed.
The structure-formation region offers an intermediate stage where correspondence learning has a structural basis while the associations are still developing. We therefore hypothesize that geometric guidance is most effective in this region. Since this region emerges at different depths depending on noise, we adapt the supervision layer to the noise timestep.
3.2  Geometric Correspondence in Geometry Foundation Models
Recent advances in geometry foundation models have demonstrated strong multi-view matching capabilities, motivating their use as a source of correspondence supervision. Probing VGGT-
Ω
\Omega
[
59
]
, we find that attention from selected layers and heads captures correspondences on both static surfaces and moving objects. As shown in
Fig.
2(b)
, attention responses remain concentrated around the same railing location across viewpoint changes in the static example, and follow the person’s hat as the person moves in the dynamic example. These observations suggest that geometry model attention can guide associations with the same scene element across both camera and object motion.
Visualization details and layer–head selection are described in
Sections
E.2
and
B.1
.
However, VGGT-
Ω
\Omega
can still produce an attention peak when the scene element represented by a source token is occluded or absent from the target view, making the peak alone an unreliable correspondence cue. As illustrated in
Fig.
6
, ambiguous or incorrect responses can exhibit visible peaks while assigning little total attention to the target frame’s spatial tokens. We call this total the target-frame attention mass and use it as a reliability cue to downweight potentially unreliable matches.

Datasets.
All three benchmarks evaluate camera-controlled video generation conditioned on a first frame, a text prompt, and a target camera trajectory. We assess long-range scene consistency with 15-second videos on RealEstate10K and DL3DV-10K, and dynamic temporal consistency with 5-second videos on OmniWorld-Game.
For all three benchmarks, we use scene-disjoint training and test splits to prevent data leakage between training and evaluation.

5.2  Results
Long-range scene consistency.
Compared with the Wan baselines,
GAD
improves cross-view matching and camera accuracy while achieving better FID, FVD, and CLIP scores across both datasets and all three backbones
Table
1
. Notably, on Wan2.2 5B, matching hit rate increases by at least 30% on each dataset. These gains demonstrate improved geometric consistency alongside better generation quality.
With Wan2.1 14B,
GAD
achieves the best results across all seven metrics on both datasets, indicating that its benefits extend to a larger backbone.
Qualitative comparisons in
Figs.
4
and
7
further show that
GAD
better preserves scene layout and geometric structure throughout long-range camera-controlled sequences.
Dynamic video consistency.
Across all three backbones,
GAD
improves subject consistency, background consistency, and motion smoothness over the corresponding Wan baseline (
Table
2
). With Wan2.1 14B, it achieves the best scores on these metrics among the evaluated methods. Improvements in both subject and background scores suggest that correspondence supervision is useful beyond static scene content, consistent with transferring relations between moving objects rather than enforcing fixed spatial locations. Lower FID and FVD and higher CLIP scores further indicate that these gains coexist with improved generation quality and text alignment. Qualitative comparisons in
Figs.
4
and
8
complement these scores:
GAD
better preserves the structure of moving characters and foreground objects, while maintaining a more stable background layout as the viewpoint changes.
Attention visualizations in
Fig.
5
further show that, compared with the Wan baseline,
GAD
focuses video attention more consistently on corresponding scene regions in both static and dynamic examples. These more localized responses accompany better preservation of scene geometry and moving-object structure in the generated videos.

5.3  Ablations
Using Wan2.2 5B on DL3DV-10K, we ablate the noise-timestep routing schedule, confidence-aware teacher weighting, and pairwise and trackwise supervision to assess their contributions.
Noise-dependent supervision.
As shown in
Table
4
, fixed-layer supervision (R2–R4) already improves geometric metrics over the Wan baseline (R1), while the proposed noise-timestep routing (R8) outperforms all other configurations (R1–R7); complete metrics appear in
Table
6
. Thus, correspondence targets are useful on their own, while their placement determines how effectively they guide generation. The lower performance of R5–R7 compared with R2–R4 further suggests that varying supervision with noise is insufficient without an appropriate layer choice.
These results support the motivation in
Section
3
: supervision should adapt to the noise timestep to target the structure-formation region rather than constrain a fixed layer throughout denoising.
Contributions of distillation components.
Table
5
shows that transferring teacher correspondences indiscriminately is insufficient: without confidence weighting, matching hit rate falls below the Wan baseline despite modest improvements in camera error. This supports accounting for uncertainty in teacher matches rather than treating every target equally. With confidence weighting, either pairwise or trackwise supervision improves all geometric metrics, while their combination performs best across all seven metrics. The joint gains are consistent with their complementary roles: pairwise supervision discriminates spatial matches within a target frame, whereas trackwise supervision extends correspondence coverage across time.
6  Conclusion
We have presented
GAD
, an attention distillation framework that transfers geometric correspondence knowledge from a frozen geometry teacher to video attention.
Motivated by geometric ambiguities in video attention and the noise-dependent emergence of scene structure,
GAD
guides cross-frame associations during structure formation while preserving the video model’s representational flexibility.
Experiments show that
GAD
consistently focuses attention on corresponding regions and improves long-range scene consistency and dynamic temporal consistency across all three video backbones, with geometric improvements across generation lengths. These gains require no additional inference modules. Our findings highlight geometric correspondence transfer through attention as a promising approach to consistent video generation and video-based world simulation.

Appendix A
Loss and Sampling Details
Sampling source–target relations.
Pairwise supervision samples valid directed frame pairs without replacement, excluding pairs within the same frame. Within each selected pair, source tokens are sampled uniformly without replacement from those with valid cached correspondences. Each selected query is compared with all spatial keys in its target frame. If fewer valid pairs or queries are available than the sampling budget, the remaining entries are masked out.
Trackwise supervision first samples one source frame containing eligible source tokens, then samples tokens that have valid correspondences in at least two other frames. Each source is matched to all of its valid target frames, excluding its own frame. For each target frame, the candidate set contains the Gaussian positive neighborhood and uniformly sampled spatial negatives without replacement from outside that neighborhood. Both schemes resample their relations during training; confidence weights affect the loss reduction rather than the probability of selecting a valid relation.

B.1  Teacher Targets and Alignment
Reference correspondences for head selection.
We select the teacher layer–head pair using reference correspondences from both static and dynamic scenes. For the static set, we randomly sample 50 DL3DV scenes and estimate per-view depth and camera parameters with VGGT-
Ω
\Omega
, retaining only high-confidence depth estimates. Inspired by CAMEO
[
34
]
, we construct correspondence labels through cycle projection. A sampled source pixel is unprojected into 3D using its depth and camera parameters, then projected into a target view and assigned to a target token. We unproject the center of that target token using the target-view depth and project it back into the source view. A correspondence is retained only if the projections remain in bounds, the projected and estimated depths agree in both directions, and the return location is sufficiently close to the source sample. When multiple samples within a source token pass these checks, we retain the correspondence with the smallest cycle error. These are geometry-derived reference labels, rather than manually annotated ground truth. For the dynamic set, we use the provided ground-truth point correspondences from 30 dynamic scenes in TAPVid-DAVIS
[
15
]
.
Layer–head evaluation and selection.
We randomly sample query tokens from the input frame of each video and examine every global-attention layer–head pair. For each query, we extract the maximum-response location in each subsequent view and its target-frame attention mass, following
Eq.
1
. We compare the predicted locations with the reference correspondences to measure correspondence error and examine the associated attention masses as reliability cues. Considering correspondence consistency across both static and dynamic tokens, we select layer 13, head 10, which provides the best overall performance in this evaluation. All layer and head indices here are zero-based, and this single pair is used for training-label extraction in all experiments.
The evaluation also reveals substantial specialization across heads. For example, layer 13, head 0 captures static-token correspondences well but fails to reliably associate dynamic tokens, whereas layer 12, head 12 captures dynamic-token correspondences well but performs poorly on static tokens. Other pairs exhibit little correspondence consistency for either type of token. These observations motivate selecting a pair using both static and dynamic scenes, rather than relying on either set alone.
Limitations of projection-based labels.
The depth-and-camera cycle projection above assumes a static scene and therefore cannot directly recover correspondences for moving scene elements. We also observe substantial errors around thin structures and closely spaced surfaces, where depth errors and token discretization can associate different surfaces. These limitations can affect methods that rely on such projection-derived supervision, including CAMEO. Extracting correspondences from VGGT-
Ω
\Omega
attention instead exploits the model’s learned cross-view consistency without imposing a static-scene projection constraint. In our observations, this alleviates these failure cases and also supports correspondences for dynamic scene elements.

Warping-based methods are sensitive to camera scale because their explicit scene initialization and geometric conditioning depend on depth estimated from the first frame. PCA projection.
For each inspected layer and denoising step, we collect the target frame’s block-output features and project the spatial tokens onto three principal components. PCA is fitted independently for each layer–step pair, with a fixed random seed and deterministic component signs. Each projected channel is scaled using its first and 99th percentiles for RGB display. Because each projection is fitted independently, we compare the spatial organization of regions within each visualization rather than matching colors across cells. As discussed in
Section
3.1

The onset of recognizable structure occurs in deeper layers at higher noise and in shallower layers at lower noise. Viewed alongside the attention maps, the PCA features help distinguish the emergence of scene structure from the development of cross-frame associations, showing that attention can still favor competing regions even when the scene layout is recognizable. This joint analysis motivates placing correspondence supervision near the structure-formation stage and adapting the supervised layer to the noise timestep.
Attention readout.
At the same layer and step, we extract queries and keys after normalization and rotary positional encoding. For the fixed source query, each head’s dot-product scores are softmax-normalized over all video keys. We then retain the target-frame slice and average the resulting probabilities over heads. This readout differs from both the block-output features used for PCA and the learned aggregation MLP used during training. Target-frame responses are displayed after normalization by each map’s maximum, with color mapping and interpolation used only for visualization. Thus, the color scale indicates relative spatial response within a map, not an absolute probability shared across layers or noise levels.

Appendix F
Limitations and Future Work
GAD
improves scene and dynamic consistency across all three video backbones by transferring geometric correspondences during training, while preserving the original inference procedure. Its current design suggests three directions for further improvement.
More reliable correspondence targets.
Our results demonstrate that attention distillation with geometric correspondence targets improves video consistency. The current implementation extracts these targets from VGGT-
Ω
\Omega
attention, making their quality dependent on the teacher’s matching ability and spatial resolution. This raises a natural question: can more reliable correspondences further improve the effectiveness of attention distillation? Stronger correspondence estimators or complementary sources of matching evidence could provide more accurate and complete supervision, particularly for ambiguous appearance, occlusion, and moving objects. The correspondence-based formulation of
GAD
provides a basis for exploring such alternatives to the current geometry teacher.
Adaptive supervision placement.
Our noise-timestep routing improves geometric metrics over fixed-layer supervision, demonstrating the value of adapting supervision depth to the denoising state. The current layer assignment depends only on the noise timestep and remains fixed throughout training. As the video model learns, the layers that benefit most from correspondence supervision may also change. Conditioning routing jointly on noise timestep and training progress could better match supervision to the model’s evolving representations, extending the current mechanism while preserving the original inference procedure.
Extension to autoregressive video generation.
GAD
improves static and dynamic consistency in Wan’s bidirectional video models. Autoregressive video generation offers a natural next setting, where preserving scene identity over long rollouts and maintaining coherent object motion remain important challenges. The principle of guiding attention with correspondences also applies to associations between newly generated content and preceding frames. Adapting the distillation objectives to the available temporal context under causal attention could help autoregressive models retain scene structure and moving-object identity as generation proceeds. This offers a promising route to extending the benefits demonstrated here to autoregressive generation.

article.headline: GAD：把几何注意力蒸馏进视频生成
article.lede: 研究者将冻结几何教师VGGT-Ω的跨帧对应关系蒸馏进视频注意力，训练后推理不增加模块。
article.problem: 视频扩散模型能生成观感不错的短视频，却难以在视角变化和物体运动中长期保持场景几何与物体结构。现有相机编码、显式几何条件、历史条件或特征对齐，并不保证注意力把不同帧中的同一场景元素关联起来；作者的分析显示，即使场景结构已经显现，视频注意力的响应仍可能分散在多个区域。
article.method: GAD 从冻结的几何基础模型 VGGT-Ω 的注意力中提取干净视频的跨帧对应关系，并用目标帧注意力质量作为可靠性权重。训练时，它按噪声时间步把监督路由到不同深度的学生层：低噪声用 L5、中噪声用 L15、高噪声用 L25，再以成对监督和跨轨迹监督联合原始流匹配损失优化。推理阶段只保留训练后的视频模型，不加载教师或聚合 MLP，也不改变采样流程。
article.results: 在 Wan2.2 5B 上，RealEstate10K 的跨帧匹配命中率从 0.263 升到 0.350，DL3DV-10K 从 0.257 升到 0.335，均达到至少 30% 的相对提升。Wan2.1 14B 在两个长视频数据集上七项指标均为最佳：RealEstate10K 旋转距离 4.724°→2.754°、匹配命中率 0.413→0.476，DL3DV-10K 旋转距离 5.497°→3.039°、匹配命中率 0.365→0.393。动态 OmniWorld-Game 上，Wan2.2 5B 的主体一致性 0.825→0.853、背景一致性 0.900→0.913、运动平滑度 0.964→0.976。表 2 中峰值显存保持 34.85GB，运行时间 69.60 秒对 70.44 秒，作者称差异在运行波动范围内，且推理不加载额外模块。
article.why_it_matters: 对交互式世界建模、机器人规划和自动驾驶仿真而言，跨帧保持同一场景元素是基本要求。GAD 把几何对应监督放在训练期，为不改推理流程的一致性提升提供了一条可行路径。
article.limitations: 局限在于，对应目标的质量受冻结 VGGT-Ω 匹配能力与空间分辨率制约，且层路由仅按噪声时间步固定、未随训练进程调整。作者也只在 Wan 双向模型上验证，自回归生成尚未覆盖；5 秒和 10 秒设置下 FID 或 FVD 存在小幅取舍。

page_papers.title: Multimodal Embodied Agents: A Unified Capability-centric Perspective from Computer-Use to Robot-Use
page_papers.abstract: Multimodal agents (MMAs) sustain interaction through reasoning, memory, tools, and feedback, most visibly as computer-use agents, while robotic systems (RSs) couple sensing and actuation under physical dynamics. We define multimodal embodied agents (MMEAs) as goal-directed systems that couple multimodal task reasoning with physical action and revise decisions from the resulting feedback. This raises a central question: what changes when a multimodal agent moves from computer-use to robot-use? We introduce PAPAV, a unified capability-centric framework of five recurring functions: Perceive the current state, Anticipate action effects, Plan a feasible course, Act through an interface or body, and Verify the outcome. Defined by function rather than architecture, these capabilities let PAPAV identify what all three share and then compare MMEAs with MMAs and with RSs. Five physical constraints, from partial observability to unverifiable outcomes, leave fewer choices fixed in advance and less room to reverse errors. Across 64 benchmarks, explicit evaluation centers on Act; only 5 assess Anticipate and 3 assess Verify, leaving both largely hidden behind task success. These constraints also frame the open challenges we identify. PAPAV therefore provides a common basis for designing reliable physical agents and measuring progress across all five capabilities rather than task success alone.

Abstract
Multimodal agents (MMAs) sustain interaction through reasoning, memory, tools, and feedback, most visibly as computer-use agents, while robotic systems (RSs) couple sensing and actuation under physical dynamics. We define
multimodal embodied agents
(MMEAs) as goal-directed systems that couple multimodal task reasoning with physical action and revise decisions from the resulting feedback. This raises a central question:
what changes when a multimodal agent moves from computer-use to robot-use?

Introduction
Multimodal agents (MMAs) have grown from one-shot generation into systems that interact over time, use external tools, and revise decisions from feedback, and they now operate browsers, desktops, and phones as computer-use agents

Discussion and Future Benchmark Design
A recurring limitation in this corpus is limited evaluation granularity. Multimodal, long-horizon, and interactive tasks increasingly couple several PAPAV capabilities across digital and embodied environments
[
239
,
220
,
152
,
20
]
, yet aggregate outcomes rarely identify the source of failure. Future benchmarks should retain end-to-end performance while adding attributable signals such as grounding correctness, failure recognition, recovery effectiveness, controlled perturbations, and intermediate checkpoints. RoboCerebra
[
65
]
and AgenticLab
[
59
]
illustrate how checking and replanning signals can improve failure attribution within the PAPAV loop.
Future benchmarks should test how information passes between PAPAV capabilities and changes later decisions. They should record whether predictions affect action selection and whether execution feedback leads to revised plans. Verification requires particular care because an apparently completed action may not satisfy the task goal. A grasp, for example, may look correct while remaining unstable. REFLECT
[
122
]
uses observations of robot execution to explain failures and guide correction. Benchmarks should assess both the accuracy of these judgments and their effect on subsequent behavior.
The evidence available to the verifier is central to this evaluation. A dedicated verifier can specialize in detecting success and failure. A shared model can reuse the actor’s representations and context, which may reduce computation. However, separate models may still miss the same failures if they use the same observations or similar training data. Benchmarks should therefore test whether additional evidence helps the verifier detect errors that the actor overlooks. Such evidence may come from another sensing modality, a physical check, a specialized success detector, or human review.
The actor and verifier should then be evaluated together. Benchmarks should report the fraction of failed executions judged successful and the fraction of successful executions judged failed. They should also identify failure types that both components miss. Detection delay, recovery success, and the extra actions or time needed for recovery show whether verification helps the task. Comparisons should control task conditions and report the resources available to each system. Reference judgments should be established independently of the agent’s verdict. These measures assess both the reliability of verification and its contribution to recovery.
These evaluations should also include realistic deployment conditions. RoboArena
[
8
]
and RobotArena
∞
\infty
[
85
]
illustrate how results can vary across sites and reconstructed environments. Benchmarks should combine controlled comparisons with physical trials or environmental perturbations. This would help determine whether verification and recovery remain effective when observations, hardware, or execution conditions change. The objective is to obtain reliable evidence about the capabilities and feedback processes required by each task.
5

Conclusion
This paper has asked what changes when a multimodal agent moves from computer-use to robot-use. To answer it, we introduced
P
A
P
A
V
, a unified capability-centric perspective that compares multimodal agents, robotic systems, and MMEAs through five functions in a shared task loop. Because each capability is defined by its contribution to the loop rather than by architecture, the digital–physical transition becomes directly comparable across research traditions.
The comparison reveals a consistent shift. Embodiment preserves the task loop but subjects it to partial observability, limited simulatability, irreversibility, real-time coupling, and unverifiable outcomes. Choices that structured interfaces or system design settle in advance for computer-use agents remain open once the same agent uses a robot, so more decisions move into the interaction itself. Reliability therefore depends on how well an agent maintains its beliefs, qualifies its predictions, authorizes its commitments, keeps execution visible, and checks outcomes as physical consequences unfold.
The benchmark analysis points to a broader lesson: end-to-end success is most informative when the underlying capabilities are also observable. Explicit evaluation currently concentrates on Act, while Anticipate and Verify remain largely hidden behind task success. Combining capability-level tests with end-to-end tasks would make failures easier to locate and reported progress easier to interpret. The open challenges we identify, from what an agent should remember to how it should act under uncertainty, follow from the same constraints and mark where the loop must be coordinated rather than merely assembled. We hope PAPAV offers a common basis for designing reliable physical agents and for measuring progress across the full interaction loop.

article.headline: 从电脑操作到机器人：多模态智能体的统一能力视角
article.lede: 一篇综述提出 PAPAV 框架，用感知、预判、规划、行动、验证五个功能角色，把电脑使用与机器人使用放进同一坐标系。
article.problem: 多模态智能体（MMA）已能操作浏览器、桌面和手机，机器人系统（RS）则把语言与感知接到物理动作上；两条研究传统各自积累，却缺少一套共同语言来描述「同一个智能体从电脑走向机器人时究竟改变了什么」。论文把多模态具身智能体（MMEA）定义为将多模态任务推理与物理动作耦合、并依据执行反馈修正决策的目标导向系统，试图回答这一迁移问题。
article.method: 作者提出 PAPAV 这一以能力为中心的统一视角，把感知（Perceive）、预判（Anticipate）、规划（Plan）、行动（Act）、验证（Verify）定义为在任务闭环中反复出现的五个功能角色，并按功能而非架构来界定，使数字与物理两类场景可以直接比较。在此基础上，论文梳理 MMA、RS 与 MM?EA 三类系统的对应关系，并据此分析基准设计与未来挑战。
article.results: 这是一篇立场与综述性论文，论文未给出具体数字，也未报告任何定量实验结果；其结论以定性对比形式给出——具身化保留了任务闭环，但引入了部分可观测、可仿真性受限、不可逆、实时耦合与结果难以验证等约束，原本由界面或系统设计预先决定的选项，在机器人场景中被推入交互过程本身。作者还指出，现有评测的显式评估集中在 Act，而 Anticipate 与 Verify 基本被端到端成功率掩盖，并以 RoboCerebra、AgenticLab、REFLECT、RoboArena 等作为可改进失败归因的示例。
article.why_it_matters: 它给出的是一套可操作的评测语言：把能力级测试与端到端任务结合，能让失败更容易定位，也便于跨数字与物理场景比较进展。对做智能体或机器人策略的研究者来说，这提供了一个整理文献与设计基准的坐标。
article.limitations: 论文属观点与综述性质，未提供新模型或定量验证，PAPAV 的五分法是否能稳定覆盖现有系统、是否会在实践中互相重叠，论文本身没有给出证据。作者也承认现有语料的评测粒度不足，聚合结果难以指认失败来源；论文提出应报告「失败被判成功」与「成功被判失败」的比例，但这些指标仍是建议而非已实施的标准。
article.figure_caption_zh: PAPAV 统一能力视角：感知、预判、规划、行动、验证这五个按功能定义的角色，在电脑使用（上）与机器人使用（下）中重复出现，从而把两类场景放到同一坐标上，并凸显动作获得物理后果后究竟改变了什么。

figure.caption: {A Unified Capability-centric Perspective (PAPAV) from computer-use to robot-use.} {perceive}{ {Perceive}}, {anticipate}{ {Anticipate}}, {plan}{ {Plan}}, {act}{ {Act}}, and {verify}{ {Verify}} are five functional roles that recur in goal-directed interaction, whether an agent operates a computer (top) or a robot (bottom). Defined by function rather than architecture, they place both settings on a common coordinate and isolate what changes once actions acquire physical consequences.

page_papers.title: AgenticRoboRL: Bringing Coding-Agent Post-Training to Agentic Robotics
page_papers.abstract: Agentic robotics systems combine planners with robot harnesses to perform complex manipulation tasks. Recent work improves these systems through better harnesses and external memory, but relies on powerful closed-source models as planners and does not improve the planners' own capabilities. In contrast, coding agents have improved substantially by post-training the model itself. We therefore investigate whether post-training can also improve robot planners. However, applying it across robot harnesses requires accommodating different execution mechanisms, including VLA skill invocation and control-code generation. To this end, we introduce AgenticRoboRL, a framework for post-training robot planners across different harnesses. The training recipe combines supervised fine-tuning with multi-turn reinforcement learning. To accommodate different execution mechanisms, harness-specific adapters connect recorded planner interactions with task outcomes, enabling a common RL training pipeline while keeping execution components fixed. On LIBERO-PRO, AgenticRoboRL raises the success rate of a 9B-parameter planner from 18.1% to 71.0% without external memory, approaching the 72.1% achieved by Codex (GPT-5.5) with external memory. These results demonstrate post-training as an effective approach for improving robot planners. We will release the framework and trained planner checkpoints.

Abstract
Agentic robotics systems combine planners with robot harnesses to perform complex manipulation tasks. Recent work improves these systems through better harnesses and external memory, but relies on powerful closed-source models as planners and does not improve the planners’ own capabilities. In contrast, coding agents have improved substantially by post-training the model itself. We therefore investigate whether post-training can also improve robot planners. However, applying it across robot harnesses requires accommodating different execution mechanisms, including VLA skill invocation and control-code generation. To this end, we introduce
AgenticRoboRL
, a framework for post-training robot planners across different harnesses. The training recipe combines supervised fine-tuning with multi-turn reinforcement learning. To accommodate different execution mechanisms, harness-specific adapters connect recorded planner interactions with task outcomes, enabling a common RL training pipeline while keeping execution components fixed. On LIBERO-PRO, AgenticRoboRL raises the success rate of a 9B-parameter planner from
18.1% to 71.0%
without external memory, approaching the 72.1% achieved by Codex (GPT-5.5) with external memory. These results demonstrate post-training as an effective approach for improving robot planners. We will release the framework and trained planner checkpoints.
1
Introduction
Figure 1:
Overview of AgenticRoboRL.
(a) Agentic robotics systems combine planners with robot harnesses for multi-turn interaction with the environment. (b) We post-train planners through SFT on successful trajectories followed by multi-turn RL. (c) On LIBERO-PRO, post-training improves a 9B planner’s success rate from 18.1% to 71.0%, approaching the 72.1% achieved by Codex (GPT-5.5)with memory. Mem denotes external memory.
Agentic robotics systems can perform complex manipulation tasks by combining a planner with a robot harness. The planner invokes VLA skills
(
Zhang et al., 2026c
)
or generates control code
(
Liang et al., 2023
;
Fu et al., 2026
)
, observes the execution results, and decides what to do next over multiple rounds of interaction. Recent work has improved performance by refining robot harnesses and storing experience from task exploration in external memory
(
Zhang et al., 2026c
;
Xu et al., 2026b
)
, with coding agents such as Codex and Claude Code
(
OpenAI, 2025
;
Anthropic, 2025
)
serving as planners. However, these approaches primarily leverage existing planner capabilities and strengthen the support available to the planner. We explore a complementary direction: enhancing planners’ own capabilities to improve the performance of agentic robotics systems.
For coding agents, enhancing the model’s own capabilities through post-training, including supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning, has proven highly effective
(
Pan et al., 2024
;
Yang et al., 2026
;
Cao et al., 2025
)
. These advances raise a natural question:
Can the post-training methods used for coding agents also improve the performance of
agentic robotics systems?
Applying these methods to robot planners is complicated by the fact that robot harnesses differ in how they carry out a planner’s response. In some harnesses the planner calls learned VLA skills, and a VLA policy executes each call. In others the planner writes control code over perception and control APIs, and a motion controller executes it. Harnesses also differ in what feedback they return to the planner and in how they decide whether the task has succeeded. Training planners across harnesses therefore requires a single pipeline that supports these different execution mechanisms.
To realize such a pipeline, we introduce AgenticRoboRL, a framework for post-training robot planners across different harnesses (Figure
1
). The training recipe combines supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with multi-turn reinforcement learning (RL). SFT trains the planner on successful demonstrations, providing a starting point for RL. During RL, we train on recorded planner requests and responses, while harness-specific adapters associate these interactions with episode outcomes. This allows the same RL pipeline to support VLA skill invocation and control-code generation without changing their execution interfaces. In both stages, only the planner is optimized, while the underlying execution components remain fixed (Figure
2
).
We evaluate the pipeline across these two execution mechanisms using a 9B planner. With RPent
(
Zhang et al., 2026c
)
, a harness that invokes VLA skills, SFT improves success on LIBERO-PRO from 18.1% to 65.1%, and RL further raises it to 71.0%, without external memory. The same checkpoint achieves 72.2% on LIBERO-Plus
(
Fei et al., 2025a
)
without additional training, compared with 19.2% for the original model. With the CaP-X harness
(
Fu et al., 2026
)
, post-training improves success from 2.7% to 28.5%.
These results establish post-training as an effective approach for improving agentic robotics systems.
Our contributions are threefold:
•
To our knowledge,
AgenticRoboRL
is the first general post-training framework to agentic robotics systems.
•
AgenticRoboRL
first fine-tunes the planner on successful demonstrations and then refines it with RL, updating only the planner while keeping execution components fixed. Lightweight harness-specific adapters link each recorded planner call to its episode outcome, so the harnesses do not need a shared low-level action representation.
•
Strong empirical results and an open release. With
AgenticRoboRL
, a 9B planner improves from 18.1% to 71.0% on LIBERO-PRO without external memory. This nearly matches Codex (GPT-5.5) with external memory (72.1%)
(
Zhang et al., 2026c
)
. With the CaP-X harness, it improves from 2.7% to 28.5%. We will release the
AgenticRoboRL
framework and trained planner checkpoints.
2
Related Work
Robot harness agents.
Language models can guide robot behavior by selecting learned skills or generating programs over perception and control APIs
(
Ahn et al., 2022
;
Liang et al., 2023
;
Singh et al., 2022
;
Huang et al., 2023
;
Mu et al., 2024
)
. In this organization, the planner chooses how to use the available capabilities, while the harness executes its decisions and returns observations. Execution feedback and reusable skill libraries support interaction over multiple turns
(
Huang et al., 2022
;
Wang et al., 2023
)
. Hierarchical systems place a language-level reasoning model above a learned low-level policy
(
Belkhale et al., 2024
;
Shi et al., 2025
)
. Recent harnesses expose these capabilities to coding agents: Harness VLA combines a frozen VLA with analytic primitives and task memory
(
Zhang et al., 2026c
)
, while CaP-X provides interfaces for generating executable control code
(
Fu et al., 2026
)
. General-purpose coding agents have also been applied to manipulation without robot-specific training
(
Kumar, 2026
;
Jia et al., 2026b
)
. Other systems improve perception, memory, safety, or skill libraries around the planner
(
Li et al., 2026
;
Xu et al., 2026b
;
Deng et al., 2026
;
Kagaya et al., 2025
;
Woods and Seifi, 2026
)
. A concurrent training-free approach, RV-ICL, provides on-demand access to a hierarchy of demonstration-video keyframes and clips
(
Bao et al., 2026
)
. AgenticRoboRL instead improves the planner through SFT and multi-turn RL while reusing the harness’s
execution components.
Training planners for embodied agents.
RL has been used to improve language and vision-language planners in embodied environments
(
Fei et al., 2025b
;
Chen et al., 2025
;
Liu et al., 2025
;
Wu et al., 2025
;
Jia et al., 2026a
)
. CaP-RL applies RL to a code model that generates a complete control program in a single turn
(
Fu et al., 2026
)
. In contrast, AgenticRoboRL trains planners that interact with the harness over multiple turns, and it applies to harnesses based on VLA skills as well as to harnesses based on control code. Closer to our supervised stage, Robo-Harness K1 and World Action Agent train 9B students on teacher trajectories collected within their respective harnesses
(
Li et al., 2026
;
Zhang et al., 2026b
)
. These methods use supervised training to transfer the capabilities of stronger agents. REAL combines SFT with online RL for mobile manipulation, using a rule-based planner for supervision and a shaped reward
(
Mi et al., 2026
)
. AgenticRoboRL instead uses teacher-agent trajectories followed by multi-turn RL with task success as the sole reward. It adapts teacher supervision when the teacher and student have different prompts, tools, or access to memory.
Post-training of tool-using agents.
Coding-agent training commonly combines supervision from successful teacher trajectories
(
Pan et al., 2024
;
Yang et al., 2026
;
Jain et al., 2025
)
with multi-turn RL on verifiable outcomes
(
Cao et al., 2025
)
. Related approaches extend to search and computer-use agents
(
Jin et al., 2025
;
Chen et al., 2026
;
Wang et al., 2025
;
Lai et al., 2026
)
. Frameworks including Agent Lightning and LEGO-RL separate agent execution from model optimization and construct training data from recorded interactions
(
Luo et al., 2025
;
He et al., 2026
;
Du et al., 2026
)
. AgenticRoboRL builds on this approach for robot harnesses: a proxy records planner calls, and harness-specific adapters associate them with episode outcomes. This interface accommodates different execution mechanisms without requiring a common low-level action representation.
3
AgenticRoboRL  Framework
Figure 2:
AgenticRoboRL training pipeline.
(a) Successful trajectories are converted into training examples for SFT. (b) The planner interacts with the environment through a robot harness, while a proxy records its model calls. (c) Recorded calls are matched with episode outcomes for RL updates, excluding episodes invalidated by infrastructure failures. Harness-specific adapters support a common training pipeline across different harnesses. Only the planner is trained; execution components remain fixed.
3.1
Overview and Problem Setup

(
Zhang et al., 2026c
)
, or executable Python code in CaP-X
(
Fu et al., 2026
)
. The harness executes these commands and returns observations and execution feedback for subsequent decisions. We update the planner, not the perception modules, motion planners, or VLA executors it invokes. Figure
2
summarizes the training pipeline: teacher supervision initializes the planner, and multi-turn interaction supplies task outcomes for reinforcement learning (RL).

3.2
Training Infrastructure
Recording the actual model interaction.
Because VLA skill invocations and generated control programs differ in representation and execution granularity, we place the shared RL interface at the model-call boundary rather than the low-level action boundary. During RL, the training unit is a recorded planner request, not a simulator step or a reconstructed full transcript. A recording proxy captures each request’s context, generated token IDs, and rollout log-probabilities at the model-serving boundary, following recent agent training frameworks
(
Luo et al., 2025
;
Du et al., 2026
;
Xu et al., 2026a
)
. Images and tool specifications are retained where applicable. This matters because a harness may prune images, omit previous reasoning, or otherwise transform its history between requests. The trainer checks its rendered prompt against the recorded prompt tokens; mismatched samples receive zero optimization weight. Training therefore uses the inputs associated with each sampled response rather than assuming that a final transcript reproduces them.
Connecting interactions to outcomes.
A harness-specific adapter reports, for every episode, five fields: the task, the initial-state identifier, the attempt index, the reward, and a validity flag. The first two define the group used for within-group comparison; the validity flag separates task failures, which remain reward-zero episodes, from infrastructure failures, which are excluded from optimization. Recorded model calls are then matched to their episode, and the pipeline checks record completeness and policy version before any sample is built. The adapter is plain conversion code with no learnable parameters: it provides a common training representation without imposing a common robot execution interface, and it does not alter the harness’s tools, prompts, or control loop. Appendix
B
lists the fields for our two harnesses.
Policy-versioned rounds.
Each round collects episodes under fixed planner weights, constructs training samples from the recorded interactions, and updates the planner before the next collection round. Multiple attempts share a task and initial-state configuration for within-group comparison. Collection, outcome processing, and optimization are separate stages; the planner is not updated during an episode.
3.3
Planner Post-Training
3.3.1
Supervised Fine-Tuning
Teacher trajectories provide an initial policy for using the harness (Figure
2
(a)). A training example pairs a teacher response with the context the
student
would receive at that turn. This context can differ from what the teacher saw, because the two planners may run under different harness configurations or chat templates. How the student context is obtained depends on the harness.
RPent.
The teacher runs with a memory module that the student does not have. We therefore reconstruct each turn’s student context offline from the recorded episode, removing memory-access calls and their results. A response is flagged as dependent on memory if it contains keywords that refer to the memory, repeats eight consecutive words of the memory text, or contains a number that appears only in a removed memory result. Teacher reasoning and text that refer to memory are rewritten and checked by a judge, while tool-call arguments are kept unchanged. Only rewrites that the judge labels OK become training targets. After this processing, each turn is used as a training target, kept only as history, or dropped. Section
4.5
compares this recipe with excluding memory-dependent responses from supervision.
CaP-X.
Teacher and student share the same harness configuration, so no memory-related context reconstruction is needed. We take the recorded model calls of successful episodes, keep those that ended normally, and re-render each prompt with the student’s chat template. The teacher’s recorded output tokens are used directly as the target.

4
Experiments
4.1
Experimental Setup
Robot environments and harnesses.
Our main experiments use RPent, the VLA-calling harness released with Harness VLA
(
Zhang et al., 2026c
)
, and evaluate planners in it on LIBERO-PRO
(
Zhou et al., 2025
)
. We additionally evaluate the base, SFT, and RL checkpoints on the 10,030 configurations of LIBERO-Plus
(
Fei et al., 2025a
)
to measure robustness without benchmark-specific training. To demonstrate the generality of the framework, we also attach it to a second harness, CaP-X
(
Fu et al., 2026
)
; its setup and results are given in Section
4.4
.
Models and comparisons.
We use Qwen3.5-9B
(
Qwen Team, 2026a
)
as the student planner and compare the original checkpoint with its SFT and RL counterparts. Qwen3.8-27B
(
Qwen Team, 2026b
)
provides teacher trajectories and serves as a larger-model performance reference. The execution components, including the VLA,
remain
frozen.
Memory.
Harness VLA provides task-specific memory of successful action sequences and global memory of rules and failure cases shared across tasks. Our 27B teacher uses the released memory files. For RPent, the 9B student is supervised using trajectories from this teacher. During RL rollouts and evaluation, the student does not access external memory.
Data split.
Each LIBERO
(
Liu et al., 2023
)
task has 50 fixed initial states. Our evaluation follows the task-specific experience setting of Harness VLA
(
Zhang et al., 2026c
)
, where the agent explores each task on initial state 0 to construct memory and is evaluated on initial states 1–10. We retain the same task set and evaluation initial states, while extending this setting with planner post-training. Teacher demonstrations and RL rollouts are collected on states 11–44, which do not overlap with the evaluation initial states. It uses the same underlying LIBERO tasks and adds perturbations that the planner
did not see during training.

For supervised fine-tuning we use AdamW with a learning rate of
10

Comparing outcomes on the same evaluation instances, RL succeeds on 1,547 instances where SFT fails, but fails on 999 instances where SFT succeeds, yielding a net gain of 548 successful episodes.

We train the 9B planner through SFT followed by RL, using trajectories collected in CaP-X rather than transferring the RPent-trained checkpoints. Table
3

The teacher data covers only 26 of the 60 tasks, namely 19 of the 20 Object tasks, five of the 20 Goal tasks, and two of the 20 Spatial tasks, and yields 979 episodes for SFT. 4.5
Ablation Study
We compare two ways of handling teacher responses that depend on memory unavailable to the student, using the RPent harness on LIBERO-PRO. The first excludes these responses from supervision (mask-only). The second rewrites them and retains those accepted by a judge as training targets (rewrite-and-filter), following the procedure described in Section
3.3.1
. The resulting datasets contain 27,110 and 40,047 target turns, respectively. As shown in Table
4
, after one epoch of training, mask-only improves the original 9B planner’s success rate from 18.1% to 55.2%, while rewrite-and-filter reaches 64.6%.
Because the datasets differ in size, one epoch corresponds to 424 optimizer steps for mask-only and 626 for rewrite-and-filter. We therefore also examine their learning curves (Figure
3
) to compare performance at similar update counts. Rewrite-and-filter achieves 60.2% at step 438, compared with 55.2% for mask-only at step 424. The advantage is thus also observed at comparable update counts, rather than only at the end of the longer training run. However, the two recipes differ in both response content and supervision coverage, so this comparison does not isolate the contribution of rewriting alone.

5
Conclusion
We introduced AgenticRoboRL to investigate whether post-training methods used for coding agents can improve how robot planners use existing harnesses. The framework combines SFT on successful demonstration trajectories with multi-turn RL, connecting recorded model calls to episode outcomes while reusing the harnesses’ execution components. Experiments with a 9B planner demonstrate improvements in both VLA skill invocation and control-code generation. On LIBERO-PRO, success increases from 18.1% to 71.0%, and the same trained planner achieves 72.2% on LIBERO-Plus without additional training. These results support post-training the planner as an effective way to improve robot-harness agents without retraining their underlying controllers. We will release the framework, teacher trajectories, and trained planner checkpoints to support further research.

We run nine RL rounds and report the checkpoint after round 6. In each round the planner weights are fixed while rollouts are collected. A round covers 64 groups, where a group is one task with one initial state, and each group is attempted six times, which gives 384 episodes. Rollouts are sampled at temperature 1.0 without truncation of the token distribution. Training with CaP-X
For CaP-X the teacher is the 27B planner in the same harness configuration as the student. We collect teacher episodes on the 26 tasks where the teacher solves at least one of the five validation episodes (initial states 45–49), and obtain 979 successful episodes with 2,370 target turns. Supervised fine-tuning uses the same learning rate, batch size, and warmup as with RPent and runs for one epoch, which is 37 optimizer steps. RL starts from this checkpoint and uses the same configuration as with RPent. Each round again covers 64 groups with six attempts. The groups are drawn from a pool of 35 tasks, which are the tasks where the SFT planner solves between one and four of the five validation episodes. Tasks that it always or never solves are left out because their groups would receive identical rewards. Rollouts on these tasks use initial states 11–44. The 35 tasks include all 26 tasks with teacher data and nine further tasks. The remaining 25 evaluation tasks are not used in training. Of the 35 tasks, 20 belong to the Object suites, nine to Goal, and six to Spatial. The reported planner is the checkpoint after 15 rounds.

Episode Limits and Sampling Settings
With RPent an episode ends after at most 100 planner turns or 7,200 seconds. With CaP-X a single response is limited to 32,768 tokens. article.headline: 把编码智能体的后训练搬到机器人规划器
article.lede: AgenticRoboRL 用 SFT 加多轮 RL 后训练机器人规划器，9B 模型在 LIBERO-PRO 上成功率从
article.problem: 现有 agentic 机器人系统主要靠改进机器人 harness 和外部记忆来提升表现，规划器本身往往直接使用 Codex、Claude Code 等闭源强模型，其自身能力并未被训练。与此同时，编码智能体已通过后训练（监督微调加强化学习）大幅进步。问题是：这套后训练方法能否迁移到机器人规划器上，并兼容 VLA 技能调用与控制代码生成这两类截然不同的执行机制。
article.method: AgenticRoboRL 把训练接口放在模型调用边界而非底层动作层：代理记录规划器每次请求的上下文、生成 token 与 rollout 概率，再由 harness 专用适配器把记录与 episode 结果（任务、初始状态、尝试序号、奖励、有效性标志）对齐。训练流程先用带记忆教师产生的成功轨迹做 SFT，再以任务成功为唯一终局奖励做多轮 RL，采用留一法组内优势和双裁剪 PPO，无 critic、无中间奖励。两阶段都只更新规划器，感知模块、VLA 执行器与运动控制器保持冻结。
article.results: 在 LIBERO-PRO 上，9B 规划器经 SFT 从 18.1% 提升到 65.1%，RL 后达到 71.0%，接近带外部记忆的 Codex（GPT-5.5）的 72.1%，并超过不带记忆的 27B 规划器（57.9%）和带记忆的 27B 教师（74.0% 以内差 3.0 个百分点）；800 个配对 episode 中，RL 相对 SFT 多解 121 个、少解 74 个（符号检验 p=0.001）。未额外训练的同一检查点在 LIBERO-Plus 上达 72.2%（原模型 19.2%，SFT 66.7%），逐实例比较净增 548 个成功 episode。换到生成控制代码的 CaP-X harness，成功率从 2.7% 升至 18.7%（SFT），再到 28.5%（RL），高于 27B 教师的 20.3%。RPent 的 RL 阶段共收集 2,304 个 episode、选取 26,052 条回复、执行 206 步优化。
article.why_it_matters: 它说明提升机器人 agent 的表现可以不重训底层控制器，而是直接后训练规划器本身，并且同一套流程能跨不同 harness 复用，为开源模型替代闭源规划器提供了一条路径。
article.limitations: 全部实验都在 LIBERO 系列仿真基准上完成，仅验证了单一 9B 学生模型；CaP-X 上的绝对成功率仍只有 28.5%，Goal 与 Spatial 套件因教师仅在 60 个任务中的 26 个上成功而几乎无提升。提升主要来自 SFT，RL 增量有限，且与“带记忆教师”的对比属于系统级参照，无法单独隔离记忆监督的贡献。
article.figure_caption_zh: AgenticRoboRL 训练流程：成功轨迹转成 SFT 样本，规划器经机器人 harness 与环境交互并由代理记录模型调用，记录再与 episode 结果匹配用于 RL（排除基础设施失败），各 harness 专用适配器共享同一流程，且只训练规划器。

journals.title: The anatomy of a personal health agent
journals.summary:
Nature, Published online: 21 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11161-8

A multi-agent framework that coordinates data science, medical reasoning and health coaching over longitudinal wearable and clinical data to provide holistic personal health support is described.
journals.blurb: 《Nature》刊文提出一种面向个人健康的智能体系统，采用多智能体框架协同数据科学分析、医学推理与健康指导，基于可穿戴设备与临床数据的纵向信息提供整体性健康支持。该工作强调跨模块协作在长期健康管理中的作用，为机器学习研究者在多智能体协同与真实健康数据建模方面提供了新思路。

journals.title: Using AI to offer personalized health advice
journals.summary:
Nature, Published online: 21 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03065-4

The use of artificial-intelligence tools in medicine is increasing. What types of technology might be on the horizon and how can such health-advice tools be tested?
journals.blurb: 《Nature》这篇简讯关注 AI 工具在医学中的应用日益增多，讨论未来可能出现哪些类型的个性化健康建议技术，以及这类工具应如何评估与测试。文章没有给出具体数据，重点在提出技术方向与验证框架的问题。对关注医疗机器学习落地的研究生来说，可作为了解评估议题的入口。
